Reasons: no auth (users, keys, tokens); Serilog files replace `app_logs`; in-process tasks
replace `data_jobs`; the remainder are deferred. The five per-source resolver cache tables
collapse into `catalog_cache` (section 5.7), which is the shape the web application had
already converged on.

`phd2_*` left this list in Phase 15A. The four tables are sections 5.15 to 5.18.

`mosaic_*` left this list in Phase 18. The four tables are sections 5.22 to 5.25.

### 5.15 phd2_logs

Mirrors `backend/app/models/phd2.py::Phd2Log`. One row per guide-log file on disk. Section 7.6
defines what fills it.

The four tables of sections 5.15 to 5.18, together with the three `scan_runs` counters of
section 5.13, arrive in **one migration, the fourth this port has** (`Data/Migrations/`, after
the three already there). `phd2_sessions.ended_at_local` (section 5.16) arrives in the **fifth**,
which adds that one column and nothing else and **carries no backfill** for the rows a fresh
column always leaves null: every existing row reads null until its session is next re-derived,
which happens for every stored session before the next correlation pass (section 7.6). A
backfill computed from `started_at_utc` plus `duration_s` would be wrong for exactly the rows
item 54 exists to fix, the sessions that spanned a daylight-saving transition, so filling the
column at migration time would plant the same error the column exists to remove. This is
consistent with the standing directive that the application has not shipped and every install is
treated as a fresh database until `main` releases run through CI/CD (HANDOFF section 5), so a
schema change here is never deferred for want of a migration. **This port has five migrations.**
Each applies and rolls back on a fresh database, which is what section 18.1 tests.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `file_path` | TEXT | no | Unique. Absolute path as walked. |
| `file_size` | INTEGER | yes | Bytes. Delta skip (section 10.3). |
| `file_mtime` | REAL | yes | Unix seconds. Delta skip, 1.0 second tolerance, the same tolerance `images` uses. |
| `parse_status` | TEXT | no | One of `ok`, `empty`, `unreadable`, `failed`. A file past the 64 MiB ceiling of section 7.6 is `failed` and is never opened. `ok` means at least one guiding section or calibration block was stored; `empty` means the file carried no guide-log content at all; `unreadable` means the file is a guide log the parser could not place; `failed` means the read or the parse threw. |
| `parse_error` | TEXT | yes | The reason, truncated to 2000 characters. Null when `parse_status` is `ok` or `empty`. |
| `phd2_version` | TEXT | yes | From the banner of the file's first run. Null for an ASIAIR build, which writes no version. |
| `log_version` | TEXT | yes | From the same banner, for example `2.5`. |
| `run_count` | INTEGER | no | Stacked runs in the file. Default 0. |
| `session_count` | INTEGER | no | Guiding sections across every run. Default 0. |
| `calibration_count` | INTEGER | no | Calibration blocks across every run. Default 0. |
| `parsed_at` | TEXT datetime | no | When this row was written. |

Index on `file_path` (the unique constraint's own index).

A file with no usable content still gets a row, with `parse_status` `empty` and zero counts, so
it is not re-read on every scan forever. The same holds for `unreadable` and `failed`: the row
is what stops a re-read, and the delta skip of section 10.3 tests the row's size and mtime
whatever its status.

### 5.16 phd2_sessions

Mirrors `backend/app/models/phd2.py::Phd2Session` column for column, with one column this port
adds and the web model does not have, `ended_at_local`, the last row of the table below. One row
per guiding section, that is one `Guiding Begins` to `Guiding Ends` block. Sessions are stored raw and never
merged at ingest: two PHD2 instances can run at once on two rigs with overlapping wall clock and
different pixel scales, so merging would mix incomparable data. Night rollups are frame-count
weighted at read time instead (section 7.6).

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `log_id` | TEXT GUID | no | FK `phd2_logs.id`, on delete cascade. |
| `run_index` | INTEGER | no | Zero-based position of the owning run within the file. |
| `section_index` | INTEGER | no | Zero-based position of this section within its run. |
| `started_at_local` | TEXT datetime | no | The naive wall clock PHD2 wrote, stored with no zone suffix, so a later timezone correction needs no re-read of the file. |
| `started_at_utc` | TEXT datetime | yes | `started_at_local` interpreted in the resolved zone. Null when no zone resolved (section 7.6); the web column is not nullable and this one is, which section 7.6 states as a deliberate departure. |
| `ended_at_utc` | TEXT datetime | yes | `ended_at_local` interpreted in the resolved zone. Null for a truncated section, which carries no `ended_at_local`, and null whenever no zone resolved, which is also when `started_at_utc` is null. |
| `duration_s` | REAL | no | End minus start when both UTC instants are known, else the local end minus the local start when no zone resolved, else the last frame's time offset, else 0. Re-derived from the two UTC instants whenever both are known (section 7.6); where they are not, the stored value stands. |
| `session_date` | TEXT date | yes | The imaging night (section 8.2), derived from `started_at_utc` and the longitude `Phd2Profiles.LongitudeResolver` answers (section 8.3, whose third step Phase 17 added). Null when `started_at_utc` is null. Derived, never authored: it is re-derived for every stored session on each correlation pass (section 7.6), so a build that changes the resolution order corrects every stored value with no migration and no guide-log re-read. |
| `equipment_profile` | TEXT | yes | The header's `Equipment Profile` line. Null when the header carries none. |
| `telescope` | TEXT | yes | Resolved from `general.phd2_profile_map` at ingest. Null means the profile was unmapped at ingest, which is the value the sole-unmapped-profile rule of section 7.6 tests. It is a snapshot, not a live value: every reader that reports a rig to a user, the night pane, the Statistics page and the correlation's own rig selection alike, re-resolves the profile against the live map through `Phd2Profiles.EffectiveTelescope` rather than trusting this column, so a profile the map no longer carries resolves to no rig on every one of them even while this column still names the rig it was mapped to before it was unmapped (section 7.6, section 12.4, section 12.5, section 12.7). |

Null for a truncated section, which has no end line. It is the table's last column because the fifth migration appends it, and it is the one column the web model has no counterpart for. |

**The 100-frame `MinFrames` gate is never applied to a stored row.** Every session stores its own
RMS and peak columns whatever its `frame_count`, and the eight columns above are null only for
the two reasons their rows give: no pixel scale to convert the pixels with, or no usable frame
to measure. The gate belongs to the rollups of section 7.6, which decline to average a session
of fewer than 100 frames and report how many they excluded. Section 7.6 governs this rule and
this table restates it rather than defining it.

The web model's `insights` column is not created: it is filled by that application's phase 3
insight detectors, which this port has no counterpart for.

| `ix_phd2_sessions_started_at_utc` | `started_at_utc` | The correlation's time-overlap range scan (section 7.6). |
| `ix_phd2_sessions_log_id` | `log_id` | The cascade and the per-log rebuild. |

Only the West and North legs measure a rate and an angle. East and South re-centre the star and
emit no completion line, which is why there are six leg columns and not twelve.

Three indexes, exactly the ones the web model declares: `ix_phd2_calibrations_log_id` on
`log_id`, `ix_phd2_calibrations_session_date` on `session_date`, and
`ix_phd2_calibrations_started_at_utc` on `started_at_utc`.

### 5.19 custom_columns

Mirrors `backend/app/models/custom_column.py::CustomColumn` (591234b lines 25 to 42) with two
columns dropped and one rule tightened. One row per column the user defines. Definitions are
catalogue rows and not settings: they are shared by every surface, they are referenced by id from
`custom_column_values`, and a settings document holds no list that could disagree with them.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `name` | TEXT | no | The label every surface shows. Trimmed on write. 1 to 60 characters, which section 12.15 states and the repository enforces; the web allows 255 and renders them in a table cell it never sizes. |
| `slug` | TEXT | no | The persisted key, unique, built by section 12.15's slug rule and **never rewritten after creation**. Always carries the `custom_` prefix, so no custom column can shadow a built-in column key in a `display.columns` list (section 5.8.2). |
| `column_type` | TEXT | no | `boolean`, `text` or `dropdown`. Stored as the lower-case word, as the web's enum does. Fixed at creation. |
| `applies_to` | TEXT | no | `target`, `session`, `rig` or, from Phase 18, `mosaic`: see "The mosaic scope" in section 12.15. Fixed at creation. |
| `dropdown_options` | TEXT JSON | yes | A JSON array of strings, in the order the user entered them, for a `dropdown` column. Null for the other two types. One TEXT column rather than the web's Postgres `ARRAY(String)`; it is a bounded list that is only ever read whole, the same argument section 5.18 makes for `phd2_calibrations.steps`. |
| `display_order` | INTEGER | no | Zero-based. Dense and distinct across the table, which the reorder of section 12.15 maintains by swapping two rows in one transaction. **No unique index**: SQLite cannot defer a constraint, so a swap would trip one mid-transaction. |
| `created_at` | TEXT datetime | no | UTC, set once. |

**Two web columns are not created.** `created_by` and, on 5.20, `updated_by`: there are no users
(section 2.3), so both would be a foreign key to a table this port does not have. The web's own
baseline migration already makes them nullable against its model (591234b
`0015_v2_baseline.py` lines 475 to 477 and 490 to 492), so nothing reads them as an identity.

Read order is `display_order`, then `created_at`, which is the web's own ordering
(`custom_columns.py` line 46) and is what makes a row that somehow shares an order still sort
stably. The repository adds `id` as a third tiebreak, so the order a reorder swap reads is total.

Two indexes:

| Index | Columns | Serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ux_custom_columns_slug` | `slug`, unique | The slug rule, and the lookup a `display.columns` entry and a stored filter both do. |
| `ix_custom_columns_display_order` | `display_order` | The read order above. |

### 5.20 custom_column_values

Mirrors `backend/app/models/custom_column.py::CustomColumnValue` (591234b lines 45 to 88). One row
per (column, subject) pair that holds a value. A subject is named by four nullable key parts, and
which of them are set is decided by the owning column's `applies_to`.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `column_id` | TEXT GUID | no | FK `custom_columns.id`, on delete cascade. |
| `target_id` | TEXT GUID | yes | FK `targets.id`, on delete cascade. Set for the target, session and rig scopes. |
| `mosaic_id` | TEXT GUID | yes | FK `mosaics.id`, on delete cascade, added by the Phase 18 migration (section 5.22). Set for the mosaic scope alone. |
| `session_date` | TEXT date | yes | The imaging night (section 8.2), set for the session and rig scopes. |
| `rig_label` | TEXT | yes | The canonical `"{telescope} / {camera}"` rig label, the one spelling `RigGroup.Label` already builds (section 12.4). Set for the rig scope alone. |
| `value` | TEXT | no | The stored value, always a string, whatever the column's type. `true` or `false` for `boolean`; one of `dropdown_options` for `dropdown`; free text for `text`. A row whose value would be empty is deleted rather than stored (section 12.15). |
| `updated_at` | TEXT datetime | no | UTC, rewritten on every upsert. |

**The value key rule.** A value row is identified by the column plus the four key parts, and the
parts a scope leaves unset are stored as SQL null, never as an empty string or a sentinel date:

| Scope | `target_id` | `mosaic_id` | `session_date` | `rig_label` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | the target | null | null | null |
| `session` | the target | null | the night | null |
| `rig` | the target | null | the night | the rig label |
| `mosaic` | null | the mosaic | null | null |

A rig value is therefore **per night and per rig**, not per rig across the library. That is the
web's own key (`SessionAccordionCard.tsx` lines 1041 to 1053 send `session_date` and `rig_label`
together) and section 12.15 says so in the reader's own words rather than leaving it to be
discovered.

**The key shape is enforced at the one write path.** `CustomColumnRepository.SetValue` checks the
key against its column's scope before it reads or writes anything, and refuses a disagreement:
a target-scope key carrying a night or a rig label, a session-scope key carrying a rig label, a
rig-scope key with no night or no rig label, a mosaic-scope key carrying a target, a night or a
rig label or carrying no mosaic id, and a key of any other scope carrying a mosaic id. The rig
label is judged set or unset and is never trimmed into shape. Six surfaces land on that one
method, so the rule lives there and in none of them (design lesson 2). The refusal is a
programming error rather than a user path: it carries no sentence, no surface shows it, and a
surface that builds its key through the four `CustomValueKey` factories (the fourth,
`ForMosaic`, added in Phase 18) cannot reach it. Without
the guard a mis-shaped row would be invisible to both reads yet still count in the value count and
in the option census, so it would show a number the reader cannot account for and could refuse an
option removal they have no way to resolve.

Four indexes, the web's four with its coalesce sentinels retyped for SQLite:

| Index | Columns | Serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uq_custom_column_value` | `column_id`, `coalesce(target_id, '')`, `coalesce(mosaic_id, '')`, `coalesce(session_date, '')`, `coalesce(rig_label, '')`, unique | The upsert. It is the reason a scope's unset parts must be null and nothing else: two rows differing only in a null against an empty string would both be legal and the surface would show whichever the reader happened to return. Declared in raw SQL inside the migration, because a fluent index cannot carry a coalesce expression. |
| `ix_custom_column_values_target` | `target_id` | The per-target read the dashboard page and the Target detail page both issue. |
| `ix_custom_column_values_column` | `column_id` | The cascade and the per-column read. |
| `ix_custom_column_values_mosaic` | `mosaic_id` | The per-mosaic read of the mosaics table and the mosaic detail header (section 12.17), and the cascade from `mosaics`. Created by Phase 20 so that Phase 18 added a foreign key and nothing else. |

The web declares `ix_custom_column_values_target` twice under two names
(`0015_v2_baseline.py` lines 495 and 496, `..._target` and `..._target_id`). The port creates it
once.

**The migration is the sixth**, `20260921173551_CustomColumns`, after
`20260919131917_Phd2SessionEndedAtLocal`. It creates both tables and their six indexes and nothing
else. Phase 15B took the fifth; by the user's ruling of 2026-09-21 this phase runs ahead of mosaics
and takes the ordinal mosaics would otherwise have used. `Down` drops the raw SQL index explicitly
before it drops the tables, so a reader of `Down` sees the whole of what `Up` made.

### 5.21 skipped_files

One row per frame the header pass opened and decided not to catalogue, with the size and
modification time it had at the time. It is the upgrade path section 10.3 step 2 used to name as
a known limit: without it every calibration frame in a library is classified new on every scan
and its header is read again over the share each time, which on a 55k-frame installation was
the whole of a thirty-minute scan. No settings key, no UI and no CLI output names the table;
`scan_runs.new_files` and `skipped_calibration` simply report their true values.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `file_path` | TEXT | no | PK, `COLLATE NOCASE` for the reason section 5.2 gives `images.file_path` the same: the known set and the writer's upsert lookup compare paths case-insensitively. |
| `file_size` | INTEGER | no | The size the walk reported when the frame was skipped. |
| `file_mtime` | REAL | no | Unix seconds, the modification time the walk reported. |
| `reason` | TEXT | no | Why no `images` row was written. The only value is `calibration` (section 7.5). A rejected file writes no row, section 10.3 step 2. |
| `recorded_at` | TEXT datetime | no | UTC, the time of the write. |

No other index: the primary key is the only lookup.

Who writes: `ScanWriter`, on a `SkippedCalibration` record, as an upsert by path riding the same
200-record batch as every other write of the run. Who reads: the known set of section 10.3 step
2, which includes every row whenever the run excludes calibration and none of them when it
includes calibration; an `images` row for the same path wins. Who deletes: the writer, when an
`Ingest` record arrives for a path that has a row, and the prune of section 10.3 step 4, under
the walked-root and discovered-set rule with both guards.

Toggling `include_calibration` therefore behaves as follows. Off to on: the next run leaves the
rows out of the known set, classifies each frame new, ingests it, and the writer removes its row.
On to off: a calibration frame already in `images` stays there (nothing is deleted by a settings
change), and a frame first seen under the new setting gets a row.

The migration is the seventh, `20261005022536_SkippedFiles`, after `20260921173551_CustomColumns`.
It creates the table and nothing else.

### 5.22 mosaics

Phase 18. Mirrors `backend/app/models/mosaic.py` with two columns dropped. One row per mosaic
project: a name, notes and the arranger's global rotation. A mosaic owns its panels (section 5.23),
and through them their nights (section 5.24); it owns no frame.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `name` | TEXT | no | `COLLATE NOCASE`, unique. Trimmed on write and never empty. Every surface that names a mosaic shows this. |
| `notes` | TEXT | yes | Free-form notes, written by the detail page's autosave (section 12.17). An emptied box stores null. |
| `created_at` | TEXT datetime | no | UTC, set once. |
| `updated_at` | TEXT datetime | no | UTC, rewritten on every write to this row, its panels or its nights. |
| `rotation_angle` | REAL | no | Default `0`. The arranger's global rotation in degrees, -180 to 180. Shipped now and unused until the arranger phase (section 19.1). |

**Two web columns are not created.** `needs_review` (ruling R11): the web only ever set it in a
baseline migration, so the Needs Review pill, Clear All Reviews and the Session Review banner are
dropped with it. `pixel_coords` (ruling R8): arranger positions are stored on the panel in one form
only (section 5.23).

One index, `ux_mosaics_name`, unique on `name`, which is the duplicate-name refusal of every create
and rename path in section 12.17 and the accepted-campaign check of section 7.7. The comparison is
case insensitive, as the web's `upper(name)` pre-check is, and the database enforces it rather than
each caller.

Deleting a mosaic cascades to its panels, through them to their nights, and to its mosaic-scope
custom values (section 5.20). It deletes no `mosaic_suggestions` row and no `images` row, and no
file.

### 5.23 mosaic_panels

Phase 18. Mirrors `backend/app/models/mosaic_panel.py` with three columns replaced. A panel is a
label plus its arranger layout (ruling R19): it names no target, because its nights may come from
any target (section 5.24).

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `mosaic_id` | TEXT GUID | no | FK `mosaics.id`, on delete cascade. |
| `panel_label` | TEXT | no | `COLLATE NOCASE`. Trimmed on write and never empty. For a detected panel it is the `images.panel_label` that produced it, for example `Panel 2`. |
| `sort_order` | INTEGER | no | Zero-based display order within the mosaic. A new panel takes one more than the mosaic's current maximum. The auto layout of the arranger reads it. |
| `canvas_x` | REAL | yes | Arranger position, left edge, in canvas units (ruling R8). No snapping. Null means the panel takes its auto layout position from `sort_order`. Shipped now and unused until the arranger phase. |
| `canvas_y` | REAL | yes | Arranger position, top edge. Null under the same rule as `canvas_x`; the two are written together. |
| `rotation` | INTEGER | no | Default `0`. One of `0`, `90`, `180`, `270`, by a check constraint. The arranger's tile rotation. |
| `flip_h` | INTEGER | no | Default `0`. Boolean. The arranger's horizontal flip. |

**Three web columns are replaced.** `target_id` is not created: a panel's targets are the targets of
its nights (ruling R19). `object_pattern` is not created: membership is the join of section 5.24, not
an `ILIKE` over `OBJECT`, so the pattern and its re-parse guard (the web's AUD-008) have nothing to
guard. `grid_row` and `grid_col` become `canvas_x` and `canvas_y` (ruling R8). The web database is
never read (section 19.1), so no column name needs to match it.

One index, `ux_mosaic_panels_mosaic_label`, unique on (`mosaic_id`, `panel_label`): a mosaic holds
one panel per label, compared case insensitively. A create that would repeat a label is
refused with the sentence of section 12.17.

### 5.24 mosaic_panel_sessions

Phase 18. Mirrors `backend/app/models/mosaic_panel_session.py` with a target and a frame label
added (rulings R19 and R19a). One row per (target, night, frame label) triple that a panel holds,
either counted or offered.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `panel_id` | TEXT GUID | no | FK `mosaic_panels.id`, on delete cascade. |
| `target_id` | TEXT GUID | no | FK `targets.id`, on delete cascade. The target whose frames this night contributes (ruling R19). |
| `session_date` | TEXT date | no | The imaging night (section 8.2). |
| `frame_label` | TEXT | yes | The `images.panel_label` value this row admits, compared case insensitively. Null admits the frames of that target and night that carry no label (ruling R19a). |
| `status` | TEXT | no | `included` or `available`, by a check constraint. `included` counts in every figure; `available` makes the target a contributor of the panel without counting the night. |

Two indexes:

| Index | Columns | Serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ux_mosaic_panel_sessions_panel_target_date_label` | `panel_id`, `target_id`, `session_date`, `coalesce(frame_label, '')` collated `NOCASE`, unique | The upsert every include and remove performs, and the one row per triple per panel. SQLite treats two nulls as distinct in a unique index, so the null label is folded to the empty string inside the index, the way `uq_custom_column_value` folds its unset key parts (section 5.20). A stored `frame_label` is never the empty string: the writer stores null for "no label". Declared in raw SQL inside the migration, because a fluent index cannot carry the expression. |
| `ix_mosaic_panel_sessions_target_date` | `target_id`, `session_date` | The membership join below, from the frame side, and the dashboard link (section 12.2). |

**The membership join (ruling R19a).** A frame belongs to a panel when its `resolved_target_id`, its
`session_date` and its `panel_label` match an `included` row of that panel, the label compared case
insensitively and a null `panel_label` matching a null `frame_label`. That is the whole of
membership: there is no `images.panel_id` (ruling R19), nothing is stamped on a frame, and a frame
changes panel only because a row changed. Because the label is part of the key, the four panels
of "NGC 7000 Panel 1" to "Panel 4", which `StripPanel` resolves to one target (section 9), can
share a night: each panel's rows admit only the frames carrying its own label. A panel's label and
the `frame_label` of its rows are separate values: "As new panel" makes a panel `Panel 1 (b)` whose
rows still admit frames labelled `Panel 1`. Every panel figure in section 12.17 (integration, frames, nights, filters,
date range) counts the LIGHT frames this join reaches and no others. A frame with a null
`session_date` or a null `resolved_target_id` belongs to no panel.

**One triple sits in at most one panel of a mosaic (ruling R19a).** At most one `included` row
per (mosaic, `target_id`, `session_date`, `frame_label`) across that mosaic's panels, the label
compared as the index compares it. Two panels may include the same night of the same target when
their frame labels differ. The database cannot state this,
because the mosaic is one join away, so `MosaicRepository` checks it in the same transaction as
every write that sets `included` and refuses the duplicate with the sentence of section 12.17. The
Available lists of section 12.17 hide such a triple, so no surface offers it. `available` rows are
not bound by the rule: the same triple may be offered in two panels until one of them includes it.
The same triple may sit in panels of two different mosaics; the rule is per mosaic.

**A merge moves the rows to the winner.** A merge (section 12.9) rewrites `target_id` from the
merged-away target to the winner on every row, in the merge's own transaction, because the winner
is where the frames now resolve and a row left on the loser would join nothing. Collisions are
resolved per (mosaic, winner, night, frame label), across the mosaic's panels and not only within
one panel, so the rewrite cannot break the one-triple rule above: when it would leave the same
triple `included` in two panels of one mosaic, the panel earlier in `sort_order` keeps its
`included` row and the other row is dropped; an `available` row that would collide with any row of
the same triple in the mosaic, of either status, is dropped. A collision is judged against the
winner's rows as they stood before the merge: two rows of the merged-away target that legally
coexisted before it (one `included` in one panel, one `available` in another) both move, and within
one panel the winner's `included` row stays over the loser's. An unmerge
does not move rows back: the manifest records no mosaic rows, and after an unmerge the reader
re-includes the nights from the detail page's Available table. That is a stated limit, not a defect.

### 5.25 mosaic_suggestions

Phase 18. Mirrors `backend/app/models/mosaic_suggestion.py`. One row per mosaic candidate detection
produced (section 7.7). Rows are written only by the detection pass and by accept and dismiss.

| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | TEXT GUID | no | PK. |
| `suggested_name` | TEXT | no | The name the mosaic takes on accept: the base name, a campaign suffix when the run split campaigns, and a ` (#n)` suffix when the name was already used (section 7.7). |
| `base_name` | TEXT | no | The panel token's base name, as the first panel's `OBJECT` spells it. |
| `target_ids` | TEXT JSON | no | Array of target ids, one per entry of `session_dates`, in its order. A target appears once for each of its panels. |
| `panel_labels` | TEXT JSON | no | Array of labels, one per entry of `session_dates`, in its order. A label may appear twice when two targets carry the same panel number; accept combines them into one panel (section 7.7). |
| `panel_patterns` | TEXT JSON | no | Array of the web's `OBJECT` pattern strings, one per entry of `session_dates`, in its order (section 7.7). Kept as the record of which token produced each entry; no query in this port matches by it. |
| `session_dates` | TEXT JSON | no | The per-panel entries, the authoritative list: an array of `{target_id, label, pattern, dates}`, one per candidate, that is one per panel-token `OBJECT` of one target (section 7.7), where `dates` is the `yyyy-MM-dd` nights of this campaign on which that `OBJECT`'s frames were taken. The three arrays above are its projections, kept so the signature and the list read without parsing it. |
| `status` | TEXT | no | `pending`, `accepted` or `rejected`. Dismiss writes `rejected`. |
| `created_at` | TEXT datetime | no | UTC, set once. |
| `confidence` | TEXT | no | `high` or `low` (section 7.7). |
| `discovery_source` | TEXT | no | `name`, `position` or `both` (section 7.7). |
| `geometry` | TEXT JSON | yes | `{panels: [{target_id, label, ra, dec}], pitches: [arcmin], fov_arcmin}`, section 7.7. Always written by detection, with null `ra` and `dec` on an entry without a position, an empty `pitches` and a null `fov_arcmin` when nothing supports them. The column stays nullable for a row no detection run wrote. |
| `flags` | TEXT JSON | no | Array of review note sentences, empty for a high confidence row (section 7.7). |
| `dedup_signature` | TEXT | no | The signature of section 7.7. |

Two indexes: `ix_mosaic_suggestions_status` on `status`, which every list read filters on, and
`ix_mosaic_suggestions_dedup_signature` on `dedup_signature`, which the dismissed-subset rule of
section 7.7 reads. `session_dates` is an array of entries, where the web keys an object by label,
because a label may repeat in this port's shape and an object would merge two targets' nights under
one key (ruling R19a).

`accepted` and `rejected` rows are kept. Detection deletes `pending` rows only (section 7.7). An
`accepted` row is read by nothing; deleting its mosaic leaves it in place.

**The migration is the eighth**, `<stamp>_Mosaics`, at the next timestamp after
`20261005022536_SkippedFiles`. It creates the four tables above with their indexes and check
constraints, the unique index of section 5.24 in raw SQL for its coalesce expression; adds `images.panel_label` with `ix_images_panel_label`, and `images.ra_deg`,
`images.dec_deg` and `images.width_px` (section 5.2); and adds the foreign key from
`custom_column_values.mosaic_id` to `mosaics.id` with its cascade (ruling R2), and nothing else for
custom columns: no column and no index. SQLite cannot add a foreign key to an existing table, so the
migration rebuilds `custom_column_values`; the raw SQL index `uq_custom_column_value` is dropped
before the rebuild and recreated after it, with the coalesce expression section 5.20 gives, and
`Down` reverses each step in the opposite order. The new columns are null on every existing row
until mosaic detection step 0 fills them (section 7.7).

## 6. File readers

Both readers are hand-rolled. Both open through `GalactiLog.Core.Io.UserFiles`, read-only.

### 6.1 FITS

Reference: FITS Standard 4.0. The web application delegates to `fitsio`, so this section
specifies the behavior `fitsio` provides and that `scanner.py` relies on, rather than a
translation of Python source.

#### 6.1.1 Block and card layout

- The file is a sequence of 2880-byte blocks.
- The header is a sequence of 80-byte ASCII card images, 36 per block, starting at offset 0
  of the primary HDU.
- Header reading stops at the card whose first 8 bytes are `END     `. The rest of that
  block is padding. Data begins at the next 2880 boundary.
- Data length is `abs(BITPIX) / 8 * NAXIS1 * NAXIS2 * ... * NAXISn` bytes, padded up to the
  next 2880 boundary.

#### 6.1.2 Card parsing

For each 80-byte card, in this order:

1. Bytes 0 to 7 are the keyword, right-padded with spaces. Trim trailing spaces.
2. If the trimmed keyword is empty, skip the card. This is the only name-based exclusion:
   `scanner.extract_metadata` drops blank-named records and nothing else
   (`if rec["name"].strip()`).
3. If the keyword is `COMMENT` or `HISTORY`, the card carries free text rather than a value.
   Take bytes 8 to 79, trim trailing spaces, and keep it. Both keywords may repeat many
   times in one header, so they are stored in `raw_headers` as a **JSON array of strings**
   under that key, in file order, rather than as a scalar that last-wins would truncate to
   one line. Every other keyword stores a scalar.
4. If the keyword is `HIERARCH`, the real keyword is the text from byte 8 up to the first
   `=`, trimmed and space-collapsed. Store under that full name. Tolerance requirement: a
   `HIERARCH` card with no `=` is skipped, never treated as a file error.
5. Otherwise bytes 8 and 9 must be `= ` for a value card. If they are not, skip the card.
6. The value field runs from byte 10 to the end of the card, minus any comment.

Value field parsing:

- A value starting with `'` is a string. It ends at the next `'` that is not doubled; a
  doubled `''` is a literal single quote. Trailing spaces inside the quotes are stripped
  (FITS strings are blank-padded); leading spaces are kept.
- After a string value closes, an optional `/` begins the comment. For non-string values,
  the comment begins at the first `/`.
- `T` or `F` alone is a logical, stored as a boolean.
- Otherwise: attempt integer parse (`long`), then floating parse (`double`, invariant
  culture). FITS permits `D` or `d` as the exponent marker; rewrite it to `E` before the
  parse. If both fail, store the trimmed text as a string.
- Complex values of the form `(re, im)` are stored as raw trimmed text. No metric reads
  them.

`CONTINUE` convention:

- A string value whose last character before the closing quote is `&` is continued. If the
  next card's keyword is `CONTINUE`, its own quoted string is appended after removing the
  `&`. Repeat while the appended fragment also ends with `&`.
- The concatenated result is stored under the original keyword. `CONTINUE` never appears in
  `raw_headers`.

Duplicate keywords: last wins, matching the Python dict comprehension in
`scanner.extract_metadata`.

#### 6.1.3 Value serialization into raw_headers

`scanner._serialize_header_value` keeps `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, and `None`, and
stringifies everything else. The C# equivalent writes into the `raw_headers` JSON object:
strings as JSON strings, integers and doubles as JSON numbers, booleans as JSON booleans,
anything else as its invariant string form. Non-finite doubles (`NaN`, infinity) are
written as strings, because JSON has no literal for them. `COMMENT` and `HISTORY` are the
one exception to scalar storage: each is a JSON array of strings (section 6.1.2 step 3).

#### 6.1.4 Pixel data

Read only when a thumbnail or preview is requested. Header ingest never reads pixels.

| BITPIX | Raw sample type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | unsigned byte | |
| 16 | signed 16-bit, big-endian | |
| 32 | signed 32-bit, big-endian | |
| -32 | IEEE 754 single, big-endian | |
| -64 | IEEE 754 double, big-endian | |

All FITS numeric data is big-endian. On x64 every multi-byte sample is byte-swapped after
read (`BinaryPrimitives.ReverseEndianness` for integers, then
`BitConverter.Int32BitsToSingle` / `Int64BitsToDouble` for floats).

Physical value: `physical = BZERO + BSCALE * raw`, with `BZERO` defaulting to 0 and
`BSCALE` defaulting to 1. This is what makes `BITPIX = 16` with `BZERO = 32768` the
standard unsigned 16-bit encoding every capture application writes. The reader emits
`float` samples after applying it; the stretch pipeline (section 11.2) then normalizes.

`BLANK` (integer data only) marks undefined pixels; treated as 0 after scaling.

Axis order: `NAXIS1` is the fastest-varying axis (width), `NAXIS2` is height. Data is read
row-major into a `[height, width]` buffer, matching the `(NAXIS2, NAXIS1)` shape that
`thumbnail._read_bayer_debayered` documents.

Three-axis data with `NAXIS3 = 3` is planar colour, channel-first `[3, H, W]`. This is the
`data.ndim == 3 and data.shape[0] == 3` branch of `thumbnail.generate_thumbnail`.

#### 6.1.5 Rejection rules

Rejected (warning log, activity event `scan`/`file_rejected`, no row written):

| Condition | Log content |
| --- | --- |
| First card keyword is not `SIMPLE`, or its value is not `T` | not a simple FITS file |
| `BITPIX` missing or not in {8, 16, 32, -32, -64} | unsupported BITPIX, with the value |
| `NAXIS` missing | missing NAXIS |
| No `END` card within the first 200 blocks | header not terminated |
| File shorter than the header claims | truncated file |
| Compressed FITS: the primary HDU carries `ZIMAGE = T`, or `NAXIS = 0` and the first extension is `XTENSION = 'BINTABLE'` carrying `ZCMPTYPE` | `compressed FITS (fpack/RICE) not supported, skipping: <path>` |

The compressed case is detected from the primary header alone. Nothing further is read: no
extension header, no data, no row. Decisions say "uncompressed only (skip fpack/RICE with
clear log line)", and skipping means skipping the file.

Header-only degradation, which writes a row but no thumbnail:

| Condition | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `NAXIS` is neither 2, nor 3 with `NAXIS3 = 3` | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data, log the shape. |
| `BITPIX = 64` | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data. Outside the decided set. |

### 6.2 XISF

Reference: XISF 1.0 specification,
`https://pixinsight.com/doc/docs/XISF-1.0-spec/XISF-1.0-spec.html`. Header parsing semantics
are defined by `backend/app/services/xisf_parser.py`; pixel data semantics come from the
specification, because the web application delegates pixel reading to the `xisf` PyPI
package.

#### 6.2.1 Monolithic file layout

Cited from `xisf_parser._parse_xisf_header`:

| Offset | Size | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 8 | Signature, ASCII `XISF0100`. Any other value is a rejection. |
| 8 | 4 | Header length in bytes, unsigned 32-bit little-endian. |
| 12 | 4 | Reserved, ignored. |
| 16 | header length | UTF-8 XML header. |
| 16 + header length | to end of file | Attached data blocks, addressed by absolute file offset. |

XML namespace `http://www.pixinsight.com/xisf`. Every element lookup is
namespace-qualified, matching `f"{{{XISF_NS}}}Image"` in the Python source.

#### 6.2.2 XML header elements

The reader takes the first `Image` element under the root. Absence is a rejection
(`No Image element in XISF header`).

`Image` attributes read:

| Attribute | Form | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `geometry` | `width:height:channelCount` | Dimensions. Channel count 1 is mono, 3 is RGB. |
| `sampleFormat` | see 6.2.4 | Sample decoding. |
| `colorSpace` | `Gray`, `RGB`, `CIELab` | `Gray` and `RGB` handled; `CIELab` skips pixel data. |
| `location` | see 6.2.3 | Where the pixel data lives. |
| `compression` | see 6.2.5 | Absent means uncompressed. |
| `byteOrder` | `little` or `big` | Default `little`. |
| `bounds` | `low:high` | Meaningful for float formats. Recorded, not applied: the MTF pipeline normalizes by observed min and max anyway (section 11.2). |
| `imageType` | `Light`, `Dark`, `Flat`, `Bias` | Fallback for `IMAGETYP` when no FITS keyword carries it. This is the `image_elem.get("imageType")` branch in `extract_xisf_metadata`. |

Child elements read:

- `FITSKeyword`, attributes `name`, `value`, `comment`. Values are unquoted by
  `_strip_fits_string`: a value that both starts and ends with `'` loses those characters
  and the remainder is trimmed.
- `Property`, attributes `id`, `type`, and either a `value` attribute or element text. When
  `value` is absent the element text is used, trimmed.
- `ColorFilterArray`, attributes `pattern`, `width`, `height`. Used for debayer when no
  `BAYERPAT` FITS keyword is present.

#### 6.2.3 Data block location

| Form | Meaning | Support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `attachment:<position>:<size>` | Absolute byte offset and byte length in the same file. | Required. What PixInsight, N.I.N.A., and SGPro write. |
| `inline:<encoding>` | Data is the base64 or base16 text content of the element. | Supported. |
| `embedded` | Data is in a child `Data` element carrying an `encoding` attribute. | Supported. |
| `url:<uri>` or `path:<path>` | Data is in a separate file (distributed XISF). | Pixel data skipped. Reading a second file is out of scope. |

`position` and `size` are decimal unsigned 64-bit. A `position + size` beyond the file
length is a rejection.

#### 6.2.4 Sample formats

| `sampleFormat` | Bytes per sample | Handling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UInt8` | 1 | Supported. |
| `UInt16` | 2 | Supported. The common case. |
| `UInt32` | 4 | Supported. |
| `Float32` | 4 | Supported. |
| `Float64` | 8 | Supported. |
| `UInt64`, `Complex32`, `Complex64` | 8, 8, 16 | Pixel data skipped, clear log line. |

Byte order follows the `byteOrder` attribute, default little-endian, the opposite of FITS.

Channel layout is planar: for `geometry = w:h:3` the block holds channel 0 in full, then
channel 1, then channel 2, giving `[3, H, W]`. That is the channels-first branch of
`generate_xisf_thumbnail`.

#### 6.2.5 Compression

| Form | Codec | Support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `zlib:<uncompressedSize>` | zlib, RFC 1950 | `System.IO.Compression.ZLibStream`. |
| `lz4:<uncompressedSize>` | LZ4 block format | `K4os.Compression.LZ4.LZ4Codec.Decode`. |
| `lz4hc:<uncompressedSize>` | LZ4 block format, high-compression encoder | Same decoder; the encoder variant does not change the block format. |
| `zlib+sh:<uncompressedSize>:<itemSize>` | zlib plus byte shuffling | Decompress, then unshuffle. |
| `lz4+sh:<uncompressedSize>:<itemSize>` | LZ4 plus byte shuffling | Decompress, then unshuffle. |
| `lz4hc+sh:<uncompressedSize>:<itemSize>` | as above | as above. |
| `zstd`, `zstd+sh` | Zstandard | Pixel data skipped, clear log line. Outside the decided codec set. |

Byte unshuffling, per the specification: the shuffled buffer of `n` items of `itemSize`
bytes stores all byte-0 values first, then all byte-1 values, and so on. To reverse, for
each item index `i` in `0..n-1` and byte index `j` in `0..itemSize-1`, the output byte at
`i * itemSize + j` is the input byte at `j * n + i`. Trailing bytes beyond `n * itemSize`
are copied verbatim.

The decompressed length must equal the declared `<uncompressedSize>`. A mismatch is a
rejection.

#### 6.2.6 Rejection rules

| Condition | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Signature is not `XISF0100` | Reject the file, no row written. |
| Header length implies a header past end of file | Reject. |
| XML does not parse | Reject. |
| No `Image` element | Reject. |
| Attachment offset or size past end of file | Reject. |
| Declared uncompressed size does not match the decompressed length | Reject. |
| `sampleFormat` is `UInt64`, `Complex32`, or `Complex64` | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data. |
| `compression` codec is `zstd` or unrecognized | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data. |
| `location` is `url:` or `path:` | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data. |
| `colorSpace` is `CIELab` | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data. |
| `geometry` channel count is neither 1 nor 3 | Ingest metadata, skip pixel data. |

"Ingest metadata, skip pixel data" writes the image row with all header-derived fields and
leaves `thumbnail_path` null. The preview modal then shows the frame's header panel with a
placeholder in place of the image.

#### 6.2.7 Pixel data block outcomes

`XisfDataBlock` returns an explicit outcome enum `XisfPixelOutcome { Ok, Skipped, Rejected }`. `XisfImageReader` forwards the outcome without inspecting reason strings. Attachment offset or size past end of file is `Rejected` at both the header layer (section 6.2.3, authoritative check) and the data-block layer (defensive re-check).

#### 6.2.8 Orientation

FITS pixel data is bottom-up: `thumbnail.generate_thumbnail` calls `np.flipud` on every
channel. XISF is top-down: `xisf_parser.generate_xisf_thumbnail` states "No vertical flip -
XISF uses top-left origin (unlike FITS)". The C# renderer preserves both behaviors exactly.

---

## 7. Metadata extraction

Port of `backend/app/services/scanner.py::extract_metadata` (FITS),
`backend/app/services/xisf_parser.py::extract_xisf_metadata` (XISF), and
`backend/app/services/csv_metadata.py::merge_csv_metrics` (CSV overlay). One C# type,
`GalactiLog.Core.Metadata.MetadataExtractor`, handles both formats: XISF header parsing
produces the same merged keyword dictionary shape as a FITS header, so everything after
keyword resolution is shared. This is the shared spine required on the second occurrence of
the pattern; the web application duplicated it across two files and the duplication is not
carried over.

### 7.1 Field table

Priority order is left to right. The first keyword that yields a parseable value wins.
"first float" means: try each keyword in order, parse as `double` with invariant culture,
skip values that fail to parse, return the first success. This is
`scanner._first_float`.

| Stored field | Source keywords, in priority order | CSV column override | Provenance value recorded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `object_name` | `OBJECT` | none | `OBJECT` |
| `exposure_time` | `EXPTIME`, `EXPOSURE` | none | the keyword that matched |
| `filter_used` | `FILTER` | none | `FILTER` |
| `sensor_temp` | `CCD-TEMP` | none | `CCD-TEMP` |
| `camera_gain` | `GAIN`, parsed as a base-10 integer | none | `GAIN` |
| `image_type` | `IMAGETYP`; XISF falls back to the `Image` element's `imageType` attribute | none | `IMAGETYP` or `xisf:imageType` |
| `telescope` | `TELESCOP` | none | `TELESCOP` |
| `camera` | `INSTRUME` | none | `INSTRUME` |
| `rotator_position` | `OBJCTROT` | `RotatorPosition` | keyword name, or `csv:RotatorPosition` |
| `median_hfr` | `HFR` when it is non-zero, else the filename pattern | `HFR` | `HFR`, `filename`, or `csv:HFR` |
| `median_fwhm` | `MEANFWHM`, `FWHM` | none | the keyword that matched. Provenance only, see 7.1.1. |
| `eccentricity` | `ECCENTRICITY`, else derived from `ELLIPTICITY` | `Eccentricity` | see 7.2 |
| `eccentricity_source` | derived, see 7.2 | derived | not itself provenance-tracked |
| `altitude_deg` | `OBJCTALT`, `CENTALT` | none | the keyword that matched |
| `arcsec_per_pixel` | derived from `XPIXSZ` and `FOCALLEN` | none | `XPIXSZ+FOCALLEN` |
| `ra_deg` | `RA` (decimal degrees), else `OBJCTRA` (sexagesimal hours), by the coordinate rule below | none | the keyword that matched |
| `dec_deg` | `DEC` (decimal degrees), else `OBJCTDEC` (sexagesimal degrees), by the coordinate rule below | none | the keyword that matched |
| `width_px` | `NAXIS1`, parsed as a base-10 integer, kept only when greater than zero | none | `NAXIS1` |
| `panel_label` | derived from `OBJECT` by the token rule of section 7.7, with the keywords in `general.mosaic_keywords`; LIGHT frames only | none | not itself provenance-tracked |
| `capture_date` | `DATE-OBS`, see 7.1.2 | none | `DATE-OBS` |
| `hfr_stdev` | none | `HFRStDev` | `csv:HFRStDev` |
| `fwhm` | none | `FWHM` | `csv:FWHM`. The only FWHM any consumer reads, see 7.1.1. |
| `detected_stars` | none | `DetectedStars` | `csv:DetectedStars` |
| `guiding_rms_arcsec` | none | `GuidingRMSArcSec` | `csv:GuidingRMSArcSec` |
| `guiding_rms_ra_arcsec` | none | `GuidingRMSRAArcSec` | `csv:GuidingRMSRAArcSec` |
| `guiding_rms_dec_arcsec` | none | `GuidingRMSDECArcSec` | `csv:GuidingRMSDECArcSec` |
| `guiding_rms_source` | derived, see 7.4 | derived | not itself provenance-tracked |
| `adu_stdev` | none | `ADUStDev` | `csv:ADUStDev` |
| `adu_mean` | none | `ADUMean` | `csv:ADUMean` |
| `adu_median` | none | `ADUMedian` | `csv:ADUMedian` |
| `adu_min` | none | `ADUMin`, as int | `csv:ADUMin` |
| `adu_max` | none | `ADUMax`, as int | `csv:ADUMax` |
| `focuser_position` | none | `FocuserPosition`, as int | `csv:FocuserPosition` |
| `focuser_temp` | none | `FocuserTemp` | `csv:FocuserTemp` |
| `pier_side` | none | `PierSide`, as string | `csv:PierSide` |
| `airmass` | none | `Airmass` | `csv:Airmass` |
| `ambient_temp` | none | weather `Temperature` | `csv:Temperature` |
| `dew_point` | none | weather `DewPoint` | `csv:DewPoint` |
| `humidity` | none | weather `Humidity` | `csv:Humidity` |
| `pressure` | none | weather `Pressure` | `csv:Pressure` |
| `wind_speed` | none | weather `WindSpeed` | `csv:WindSpeed` |
| `wind_direction` | none | weather `WindDirection` | `csv:WindDirection` |
| `wind_gust` | none | weather `WindGust` | `csv:WindGust` |
| `cloud_cover` | none | weather `CloudCover` | `csv:CloudCover` |
| `sky_quality` | none | weather `SkyQuality` | `csv:SkyQuality` |
| `raw_headers` | every non-blank card name | not overridden | not applicable |

Rules the table encodes, restated because getting them wrong is silent data corruption:

- `HFR` and `FWHM` are different metrics on different scales. HFR-family keywords go to
  `median_hfr`; `MEANFWHM` and `FWHM` go to `median_fwhm`. Never cross them. This is called
  out explicitly in `scanner.extract_metadata`.
- HFR keyword-versus-filename order matches
  `_first_float(header, "HFR") or _parse_hfr_from_filename(...)`, and Python's `or` falls
  through on `0.0`. So a header `HFR` of exactly zero, which is how some capture software
  writes "star detection failed", is treated as absent and the filename pattern is tried.
  Preserved deliberately.
- HFR filename fallback: regex `(\d+\.\d+)HFR`, case-insensitive, searched anywhere in the
  file name. From `scanner._HFR_PATTERN`. Matches the N.I.N.A. default file pattern.
- `camera_gain` parses `GAIN` as a base-10 integer, matching Python's `int(v)`. A `GAIN` of
  `"120.0"` or `"high"` yields null plus one Debug log line naming the file and the value.
  This is stricter than `int(float(v))` on purpose: a fractional gain is a header the port
  does not understand, and guessing at it is worse than recording nothing.
- Plate scale: `arcsec_per_pixel = 206.265 * XPIXSZ / FOCALLEN`, where `XPIXSZ` is in
  micrometres and `FOCALLEN` in millimetres. Null when either is missing, non-numeric, or
  not strictly positive. From `units.arcsec_per_pixel`. `XPIXSZ` is assumed to be the
  binned-effective pixel size, as N.I.N.A. writes it; no `XBINNING` correction is applied.
- Coordinates (Phase 18), port of `coordinates._parse_ra` and `_parse_coord` as
  `mosaic_detection._frame_coords` uses them. Each value is trimmed and parsed as a `double` with
  invariant culture first; a value that parses is taken as degrees as it stands, for `OBJCTRA` as
  well as `RA`. A value that does not parse is split on whitespace and must yield exactly three
  parts, each a `double`, or it yields nothing. For right ascension the three are hours, minutes
  and seconds and the result is `(h + m / 60 + s / 3600) * 15`. For declination the leading `+` or
  `-` is removed before the split, the result is `d + m / 60 + s / 3600`, and it is negated when
  the trimmed value began with `-`, which is what keeps `-00 30 00` negative. Colon-separated
  values such as `05:35:17` are not parsed, as in the web. A value that parses to `NaN` or infinity
  yields nothing, where Python's `float()` would accept it and store a NaN centre. `RA` falls back to `OBJCTRA` and `DEC`
  to `OBJCTDEC` independently, so a frame may take its right ascension from one keyword and its
  declination from the other. The pair is stored only when both values exist and the declination
  lies in -90 to 90 inclusive; otherwise both columns are null. A stored right ascension is
  normalised into 0 to less than 360 by a floating modulo that maps a negative value upward.
- `width_px` is `NAXIS1` only. The web falls back to `NAXIS2` when `NAXIS1` is absent; ruling R10
  names `NAXIS1` and a frame without it carries no usable width.

#### 7.1.1 The two FWHM columns

Two columns exist and they are not interchangeable:

| Column | Source | Unit | Who reads it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fwhm` | N.I.N.A. Session Metadata CSV, column `FWHM` | arcseconds | Everything. Every screen, chart, filter, sort, and aggregate. |
| `median_fwhm` | FITS or XISF header `MEANFWHM` or `FWHM` | undeclared, application-specific | Nothing except the raw header panel. |

`median_fwhm` is stored so a frame's header content is not silently discarded and so the raw
header panel can show it alongside its provenance string. It is never displayed as "FWHM"
anywhere, never charted, never filtered on, never averaged, and never mixed into a median
with `fwhm`. This matches the web application, where `Image.fwhm` is the value in every
display path and `median_fwhm` is surfaced nowhere.

Consumption sites that must read `fwhm` and not `median_fwhm`: the dashboard metric filter
`fwhm` (section 12.2), every FWHM figure on target detail, in its nights ledger and in its session pane
(section 12.4), the frame table's FWHM column (section 12.4), the statistics equipment
median FWHM and its filter breakdown (section 12.5), and the FWHM chart series
(section 13). Section 11 does not read either.

`fwhm` is already in arcseconds, so it never passes through the plate-scale conversion.
`median_hfr` is in pixels and does. `units.py` states this rule.

#### 7.1.2 DATE-OBS and the assumed zone

The FITS standard defines `DATE-OBS` as UTC unless the value carries an explicit offset.
Python's `datetime.fromisoformat`, which the web application uses, returns a naive value for
the usual offsetless form and the web application then stores it in a `timestamptz` column,
so PostgreSQL applies the session zone. The port does not inherit that ambiguity.

Parse rule:

1. Parse the value as ISO-8601, accepting the FITS forms `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss`,
   `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.fff` with any fractional length, and `yyyy-MM-dd`.
2. If the value carries a zone designator (`Z` or an explicit offset), convert it to UTC.
3. If it does not, **treat it as UTC**, per the FITS standard. Do not apply the machine's
   local zone, do not apply `general.timezone`, and do not apply `general.observer_timezone`.
4. Store as `TEXT` ISO-8601 UTC with a `Z` suffix (section 5.1).
5. A value that does not parse yields null plus a warning naming the file. The frame is then
   excluded from the timeline, the calendar, and every session analytic, because
   `session_date` derives from `capture_date` (section 8.2).

This matters beyond storage: `capture_date` feeds `compute_session_date` directly, so a
wrong zone assumption moves frames between nights.

XISF keyword resolution, from `xisf_parser.extract_xisf_metadata`: FITS keywords are read
first, then native XISF properties fill only the gaps, using this map.

| XISF property id | FITS keyword filled |
| --- | --- |
| `Observation:Object:Name` | `OBJECT` |
| `Instrument:ExposureTime` | `EXPTIME` |
| `Instrument:Filter:Name` | `FILTER` |
| `Instrument:Sensor:Temperature` | `CCD-TEMP` |
| `Instrument:Camera:Gain` | `GAIN` |
| `Instrument:Telescope:Name` | `TELESCOP` |
| `Instrument:Camera:Name` | `INSTRUME` |
| `Observation:Time:Start` | `DATE-OBS` |

`raw_headers` for an XISF file holds every FITS keyword and every XISF property, both keyed
by their own names. Property ids therefore appear in the raw header panel and are queryable
in the header query builder.

### 7.2 Eccentricity and its provenance

Port of `scanner._eccentricity_from_header` and `xisf_parser._eccentricity_from_values`.

1. If `ECCENTRICITY` parses to a number, store it and set `eccentricity_source = "header"`.
2. Otherwise, if `ELLIPTICITY` parses to a number, compute
   `axisRatio = 1 - ellipticity`, then `v = 1 - axisRatio * axisRatio`. If `v < 0`, store
   null and null source. Otherwise store `sqrt(v)` with
   `eccentricity_source = "ellipticity"`.
3. Otherwise both are null.
4. If the CSV supplies a non-null `Eccentricity`, it wins and
   `eccentricity_source = "csv"` (section 7.4).

Eccentricity and ellipticity are different quantities. A value converted from an
`ELLIPTICITY` written by one application is not comparable with a native `ECCENTRICITY`
written by another, which is why the source rides along and why aggregations pool only
same-source values (section 12.4).

### 7.3 Provenance record

New in this port, required by the decisions ("Per-frame ingest provenance: which keyword or
CSV column produced each stored metric, viewable in raw header panel").

`images.provenance` holds a flat JSON object mapping stored field name to the provenance
string from the table in 7.1. Only fields that received a value are present. Example:

`{"exposure_time":"EXPTIME","median_hfr":"csv:HFR","eccentricity":"ellipticity","altitude_deg":"CENTALT","arcsec_per_pixel":"XPIXSZ+FOCALLEN"}`

Provenance is written by the same code path that resolves the value, never by a second
pass. The raw header panel (section 12.4) renders each stored metric with its provenance
string as secondary text.

### 7.4 CSV backfill

Port of `csv_metadata.py`. Two files, both looked up in the frame's own parent directory:
`ImageMetaData.csv` and `WeatherData.csv`.

Parsing:

- UTF-8 with BOM tolerance (`encoding="utf-8-sig"`).
- `ImageMetaData.csv` is keyed by the last path segment of its `FilePath` column, split on
  both `/` and `\` because the column holds Windows paths.
- `WeatherData.csv` is keyed by its `ExposureStartUTC` column, trimmed.
- The image row's `ExposureStartUTC` joins it to a weather row.
- Blank, whitespace-only, and `NaN` cells convert to null. The literal string `NaN` is also
  null for string columns.
- `HFR == 0.0` means star detection failed in N.I.N.A.; it converts to null.
- Both files are cached in memory keyed by path, invalidated when the file's modification
  time changes.

Merge rule, from `merge_csv_metrics`, and the single most important behavior in this
section:

> A real CSV value takes priority over the header-derived value. A null CSV value must
> never erase a header-derived value.

Concretely, for each mapped column: if the CSV value is null and the metadata already holds
a non-null value for that field, skip. Otherwise assign. Fields the header never set are
still written as null, which keeps the record shape stable.

Provenance follow-on rules:

- If the CSV supplied a non-null `Eccentricity`, set `eccentricity_source = "csv"`.
- If the CSV supplied a non-null value for any of `GuidingRMSArcSec`, `GuidingRMSRAArcSec`,
  or `GuidingRMSDECArcSec`, set `guiding_rms_source = "csv"` for the whole triple, because
  a frame's guiding numbers come from one measurement. A CSV silent about guiding stamps
  nothing.

### 7.5 Calibration frames

`image_type`, uppercased, in {`BIAS`, `DARK`, `FLAT`, `DARKFLAT`, `BIASFLAT`} marks a
calibration frame (`scanner.CALIBRATION_FRAME_TYPES`). Calibration filtering happens at
ingest, not during the directory walk, because the header is already open at ingest and
opening every candidate during the walk costs an extra file open per file on a network
share. When `general.include_calibration` is false (the default), a calibration frame is
counted in `skipped_calibration` and no row is written to `images`; section 10.3 step 2's
`skipped_files` row records the decision. Calibration frames never get a thumbnail and never
go through target resolution.

`MetadataExtractor` stores `image_type` trimmed and upper-cased; the raw value stays in
`raw_headers`. An absent or blank `IMAGETYP` stores `LIGHT` with provenance source `default`
and a warning note in the extraction result. `CalibrationFrames.IsCalibrationFrame` keeps its
own normalisation, because the CSV backfill can hand it a raw value that never passed through
the extractor.

Every listing and aggregation query filters `image_type = 'LIGHT'`, matching the first
`where_parts` entry in `target_listing.list_targets_aggregated`. That predicate is one shared
constant, `GalactiLog.Data.Queries.SqlFragments.LightFrameOnly`, referenced by the listing,
facets, distinct header keys and search queries, so the four cannot drift apart.

### 7.6 PHD2 guide logs

Port of `backend/app/services/phd2_parser.py`, `phd2_metrics.py`, `phd2_profiles.py` and
`phd2_correlation.py`, and of the ingest half of `backend/app/worker/tasks_phd2.py`. The guide
log is the second source of a frame's guiding RMS, beside the N.I.N.A. CSV sidecar of section
7.4, and the only one that measures the guiding of an exposure the sidecar said nothing about.

**File safety.** A guide log is a user file. It is opened through
`GalactiLog.Core.Io.UserFiles` in shared-read mode, read whole, and closed. No guide log is
written, moved, renamed, truncated or deleted by any path in this section, and none ever will
be: `FileSafetyTest` (section 2.1.3) fails the build if a write-capable call appears anywhere in
`Core/Phd2` or `Data/Ingest/Phd2*`. Everything this section changes is catalogue rows. Dropping
a `phd2_logs` row for a log that is gone from disk (below) deletes database rows and nothing
else.

#### Discovery

A discovered file is a guide log when its file name matches, case-insensitively:

```
^PHD2_GuideLog_.*\.txt$
```

`GalactiLog.Core.Scanning.FileWalker` reports matching paths to the guide-log callback during
the same walk that discovers frames, so no second traversal of the library is made. Port of
`scanner.PHD2_LOG_RE` and `scanner.is_phd2_guide_log`.

The sibling `PHD2_DebugLog_*` files are never read. They are large, unstructured, and carry
nothing the guide log does not.

**Scope: the scan roots only** (coordinator ruling F3). A guide log outside the effective roots
of the run is not discovered and is not ingested. A separate "guide log folders" list is a
recorded candidate and is not built here. The include and exclude filters of section 10.2 apply
to a guide log exactly as they apply to a frame, because it is the same walk.

#### Parser contract

`GalactiLog.Core.Phd2.Phd2LogParser` is pure: text in, records out, no file IO, no database, no
settings. The caller reads the file and hands over the string, which keeps the grammar testable
against fixture strings and keeps network latency out of the parse. Log version 2.5 is the
layout every pattern below is written against.

One physical file often holds several stacked runs, because PHD2 was restarted and appended to
the same file. **Runs are segmented on the banner line and never on `Log enabled at`:** stacked
runs repeat the same `Log enabled at` timestamp while `Log closed at` advances, so segmenting on
the latter would merge them.

Timestamps in a guide log are local wall clock with no zone. The parser returns them exactly as
written, as naive values. Converting to UTC needs a zone and belongs to the metrics step below,
never here.

**Run-level patterns.** `TS` below is the shared timestamp group
`(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2})`.

| Name | Pattern | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Banner` | `^PHD2 version(?: (\S+) \[([^\]]*)\])?, Log version ([\d.]+)\. Log enabled at ` + `TS` | Starts a run. **The version and platform tag are one optional unit**, which is the ASIAIR shape: the desktop build writes `PHD2 version 2.6.14 [Windows], ...` and the PHD2 embedded in an ASIAIR writes `PHD2 version, ...` with both left out. Without the optional group those files match nothing at all. Groups 1 and 2 are null for an ASIAIR build and are recorded as null, because nothing else in the file says which build produced it. |
| `LogClosed` | `^Log closed at ` + `TS` | Ends a run. |
| `LogSummary` | `^Log Summary: calcnt:(\d+) gcnt:(\d+) gdur:(\d+) gacnt:(\d+)` | PHD2's own count of what it wrote. Compared against the parsed counts as a free self-check; a mismatch is a warning on the run, never an error, because a run killed before its summary is written is normal. |
| `GuidingBegins` | `^Guiding Begins at ` + `TS` | Opens a guiding section. |
| `GuidingEnds` | `^Guiding Ends at ` + `TS` | Closes it. One with no open section increments the run's orphan count. |
| `CalibrationBegins` | `^Calibration Begins at ` + `TS` | Opens a calibration block. |
| `CalibrationComplete` | `^Calibration complete, mount = (.+?)\.?$` | Closes it and sets its mount name. |
| `AxisComplete` | `^(West\|North) calibration complete\. Angle = ([-\d.]+) deg, Rate = ([-\d.]+) px/sec, Parity = (\S+)` | Only the West and North legs measure a rate and an angle. East and South re-centre the star and emit no completion line. |

A section still open when the file ends, when a new banner arrives, or when the next block
starts is marked truncated: PHD2 was killed, or the run boundary swallowed the end line.

**Header patterns.** One header record per section, never per file. A file in the reference
corpus carries a misconfigured one-off pixel scale in a single section's header, so a file-level
pixel scale would corrupt every arcsecond conversion in that file. Each line is trimmed before
matching, because some builds emit the camera line with a leading space, and every pattern is
anchored so `RA Guide Speed =` and `RA =` cannot be confused for one another.

| Name | Pattern | Fills |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Profile` | `^Equipment Profile = (.+)$` | `equipment_profile` |
| `PixelScale` | `^Pixel scale = ([\d.]+) arc-sec/px(?:, Binning = (\d+))?(?:, Focal length = ([\d.]+) mm)?` | `pixel_scale_arcsec`, binning, `focal_length_mm`. **Absent entirely on an ASIAIR log.** |
| `Camera` | `^Camera = ([^,]+)` | `guide_camera` |
| `Exposure` | `^Exposure = ([\d.]+) ms` | `exposure_ms` |
| `Mount` | `^Mount = ([^,]+)` | `mount_name`, then the sub-searches `xAngle = ([-\d.]+)`, `xRate = ([-\d.]+)`, `yAngle = ([-\d.]+)`, `yRate = ([-\d.]+)` and `parity = (\S+)` over the same line. |
| `NormRates` | `^Norm rates RA = ([\d.]+)"/s.*?Dec = ([\d.]+)"/s(?:; ortho\.err\. = ([-\d.]+) deg)?` | normalised rates and `ortho_error_deg` |
| `XAlgo` | `^X guide algorithm = ([^,]+)` | `algo_ra`, plus the sub-searches `Hysteresis = ([\d.]+)`, `Minimum move = ([\d.]+)` and `Aggression = ([\d.]+)` over the same line. |
| `YAlgo` | `^Y guide algorithm = ([^,]+)` | `algo_dec`, plus `Minimum move` and `Aggression` over the same line. PHD2 writes the two axes in different units on adjacent lines: the X aggression is a fraction, the Y aggression is a percentage with the sign stripped. |
| `Backlash` | `^Backlash comp = (\w+)(?:, pulse = ([\d.]+) ms)?` | backlash enabled and pulse |
| `MaxDuration` | `^(?:Calibration step = [^,]+, )?Max RA duration = ([\d.]+), Max DEC duration = ([\d.]+)(?:, DEC guide mode = (\w+))?` | max durations and `dec_guide_mode`. **The optional leading group is the ASIAIR shape**, which prefixes the line with a placeholder calibration step; without it the whole line goes unrecognised and all three fields are dropped. |
| `GuideSpeeds` | `^RA Guide Speed = ([\d.]+) a-s/s, Dec Guide Speed = ([\d.]+) a-s/s` | `ra_guide_speed`, `dec_guide_speed`, plus the sub-searches `Cal Dec = ([-\d.]+)`, `Last Cal Issue = ([^,]+)` and `Timestamp = (\d{1,2}/\d{1,2}/\d{4} \d{1,2}:\d{2}:\d{2} [AP]M)` over the same line. |
| `Pointing` | `^(?:RA = ([-\d.]+) hr, )?Dec = ([-\d.]+) deg, Hour angle = ([-\d.]+) hr, Pier side = (\w+), Rotator pos = ([^,]+)(?:, Alt = ([-\d.]+) deg, Az = ([-\d.]+) deg)?` | RA, `dec_deg`, `hour_angle_hr`, `pier_side`, rotator position, `alt_deg`, `az_deg`. **Two shapes:** the desktop seven-field line, and the ASIAIR line that omits RA, Alt and Az entirely. Both optional groups are greedy so a desktop line still fills all seven. Anchoring on `Dec = ` is safe: it is the only line that starts that way, and `Dec Guide Speed` appears only mid-line. |
| `LockPosition` | `^Lock position = ([-\d.]+), ([-\d.]+), Star position = ([-\d.]+), ([-\d.]+), HFD = ([-\d.]+) px` | lock and star position, HFD |

The `Last Cal Issue` line carries a United States twelve-hour timestamp,
`M/d/yyyy h:mm:ss tt`, which is a different format from every other timestamp in the file and
is parsed with the invariant culture.

A header line matching no pattern is ignored. An empty cell and the literal `N/A` both parse to
null for a numeric field, and a numeric field that does not parse is null rather than zero.

**Guiding CSV rows.** Row mode opens on a byte comparison against the log version 2.5 header
line, not on a fuzzy prefix match:

```
Frame,Time,mount,dx,dy,RARawDistance,DECRawDistance,RAGuideDistance,DECGuideDistance,RADuration,RADirection,DECDuration,DECDirection,XStep,YStep,StarMass,SNR,ErrorCode
```

A line that begins `Frame,Time` and is not that exact string never enters row mode, and the run
records a warning naming the line. A PHD2 release that adds or renames one column would
otherwise drop every frame silently, with a frame count of zero, no error and nothing in the
file to point at.

The eighteen columns map to `phd2_frames` (section 5.17) in order: `Frame` to `frame_index`,
`Time` to `time_offset`, `mount` to the DROP test, `dx`, `dy`, `RARawDistance` to `ra_raw`,
`DECRawDistance` to `dec_raw`, `RAGuideDistance` to `ra_guide`, `DECGuideDistance` to
`dec_guide`, `RADuration` to `ra_duration_ms`, `RADirection` to `ra_direction`, `DECDuration`
to `dec_duration_ms`, `DECDirection` to `dec_direction`, `XStep` and `YStep` parsed past and not
stored, `StarMass` to `star_mass`, `SNR` to `snr`, `ErrorCode` to `error_code`.

**DROP rows.** A row whose `mount` field, unquoted and upper-cased, equals `DROP` sets
`dropped`. A DROP row carries a nineteenth quoted field holding the star-loss reason, which is
why a row is read with a CSV reader that honours quoting rather than by splitting on commas. The
reason is counted into `phd2_sessions.star_lost_reasons` and is not stored per frame.

A row of fewer than eighteen fields, or one whose frame number or time does not parse, is a file
truncated mid-write. The section is marked truncated, the row and every CSV row after it are
counted into `discarded_rows`, and the parse continues: the rows after a corrupt one are still
CSV rows, and their count is what tells a reader whether a clipped tail or the body of a session
was lost. Structural lines (a `Guiding Ends`, the next banner, an `INFO:` event, a header line)
are all matched before row mode is consulted, so discard mode cannot swallow them.

**Events.** An `INFO:` line carries no timestamp of its own, so it is stamped with the `Time`
of the most recent CSV row in the same section, zero before the first row. Five patterns, seven
event kinds, the settling pattern yielding three of them:

| Kind | Pattern | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `settle_start` | `^INFO: SETTLING STATE CHANGE, (.+)$` with a detail beginning `settling started` | |
| `settle_done` | the same pattern, detail beginning `settling complete` | |
| `settle_failed` | the same pattern, detail beginning `settling failed` | The prefix test is case-insensitive. Any other settling detail is dropped. |
| `dither` | `^INFO: DITHER by (.+)$` | |
| `lock_shift` | `^INFO: SET LOCK POSITION, (.+)$` | |
| `star_lost` | `^INFO: STAR LOST during calibration, (.+)$` | |
| `param_change` | `^INFO: Guiding parameter change, (.+)$` | |

An `INFO:` line matching none of these is dropped. An event outside a guiding section is
dropped.

**Calibration block.** Step-row mode opens on the exact header `Direction,Step,dx,dy,x,y,Dist`.
Each step row is seven comma-separated fields, `direction` a string and the other six numbers; a
row of any other shape or with an unparsable number is skipped without ending the block. The
West and North completion lines fill the six leg columns. The block closes on
`Calibration complete`, which also sets `completed` and the mount name.

**The size ceiling.** A guide log larger than **64 MiB** is recorded with `parse_status`
`failed` and a reason naming both the file's size and the ceiling, and **is never opened**. The
test is on the size the walk already stat'ed, so the ceiling costs no read. A real guide log is
a few megabytes at most; a file past this ceiling is a debug log renamed, a concatenation
accident or a runaway, and the parser reads a whole file into memory, so opening one would cost
a user's session rather than one row. The row is what stops the file being reconsidered on every
scan, exactly as it does for any other failure, and raising the ceiling is a change to this
sentence and nothing else.

**Progress and batching.** The pass reports progress **per guiding section within a log**, not
only per file: one log can hold hundreds of sections and several hundred thousand frame rows, and
a per-file numerator leaves a reader watching a motionless counter for minutes. Frame rows are
inserted in batches inside the **one transaction** that replaces a log (section 10.3 step 3), so
the batching is an insert-shaping decision and never a durability one: a log is still replaced
whole or not at all.

**Unreadable against empty.** A text carrying no guide-log content at all yields no run and is
recorded as `parse_status` `empty`. A text that clearly is a guide log, because some line begins
with one of the markers `PHD2 version`, `Guiding Begins at`, `Guiding Ends at`,
`Calibration Begins at`, `Calibration complete,`, `Log Summary:`, `Log closed at`, `Frame,Time`
or `Direction,Step`, and that yields no run, is an error: the parser throws
`Phd2UnreadableLogException` naming the first line it could not place, and the ingest records
`parse_status` `unreadable` with that message. The two cases used to share one status in the web
application, and ten real ASIAIR logs holding 74 unseen guiding sections sat in it for a year
with nothing in the product saying so.

#### Timezone resolution (ruling F1)

PHD2 writes local wall clock with no zone. **The port never assumes the machine's zone.** For
each guiding section and each calibration block, the zone is resolved from the section's own
equipment profile, in this order:

1. The profile's own `timezone` in `general.phd2_profile_map`, when it is non-empty and the
   platform can load it. Source `profile`.
2. `general.observer_timezone`, when it is non-empty and loadable. Source `global`.
3. Nothing. Source `unset`.

A per-profile zone the platform cannot load degrades to step 2 and reports as `global`, because
the global value is what will be used. A bad global value is reported once per pass rather than
once per section (section 10.9, `phd2_timezone_invalid`). A section whose header names no
equipment profile resolves through steps 2 and 3 only.

**What is stored when the zone is `unset`.** The session row is written in full, with
`started_at_local` and `ended_at_local` holding the wall clocks exactly as PHD2 wrote them, and
with `started_at_utc`, `ended_at_utc` and `session_date` all null. Every frame row, every event
and every count is stored. The session is simply not reachable by anything keyed on a UTC
instant: the correlation below skips it, and the pass writes one warning naming the profiles it
held back (section 10.9, `phd2_timezone_unset`). Nothing is lost and nothing is invented.
Configuring a zone later and saving it fills the three columns from the two wall clocks already
stored, by the re-derive below, with no re-read of any log file.

**Re-deriving session times.** `started_at_local` and `ended_at_local` are the stored sources of
truth for a session's time and **are never rewritten** after the ingest that read them.
`started_at_utc`, `ended_at_utc` and `session_date` are derived from them under the resolution
order above, and they are **re-derived for every stored session**, through the same members the
ingest uses rather than a second copy of the arithmetic, before every correlation pass inside a
scan and before every out-of-scan re-run. A row is written only where a derived value differs
from the stored one, **including a difference to null** when a zone the user had configured is
removed. The same re-derive runs over `phd2_calibrations`, whose two time columns have the same
shape and which has no end of any kind, so nothing is invented for the column it does not have.

**The end is re-derived from the stored local end, exactly as the start is**, and never
reconstructed from `started_at_utc` plus `duration_s`. The reconstruction is what a stored
`ended_at_local` replaces, and it carried one residual error: a session ingested with no zone
stores a `duration_s` measured between two local wall clocks, which is an hour short or an hour
long across a daylight-saving transition, so the first re-derive after a zone was configured
ended that session an hour out with no stored end to contradict it. Converting the stored local
end through the resolved zone has no such term. `duration_s` is re-derived alongside, as the
difference of the two re-derived instants, whenever both are known; where they are not, which is
a truncated section or a zone that still does not resolve, the stored value stands.

This is the whole mechanism behind "set the zone later, then save": a log whose file has not
changed is never re-read, its `phd2_logs` row is skipped by the delta test of section 10.3, and
its sessions still gain their UTC instants and their nights from the wall clocks already in the
database. It also means a zone corrected downwards converges without any special case: the
re-derive writes the new values, the correlation re-derives the nights those sessions now belong
to, and nothing is left holding an instant computed under the old zone.

**Why a stored guiding value is never cleared because the zone is blank.** Whether a stored
value is wrong depends on the zone that was configured when it was derived, and nothing records
that. An empty setting now says nothing about a value written last week under a correct one.

A session with no resolved zone has a null `session_date` and so belongs to no night, which
means the hold-out cannot be expressed over `session_date`. It is expressed over the one time
column such a session always has, and over one date test on each side:

- An **unzoned candidate** of an imaging night is a session with a null `started_at_utc` whose
  naive `started_at_local` falls on a calendar date within one day either side of that night.
- A **zoned session** of that night is a session whose own `session_date` is within one day
  either side of it.

Both use the same one-day widening the night lookups elsewhere in this section use, and it is
sound for the same reason: no zone shifts a wall clock by more than about fourteen hours.

**The clear-side hold-out.** The correlation's re-derive clear (below) leaves a night alone when
it has at least one unzoned candidate and no zoned session at all. Such a night is not cleared,
and it is refilled normally, which fills nothing, because an unzoned session contributes no
samples. A night that mixes a zoned session with an unzoned one is cleared and refilled
normally, with the unzoned sessions dropped from the fill. A night with no guiding session of
either kind is cleared normally, which is the case of a guide log deleted from disk with nothing
else left on that night, whose values must go. **The hold-out takes precedence over that clearing
rule whenever an unzoned candidate remains within a day of the night**, so a guide log deleted
while another rig's session on that same night still has no time zone does not clear: the
deleted log's guiding figures stay on the frames until a zone resolves for that rig, its own logs
are also gone, or the frames are rescanned.

The widened date test is used rather than the time-overlap lookup the fill uses, because an
unzoned session has no instant to overlap with and a zoned one would have to be matched against
a span computed over the night's **already filled** frames, which is a second query and a second
definition of "the night's guiding". One definition, two date tests, and the error it can make is
the safe one: a zoned session found a day wide of its night makes the pass clear where the
hold-out would have kept, which is the behaviour that shipped before the hold-out existed.

Phase 15A's correlation implemented the fill-side exclusion, that is, an unzoned session
