contributes no samples; Phase 15B added the clear-side hold-out above, with the fifth migration's
`ended_at_local` beside it. No `csv` value is at risk on either side, because the clear is scoped
by the never-overwrite predicate below.

The site resolves by the same shape and independently per coordinate: the profile's own
`latitude` or `longitude` when it is not null, otherwise `general.observer_latitude` or
`general.observer_longitude`, otherwise null. The longitude is what the imaging-night
arithmetic of section 8.3 consumes.

**The longitude has a third step and the latitude does not (Phase 17, user ruling U4).** When
neither the profile nor `general.observer_longitude` gives a longitude,
`Phd2Profiles.LongitudeResolver` falls back to the configured `general.observer_timezone`,
converted as `utcOffsetHours * 15` at the session's own resolved start instant, which is the
same step 3 `SessionDate.ResolveLongitude` gives a frame (section 8.3). It is taken here and not
by a later phase because every consumer of a guiding night joins it to frames on strict
`session_date` equality: without it, a library with a zone set and no longitude configured files
a 21:42 local session under the next date while the frames of that same evening are filed under
their own, and the two never meet. Section 8.3 states the full order, why the latitude gains no
such step, and that the web has the same split.

**A stored `session_date` written under the old order corrects itself on the next pass.** It is a
derived column, the re-derive below rebuilds it for every stored session from the two wall clocks
already in the database, and `general.phd2_correlation_pending` keeps the obligation across a
crash or an exit. No guide log is re-read, and there is no migration: an installed library gains
the corrected dates the first time a correlation pass runs on the new build.

#### Metrics

`GalactiLog.Core.Phd2.Phd2Metrics` reduces one parsed guiding section to one `phd2_sessions`
row. Pure functions over the parser's records: no database, no settings object beyond the
resolved zone and longitude handed in.

Two conventions decide whether a reader trusts the number:

1. **RMS excludes frames inside dither and settling windows.** PHD2's own on-screen RMS excludes
   them and a reader will put the two figures side by side. Without the exclusion every dithered
   session reads several times worse than PHD2 said it was.
2. **RMS is a population standard deviation**, matching PHD2's own definition of the figure it
   displays. It is computed over the raw RA and Dec distances of the counted frames, not over
   their deviation from a fitted mean.

**The window rule, one implementation.** A window opens on the first `dither` or `settle_start`
that is not already inside one, and closes on the next `settle_done` or `settle_failed`. A
window still open at the end of the section closes at the last frame's time offset, because PHD2
was still settling when the section ended. A frame at time `t` is inside a window when
`start < t <= end`: the lower bound is exclusive and the upper bound inclusive, because an
`INFO:` line is stamped with the time of the **preceding** CSV row, so a frame at exactly
`start` was written before the dither began and is a legitimately guided sample, while a frame
at exactly `end` was written while PHD2 was still settling. The rule has one implementation,
which takes `(kind, time offset)` pairs and is fed both from the parser's events and from the
`events` JSON read back out of `phd2_sessions`. Two implementations would eventually disagree,
at which point a per-frame figure and the session figure printed beside it would stop describing
the same thing.

**Counted frames** are the frames that are neither dropped nor inside a window. From them:

- `rms_ra_arcsec` and `rms_dec_arcsec`: the population standard deviation of `ra_raw` and
  `dec_raw`, multiplied by the section's `pixel_scale_arcsec`, rounded to six decimals through
  `PythonNumerics.RoundLikePython` (below). `rms_total_arcsec` is the hypotenuse of the two.
- The filtered triple: the same computation over values that survive **one pass** of the
  excursion filter, which drops any value whose absolute size exceeds five times the unfiltered
  sigma. One pass, never iterated to convergence. One cable snag can inflate a session RMS
  several-fold, so both figures are stored and neither replaces the other.
- `peak_ra_arcsec` and `peak_dec_arcsec`: the largest absolute raw distance, scaled.

**Rounding matches the web's, by rule and not by coincidence.** Every value the web's own
`round()` rounds, this port rounds through `PythonNumerics.RoundLikePython(double value, int
digits)`, never `Math.Round(double, int)`. The two disagree on a genuine tie: .NET's `Math.Round`
rounds the shortest decimal representation of a double half to even, while Python's `round`
rounds the exact binary value half to even, and a value such as a two-sample median of
three-decimal timestamps lands on a tie under the second rule that the first rounds the other
way. `RoundLikePython` reproduces Python's behaviour exactly (measured against real Python 3.14
output on real data, not assumed from the specification of either language) by formatting the
value with the `"F"` format specifier at InvariantCulture and parsing the string back, which on
this runtime's format implementation performs the same exact-value half-to-even rounding Python's
`round` does. Every site that rounds a figure the web also rounds calls it: `rms_ra_arcsec`,
`rms_dec_arcsec` and the filtered pair above; `peak_ra_arcsec` and `peak_dec_arcsec`;
`settle_median_s`; `snr_mean`; and the correlation's own `guiding_rms_ra_arcsec`,
`guiding_rms_dec_arcsec` and `guiding_rms_arcsec` below, each to six decimals.

**Accumulation matches the web's, by rule and not by coincidence, in three separate shapes,
because the Python this port ports uses three.** Rounding alone is not enough when two different
sums land on two different doubles before either is rounded, which cost this port one stored
decimal on 1 of 937 real guiding sessions before it was found (`snr_mean`, from `Enumerable.Average`
against `statistics.fmean`, on a real corpus, `fix-f-report.md`).

- **`PythonNumerics.ExactMean`**, a port of `statistics.fmean`, which sums exactly through
  `PythonNumerics.ExactSum` (a Shewchuk correctly-rounded sum, from CPython's `math.fsum`) before
  dividing by the count. Used for `snr_mean` and `star_mass_mean`.
- **`PythonNumerics.CompensatedSum`**, a port of CPython 3.12's builtin float `sum()`, which is
  Neumaier-compensated rather than a naive running total. Used for the night rollup's
  `unguided_seconds` and for the per-rig guided hours the Statistics scorecard reads.
- **The naive left-to-right loop**, wherever the Python this port matches is itself an explicit
  `+=` loop rather than a call to `fmean` or `sum()`: the drop metrics above and the frame-count
  weighted RMS the night and rig rollups both use.

**The four members that reproduce a CPython rule live in
`GalactiLog.Core.Metrics.PythonNumerics`, not in `Phd2Metrics` (Phase 17).** `RoundLikePython`,
`ExactSum`, `ExactMean` and `CompensatedSum` are arithmetic, not guiding: they arrived here
because PHD2 was the first port that needed them, and Phase 17's Analysis statistics are their
second consumer, which is where a spine is extracted rather than copied or reached into across a
namespace (design lesson 1). `Phd2Metrics` calls them at their new home and keeps no copy of any
of them, so every figure in this section and every figure in section 12.14 rounds and accumulates
through one file. Nothing about the rules above changes; only where they live does.
`Phd2Metrics.WeightedRms` stays where it is, because a frame-count weighted RMS is a guiding
figure and not a CPython rule.

**This pins the port's parity on those figures to CPython 3.12 or later on the web's own side.**
The builtin `sum()` gained its float compensation in CPython 3.12, and `math.fsum` has been
Shewchuk since 2.6; the web backend already requires 3.12 or later
(`backend/pyproject.toml`, `python:3.12-slim`). A web deployment on Python 3.11, where the
builtin `sum()` is still a naive loop, would produce a different last decimal on the two
compensated sites, and the port would then be the one agreeing with a newer interpreter rather
than with that deployment.

**Pixels to arcseconds.** Every arcsecond figure is a stored pixel value multiplied by the
owning section's `pixel_scale_arcsec`. Nothing is stored in arcseconds at the frame grain, so a
corrected pixel scale never needs a data migration.

**Drop metrics**, over every frame including those inside windows: `drop_count` is the number of
DROP rows; `max_drop_run` is the longest consecutive run of them; `unguided_seconds` is the
elapsed time across those runs, measured from the last good frame before each run to the first
good frame after it, or to the section's last frame when the run reaches the end. Run length
matters more than raw count: a star reappearing many minutes later is probably a different star
and the target is likely off frame, so elapsed unguided time is the figure worth surfacing.

**Dither and settle metrics**: `dither_count` is the number of `dither` events; `settle_count`
counts settles that completed or failed; `settle_failed_count` counts the failures;
`settle_median_s` is the median of the settle durations, one per settle that started and then
completed or failed, null when none did. **A failed settle is timed like a completed one**: it
consumed that time, and excluding it would bias the median low on exactly the nights that went
worst. The three figures are consistent with one another by construction: `settle_count` is the
number of durations the median is taken over, and `settle_failed_count` is the subset of them
that ended in a failure.

**Star-lost reasons**: the DROP rows' reason strings counted into a JSON object, with an absent
reason counted as `unknown`.

**SNR and star mass include DROP rows**, deliberately: PHD2 still reports them there, and a
collapsing SNR trend during a star-loss burst is the whole diagnostic. **Pulse counts and pulse
totals cover every non-dropped frame including dither windows**, also deliberately: the
corrections issued to chase a dither are real mount commands.

**`MinFrames` is 100.** A session of fewer than 100 frames contributes its event counts, its
drop metrics and its settle metrics to every rollup, and contributes **no RMS**. A twenty-frame
fragment around an autofocus run gives a standard deviation with no statistical meaning, and
roughly seventy of the eight hundred sessions in the reference corpus are that short. The gate
applies to the rollup, not to the row: a short session still stores its own RMS columns, and the
rollup declines to average them.

**Night rollups are frame-count weighted.** A night's RMS in a given axis is
`sqrt(sum(n_i * rms_i^2) / sum(n_i))` over the sessions that pass `MinFrames` and carry a value,
`n_i` being each session's `frame_count`. Counts sum, `max_drop_run` takes the maximum,
`unguided_seconds` sums, and the night's settle median is the median of the per-session medians.
The count of sessions the gate excluded is reported alongside, so a screen can say why a number
moved.

#### Correlation

`GalactiLog.Data.Ingest.Phd2Correlation` fills a LIGHT frame's guiding columns from the stored
guide frames. It runs after the guide-log ingest of section 10.3 and again out of scan after a
settings save that could change its answer, and it is the only writer of a `phd2`-sourced value.

**What triggers the out-of-scan re-run.** One re-run per save, dispatched when the save changed
any of these:

- `general.phd2_profile_map`, compared **in its normalised form** (section 5.8.1) rather than as
  stored text, so re-saving a legacy-shaped document unchanged queues nothing while a real
  mapping change always queues.
- `general.observer_timezone`, which is step 2 of the resolution order above and therefore the
  zone of every profile that carries none of its own.
- `general.observer_latitude` or `general.observer_longitude`, which are the site behind a
  session's imaging night (section 8.3) and can move a session from one night to another.

A save that changes two or more of them queues one re-run, not two. A save that changes none of
them queues nothing. The re-run begins with the time re-derive described above, because a
changed zone or longitude is exactly what makes a stored `started_at_utc` or `session_date`
stale.

**The obligation survives a crash.** The same save that queues the re-run sets
`general.phd2_correlation_pending` to true (section 5.8.1), and the pass that completes clears
it. A pass that is cancelled, that fails or that is cut off by the application exiting leaves it
true, so the work is still owed rather than silently dropped. While it is true the next
correlation pass, whichever trigger brings it, widens its scope to every invalidated night
instead of only the nights an ingest touched and the nights holding an unfilled frame, and the
application queues one out-of-scan re-run when the GUI starts (section 12.11). A re-run is
therefore at worst deferred to the next start, never lost.

**Rig selection.** For one imaging night, the guiding sessions that describe a given rig are
chosen in this order:

1. Sessions whose rig matches. A session's rig is resolved live from `general.phd2_profile_map`
   through `Phd2Profiles.EffectiveTelescope(equipmentProfile, profileMap)`, never from the value
   frozen in the stored `phd2_sessions.telescope` column at ingest, so a profile the map no
   longer carries resolves to no rig here even though the column still names the rig it was
   mapped to before it was unmapped. Both sides of the comparison are user data written at
   different times, so the rig name is expanded to its canonical form plus every alias through
   `AliasMap.TelescopeMatchSet` (section 9.1) before comparing. A raw string comparison would
   miss a night shot on a telescope whose profile was mapped under a different spelling of the
   same rig.
2. When none match and no session on the night carries a telescope at all, and the night's
   sessions name exactly one distinct equipment profile, that sole unmapped profile's sessions
   are used. An unmapped profile is the pre-configuration state and attributing it is a helpful
   guess. A profile mapped to a different rig is a decision the user already made, and
   overriding it would put the guided rig's numbers on the other rig's frames.
3. Otherwise nothing. Two unmapped profiles on one night attribute nothing, and on a night
   whose frames span more than one rig the sole-unmapped-profile fallback of step 2 is vetoed
   outright: guessing which rig a target used would attach wrong guiding numbers to real data,
   which is worse than showing none.

The multi-rig count in step 3 is taken over the night's **full** rig set, the rigs of every
LIGHT frame on the night, not over the subset still needing a value. A rig whose frames all
already carry a CSV value is invisible to the unfilled query, and once it drops out of the count
a two-rig night reads as single-rig. The count is taken over canonical names, while the
attribution itself keys on the raw stored spellings, because one physical rig regularly appears
under several spellings in one night's headers and counting raw strings would read it as two.

**Pooling.** The sessions attributed to a rig are turned into one time-ordered stream of
`(instant, ra_arcsec, dec_arcsec)` samples, the instant being the session's `started_at_utc`
plus the frame's `time_offset`. DROP frames and frames inside a dither or settle window are
excluded, by the same one rule the session metrics use. The streams of several sessions are
concatenated, because PHD2 restarting mid-exposure produces two sessions covering one frame and
both describe how that frame was guided. **Sessions of a different rig are never pooled**: their
samples describe a different optical train.

For each unfilled LIGHT frame with a capture time and a positive exposure, the samples falling
in `[capture, capture + exposure]` are taken and their population standard deviations become
`guiding_rms_ra_arcsec` and `guiding_rms_dec_arcsec`, each rounded to six decimals through
`PythonNumerics.RoundLikePython`, with `guiding_rms_arcsec` the hypotenuse of the two rounded values
and rounded the same way, and `guiding_rms_source` is set to `phd2`. Two coverage gates, both of which leave the columns
null rather than writing a weak figure: at least **10** samples in the window, and the samples
must span at least **50 percent** of the exposure. `MinFrames` of 100 is a session gate and does
not apply here: an exposure window is seconds to minutes long, so a hundred samples would
exclude every sub shorter than about a minute at a half-second guide exposure. Twenty samples
from the first ten seconds of a five-minute sub say nothing about the other 290, which is what
the coverage gate refuses.

Sessions are found by **time overlap, not by date equality**: a session whose own `session_date`
lands a day off the frames it covers, which happens whenever the longitude behind it is unset,
is still found. The lookup window starts 24 hours before the night's first exposure, because
PHD2 sessions run for hours and one can already be running when the night's first frame opens.
It is served by `ix_phd2_sessions_started_at_utc` (section 5.16).

**The never-overwrite guarantee, stated once and enforced structurally (ruling F6):**

> **A value whose `guiding_rms_source` is `csv` is never overwritten, never cleared and never
> read as a candidate for filling, by any path in this section.**

That guarantee is not a check each caller remembers. One write method in `Phd2Correlation`
carries the predicate `guiding_rms_source IS NULL OR guiding_rms_source = 'phd2'` inside the
update statement itself, and it is the only method in the solution that writes a `phd2` source,
so no caller can defeat it by forgetting a check. A test feeds it a `csv` row and asserts the row
is unchanged.

**Re-derivation.** A pass given an explicit set of nights, which is what a guide-log ingest and
an out-of-scan re-run both dispatch, clears the `phd2`-sourced values on those nights before
refilling them: a re-ingested log, an edited map or a changed zone can invalidate a value that
was correct when it was written, and a frame that no longer qualifies would otherwise keep
yesterday's number forever. A pass given no set visits only the nights holding a LIGHT frame
with no guiding RMS at all, fills what qualifies and re-derives nothing. In both modes the clear
is scoped to `guiding_rms_source = 'phd2'` by the same predicate above, and in both modes it
respects the unzoned-night hold-out described earlier, trivially so in the incremental mode,
which clears nothing at all.

The nights an out-of-scan re-run invalidates are the union of the nights holding a
`phd2`-sourced frame, whose attribution may now be wrong, and the nights holding a guiding
session, which may now attribute where it did not before. The second set is taken after the time
re-derive, so a session that just moved to another night puts both its old night and its new one
in the set. That set is bounded by the guide-log corpus, not by the size of the frame catalogue.

#### A session with no pixel scale

The PHD2 build embedded in an ASIAIR writes no `Pixel scale` line. Such a session is parsed,
stored and counted like any other: its `phd2_frames` rows hold the same pixel distances, its
drop, dither, settle and star-loss metrics are complete, and its `pixel_scale_arcsec` is null.

Its arcsecond columns are null, and **it is never correlated**: a frame's guiding RMS is an
arcsecond figure, and with no scale there is nothing to convert the pixels with. An arcsecond
figure derived from an assumed scale would be invented rather than measured.

The pass writes one warning per pass naming every profile whose sessions carried no pixel scale
(section 10.9, `phd2_pixel_scale_missing`), so a reader who sees no guiding on an ASIAIR night
is told why rather than left to guess. The web application is silent in this case; the port is
not, which is recorded in section 7.6's departures below.

#### Departures from the web application

- `phd2_sessions.started_at_utc`, `ended_at_utc` and `session_date` are nullable here and the
  first is not nullable in the web model. The web application falls back to the server's own
  zone when nothing is configured, which on that deployment silently stored a whole corpus six
  hours early and filled 172 frames with an RMS measured six hours away from the exposure.
  Ruling F1 refuses that fallback, and a session with no zone therefore has no UTC instant to
  store.
- The missing pixel scale warning above has no counterpart in the web application, which
  declines silently.
- `phd2_sessions.discarded_rows` is stored here and lives only on the web parser's in-memory
  record.
- `phd2_sessions.ended_at_local` is stored here and has no counterpart in the web model at all.
  It is what lets a session's UTC end be re-derived from a wall clock rather than reconstructed
  from a duration, which is the one place a daylight-saving transition could still move a stored
  instant (section 5.16).
- The guide-log orphan drop is guarded **per walked root** here, and the web application guards
  it over the whole guide-log corpus with one 50 percent limit and no zero-discovery guard at
  all. Both guards of section 10.3 step 4 apply to guide-log rows, through the same shared
  arithmetic rather than a second implementation. The reason is that the two sides must agree:
  with two scan roots and one drive unplugged, a corpus-wide test would drop that drive's
  guide-log rows in the same run in which the frame-side guards keep its frame rows.
- The web model's `insights` column is not created (section 5.16).
- `phd2_sidereal.py`, the timezone cross-check, is not ported at all and has no owner
  (section 19.1). `phd2_stats.py`, the statistics aggregates, is not ported in Phase 15A and is
  ported in Phase 15B as `GuidingStatsQuery` (section 12.5).

### 7.7 Panel tokens and mosaic detection

Phase 18. Port of `backend/app/services/panel_tokens.py`, `mosaic_detection.py` and the accept half
of `mosaic_suggestions.py`, amended by the plan's rulings R4 to R6, R10 and R19. The token rule and
every grouping, scoring and naming step are pure functions over records in
`GalactiLog.Core.Mosaics.PanelTokens` and `GalactiLog.Core.Mosaics.MosaicDetection`; the pass that
reads the catalogue and writes suggestions is `GalactiLog.Data.Ingest.MosaicDetectionPass`. Detection
reads frame geometry from the `images` columns of section 5.2 and never from `raw_headers`; it reads
`OBJECT` with `json_extract`, as the dashboard group key does (section 12.2).

#### The token rule

A panel token is a trailing panel number in `OBJECT`. Two patterns are tried in order; the first
that matches wins, and a name neither matches carries no token, so its frame's `panel_label` is
null and it never becomes a panel candidate.

1. **The keyword pattern**, matched case insensitively and culture invariantly:
   `^(.+?)\s*[-_\s]?\s*(K)\s*[-_\s]?\s*(\d+)\s*$`, where `K` is the alternation of
   `general.mosaic_keywords`, each keyword regex-escaped, in the stored order. Group 1, trimmed, is
   the **base name**; group 2 is the keyword as `OBJECT` spells it; group 3 is the **panel
   number**, as written. The pattern is skipped when the keyword list is empty.
2. **The tile pattern**: `^(.+?)[\s_-]+(\d+-\d+)\s*$`. Group 1, trimmed, is the base name and
   group 2, a row and column pair, is the panel number. It carries no keyword.

The **panel label** is `Panel ` followed by the panel number, whichever keyword matched, so
`NGC 7000 P3` and `NGC 7000 Panel 3` both label `Panel 3`. The base is the name with the token
removed; it is what panels of one mosaic share.

| `OBJECT` | Keywords | Base name | Number | `panel_label` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `M 31 Panel 2` | `Panel`, `P` | `M 31` | `2` | `Panel 2` |
| `NGC 7000 P3` | `Panel`, `P` | `NGC 7000` | `3` | `Panel 3` |
| `IC 1396 P1` | `Panel`, `P` | `IC 1396` | `1` | `Panel 1` |
| `Sh2-155 Panel 1` | `Panel`, `P` | `Sh2-155` | `1` | `Panel 1` |
| `M31 panel2` | `Panel`, `P` | `M31` | `2` | `Panel 2` |
| `NGC 7000_Panel_4` | `Panel`, `P` | `NGC 7000` | `4` | `Panel 4` |
| `IC1805_1-2` | `Panel`, `P` | `IC1805` | `1-2` | `Panel 1-2`, by the tile pattern |
| `North America Nebula` | `Panel`, `P` | none | none | null: no token |
| `M 31 Tile 2` | `Panel`, `P` | none | none | null: `Tile` is not a keyword and `2` is not a row and column pair |
| `NGC 7000 Panel 1` | `P` | none | none | null: `Panel` is not in the list, and `P` must be followed by digits |

The number is the trailing digit run, anchored to the end of the name, so `Sh2-155 Panel 1` keeps
the digits of its base, and a base needs at least one character. `Pelican 2` under `P` carries no
token because the only `P` is followed by letters, not by a separator and digits, and `2` alone is
not a row and column pair.

**The pattern per entry.** Each suggestion entry stores the web's `OBJECT` pattern for its token in
`mosaic_suggestions.panel_patterns`: `%<base>%<keyword>%<number>%` for a keyword match and
`%<base>%<number>%` for a tile match, with base and keyword as the first matching `OBJECT` spells
them. No query in this port matches by it: membership is the join of section 5.24, and a candidate's
frames are found by re-parsing `OBJECT` with the token rule, so the web's prefix guard against `1`
matching `Panel 12` (AUD-008) has nothing to guard.

#### Step 0: relabel and backfill

Every run begins with two maintenance passes, inside the detection job. Step 0 also runs alone,
once, in the startup that applies the Mosaics migration, in the App and the CLI alike, before any
page reads, so rows a scan wrote before the upgrade carry their labels from the first read on; it
logs one line with both counts, and a failure there is logged and does not block startup.

1. **Relabel (ruling R6).** For each distinct `OBJECT` among LIGHT frames, the label is computed
   with the current keywords, and every LIGHT row whose stored `panel_label` differs from it,
   null compared as a value, is rewritten. Rows whose label is unchanged are not written. This is
   what makes a keyword change on the Mosaics page reach the frames already catalogued. The count
   of rewritten rows is reported as `relabelled`.
2. **Backfill (ruling R10).** Every LIGHT row whose `ra_deg`, `dec_deg` and `width_px` are all
   null has `RA`, `DEC`, `OBJCTRA`, `OBJCTDEC` and `NAXIS1` read from `raw_headers` and put
   through the rules of section 7.1, and whatever they yield is written. This fills the rows a
   scan catalogued before Phase 18. A row whose headers yield nothing stays null and is visited
   again on the next run, one `json_extract` per such row; that is the known ceiling, and the
   upgrade path is a marker column if it is ever measured. The count of rows written is reported
   as `backfilled`.

#### Candidates

A **candidate** is one distinct panel-token `OBJECT` within one target, the web's
`_build_candidates` rule (ruling R19a). The pass reads, for every target with no `merged_into_id`,
the distinct `OBJECT` strings of its LIGHT frames whose `panel_label` is not null, re-parses each
with the token rule, and makes one candidate per string. Several panels resolved to one target, as
`StripPanel` makes "NGC 7000 Panel 1" to "Panel 4" resolve to NGC 7000 (section 9), therefore yield
one candidate each, each with its own centre and its own nights. Within one target, a second
`OBJECT` that parses to the same base, compared case insensitively, and the same number as an
earlier one yields no candidate of its own, as in the web; its frames carry the same label, so they
still count once their nights are included (section 5.24). A target with no token `OBJECT` yields
no candidate, which is the web's never-absorb rule. Candidates are ordered by target id, ordinal,
and then by `OBJECT`, ordinal; every "first" below is in that order.

A candidate's **frames** are its target's LIGHT frames carrying its `OBJECT`, so its centre is a
per-`OBJECT` centre and never the target's. From them:

- **The centre** is the robust centre below, over the frames with a stored position, or none when
  no frame has one.
- **The field of view**, in arcminutes, is `width_px * arcsec_per_pixel / 60` of the earliest frame
  by `capture_date`, then `id`, that carries both, or none. The web takes the first frame its query
  returned, which is not a defined order; this port fixes one.
- **The nights** are the distinct non-null `session_date` values: the nights on which this
  `OBJECT` was shot, which become the `dates` of its entry in `mosaic_suggestions.session_dates`
  (section 5.25), not every night of the target.

**The robust centre** (`robust_median_center`). The declination is the median of the frames'
declinations. The right ascension is unwrapped around a reference so the 0 and 360 seam does not
collapse to 180: the reference is the median of the raw right ascensions; each frame's offset from
it is brought into -180 to less than 180 by `((ra - ref + 180) mod 360) - 180` with a floating
modulo that maps a negative value upward; each offset is multiplied by `cos(median declination)`,
taken as `1e-9` when it is exactly zero; and the centre's right ascension is
`(ref + median offset / cos) mod 360`. A median of an even count is the mean of the two middle
values. The median, not the mean, is the outlier rule: a single frame with a corrupt header cannot
move the centre, and the web applies no other rejection.

**Separation** between two centres is the haversine great-circle distance,
`2 * asin(sqrt(a))` with `a = sin(dDec / 2)^2 + cos(dec1) * cos(dec2) * sin(dRa / 2)^2` clamped
to 0 to 1, in degrees, multiplied by 60 for arcminutes.

**The tolerance**, one value for the whole run: `general.mosaic_position_tolerance_arcmin` when it
is greater than zero; otherwise a quarter of the smallest field of view among all candidates, but
not less than 1.0 arcminute; otherwise, when no candidate has a field of view, 12.0 arcminutes, the
web's `DEFAULT_TOLERANCE_ARCMIN`. Two centres closer than the tolerance are the same position.

#### Grouping

Three paths run in order. A **group** is an ordered list of entries, each a candidate; its entries
are sorted by panel number, the number split on `-` and compared as a sequence of integers, with a
number that does not parse sorted after every one that does, and ties keeping candidate order. The
group's base name is its first entry's base.

1. **By name.** Candidates are grouped by base name compared case insensitively. A base with at
   least two distinct panel numbers becomes a group, keeping the first candidate of each number.
   Its positions are **distinct** when at least one pair of its entries with a centre is at least
   the tolerance apart; then its discovery source is `both`, otherwise `name`. Every target with an
   entry in a name group is consumed.
2. **By position.** The candidates whose target is not consumed and that have a centre are
   clustered by single link: two candidates join when their separation is at most the **reach**,
   three times the median field of view of these candidates, or ten times the tolerance when none
   has one, and joining is transitive. A cluster becomes a group when it holds at least two
   distinct targets and at least two distinct panel numbers; its discovery source is `position`.
   Entries are not collapsed by number: two targets carrying `Panel 1` stay two entries, and accept
   combines them into one panel.
3. **One panel.** Every candidate whose target is in no group from the first two paths is grouped
   by base name compared case insensitively, and each such base becomes a one-panel group with
   discovery source `name`, provided that base, compared case insensitively, has no entry in any
   name or position group. A leftover candidate of a base that is already grouped is dropped, as
   the web drops it, so the path never duplicates a suggestion. The plan's fixture keeps a lone `IC 1396 P1` as a
   low confidence suggestion, so the port surfaces a first panel the reader may be starting a
   mosaic with, and dismissing it keeps it away under the rule below.

Groups are emitted name groups first, then position groups, then one-panel groups, each set ordered
by base name, ordinal and case insensitive. The order decides which campaign takes a ` (#n)` suffix.

#### Confidence and flags

Each group is checked in this order, and each failing check adds one review note to `flags`, in the
words below. A group is `high` confidence when it has no flag and its discovery source is `both`;
every other group is `low`.

| Check | Fails when | Review note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positions not distinct | Any two entries with a centre are closer than the tolerance. | "Positions not distinct: two panels share a sky centre within tolerance (possible duplicate or mislabel)." |
| Unrelated names | A position group's entries carry more than one base name, compared case insensitively. | "Position-grouped targets have unrelated base names." |
| No position | At least one entry has no centre. | "Some panels have no usable sky coordinates." |
| Irregular geometry | At least three entries have a centre, at least one entry has a field of view, and the largest separation between two entries is more than 8 times the median field of view. | "Panel spread is far larger than the field of view (irregular geometry)." |
| Mixed plate scales | At least two entries have a field of view and the largest is more than 1.5 times the smallest. | "Mixed plate scales across panels." |
| Mixed keywords | The entries' keywords, compared case insensitively, with the tile pattern counted as one more kind, hold more than one value. | "Panels name their number with different keywords." |
| One panel | The group has one distinct panel number. | "Only one panel found." |

The first five are the web's checks with its constants. The web's first note does not name the
check; the port's prefixes "Positions not distinct" so the reader meets the same words the list
pill and the fixture use. Mixed keywords and one panel are the port's own, from the plan: the first
catches `NGC 7000 Panel 1` beside an unrelated `NGC 7000 P2`, and the second keeps a one-panel
group from ever reading as high.

**Geometry** (`mosaic_suggestions.geometry`): `panels`, one object per entry in entry order with
its `target_id`, `label`, and `ra` and `dec` rounded to 6 decimals or null; `pitches`, the
separation in arcminutes of every pair of entries with a centre, rounded to 3 decimals, in pair
order; and `fov_arcmin`, the median field of view of the entries that have one, rounded to 2
decimals, or null. Rounding is half to even, Python's `round` and `Math.Round`'s default alike.

#### Campaigns and names

A group's nights are the union of its entries' nights. When `general.mosaic_campaign_gap_days` is
greater than zero, the distinct nights are sorted and split into **campaigns**: a new campaign
starts wherever two consecutive nights are more than that many days apart. When it is zero, or the
split yields one campaign, the group is one suggestion over all its nights, named with the base name
alone. A group with no nights at all is one suggestion with no nights.

When the split yields two or more campaigns, each campaign is its own suggestion over the entries
that have at least one night in it, each entry's nights narrowed to the campaign. A campaign whose
entries carry fewer than two distinct panel numbers is skipped, except in a one-panel group, where
one is enough. Its name is the base name, a space and the campaign's **date range suffix** built
from its first and last night: `(Mar 2026)` when both fall in one month, `(Mar 2026 - May 2026)`
otherwise, with English three-letter month abbreviations whatever the culture. Its geometry keeps
the campaign's entries, recomputes the pitches over them alone, and carries the group's field of
view unchanged.

**Unique names.** Within one run, no two suggestions share a name and no suggestion takes the name
of an existing mosaic: the set of used names starts as the existing mosaic names, and a name
already in it, compared case insensitively, becomes `<name> (#2)`, then `(#3)`, and so on, the first
free one. The web compares this set case sensitively against a case-insensitive unique mosaic name;
the port compares it the way `mosaics.name` is unique.

**The dedup signature** is `<base>|<target ids>|<labels>`: the base name as stored, then the
entries' target ids sorted ordinally and joined with `,`, then the entries' labels sorted ordinally
and joined with `,`, duplicates kept in both. It does not depend on order, nights, geometry, frame
counts or the suggested name, so a re-run over the same panels yields the same signature.

#### Writing suggestions

Detection is idempotent (ruling R5). The write is one transaction, so a failed run leaves the
previous list in place:

1. Read every `rejected` row's signature together with the union of its nights. Several dismissed
   rows sharing a signature pool their nights.
2. Delete every `pending` row. `accepted` and `rejected` rows are untouched.
3. Read the existing mosaic names and the **covered triples**: every (target, night, frame
   label) held by an `included` row in any mosaic.
4. For each suggestion in emission order, skip it when its name before the unique-name step equals
   an existing mosaic's, compared case insensitively, because that campaign was already accepted;
   skip it when it has at least one (target, night, label) triple, each entry's target and label
   with each of its nights, and every triple is covered, which catches
   an accepted mosaic since renamed; skip it when its signature matches a dismissed signature and
   its nights are a subset of that signature's dismissed nights. Otherwise give it its unique name
   and insert it as `pending`.

A dismissed suggestion therefore stays away only while nothing new is shot: a later night over the
same panels is not a subset and the suggestion returns, and a different set of targets or labels is
a different signature. A target already in a mosaic is still read, so a new campaign of an accepted
base can surface; the name and covered-triple checks are what keep an accepted campaign from coming
back.

#### When it runs

On the Mosaics page's Run Detection button and at the end of every scan, after duplicate detection
(section 10.3 step 6, ruling R4). A scan that is cancelled or fails does not run it. Either way it
registers with the job registry as kind `mosaic_detection`, titled "Mosaic detection", with no
cancel delegate, reporting the steps "Relabelling frames", "Filling positions", "Grouping
candidates" and "Writing suggestions", and ending with the summary "n suggestions". The button is
disabled while a scan runs, with the tooltip "A scan is running. Detection runs when it ends.", and
while a detection job runs. Two passes never overlap: a pass waits for the one in flight to finish
before it starts. A manual run requested while the resolution lease is held (a manual resolution or
the reference thumbnail regeneration) is refused rather than queued, and its job ends Cancelled.

It writes `mosaic_detection_complete` (`scan`, info) with `{trigger, suggestions, relabelled,
backfilled}` when it ends, and `mosaic_detection_failed` (`scan`, error) with `{trigger, reason}`
when it throws, where `trigger` is `scan` or `manual` (section 10.9). A failure inside a scan does
not fail the scan, and its row is parented to that scan's `scan_started`. The headless CLI scan runs
the pass the same way.

#### Accept and dismiss

**Accept** takes a pending suggestion and the set of checked labels, which is every label unless the
reader unchecked some (section 12.17). It is refused with "Select at least one panel to accept."
when none is checked, and with "A mosaic named \"<name>\" already exists." when the suggested name
is taken. Otherwise, in one transaction, it creates the mosaic with the suggested name; creates one
panel per distinct checked label, in entry order, with `sort_order` from 0; writes, for each checked
entry, an `included` row for each of its `dates` with the entry's one target and `frame_label` set
to the panel's label, in the panel of that label; and writes an `available` row, same target and
frame label, for each other night of that target whose LIGHT frames carry that label. An unchecked
label creates no panel. Entries sharing a label share one panel. Two panels of one target sharing a
night do not collide, because their frame labels differ (ruling R19a). Where two entries would
include the same triple, the first in entry order takes it as `included` and the later as
`available`, the rule of section 5.24.
Accept sets the suggestion `accepted`. It asks nothing (ruling R13).

**Dismiss** sets the suggestion `rejected` and keeps its signature and nights, which is what the
subset rule above reads. It deletes nothing else. Its confirm says that a dismissal is not
permanent (section 12.17).

**Departures from the web, in one place.** No `needs_review` and no review clearing (ruling R11).
Membership is the join of section 5.24 on target, night and frame label rather than
`images.panel_id` and the retro-link that stamps it (rulings R19 and R19a), so accept claims no
frame. Detection runs at scan end as well as on the button
(ruling R4) and reads stored geometry rather than header JSON (ruling R10). Labels are recomputed by
step 0 rather than at ingest alone (ruling R6). One-panel groups, the mixed keywords note and the
"Positions not distinct" prefix are additions; candidate order, the field-of-view frame and the
case of the unique-name comparison are fixed where the web left them to query order or compared
case sensitively. A candidate's nights are collected from its own target's frames carrying its
`OBJECT` only, where the web runs an `ILIKE` of the panel pattern over every target's `OBJECT`;
its centre is likewise taken over that one `OBJECT` string's frames of that target. Progress and outcomes go to the job registry and the Activity feed; nothing
pushes a toast.

---

## 8. Session derivation

### 8.1 Session identity

A session is the pair (target, session date). The session date is the astronomical night a
frame belongs to. Frames captured either side of local midnight on the same night carry the
same session date.

### 8.2 Session date algorithm

Port of `backend/app/services/session_date.py::compute_session_date`.

Local solar noon at longitude `lon` occurs at UTC hour `12 - lon / 15`. Subtracting that
offset from the UTC capture instant and taking the date gives a value that is constant
between one local solar noon and the next.

```
computeSessionDate(captureUtc, useImagingNight, longitude):
    if captureUtc is null:            return null
    if not useImagingNight:           return captureUtc.Date
    if longitude is null:             return captureUtc.Date     # UTC-midnight fallback
    offsetHours = 12.0 - longitude / 15.0
    return (captureUtc - TimeSpan.FromHours(offsetHours)).Date
```

`use_imaging_night` defaults to true.

### 8.3 Longitude resolution order

`GalactiLog.Core.Sessions.SessionDate.ResolveLongitude` tries, in order:

1. The frame's own raw headers: `SITELONG`, then `OBSLONG`, then `LONG-OBS`, each parsed as
   a double, **first parseable finite value wins**. This is `session_date._LONGITUDE_KEYS` and
   `extract_longitude`, and the web ingest prefers it over the configured value
   (`effective_lon = site_lon if site_lon is not None else general.observer_longitude` in
   `worker/tasks_scan.py`).
2. `general.observer_longitude` from settings, through the one rule below.
3. The configured `general.observer_timezone` (an IANA zone name), converted to an
   approximate longitude as `utcOffsetHours * 15` using the offset in effect at the
   frame's capture instant. This step is added by the decisions ("observer longitude, FITS
   SITELONG fallback, user tz") and has no counterpart in the web application. It is
   deliberately coarse: a whole-hour zone offset places the noon boundary within 30 minutes
   of true local solar noon, which never moves a frame across a night boundary in practice.
4. No longitude resolvable. Fall back to UTC-midnight grouping and emit the fallback
   warning exactly once per scan run, never once per frame. Port of
   `session_date.warn_imaging_night_fallback`, whose docstring states this rate-limit
   requirement explicitly. The warning text names the missing headers and points at the
   Settings observer location field.

Longitude sign convention: positive east, matching FITS `SITELONG` and the web
application's `observer_longitude`.

**Step 1 skips a header value that is not finite.** `double.TryParse` under `NumberStyles.Float`
accepts the literals `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`, so a header carrying one of them used to
win the step and then raise out of the imaging-night arithmetic. The next key is tried, then step
2, exactly as for a value that does not parse at all. The narrow rule is deliberate: it is the one
shape of header value that cannot produce an answer.

**A finite header value outside minus 180 to 180 wins step 1 exactly as written.** It is not
skipped, not clamped and not treated as unset. Some capture software writes site longitude in the
0 to 360 east convention, so reading 250 as unset would silently move the session dates of real
libraries, which is the one thing a change here may never do. The present behaviour is pinned by a
characterisation case: a `SITELONG` of 250 files a 2025-06-15 03:00 UTC capture as 2025-06-15 and
a `SITELONG` of minus 200 files it as 2025-06-14. **Whether that is right is not ruled**, and the
question is carried rather than answered. The guide-log side has no equivalent exposure, because
`Phd2Header` carries no site field.

**Step 2 has one rule and one implementation, `SessionDate.UsableLongitude`, read by both sides.**
A stored `general.observer_longitude` counts only when it is a finite number inside minus 180 to
180, the bounds included. **Anything else is unset and falls through to step 3, and is never
clamped to the nearer limit**: a value that cannot describe a site is not evidence about where the
site is, and a clamp would invent one. Before Phase 17 the guide side coerced the stored value and
the frame side read it raw, so a hand-edited out-of-range, `NaN` or infinite longitude filed a
frame and the same evening's guiding under two dates, with an empty guiding chart and no error.
One rule in one place is what closes that. `ValidateGeneral` refuses an out-of-range longitude on
every save, so only a hand-edited settings document reaches the rule with anything to reject.

**Steps 1 and 3 are deliberately not range coerced**, and the reasons differ. A `SITELONG` header
belongs to one frame and has no counterpart on the guide side, so it cannot make the two sides
disagree. A zone-derived longitude is legitimately past a legal one: a UTC+14 zone answers 210.

`general.observer_latitude` needs no such rule at all: latitude plays no part in the imaging-night
arithmetic of section 8.2 and neither side reads it there.

**`Phd2Profiles.LongitudeResolver` resolves a guiding session's longitude by exactly this order
(Phase 17, user ruling U4, HANDOFF 5.1 item 11e answered).** Before Phase 17 it had no step 3: it
tried the profile's own `longitude`, then `general.observer_longitude`, then null, and never fell
back through the observer timezone the way `SessionDate.ResolveLongitude` does. The consequence
was a split that only shows up on a library with a zone configured and no longitude anywhere: a
frame's night resolved through step 3 while a guiding session of the same evening resolved to no
longitude at all, fell back to UTC-midnight grouping, and was filed under the **next** date. The
two sides then disagreed on the calendar date of one evening, and because every consumer of a
guiding night joins on strict `session_date` equality (section 12.14), the guiding figures joined
nothing at all, silently: an empty chart with no error and no warning. On the user's own library
this would have dropped all five joinable PHD2 nights.

The order is now the one above, member for member:

1. The profile's own `longitude` in `general.phd2_profile_map`, when it is not null. This is the
   guide-log analogue of step 1's header, the nearest thing a session has to its own site.
2. `general.observer_longitude` from settings.
3. **The configured `general.observer_timezone`, converted as `utcOffsetHours * 15` using the
   offset in effect at the session's own start instant**, exactly as step 3 above does at the
   frame's capture instant. The session's start instant is the one the zone resolution of section
   7.6 already produced, so this step needs nothing the resolver does not already hold.
4. No longitude resolvable. UTC-midnight grouping, as before.

`general.observer_latitude` and the profile's own `latitude` are untouched: latitude plays no part
in the imaging-night arithmetic of section 8.2 and gains no step.

**No guide log is re-read.** `session_date` is a derived column and is re-derived for every stored
session through the existing re-derive of section 7.6, from the two wall clocks already in the
database, on the next correlation pass. The pass that a settings save dispatches already begins
with that re-derive, and `general.phd2_correlation_pending` already makes the obligation survive a
crash, a cancellation or an exit, so an installed library **upgrades on its own**: the first pass
after this build files every session on the night its frames are on, with no user action and no
file read. Nothing in this ruling adds a column, a migration or a trigger.

**This departs from the web, which has the same split.** `phd2_profiles.py` has no
timezone-to-longitude step either, and the web documents the split the way this section used to.
The port closes it because the port is the one that has to answer for an empty PHD2 correlation
chart with no error on it.

**One split survives the ruling, and it is named here rather than left to be rediscovered.** Over
the sixteen combinations of the four inputs (`general.observer_longitude`,
`general.observer_timezone`, the profile's own `timezone`, and the frame's own `SITELONG`) twelve
agree and four do not. Three of the four are the null-date rows spec 5.16 already gives by design,
where no zone resolves for the session at all and it has no UTC instant. **The fourth is the cell
where a profile zone is set, the global zone is empty, no longitude is configured anywhere, and
the frames carry their own `SITELONG`.** The session has an instant, from its profile zone, but
step 3 above reads the **global** key, finds it empty, falls to step 4 and files the evening a day
late, which is exactly the symptom this ruling exists to close. The frame, meanwhile, resolves its
own header and is filed correctly, so the two sides disagree by one day and the guiding joins
nothing.

**It is a trade and not an oversight.** Reading the profile zone at step 3 would close that cell
and open its neighbour in exchange, the one where the profile zone is set, no longitude is
configured and the frames carry no `SITELONG`: there the session would resolve a longitude and the
frame would not, and the same one-day disagreement would appear with the sides swapped. One
longitude rule cannot close both, so step 3 reads the global key on both sides and the surviving
cell is recorded. A library that configures either an observer longitude or a global timezone
never reaches it.

### 8.4 Astronomical night hours

Port of `backend/app/services/astro_night.py`. Used only by the statistics timeline's
efficiency percentage and by the imaging calendar tooltip; no ingest path depends on it.

Definition: astronomical night is the interval during which the sun's altitude is below
-18 degrees.

```
darkHoursForNight(date, latitude, longitude):
    samples = 144                     # every 10 minutes
    intervalHours = 24.0 / samples
    start = date at 12:00:00 UTC
    darkCount = 0
    for i in 0 .. samples-1:
        t = start + i * intervalHours hours
        if sunAltitudeDegrees(t, latitude, longitude) < -18.0:
            darkCount += 1
    return darkCount * intervalHours
```

The window starts at 12:00 UTC on the given date and runs 24 hours, exactly as the Python
implementation does. Note that this is UTC noon, not local noon; the count is a duration,
so a whole-day window at any phase yields the same total for a night at moderate latitude.
The port keeps the same window so results match.

`AstroNight.NightBounds(sessionDate, latitude?, longitude?, TimeZoneInfo)` is the interval rather
than the duration, and it samples a different window. It anchors a 24 hour window on 12:00 in the
supplied display zone, takes the longest contiguous dark run inside that window, and refines both
edges by 1 minute bisection; it returns local wall-clock `DateTime`s of kind `Unspecified`, or
null when no coordinates are configured or no sample is dark. `darkHoursForNight` above keeps the
12:00 UTC window untouched. The two figures can therefore differ by up to one sample at a site
whose UTC window splits the night into two dark runs; the pinned rows measure at most 0.15 hours
of difference against a 0.1667 hour sample. The interval needs a contiguous run because it is
drawn as a band behind the night strip (sections 12.4 and 13), and a duration does not.

Monthly and weekly totals are the sum of per-night values, rounded to one decimal, from
`dark_hours_for_month` and `dark_hours_for_week`. Weeks are ISO weeks: week 1 contains
4 January, and the week starts on the Monday. Both are memoized in a
`ConcurrentDictionary` keyed by (year, period, latitude, longitude), matching the Python
`lru_cache` sizes of 512 and 2048 in spirit; a plain unbounded dictionary is fine here
because the key space is bounded by the user's catalogue span.

`darkHoursForNight` is memoized on the same terms, in a third `ConcurrentDictionary` keyed by
(date, latitude, longitude). The Python implementation memoizes the month and week totals only,
but three callers ask for single nights repeatedly: the calendar tooltip asks per cell, the
monthly total asks for every night of the month, and the weekly total asks for seven of the same
nights again. Each miss is 144 solar position evaluations, so the per-night memo removes the
duplicated work that the month and week memos alone leave in place.

Sun altitude uses the low-precision solar position algorithm, accurate to roughly
0.01 degrees, which is three orders of magnitude better than a 10-minute sampling grid
needs.

**Unit convention, stated once and applied to every line below.** Every named quantity
carries its unit as a suffix: `*Deg` is degrees, `*Rad` is radians, `*Hours` is hours.
`Math.Sin`, `Math.Cos`, `Math.Asin`, and `Math.Atan2` in C# take and return **radians only**,
so every degree quantity is converted with `rad(x) = x * PI / 180` before it reaches a trig
call, and every radian result is converted with `deg(x) = x * 180 / PI` before it is compared
with a degree threshold. Transcribing this pseudocode literally must produce correct output;
there are no implicit conversions anywhere in it.

```
sunAltitudeDegrees(utc, latDeg, lonDeg):
    n        = julianDate(utc) - 2451545.0                        # days since J2000.0

    lMeanDeg = mod360(280.460 + 0.9856474 * n)                    # mean longitude, degrees
    gMeanDeg = mod360(357.528 + 0.9856003 * n)                    # mean anomaly, degrees

    lamDeg   = lMeanDeg
             + 1.915 * sin(rad(gMeanDeg))
             + 0.020 * sin(rad(2.0 * gMeanDeg))                   # ecliptic longitude, degrees
    epsDeg   = 23.439 - 0.0000004 * n                             # obliquity, degrees

    lamRad   = rad(lamDeg)
    epsRad   = rad(epsDeg)

    raRad    = atan2(cos(epsRad) * sin(lamRad), cos(lamRad))      # right ascension, radians
    decRad   = asin(sin(epsRad) * sin(lamRad))                    # declination, radians

    gmstHours = mod24(18.697374558 + 24.06570982441908 * n)       # Greenwich sidereal, hours
    lstDeg    = mod360(gmstHours * 15.0 + lonDeg)                 # local sidereal, degrees
    haDeg     = mod360(lstDeg - deg(raRad))                       # hour angle, degrees

    latRad   = rad(latDeg)
    haRad    = rad(haDeg)

    altRad   = asin(sin(latRad) * sin(decRad)
                  + cos(latRad) * cos(decRad) * cos(haRad))       # altitude, radians
    return deg(altRad)                                            # altitude, degrees
```

`mod360(x)` and `mod24(x)` return a non-negative remainder: `((x % m) + m) % m`. C#'s `%` on
a negative operand returns a negative value, and `n` is negative for any date before 2000,
so the plain operator is not sufficient.

`julianDate(utc)` is `utc.ToOADate() + 2415018.5`, exact for the `DateTime` range this
application sees.

The Python implementation uses astropy's full ephemeris. The two agree to well under the
0.1 degree needed to place a sample on the correct side of the -18 degree threshold. The
Core test asserts against published USNO twilight times rather than against astropy, so the
test project needs no ephemeris of its own (section 18.1).

When `observer_latitude` or `observer_longitude` is not configured, dark hours are
unavailable and the efficiency percentage is null. The statistics page hides the efficiency
series rather than showing zero.

---

## 9. Target resolution

Single entry point: `GalactiLog.Core.Targets.TargetResolver.Resolve(objectName)`. Port of
`backend/app/services/target_resolver.py::resolve_target`. Every path that turns a FITS
`OBJECT` string into a target goes through it; there is no second resolution path. This is
the design-lessons choke point applied to identity.

### 9.1 Normalization

Port of `simbad.normalize_object_name` and `normalize_catalog_id`.

| Function | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `Normalize(name)` | Trim outer whitespace, collapse every internal whitespace run to a single space, uppercase. Used as the DB matching key. |
| `NormalizeDisplay(name)` | Same, without uppercasing. Used for display-quality names. |
| `NormalizeCatalogId(id)` | Null or blank in, null out. Otherwise `Normalize(id)`. Null-safe because `catalog_id` is nullable. |
| `StripPanel(name)` | Remove a trailing mosaic panel token, then trim. The token is section 7.7's keyword rule (`PanelTokens`) over the default keywords `Panel` and `P` from `GeneralSettings`, never the stored `general.mosaic_keywords`: a custom keyword affects detection, not resolution. Token-bounded and case-insensitive: the keyword follows a space, hyphen or underscore and is followed by digits, so `IC 1396 P1` becomes `IC 1396` and `M 31 Panel 2` becomes `M 31`, while `PK 164+31.1`, `NGC 7000 P` and `HIP 12345` stay whole. A tile token (`2-1`) is not stripped, and neither is a comet designation's half-month token (`C/2023 P1`). The web's `_PANEL_RE` knew only `Panel`. The strip is kept so `M31 Panel 2` resolves to M31 rather than creating a second target; mosaic panels are told apart by `images.panel_label` and the frame label of section 5.24, not by target. |
| `Compact(s)` | Uppercase, then remove spaces, hyphens, and underscores. Used for the substring filter tier in dashboard search. `target_listing._compact` uppercases, so the port does too; both sides of every comparison pass through this function, so the case only has to be consistent. |

`normalization.py` in the web application is a different concern: it maps user-configured
filter and equipment aliases to canonical names at query time. That is
`GalactiLog.Core.Aliases.AliasMap` here, covered in section 12.2, and it never mutates
stored data.

### 9.2 Resolution pipeline

```
Resolve(objectName):
    normalized = Normalize(objectName)

    1. Negative cache check
       row = catalog_cache[("resolver", normalized)]
       if row is a fresh negative:  return null

    2. Existing target lookup            -> FindTargetByName, section 9.5
       if found:                         return target.id

    3. Offline catalog lookup            -> section 9.3
       if found:                         create or link the target, return its id

    4. SIMBAD, through the cache          -> section 9.4, 9.6
    5. If SIMBAD produced nothing, SESAME with resolvers NV, through the cache

    6. If both produced nothing, solar-system name check  -> section 9.8
       if the name matches:              create or link a user_defined target, return its id

    7. If that produced nothing either:
          write a negative cache row for ("resolver", normalized)
          return null

    8. A resolved identity was produced. Match by identity (section 9.5).
       if found:                         return target.id

    9. Create the target (section 9.7).
```

Step 6 runs regardless of network state: it is a name-pattern test over the string itself, so
the per-scan circuit breaker below suppresses the online stages and the negative-cache write of
step 7, never the solar-system check. A name the check claims is therefore never
negative-cached, whether or not any online source was reachable.

`TargetResolver.Resolve` accepts a `CancellationToken` that is honored by the retry backoff and
by every HTTP call, so the scan writer can cancel a resolution mid-retry. Phase 4 adds a
per-scan online circuit breaker: after the first transient network failure in a scan, remaining
names skip the online stage for that scan, because a black-holed network costs up to 96 seconds
per name (15 s timeout, 3 attempts, 1 s and 2 s backoff, two sources).

Three distinct `catalog_cache.source` values are in play and they must not be conflated:

| Source | Written by | Meaning of a negative row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `simbad` | Step 4, keyed on the normalized name and, when different, the mapped name | SIMBAD was queried and returned no match. |
| `sesame` | Step 5, keyed on the normalized name | SESAME was queried and returned no match. |
| `resolver` | Step 7, keyed on the normalized name | The whole pipeline, offline, online and solar-system, produced nothing for this name. This is the only row step 1 reads. |

Step 1 checks `resolver` and only `resolver`. Checking `simbad` there would suppress the
offline lookup for every name SIMBAD happens not to know, which is exactly backwards for an
offline-first pipeline.

Step 3 is new in this port and is the "offline-first" requirement from the decisions. The
web application always goes to SIMBAD first because it runs on a server with reliable
network; a desktop application on an imaging PC frequently has none. Placing the bundled
catalogs ahead of the network changes which source wins for names both can resolve, so the
offline result is enriched with the same fields the SIMBAD path produces (`primary_name`,
`catalog_id`, `common_name`, `ra`, `dec`, `object_type`) and the online step is skipped
entirely when the offline hit is exact.

A resolved identity is never negative-cached. That is called out in `resolve_target`: a
single create collision must not cascade nulls across a whole scan batch.

### 9.3 Offline catalog lookup order

Bundled files, copied verbatim from `backend/data/catalogs/` into the application's
`Catalogs` content directory and loaded into SQLite on first run (guarded by
`general.catalogs_loaded_version`):

| File | Size | Table | Loaded as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `openngc.csv` | 3.9 MB | `openngc_catalog` | Semicolon-delimited. Columns `Name`, `Type`, `RA`, `Dec`, `Const`, `MajAx`, `MinAx`, `PosAng`, `B-Mag`, `V-Mag`, `SurfBr`, `Common names`, `M`. |
| `names.dat` | 95 KB | in-memory only | Stellarium common names. Fixed-width, section 9.3.2. |
| `caldwell.csv` | 3 KB | `static_catalog_entries` (`caldwell`) | |
| `abell.csv` | 138 KB | `static_catalog_entries` (`abell`) | |
| `arp.csv` | 22 KB | `static_catalog_entries` (`arp`) | |
| `sac.csv` | 15 KB | `static_catalog_entries` (`sac`) | |
| `herschel400.csv` | 8 KB | `static_catalog_entries` (`herschel400`) | |

Lookup order for a normalized name. The panel token is stripped first (`StripPanel`, section
9.1), and every step below looks up the stripped name, the designation and the common name alike,
the web's order: `NGC 7000 Panel 1` and `IC 1396 P1` resolve offline to NGC 7000 and IC 1396 on a
catalogue that holds no target for either yet. The strip uses the default keywords only, so a
custom keyword in `general.mosaic_keywords` affects detection (section 7.7), not resolution.
A panel name negatively cached before the upgrade (section 5.7) stays unresolved until that cache
row expires; Retry unresolved or smart rebuild's link pass resolves it sooner.

1. **Direct catalog designation.** If the stripped name matches a catalog pattern (section 9.4.1),
   normalize it and look it up:
   - `NGC n` or `IC n`: `openngc_catalog.name`, after `NormalizeNgcName`.
   - `M n`: `openngc_catalog.messier`, where the stored form is `M` plus the number
     zero-padded to three digits (`M 031`). Port of `openngc.lookup_openngc`, which builds
     `f"M {messier_match.group(1).zfill(3)}"`.
   - `Caldwell n` or `C n`: `static_catalog_entries` where `catalog_name = 'caldwell'`, then
     follow its `ngc_name` into `openngc_catalog`.
   - `Abell n`, `Arp n`: same shape against their own discriminators.
2. **Common name.** Look the lowercased, stripped name up in the override map
   (section 9.4.2), then in the Stellarium names map. Both yield a SIMBAD-style identifier
   such as `NGC 7000` or `Sh2-155`, which re-enters step 1.
3. **Descriptive suffix strip.** If the name contains ` - `, take the part before it and
   retry steps 1 and 2 on that.
4. **Sharpless and LBN rewrites.** `Sh2 174`, `SH2-174`, `S2_174`, and similar all rewrite
   to `SH 2-174`. `LBN 672` stays `LBN 672`. Ports of `_SH2_RE` and `_LBN_RE` in
   `simbad._get_simbad_id`.

`NormalizeNgcName`, from `openngc.normalize_ngc_name`: regex
`^(NGC|IC)\s*0*(\d+)([A-Z]?)$`, case-insensitive, rewritten as
`<PREFIX> <number><suffix>`. `NGC0031` becomes `NGC 31`, `IC0002` becomes `IC 2`.

RA and Dec parsing from OpenNGC, from `openngc.parse_ra_hms` and `parse_dec_dms`:

- RA `HH:MM:SS.ss` to degrees as `(h + m/60 + s/3600) * 15`. Exactly three colon-separated
  parts, otherwise null.
- Dec `+DD:MM:SS.s` to degrees as `sign * (d + m/60 + s/3600)`, with the sign taken from a
  leading `-`. Exactly three parts, otherwise null.

Enrichment from OpenNGC, from `openngc.enrich_target_from_openngc`, applied to a newly
created target and by the "rebuild targets" maintenance action:

- Fill `constellation`, `size_major`, `size_minor`, `position_angle`, `v_mag`, and
  `surface_brightness` only where the target's own value is null.
- If `common_name` is null and the OpenNGC row carries `Common names`, take the first
  semicolon-separated entry, trimmed, and rebuild `primary_name` from it.
- Skip entirely when `user_defined` is true.

#### 9.3.2 names.dat format

Port of `stellarium_names.parse_names_dat`. Fixed-width, one record per line:

| Columns | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| 0 to 4 | Catalog prefix, trimmed. |
| 5 to 19 | Object identifier, trimmed. |
| 20 onward | Remainder, searched with regex `_\("(.+?)"\)` for the common name. |

Lines shorter than 21 characters, blank lines, lines beginning with `#`, lines with no
regex match, and lines with an empty prefix or identifier are skipped. The common name is
lowercased and used as the dictionary key; the first occurrence of a name wins, later
duplicates are ignored.

Prefix to SIMBAD identifier mapping (`PREFIX_MAP`), joined with a space except for `Sh2-`
which is joined with nothing:

`NGC`, `IC`, `M` map to themselves; `SH2` to `Sh2-`; `B` to `Barnard`; `CR` to `Collinder`;
`MEL` to `Melotte`; `LDN`, `LBN`, `RCW`, `HCG`, `ARP`, `DWB` to themselves; `VDB` to `vdB`;
`CED` to `Ced`; `GUM` to `Gum`; `PAL` to `Palomar`; `ST` to `Stock`; `ACO`, `PGC` to
themselves; `SNRG` to `SNR G`. An unmapped prefix passes through unchanged.

### 9.4 Online resolution

The whole resolution pipeline is synchronous using `HttpClient.Send` with a 15 second timeout. Async is the upgrade path only if UI responsiveness demands it, since resolution runs on the scan writer task (section 5.1).

#### 9.4.1 Catalog priority

Port of `simbad.CATALOG_PATTERNS`, an ordered list where a lower index wins. This decides
which of several designations becomes the target's `catalog_id`.

| Index | Pattern | Catalog |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `^M\s*\d+$` | Messier |
| 1 | `^NGC\s*\d+$` | NGC |
| 2 | `^IC\s*\d+[A-Z]?$` | IC |
| 3 | `^(Caldwell\|C)\s+\d+$` | Caldwell |
| 4 | `^SH?\s*2[\s\-_]+\d+$` (case-insensitive) | Sharpless, all variants |
| 5 | `^(PN\s+A66\s+\d+\|Abell\s+\d+)$` | Abell planetary nebulae |
| 6 | `^Arp\s*\d+$` | Arp |
| 7 | `^HCG\s*\d+$` | Hickson compact group |
| 8 | `^B\s+\d+$` | Barnard |
| 9 | `^vdB\s*\d+$` | van den Bergh |
| 10 | `^LBN\s+[\d.+\-]+$` | LBN |
| 11 | `^LDN\s+\d+$` | LDN |
| 12 | `^(Cr\|Collinder)\s+\d+$` | Collinder |
| 13 | `^(Mel\|Melotte)\s+\d+$` | Melotte |
| 14 | `^RCW\s+\d+$` | RCW |
| 15 | `^Pal\s+\d+$` | Palomar |
| 16 | `^(Tr\|Trumpler)\s+\d+$` | Trumpler |
| 17 | `^Stock\s+\d+$` | Stock |
| 18 | `^(Ced\|Cederblad)\s+\d+$` | Cederblad |
| 19 | `^Simeis\s+\d+$` | Simeis |
| 20 | `^DWB\s+\d+$` | DWB |
| 21 | `^SNR\s+G[\d.+\-]+$` | SNR G |
| 22 | `^Cl\s+Berkeley\s+\d+$` | Berkeley |
| 23 | `^Cl\s+King\s+\d+$` | King |
| 24 | `^Gum\s+\d+$` | Gum |

Patterns are matched against `NormalizeDisplay(name)` and anchored with `IsMatch` from the
start, matching Python's `re.match`.

`ExtractCatalogId(aliases, mainId)`: evaluate every alias plus the main identifier, keep the
one with the lowest priority index. If none match, fall back to `NormalizeDisplay(mainId)`
with a leading `NAME ` prefix stripped (a SIMBAD common-name marker, not a designation).

#### 9.4.2 Common name override map

Port of `simbad.COMMON_NAME_MAP`, copied verbatim into `GalactiLog.Core.Targets.CommonNameOverrides`. The dictionary holds 72 entries covering three classes: abbreviations Stellarium does not carry (`rho oph`), entries where Stellarium maps to a less-preferred designation (`pinwheel galaxy` to `M 101` rather than the NGC number), and entries where Stellarium maps to the wrong object (`horsehead nebula` to `Barnard 33` rather than `IC 434`). Caldwell 1 to 50 mappings are included; full Caldwell 1 to 109 coverage comes from the bundled `caldwell.csv` consulted first in the offline catalog lookup order (section 9.3). Copy the dictionary literally; do not regenerate it.

Lookup key is the lowercased, panel-stripped name.

#### 9.4.3 SIMBAD request format

Two calls, both `https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr`, 15 second timeout, from `simbad.py`.

Call 1, the object query. `POST` to `/simbad/sim-script`, form field `script`:

```
format object "%MAIN_ID|%OTYPELIST|%COO(d;A)|%COO(d;D)"
query id <sanitized name>
```

Sanitization strips every character outside printable ASCII, and strips tab, carriage
return, and newline, then trims. An empty result after sanitization returns null without a
request.

Response parsing:

- If the body contains `::error::`, SIMBAD found no match. Return null.
- Otherwise take the text after the last `::data::`, split into lines, drop blank lines,
  lines starting with `~`, and lines consisting only of `:` characters.
- Split the first remaining line on `|`. Fewer than 4 fields means no usable result.
- Fields are `main_id`, `object_type` (an OTYPELIST, comma separated), `ra` in degrees,
  `dec` in degrees. Empty RA or Dec fields yield null.

Call 2, the alias query. `GET` to `/simbad/sim-tap/sync` with query parameters
`request=doQuery`, `lang=adql`, `format=tsv`, and:

```
SELECT id FROM ident JOIN basic ON ident.oidref = basic.oid WHERE basic.main_id = '<escaped main_id>'
```

The `main_id` is escaped by doubling every single quote, per the SQL standard, so the value
cannot break out of the literal. This escaping is mandatory and is the ADQL injection
guard; do not build the query by concatenation without it. The response is TSV; the first
line is the header `id` and is discarded. Remaining non-blank lines are trimmed and have
surrounding double quotes stripped.

The order matters: call 1 supplies the canonical `main_id`, and call 2 is keyed on that
`main_id`, not on the user's input.

#### 9.4.4 SESAME request format

Port of `sesame.py`. Fallback only, invoked when SIMBAD produced nothing.

`GET https://cds.unistra.fr/cgi-bin/nph-sesame/-ox/NV?<name with spaces replaced by +>`.

Resolvers `NV` means NED and VizieR only; SIMBAD is deliberately excluded because it has
already been tried. Response is XML. Iterate `Resolver` elements in document order and take
the first that carries both `jradeg` and `jdedeg`. From that element read `oname` (falling
back to the query name), `otype` trimmed, and every `alias` child's text. The resolver's
`name` attribute is recorded for diagnostics.

#### 9.4.5 Alias curation and naming

Port of `simbad.curate_aliases`, `extract_common_name`, and `build_primary_name`. Applied
identically to SIMBAD and SESAME results, which is why both go through
`curate_simbad_result`.

`CurateAliases(rawAliases, fitsNames)`:

- For each raw alias, take `NormalizeDisplay(alias)`.
- If it starts with `NAME ` (case-insensitive), strip the prefix, title-case the remainder,
  and keep it.
- Else if it matches any catalog pattern, keep the normalized form.
- Else drop it. This discards coordinate and survey identifiers: `2MASS`, `USNO`, `GSC`,
  `TYC`, `SDSS`, `WISE`, `GAIA`, `UCAC`, `IRAS`, bracket-prefixed forms such as `[BFS98]`,
  and bare RA-style numeric strings.
- Append every supplied FITS name, normalized.
- Deduplicate by the key `alias.ToUpperInvariant().Replace(" ", "")`, keeping the first
  occurrence and preserving order.

`ExtractCommonName(rawAliases, fitsNames)`: the first `NAME ` alias, prefix stripped and
title-cased. Failing that, the first FITS name that is panel-stripped, non-empty, and does
not match any catalog pattern. Failing that, null.

`BuildPrimaryName(catalogId, commonName)`:

| Inputs | Result |
| --- | --- |
| both present | `"{catalogId} - {commonName}"` |
| catalog only | `catalogId` |
| common only | `commonName` |
| neither | `"Unknown"` |

### 9.5 Identity matching

Port of `target_resolver.find_target_by_name` and `match_target_by_identity`. Every lookup
excludes merged-away targets (`merged_into_id IS NULL`).

`FindTargetByName(objectName)`:

1. `normalized = Normalize(objectName)`. Search targets whose `aliases` array contains
   `normalized`.
2. If not found, `stripped = StripPanel(normalized)`. If it differs, search aliases for it.
3. If not found, search for `primary_name == NormalizeDisplay(objectName)` (case
   preserved).

`MatchTargetByIdentity(resolved, objectName)`, identity first:

1. `catNorm = NormalizeCatalogId(resolved.catalogId)`. If non-null, search for a target with
   that `catalog_id_normalized`. Catalog identity is the stable primary key for a target.
2. Otherwise, or if that misses, fall back to `FindTargetByName(objectName)`.
3. On a match, add `StripPanel(Normalize(objectName))` to the target's `aliases` if it is
   not already present (compared uppercase), so the next direct lookup hits and the linkage
   is visible in the UI.
4. Never creates.

This ordering is what prevents duplicate targets. The web application's
`_create_target` docstring names the failure mode it eliminates: insert, then rename during
enrichment, then collide.

### 9.6 Cache and negative cache

One table, `catalog_cache`, keyed by (`source`, `key`). Port of
`backend/app/services/catalog_cache.py`.

| Row shape | Meaning | Effect on the next lookup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `payload` non-null, `negative = 0` | Positive result | Returned immediately, authoritative, no network call. |
| `payload` null, `negative = 1` | The source was queried and found nothing | Returns null immediately, no network call. |
| no row | Never queried | Perform the network call. |

TTLs, from `catalog_cache.py` defaults, overridden by the decisions which require a TTL on
the negative cache:

| Row type | TTL | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | none, cached forever | Catalog identity does not change. Cleared only by the reset-database action. |
| Negative | 7 days | A name that failed to resolve today may resolve after a catalogue update or after the user's network comes back. Seven days is short enough to self-heal and long enough that a rescan of an unresolvable library does not hammer CDS. |

An expired row is treated as a miss, not as a hit; it is overwritten by the fresh result.

Retry with backoff around the network call: 3 attempts total, sleeping
`1 * 2^n` seconds before attempt `n+2`, so 1 second before the second attempt and 2 seconds
before the third. A non-transient failure, defined as any HTTP 4xx other than 429, is not
retried, does not consume an attempt, and does not write a cache row; it propagates as
`NonTransientException`. Timeouts, connection failures, 5xx, and 429 are transient. A network
failure after all retries propagates as an exception and is never negative-cached, so an
offline evening cannot poison the resolver cache for the 7 day TTL.

SIMBAD's dual-key case, preserved from `resolve_target_name_cached`: the resolver may need
either the original normalized name or the mapped name from the override or Stellarium maps.
Both cache keys are checked before any network call, in that order. When a mapped name is
the one that resolves, the payload is written under both keys. That second write is a cache
write of data already fetched, not a second network call.

`skipSimbad` mode, used by the "rebuild targets" maintenance action: consult the cache only,
never call out. This is how a full rebuild runs offline.

Who writes these rows: during a scan, the scan writer task, as part of the per-record
sequence in section 5.1. The network call itself happens on that task, which is why a slow
CDS response slows ingest; the cache is what keeps that to once per distinct new name rather
than once per frame. Outside a scan, the maintenance actions write them through
`CatalogCacheRepository` on their own short-lived context.

### 9.7 Target creation, duplicates, and unresolved names

Creation, port of `target_resolver._create_target`:

1. Build the in-memory target from the resolved identity: `primary_name`, `catalog_id`,
   `catalog_id_normalized`, `common_name`, `aliases` (curated, plus the panel-stripped
   incoming name), `ra`, `dec`, `object_type`.
2. Enrich from OpenNGC before any insert or match, so `primary_name` is final. Enrichment
   may rewrite `primary_name`; it never changes `catalog_id`, so the normalized identity
   computed in step 1 stays valid.
3. `MatchTargetByIdentity` against the final identity. If a target already carries it, link
   to that target and return, rather than inserting a colliding row.
4. Otherwise insert.
5. After insert, attach catalog memberships (section 9.8), and fill `sac_description` and `sac_notes` from `static_catalog_entries` where `catalog_name = 'sac'` using null-only fill so existing values are never overwritten. For Herschel 400 membership rows, store the row's NGC or IC id as `catalog_number` because the unique constraint on (`catalog_name`, `catalog_number`) requires it.

The web application's `_create_target` wraps the insert in an `IntegrityError` handler that
