re-queries by the final `primary_name` and then by `catalog_id_normalized`, because several
Celery workers resolve names concurrently and can race to create the same target. **That
retry is deliberately absent here.** Resolution runs only on the single scan writer task
(section 5.1), so step 3 and step 4 are not separated by any other writer, and a unique
violation on `primary_name` or `catalog_id_normalized` is a genuine bug rather than an
expected race. It propagates, fails the record, and is logged at error level. Do not
reintroduce the handler; it would hide the bug it was never needed for here.

Manual creation (PAR-001), port of `backend/app/api/merges.py` `POST /custom` and
`POST /orphan-create`. The user creates a target from the Settings Targets tab (section 12.7)
rather than from a resolved identity, so this path skips step 2's enrichment and step 3's
identity match and writes what the user typed:

1. Trim the primary name. An empty name is refused with `Primary name is required` and nothing
   is written.
2. Build `aliases` from the comma-separated list the user typed, in the order typed,
   deduplicated case-insensitively, and add the normalized form (section 9.1) of every typed
   alias and of the primary name. The literal primary string is not stored as an alias, because
   `primary_name` is matched on its own; its normalized form is, so a later scan whose `OBJECT`
   is the upper-case name links to this target. Port of `_build_aliases`.
3. Conflict check, over active targets only (`merged_into_id` null), case-insensitive, of the
   new name and every one of its aliases against each active target's `primary_name` and each
   of its aliases:

   | Conflict | Refusal text |
   | --- | --- |
   | The name or any alias matches an active target's `primary_name` or one of its aliases | `Name already in use by "<target>". Use the merge action to attach these frames to it.` |
   | The normalized catalog id matches an active target's `catalog_id_normalized` | `Catalog ID already belongs to "<target>".` |

   Either refusal writes nothing and leaves the form holding what the user typed. A merged-away
   target never causes a refusal, which is what the partial unique indexes of section 5.3 are
   for.
4. Insert with `name_locked = 1`, and `user_defined` from the form's checkbox. `ra` and `dec`
   are stored as typed or left null. `object_type` stores the chosen display category literal
   or the free text the user typed under "Other", and null when nothing was chosen;
   `ObjectTypeCategories.Categorize` (section 9.8) already passes a stored category name
   through unchanged and reports anything it does not recognise as `Other`, so no new mapping
   is needed for a free-text value.
5. Retro-link. **Frame-driven, not candidate-driven** (Task 3 review escalation 1, a coordinator
   product correction; the approved spec read the candidate-driven text below and the user is
   told of the correction): link every unresolved LIGHT frame whose normalized `OBJECT` equals the
   created target's name or any of its aliases, by setting `resolved_target_id` to the new target
   on every such frame whose `resolved_target_id` is null. Then, for every `merge_candidates` row
   still `pending` whose `source_name` matches one of the new target's names case-insensitively,
   close it as accepted (its `suggested_target_id` set to the new target, its status to `accepted`
   and its `resolved_at` stamped) when one exists; a pending candidate is never required for the
   frames to move. Create from unresolved is the same path with the unresolved name already in the
   alias list, so the frames it names move and its own candidate, when one exists, closes in the
   same transaction as the insert. (Superseded text, kept for the record of what was approved: "For
   every `merge_candidates` row still `pending` whose `source_name` matches one of the new target's
   names case-insensitively, set `resolved_target_id` to the new target on every LIGHT frame whose
   `OBJECT` equals that `source_name` and whose `resolved_target_id` is null, then set that
   candidate's `suggested_target_id` to the new target, its status to `accepted` and its
   `resolved_at`." That wording left a row whose candidate was dismissed, or never written,
   permanently unresolved even though its frames plainly named the new target.)
6. Emit `target_created` (section 10.9) with `source` `manual`, carrying the linked frame count
   and the distinct unresolved name count the retro-link closed in its details.

The insert (step 4) and the retro-link (step 5) are two separate `SaveChanges` calls, because the
retro-link's own frame lookup runs its own commands under the same connection and cannot share a
transaction with the first save without changing that lookup's signature for its other callers. If
the second `SaveChanges` throws, the target row from the first save is already committed and is
not rolled back with it, so the outcome is a target that exists with an incomplete retro-link
rather than no target at all. This reports a distinct outcome, `CreatedWithoutBookkeeping`, and a
sentence naming it, rather than the create refusal's "The target could not be created": that
sentence would be false (the target was created) and would send the user into an immediate
re-submit that the name conflict then refuses against the very row this path just made.

No catalog enrichment runs on this path and no network call is made: a `user_defined` target is
one nothing in a catalog describes, and a name-locked one has already been named by its owner.

**The name-locked rule (ruling D5).** No automatic pass ever re-resolves a `name_locked` target.
A scan (section 10.3), the retry action under "Unresolved handling" below, duplicate detection
below and smart rebuild
(section 12.7) may link frames to such a target by name or alias and may add an alias to it, and
they write nothing else: `primary_name`, `catalog_id`, `catalog_id_normalized`, `common_name`,
`ra`, `dec` and `object_type` stay as the user left them. A manually created target is inserted
`name_locked`, so both flags are set on every row the Create target form writes, and either flag
alone is enough to stop the write. The explicit re-resolve action on Target detail keeps its
narrower rule, stated below, because a user who asks for a re-resolve is asking for exactly that.
A test pins the automatic case: create a user-defined target, scan frames whose `OBJECT` is its
name, and assert every column above is unchanged while its LIGHT frame count grew.

Duplicate detection, port of `worker/tasks_target_dedup.py`, run at the end of every scan
that ingested at least one new file, over distinct unresolved `OBJECT` strings that do not
already have a `merge_candidates` row in any status:

- **Pass 1, per unresolved name.**
  1. Try resolution. If it resolves to an identity an existing target already carries,
     write a candidate with `method = "simbad"`, `similarity_score = 1.0`, and reason text
     `SIMBAD resolves "<name>" to the same object as "<target>"`.
  2. If it resolves but no existing target matches, create the target and assign the frames
     directly. No candidate is written; a correct answer beats a suggestion.
  3. If it does not resolve, run trigram similarity against every active target's
     `primary_name` and each of its aliases, taking the maximum. If the best score exceeds
     0.4, write a candidate with `method = "trigram"` and reason text
     `Name is <score as percent>% similar to "<target>"`.
  4. Otherwise write a candidate with `method = "orphan"`, score 0, and reason text
     `No match found in SIMBAD or existing targets`.
- **Pass 2.** Detect active targets that share a normalized name or an alias with each other
  and propose merging them. The groups are built with union-find over the normalized
  `primary_name` and every normalized alias, so a chain of three targets sharing two different
  names is one group, not two candidates. Within a group the winner is the target with the most
  LIGHT frames, ties broken by ordinal comparison of `primary_name`; every other member becomes
  a candidate with `method = "duplicate"`, `similarity_score = 1.0`,
  `source_image_count` = that member's LIGHT frame count, and reason text
  `Shares alias "<shared name>" with "<winner>"`.

Network behaviour of the two passes: the first transient network failure stops Pass 1 and the
run reports that it stopped on a network failure, so the names it never examined are left for
the next run rather than judged unresolvable. Pass 2 still runs, because it compares existing
rows and needs no network. A non-transient catalog rejection skips that one name and the pass
carries on.

Trigram similarity, since SQLite has no `pg_trgm`: implemented in
`GalactiLog.Core.Targets.Trigram` to match PostgreSQL's `similarity()`. Both strings are
lowercased; each word is padded with two leading spaces and one trailing space; the set of
distinct 3-character substrings is taken; similarity is `|intersection| / |union|`. The 0.4
threshold is carried over unchanged.

`similarity()` is the only trigram function implemented. The web application also uses
PostgreSQL's `word_similarity()` in its dashboard fuzzy-search tier; an approximation of it
is not ported, because approximating a scoring function nothing can test against trades a
known behavior for an unknown one. Dashboard search uses `similarity()` at the same 0.4
threshold against each of `primary_name`, `catalog_id`, `common_name`, and each alias
separately, taking the maximum, and never against a concatenated blob of all of them. Names
are short enough that the two functions rank the same candidates.

Unresolved handling:

- Frames whose `OBJECT` resolves to nothing keep `resolved_target_id` null and are grouped
  in the dashboard under a synthetic key `obj:<OBJECT string>`. An empty or missing `OBJECT`
  groups under `obj:__uncategorized__`. Port of the `gk` group-key expression in
  `target_listing.list_targets_aggregated`.
- The Diagnostics page lists distinct unresolved names with their frame counts.
- The retry action clears every negative cache row, then re-runs resolution for each
  distinct unresolved `OBJECT`, assigning frames where it now succeeds. Port of the web
  application's `retry_unresolved` task.
- A scan and the retry are the same writer of targets and of the negative cache, so they
  exclude each other in both directions: the retry refuses while a scan is running, and a scan
  refuses while the retry is running. The refusal lives in the services, not in the buttons, so
  every surface that offers either action inherits it. The Run scan button greys while the retry
  runs, and the retry's own action reports that a scan is in progress and touches nothing.
- Filename-based target inference is deferred and is not implemented.

Merge and unmerge, port of `backend/app/services/target_merge.py`:

- A merge records a manifest (section 5.11) before moving anything: the exact set of image
  ids on the loser, the session notes re-keyed to the winner, the session notes appended
  to an existing winner note along with the winner's prior text, and the aliases the merge
  added to the winner.
- There are two merge shapes and both write a manifest: a target merged into a target, and an
  unresolved `OBJECT` name merged into a target. The second has no loser `targets` row, so its
  manifest carries a null `loser_id` and names what it absorbed in the payload's `source_name`.
  The history lists manifests, so both shapes appear in it and both can be undone.
- On merge, the winner absorbs the loser's `primary_name` and every loser alias into its own
  `aliases` array, deduplicated case-insensitively, matching `target_merge.py`. The loser keeps
  its own columns but is excluded from every lookup by `merged_into_id`.
- Session notes on a date the winner has no note for are re-keyed. On a date the winner
  already has a note, the loser's text is appended as
  `"<winner text>\n\n--- merged from <loser name> ---\n<loser text>"` and the loser's own
  row is left in place so it reappears after an unmerge.
- The loser gets `merged_into_id` and `merged_at` set; the row is never deleted.
- Unmerge consumes and deletes the manifest, restoring exactly what it records. There is no
  fallback path: this port has no pre-manifest merges to be compatible with.
- Undo is exact only in reverse order. When a manifest's winner has itself since been merged
  away, undoing that manifest is refused and nothing is written: the later merge has moved the
  frames on again, so restoring from the earlier manifest would take rows the earlier merge
  never moved. The surface says which merge has to be undone first.

Re-enrichment, the action behind Target detail's re-resolve: it clears the `resolver` negative
cache row for the target's `primary_name`, resolves the name again, and writes back
`catalog_id`, `catalog_id_normalized`, `common_name`, `ra`, `dec`, `object_type`,
`sac_description` and `sac_notes`. A null answer never overwrites a non-null column, so a
catalog that has since gone quiet cannot erase what is already known. `primary_name` is written
only when `name_locked` is unset, so a user's rename survives. A `user_defined` target is a
no-op: nothing in a catalog describes it.

### 9.8 Catalog membership and object type

Membership, port of `catalog_base.match_ngc_catalog_for_target`: for a target, take its
`catalog_id` plus every alias as the identifier set. For each row of
`static_catalog_entries`, normalize its `ngc_name` with `NormalizeNgcName` and, if the
result is in the identifier set, upsert a membership row with that catalog's name and
number and the row's `payload` as metadata. Idempotent by the unique constraint on
(`target_id`, `catalog_name`). Messier membership comes from a non-null
`openngc_catalog.messier` for the matched row.

Object type: `targets.object_type` stores SIMBAD's raw OTYPELIST verbatim, a comma-separated
list whose first element is the primary type. Display categories come from
`ObjectTypeCategories.Categorize`, a port of `target_helpers.SIMBAD_CATEGORY_MAP`:

| Category | SIMBAD codes |
| --- | --- |
| Emission Nebula | `HII`, `sh` |
| Reflection Nebula | `GNe`, `RNe` |
| Dark Nebula | `DNe`, `Cld`, `MoC` |
| Planetary Nebula | `PN` |
| Supernova Remnant | `SNR` |
| Galaxy | `G`, `H2G`, `GiG`, `GiC`, `GiP`, `rG`, `AGN`, `Sy2`, `LIN`, `QSO`, `PoG`, `IG` |
| Open Cluster | `OpC`, `Cl*` |
| Globular Cluster | `GlC` |
| Star | `*`, `**`, `Ae*` |

A stored `object_type` matches a code when it equals the code exactly or begins with the
code followed by a comma. Anything mapped by no code is `Other`. Frames with no resolved
target are `Unresolved`. The solar system categories `Planet`, `Moon`, `Sun`, `Comet`, and
`Asteroid` are never produced by SIMBAD mapping. They are produced by the name-pattern
classifier of pipeline step 6 (section 9.2), which recognises the Sun, the Moon, the eight
planets, `C/` and `P/` comet designations and numbered asteroid designations, creates the target
with `object_type` `user_defined` and stores the category literal; the constellation
abbreviations that collide with those names are excluded. A target created that way carries the
category directly, so `Categorize` passes a stored category name through unchanged rather than
mapping it. The full toggle list on the dashboard is the nine categories above, plus the five
solar system categories, plus `Other` and `Unresolved`. `Categorize` also accepts OpenNGC Type
codes directly (OCl open cluster, GCl globular cluster, Neb, HII, RNe, EmN, DrkN nebula families,
G galaxy, PN planetary nebula, SNR, *, **, Ast asterism, Dup duplicate, Other) so offline-resolved
targets categorize without a translation layer.

Constellation comes from OpenNGC enrichment (section 9.3) as a three-letter IAU code.

---

## 10. Scan pipeline

Owner: `GalactiLog.Data.Ingest.ScanCoordinator` (no Avalonia dependency; see 4.2). One scan at a time, process-wide. A
trigger arriving while a scan runs sets a pending flag; the coordinator starts one more scan
when the current one finishes and then clears the flag. This is the port of the web
application's `SCAN_PENDING_KEY` behavior without Redis. The follow-up scan the pending flag
starts is always a full scan of every configured root: a targeted run or a path-override run
that was answered `AlreadyRunning` is therefore followed by a full scan, not by a repeat of
its own narrower file or root list. Cancelling clears the pending flag as well, so a shutdown
drain is never defeated by a follow-up it cannot reach.

### 10.1 Roots

`general.scan_roots` is a list of absolute directory paths. Every root is walked. Unlike the
web application, which has one `FITS_DATA_PATH` and expresses multiple roots as
`include_paths` beneath it, this port has genuinely independent roots, because an imaging PC
commonly has one local capture folder and one NAS share.

Each root carries its own confinement boundary: a file is only ingested if its resolved
absolute path is a descendant of the root it was discovered under. Symbolic links and
junctions are followed during the walk (matching `follow_symlinks=True` in
`scanner._walk_supported_files`), but a followed link that lands outside every root is
skipped.

The list may not hold a duplicate path, nor a pair where one root is nested under another, and
the rule is enforced on the write path rather than at load: `SettingsStore.SaveGeneral` and
`SettingsStore.MutateGeneral` validate the list inside their own gate and throw
`SettingsValidationException` for either shape, so no surface can store one. Walking an ancestor
already visits the descendant, so a nested pair would ingest and queue every file beneath the
inner root twice.

Supported extensions, from `scanner.SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS`: `.fits`, `.fit`, `.fts`,
`.xisf`. Matched case-insensitively on Windows.

### 10.2 Include and exclude filters

Port of `backend/app/services/scan_filters.py`. Two mechanisms, both stored in
`general.scan_filters`.

**Path filters.** `include_paths` and `exclude_paths` are absolute directory paths. Each is
validated at load time to resolve under one of the configured scan roots; a path outside
every root is a configuration error surfaced in Settings, not silently dropped. This is the
trust-boundary validation referenced in section 2.3. `ScanFilterConfig.Validate` runs inside `SettingsStore.SaveGeneral` before persisting, rejecting invalid regexes, non-absolute roots, and rules whose target type is unknown, so a bad filter never reaches the scanner.

- Effective roots: if `include_paths` is empty, the roots are `scan_roots`. Otherwise the
  roots are `include_paths` with duplicates removed and with any path nested under another
  include path dropped, preserving the original order. Walking an ancestor already visits
  the descendant; keeping both enumerates and queues every nested file twice.
- A directory whose resolved path is at or under any `exclude_paths` entry is not walked.
- When `include_paths` is non-empty, a file must resolve under one of them or it is not
  included.

**Name rules.** Each rule is `{id, action, type, pattern, target, enabled}`:

| Field | Values | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | `include`, `exclude` | Any other value is a validation error. |
| `type` | `glob`, `substring`, `regex` | |
| `pattern` | non-empty string | A `regex` pattern that fails to compile is a validation error. |
| `target` | `file`, `folder` | |
| `enabled` | boolean | A disabled rule never matches. |

Matching semantics, from `NameRule.matches`:

| Type | Semantics |
| --- | --- |
| `glob` | Case-sensitive full-string glob, equivalent to `fnmatch.fnmatchcase`. |
| `substring` | Case-insensitive containment, equivalent to a casefolded `in`. |
| `regex` | .NET regex, unanchored search, equivalent to `re.search`. Compiled with a 250 ms match timeout so a catastrophic pattern cannot hang a scan. |

Evaluation order for a file, from `should_include_file`, and this order is the contract:

1. Path excludes. Under any `exclude_paths` entry means excluded.
2. Include-path narrowing. When `include_paths` is set, not under one means excluded.
3. Compute the path relative to its root. The last segment is the file name; the preceding
   segments are the ancestor folders.
4. Exclude name rules. A `file` rule matching the file name, or a `folder` rule matching any
   ancestor segment, means excluded.
5. Include narrowing per target type. If any enabled `file` include rules exist and none
   match the file name, excluded. If any enabled `folder` include rules exist and none match
   any ancestor segment, excluded.
6. Otherwise included.

Deliberate divergence at step 5: `scan_filters.should_include_file` selects include rules
with `r.action == "include" and r.target == "file"` and never tests `r.enabled`, so a
disabled include rule still narrows the scan in the web application while a disabled exclude
rule correctly does not (`NameRule.matches` returns false early for disabled rules, which
only reaches the exclude path). Disabling the only include rule there silently excludes
everything. This port tests `enabled` on both actions, so disabling a rule means the rule
does nothing. Behavior differs from the web application only for a configuration that is
already broken there.

Directory pruning, from `should_walk_dir`, applied before descending: a directory is not
walked if it is under an `exclude_paths` entry, or if any `folder` exclude rule matches any
segment of its path relative to the root, including its own name. Pruning at the directory
level is what keeps a scan off a `WORK_AREA` or `CALIBRATED` subtree entirely rather than
walking it and rejecting each file.

**Test-a-path tool.** Port of `ScanFilterConfig.test_path`. Given a path and an optional
kind (`file`, `folder`, or `auto`), returns a verdict and the ids of the rules that decided
it:

| Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `included` | The walker would ingest it. `matchedRuleIds` lists the include rules that matched. |
| `excluded_by_path` | An `exclude_paths` entry, or outside every include path, or outside every root. |
| `excluded_by_rule` | An exclude name rule matched. `matchedRuleIds` holds the first matching rule id. |
| `excluded_by_missing_include` | Include rules exist for this target type and none matched. |

In `auto` mode the on-disk type decides when the path exists; otherwise a path with a
file extension is treated as a file and one without as a folder. The path is resolved and
confined to a scan root before any filesystem access, so the tool cannot be used to probe
for the existence of arbitrary host paths. That confinement is required even without
authentication because it also makes the verdict match what the walker would actually
decide.

### 10.3 Header pass

Phase 1 of a scan, and the only phase that writes image rows.

1. **Walk.** Depth-first over each effective root using `DirectoryInfo.EnumerateFileSystemInfos`
   with `MatchCasing.CaseInsensitive`; the returned infos carry each entry's attributes, size
   and last-write time from the directory listing, so the walk takes no further stat per entry,
   which on a share is two round trips saved per file. Directories are pruned per 10.2 before
   descent.
   Inaccessible entries (permission denied, stale network handle) are logged at warning and
   skipped; they never fail the scan. Progress is reported every 50 discovered files, mirroring
   `scan_directory`.
2. **Classify.** For each discovered file, compare against the known set loaded from
   `images` (path, `file_size`, `file_mtime`):
   - Not in the known set: new file.
     A calibration frame skipped by `include_calibration` (section 7.5) is recorded in
     `skipped_files` (section 5.21) with its size and modification time. Whenever the run
     excludes calibration the known set includes those rows, so the frame is classified
     unchanged and is not read again until it changes. A run that includes calibration leaves
     them out of the known set, so the frame is classified new and ingested. Remaining limit: a
     rejected file writes no row and is read again on every scan, because a rejection can be a
     transient share fault or a parser gap a later version fixes.
   - In the known set and either the size differs or the modification time differs by more
     than 1.0 seconds: changed file, re-ingest. The one-second tolerance is from
     `scan_directory` and absorbs filesystem timestamp granularity differences across SMB.
   - Otherwise: unchanged, skip.
3. **Ingest.** For each new or changed file (section 10.6 covers concurrency):
   read the header, extract metadata (section 7), apply CSV backfill, decide calibration
   (section 7.5), compute the session date (section 8), resolve the target (section 9), and
   hand a completed record to the writer. This step is `FrameReader.TryRead`, shared with the CLI.
   The extracted metadata carries `ra_deg`, `dec_deg` and `width_px` (section 7.1), and
   `ScanWriter` writes them with the row together with `panel_label`, computed from `OBJECT` by
   the token rule of section 7.7 with the `general.mosaic_keywords` read once at the start of the
   run, for a LIGHT frame, and null for any other (Phase 18, rulings R6 and R10). Rows written
   before Phase 18 are labelled by the step 0 that the startup applying the Mosaics migration runs
   (section 7.7), not by this step.
   One file whose header read, metadata extraction or session-date derivation fails for any
   reason is one failed file, recorded `file_rejected` with its reason and counted in
   `scan_runs.failed`; the scan continues and ends `complete`. It writes no `images` row, so
   step 2's remaining limit applies and it is read again on the next scan.
4. **Prune.** After the walk completes and only if it was not cancelled, delete every
   `images` row whose `file_path` was not in the walk's discovered set and which lies under
   one of the walked roots. Rows under a root that was removed from configuration are left
   alone; deleting them would lose data the moment a user temporarily unplugs a drive.
   Deleting a row never touches the file. Rows under a subtree that `exclude_paths` (or any
   other filter rule) removed from the walk are pruned like any other undiscovered row: this
   is intended, so that excluding a folder and rescanning takes its frames out of the
   catalogue, and clearing the exclusion and rescanning puts them back. The walked roots are
   the effective roots for the run, so narrowing with `include_paths` prunes only inside the
   narrowed subtree. Deletion count is recorded as `scan_runs.removed`. `skipped_files` rows
   (section 5.21) are pruned under the same walked-root and discovered-set rule: zero discovery
   under a root holds its rows back whether or not an `images` row exists there, the safety
   limit guard follows the `images` prune, and `removed` does not count them.
5. **Guide logs.** The PHD2 pass of section 7.6, run only when `general.phd2_scan_enabled` is
   true. It is described below.
6. **Post-passes.** Duplicate detection (section 9.7), then mosaic detection (section 7.7,
   ruling R4), then reference thumbnails (section 11.4), then activity retention pruning. Mosaic
   detection runs only when the scan completed, after duplicate detection so that it reads the
   targets that pass left behind; it registers as its own job, and its failure does not fail the
   scan.

**The guide-log pass (Phase 15A).** It runs after the header pass has finished, never beside it:
the writer of section 5.1 owns the single write connection until the frame ingest is done, and
the guide-log pass is a second writer that takes it afterwards. It registers with the job
registry (section 12) as its own job. When `general.phd2_scan_enabled` is false the pass does not
run at all, the three `scan_runs` counters are written as zero, and nothing in `phd2_*` is read,
written or pruned; turning the key off is not a deletion.

1. **Candidates.** The paths the walk of step 1 reported through its guide-log callback
   (section 7.6). The walk is not repeated.
2. **Delta skip.** A candidate whose `phd2_logs` row exists and whose size matches and whose
   modification time differs by no more than 1.0 seconds is skipped without being opened. PHD2
   never rewrites a closed log, so a stored log is otherwise never read again.
3. **Ingest.** Each remaining candidate is read through `UserFiles` in shared-read mode, parsed,
   and stored, except one past the 64 MiB ceiling of section 7.6, which is recorded `failed`
   from its stat'ed size and never opened. One file is one transaction: the old rows are deleted
   and the new ones inserted together, so an interrupted re-parse can never leave a log half
   replaced, and the frame rows are inserted in batches of 5000 inside that one transaction.
   Progress is reported per guiding section within a log, not only per file: the envelope's own
   step and total stay the file counters (so the registered job's percentage does not jump
   backwards mid-file and a mid-file total is never what opens the job), and the section a log is
   currently on is named in the message alone. A file that cannot be read or
   parsed writes a row with `parse_status` `unreadable` or `failed` and its reason (section
   5.15), and **is not read again** until its size or its modification time changes. One bad
   file never stops the pass.
4. **Orphan rows.** A `phd2_logs` row whose `file_path` no longer exists on disk is deleted,
   taking its sessions, frames and calibrations with it through the foreign key cascade. Rows
   only, never files. Existence is the only test used: a log outside this run's effective roots
   is not a deleted log, so a run narrowed by `include_paths` drops nothing.
5. **Correlation.** The correlation of section 7.6 runs last, over the imaging nights this pass
   ingested and over the nights the orphan drop of step 4 emptied. It begins with the session
   time re-derive of section 7.6, so a zone configured since the last scan takes effect without
   any log being re-read. It registers as its own job. **With no night to visit it does not run,
   registers no job and writes no event**, and the guide-log pass itself writes
   `phd2_pass_complete` only when it had at least one log to report on (section 10.9): a library
   with no guide logs produces no PHD2 row in the Activity feed on any scan. The same pass runs
   out of scan, once per save, when a settings save changed the normalised profile map,
   `general.observer_timezone`, `general.observer_latitude` or `general.observer_longitude`
   (section 7.6, section 12.7); **that out-of-scan pass writes its completion row even when it
   visited no night**, unlike the in-scan silence rule above, because the row is the settings
   save's own completion signal to the reader (section 10.9).

**How the guide-log orphan drop meets the two guards above.** It meets them by using them. A
guide log is discovered only under a walked root, so it has a root by construction: a
`phd2_logs` row belongs to the walked root its `file_path` sits under. **Both guards are
therefore evaluated per walked root, exactly as step 4 evaluates them for frames**, and the
arithmetic is the frame side's own rather than a second copy of it: `OrphanPruner` already
holds `known`, `missing`, the `missing >= max(1, known) * 0.5` test and the override rule, and
the guide-log pass calls that shared code with `phd2_logs` rows in place of `images` rows.

1. **Zero discovery.** When a walked root that holds stored guide-log rows yielded no guide log
   in this run, no `phd2_logs` row under that root is deleted and `phd2_orphan_prune_skipped` is
   written at warning naming the root. This guard is absolute: **the per-run cleanup override
   reaches guard 2 only and never this one**, exactly as guard 1 of step 4 is absolute for
   frames.
2. **The 50 percent safety limit.** Evaluated only for a root guard 1 let through. When that
   root's missing rows reach `max(1, known) * 0.5` and the override is off, nothing under it is
   deleted and `phd2_orphan_prune_limited` is written at warning with both counts and the root.
   When the override is on, those rows are deleted and `phd2_orphan_prune_forced` is written at
   warning. The override is the same per-run argument the Library tab's checkbox sets (PAR-013
   above); it is not a second control.

A root this run did not walk, because the run was scoped by `include_paths` or because its walk
failed, prunes nothing: its guide-log rows are left alone, the same treatment step 4 gives
`images` rows under a root that left the configuration.

**The two sides must agree, which is why this is per root.** With two scan roots and one drive
unplugged, a corpus-wide zero-discovery guard never fires and a corpus-wide 50 percent limit can
pass, so the unplugged drive's guide-log rows would be dropped in the same run in which the
frame-side guards kept that drive's frame rows. A library would then hold frames whose guiding
had been silently deleted underneath them.

**Per-run arguments (PAR-013).** `ScanCoordinator.RunAsync` takes two arguments that are not
settings keys and are not carried from one run to the next (section 5.8.1), carried as one
`ScanRunOptions` record that is itself a trailing optional parameter after the cancellation token,
so every one of the sixty existing call sites in the solution keeps building unchanged:

- The run's scope, all frames or light frames only. `general.include_calibration` is the value
  the Library tab's radio pair starts from (section 12.7); the run uses the argument, so
  choosing light frames only for one run never rewrites the stored default. The argument reaches
  step 2's known set and step 3's calibration decision (section 7.5) and nothing else. A run
  scoped to light frames classifies calibration frames as skipped exactly as a stored `false`
  does, with the same remaining limit step 2 records.
- The orphan cleanup override for step 4, below. It is off on every trigger by default, and only
  a manual run can set it: the watcher, the scheduler, the first-run scan and the CLI always
  pass it off, because an unattended run must not be the thing that decides a storage volume is
  gone.

Orphan pruning has two guards, both from the web application's
`backend/app/services/orphan_cleanup.py`, both evaluated per walked root so one dead share does
not stop a healthy root from being cleaned in the same run:

1. **Zero discovery.** If the walk discovered no file under a root that previously had rows,
   pruning for that root is skipped and a warning is logged (`orphan_prune_skipped`, section
   10.9). An unmounted network share must not silently empty the catalogue. This guard is
   absolute: **the cleanup override reaches guard 2 only and never this one**, so a walked root
   whose whole tree is gone (an unplugged drive, a folder deleted outright) is treated exactly
   like an unreachable share and its rows are never deleted, forced or not; the only event it can
   ever write is `orphan_prune_skipped`. A root that produced nothing at all carries no evidence
   that anything was deleted, and ticking the cleanup checkbox cannot manufacture that evidence.
   Verified on the launched application: deleting an entire scan root and forcing the cleanup
   still leaves every row and repeats `orphan_prune_skipped`, not `orphan_prune_forced`.
2. **The 50 percent safety limit.** Evaluated only for a root guard 1 let through, that is, a root
   the walk discovered at least one file under. Let `known` be the number of catalogued rows under
   the root and `missing` the number of those whose path the walk did not discover. When
   `missing >= max(1, known) * 0.5` and the override is off, nothing under that root is deleted
   and `orphan_prune_limited` is written at warning with both counts. Half a library
   disappearing between two scans is far more often a storage fault than a deliberate deletion.
   When the override is on, those rows are deleted and `orphan_prune_forced` is written at
   warning naming the removed count, the total and the percentage, so a forced pass that emptied
   half the catalogue is in the Activity feed and not only in the run counters. The override
   applies to this guard alone (never to guard 1 above): a partial loss under a root the walk
   still found files under is what the checkbox is for, and a total loss is not.

Both guards, and the deletion either of them permits, touch database rows and nothing else. No
file, folder or image on disk is deleted, moved, renamed or modified by any outcome of step 4,
forced or not (section 2.1: "Missing files on rescan: delete DB rows, never touch disk"). The
web application's counterpart also unlinks each deleted row's thumbnail; that has no counterpart
here, because `images.thumbnail_path` is never written (section 5.2). `OrphanPruner` performs no
filesystem access at all, and `FileSafetyTest` (section 2.1.3) fails the build if that stops
being true.

### 10.4 Progress envelope

Reported by `ScanCoordinator` as an immutable record, matching the web application's
`ProgressEnvelope` in `backend/app/schemas/scan.py` and the fields carried in the
`scan:state` hash:

```
record ScanProgress(
    string Task,        // one of the task vocabulary below
    int Step,
    int TotalSteps,
    double Percent,     // derived, never stored
    string Message)
```

Task vocabulary, closed set, in the order a full scan emits them:

| `Task` | Phase | `TotalSteps` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `discovery` | The directory walk (10.3 step 1) | 0, no fixed total |
| `classify` | Comparing discovered paths against the known set (10.3 step 2) | discovered file count |
| `ingest` | Header read, extraction, resolution, write (10.3 step 3) | new plus changed file count |
| `prune_orphans` | Deleting rows for files no longer on disk (10.3 step 4) | candidate row count |
| `phd2_ingest` | Reading and storing discovered PHD2 guide logs (10.3 step 5) | discovered guide-log count |
| `phd2_correlate` | Filling frame guiding RMS from guide frames (7.6) | imaging nights to visit |
| `dedup` | Duplicate detection (9.7) | distinct unresolved name count |
| `mosaic_detection` | Mosaic detection (7.7), only when the scan completed | 4, the pass's steps; a negative total on the terminal envelope reports a pass that threw |
| `ref_thumbnails` | Reference thumbnail pass (11.4) | targets needing one |
| `prune_activity` | Applying the activity retention window | 0, no fixed total |

`prune_orphans` and `prune_activity` are separate tasks with separate names; an earlier draft
used one `prune` for both, which made a status bar reading "prune 12/400" ambiguous.

`Percent` is always derived at read time as `TotalSteps > 0 ? 100.0 * Step / TotalSteps : 0`.
A phase with no fixed total reports `TotalSteps = 0` and carries its running count in
`Message`. The decisions name the envelope as `{task, step, total, percent, message}`;
`TotalSteps` is that `total`.

The two `phd2_*` tasks are emitted only when `general.phd2_scan_enabled` is true. A pass that
found no guide log still emits `phd2_ingest` once with `TotalSteps` 0, so a reader can tell "the
pass ran and found nothing" from "the pass did not run". A `phd2_correlate` pass that throws
reports one terminal envelope whose `TotalSteps` is negative, which is the signal the registered
job (section 12) reads to end `failed` rather than `succeeded`; a negative total is otherwise
inert, because `Percent` is defined only for `TotalSteps > 0` and every determinate-percent
reader already guards on that same test.

Alongside the envelope, `ScanCoordinator` exposes the counters that feed the completion
summary and `scan_runs`: `discovered`, `newFiles`, `changedFiles`, `completed`, `failed`,
`skippedCalibration`, `removed`, `phd2Found`, `phd2Ingested`, `phd2Failed`.

The three PHD2 counters carry the meanings section 5.13 gives their `scan_runs` columns:
`phd2Found` is every guide log the walk discovered, whether or not the delta skip opened it;
`phd2Ingested` counts the logs this pass parsed and stored, so a rescan that skipped every
unchanged log reports a found count with an ingested count of zero, which is the correct reading
of a rescan that found nothing new; `phd2Failed` counts the logs recorded as `unreadable` or
`failed`. A log recorded as `empty` is neither ingested nor failed. All three are zero when the
key is off.

Delivery to the UI: `ProgressChanged` is raised on the coordinator's thread, throttled to at most 10 updates per second; UI marshaling is the subscriber's job. The status bar binds to it directly. No polling.

### 10.5 Cancellation

One `CancellationTokenSource` per scan run, owned by the coordinator. The token is checked:

- Once per discovered file in the walk loop.
- Once per file before ingest begins.
- Between phases.

Cancellation is cooperative and leaves the database consistent: every file already ingested
stays ingested, orphan pruning is skipped entirely, and the run is recorded with
`state = "cancelled"`. The status bar's cancel button and the CLI's Ctrl+C both trigger it.
Application shutdown cancels and waits up to 5 seconds for the writer to drain.

### 10.6 Concurrency model

| Stage | Concurrency | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Directory walk | 1 task per effective root, at most 4 concurrent | Network shares benefit from overlapping directory reads; more than 4 does not. |
| Header read, metadata extraction, CSV backfill, session date | `Environment.ProcessorCount` clamped to [2, 8] parallel reader tasks | CPU-bound parsing over I/O-bound reads. None of these steps touches the database. |
| Everything database-facing | 1 task, `ScanWriter` | Section 5.1. |
| Thumbnail generation | 2 | Memory-bound; a full-frame decode of a 60-megapixel sensor is large. Enforced in the thumbnail cache, which every render passes through, so the on-demand worker's two pumps and the scan thread's reference pass (section 11.4) share one budget of two rather than each holding their own. |

Structure:

1. The walk feeds a `Channel<FileInfo>`.
2. N reader tasks consume it, parse the file, and produce a `ParsedRecord` (metadata,
   provenance, raw headers, file stat, the resolved `OBJECT` string) into a second
   `Channel<ParsedRecord>` with capacity 256. A reader performs no database access at all,
   not even a read: everything it needs is in the file and in the immutable settings snapshot
   taken at scan start.
3. One `ScanWriter` task consumes that channel and performs, sequentially per record: image
   upsert, target resolution (offline catalog lookup, cache read, online call if needed,
   cache write), target create if the identity is new, catalog membership rows, activity
   events. `SaveChanges` is called once per batch of 200 records, and once at the end.

The capacity-256 bound is the backpressure that stops readers from outrunning the writer and
exhausting memory on a large library.

Resolution living on the writer task is what removes the need for a per-name lock: only one
task ever looks up an identity and then inserts it, so the check-then-insert sequence cannot
interleave with itself. It also means a slow SIMBAD call stalls the writer while readers keep
filling the channel, which is the correct trade for a cache that turns the call into a
once-per-distinct-new-name cost.

The CSV cache is a `ConcurrentDictionary` keyed by CSV file path holding (modification time,
parsed rows), because readers are parallel and frames from one folder land on several of
them. Each CSV is parsed once.

### 10.7 Watcher

`GalactiLog.App.Services.WatcherService`. Enabled by `general.watcher_enabled`.

Known ceiling (Phase 4 ruling): a debounced batch that arrives while a scan is running receives
`AlreadyRunning`; the coordinator's pending flag then schedules a full follow-up scan, not the
targeted batch. No file is lost because the full walk finds it. Upgrade path if it matters: a
pending targeted-path set merged into the follow-up run.

- One `FileSystemWatcher` per scan root, `IncludeSubdirectories = true`,
  `InternalBufferSize = 65536`, watching `NotifyFilters.FileName | LastWrite | Size`.
- Events for `Created`, `Changed`, and `Renamed` are collected into a set of paths.
- Debounce: a `general.watcher_debounce_ms` timer, default 30000, restarts on each event. When it fires, the collected paths are
  passed to `ScanCoordinator` as a targeted ingest, not a full walk. A capture run writes a
  frame every few minutes, so 30 seconds is well inside the gap while still absorbing the
  several events a single file write produces.
- Paths are filtered through the same `ScanFilterConfig` before ingest.
- A file is only ingested once it can be opened for read and its size has been stable across
  two consecutive checks `general.watcher_stability_check_ms` apart, default 2000. This avoids reading a frame N.I.N.A. is still
  writing.
- `Error` events (buffer overflow) are logged and trigger a full scan, because the watcher
  has lost events.
- `FileSystemWatcher` is unreliable on SMB shares, which is exactly why the interval
  scheduler exists.

### 10.8 Scheduler

`GalactiLog.App.Services.ScanScheduler`. Enabled by `general.auto_scan_enabled` (default
true), interval `general.auto_scan_interval_minutes` (default 240). A
`PeriodicTimer` triggers a full scan. The timer resets after any scan finishes, from any
trigger, so a manual scan pushes the next scheduled one out by a full interval. Skipped
while a scan is running.

### 10.9 Activity events emitted

| Category | Event type | Severity | When | Details payload |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `scan` | `scan_started` | info | A scan begins | `{trigger, roots}` |
| `scan` | `scan_complete` | info | A scan finishes normally | `{discovered, new, changed, completed, failed, skipped_calibration, removed, phd2_found, phd2_ingested, phd2_failed, duration_ms}`. The three PHD2 members are present and zero when `general.phd2_scan_enabled` is off. |
| `scan` | `scan_cancelled` | warning | Cancelled | counters so far |
| `scan` | `scan_failed` | error | Unhandled failure | `{error}` |
| `scan` | `file_rejected` | warning | A file failed a rejection rule (section 6), or its header read, metadata extraction or session-date derivation threw during ingest (section 10.3 step 3) | `{path, reason}` |
| `scan` | `orphans_pruned` | info | Rows removed, count above zero | `{count}` |
| `scan` | `orphan_prune_skipped` | warning | A root with catalogued rows discovered no files, so its pruning was skipped (section 10.3 step 4) | `{root, known_rows}` |
| `scan` | `orphan_prune_limited` | warning | Missing rows under a root reached the 50 percent safety limit and the run was not forced, so that root's pruning was skipped (section 10.3) | `{root, missing_rows, known_rows}` |
| `scan` | `orphan_prune_forced` | warning | A forced run deleted rows past the safety limit (section 10.3) | `{root, removed, known_rows, percent_removed, forced}`. `removed` is the walked root's missing-row count, the figure the guard evaluated and the pass intended to delete, not the delete statement's own affected-row count; the two agree for one root and could disagree only if two walked roots overlapped, which the write path already refuses (section 10.3). `scan_runs.removed` and this event's `removed` carry the same figure. |
| `scan` | `phd2_pass_complete` | info | The guide-log pass finishes **having something to report**, that is having found, ingested, failed, skipped as unchanged or removed at least one guide log (section 10.3 step 5) | `{found, ingested, skipped_unchanged, empty, failed, removed, duration_ms}`. **A pass that found no guide log under any walked root and holds no stored `phd2_logs` row writes nothing at all.** With `phd2_scan_enabled` defaulting to true, the alternative is a row in the feed on every scan of every library that has no guide logs, forever: a library with nothing to say about guide logs stays silent. |
| `scan` | `phd2_log_failed` | warning | One guide log could not be read or parsed, one event per file | `{path, parse_status, reason}`. `parse_status` is `unreadable` or `failed` (section 5.15). |
| `scan` | `phd2_timezone_unset` | warning | At least one guiding session that could have met a frame of a night this pass visited resolved to no timezone (section 7.6). **Once per pass**, whatever the mix of nights and profiles | `{profiles, setting}`. `profiles` is the sorted distinct profile names, capped at 50 (the message names the uncapped count beside the capped list, so a reader who sees "63 equipment profiles" beside 50 names knows which figure is which), with a section carrying no profile named `(no equipment profile)`; `setting` is the literal `phd2_profile_map`. **It names only the profiles the pass actually held back**, matched to a visited night by the calendar date of each unzoned session's `started_at_local` plus or minus one day (section 7.6), never every unzoned profile in the corpus: an unconfigured rig that never meets a frame this pass would have written costs the reader nothing, and naming it after every scan is how an Activity feed stops being read. A scan runs the guide-log pass and then the correlation, and each can raise this row on its own scoping rule; the correlation's own copy names only the profiles the guide-log pass did not already name in its own copy, and emits nothing when none remain, so the two never repeat one profile inside the same scan. |
| `scan` | `phd2_timezone_invalid` | warning | A configured zone name, per profile or global, could not be loaded and was ignored. Once per pass | `{zone, scope, profiles}`. `scope` is `profile` or `global`. When more than one zone is broken in the same pass, a broken global (observer) zone is reported ahead of a broken profile zone, because it stands behind every profile that names no zone of its own and is both the larger fact and the one to fix first; `profiles` still lists every profile any broken zone affected, not only the reported zone's. |
| `scan` | `phd2_pixel_scale_missing` | warning | At least one stored guiding session carried no pixel scale, so it can never be correlated to arcseconds (section 7.6, the ASIAIR case). **Once per pass** | `{profiles, session_count}` from the guide-log pass. A scan's correlation can raise this row too, over the profiles the guide-log pass did not already name; its copy carries `{profiles}` alone, because `session_count` is a figure only the pass that just read the logs can give. |
| `scan` | `phd2_orphan_prune_skipped` | warning | A walked root holding stored guide-log rows discovered no guide log, so its rows were kept (section 10.3) | `{root, known_rows}` |
| `scan` | `phd2_orphan_prune_limited` | warning | A walked root's missing guide-log rows reached the 50 percent safety limit and the run was not forced | `{root, missing_rows, known_rows}` |
| `scan` | `phd2_orphan_prune_forced` | warning | A forced run deleted a walked root's guide-log rows past the safety limit | `{root, removed, known_rows, percent_removed, forced}` |
| `scan` | `phd2_correlation_complete` | info | A correlation pass finishes. **Inside a scan**, only a pass that **visited at least one night** writes this row; with no night to visit that pass runs no job and writes nothing, the same silence rule `phd2_pass_complete` follows. **The out-of-scan re-run a settings save dispatches always writes this row when it finishes, whether or not it visited a night**, because `trigger` `settings_change` is the reader's only signal that their saved mapping, zone or site took effect; withholding it on an empty pass would leave a save that changed nothing correlatable looking as if it had not been read at all | `{nights, frames_considered, filled, cleared, below_gate, trigger}`. `trigger` is `scan` or `settings_change`. The out-of-scan re-run fires on a change to the normalised profile map, to `observer_timezone`, or to `observer_latitude` or `observer_longitude`, once per save (section 7.6). |
| `scan` | `phd2_correlation_failed` | error | The correlation, or the session time re-derive that begins it, threw (section 7.6). Written inside a scan parented to `scan_started`, and in the out-of-scan re-run parentless | `{trigger, reason}`. `trigger` is `scan` or `settings_change`; `reason` is the exception's message. |
| `scan` | `phd2_correlation_unattributed` | warning | Guiding sessions on a night were attributed to no rig (section 7.6 rig selection step 3) | `{profiles, nights}` |
| `scan` | `mosaic_detection_complete` | info | A mosaic detection pass finishes, from a scan or from the Mosaics page's Run Detection (section 7.7) | `{trigger, suggestions, relabelled, backfilled}`. `trigger` is `scan` or `manual`. Inside a scan, parented to `scan_started`. |
| `scan` | `mosaic_detection_failed` | error | A mosaic detection pass threw (section 7.7). The scan that hosted it still ends normally | `{trigger, reason}` |
| `user_action` | `mosaic_action_failed` | warning | One item of a bulk Accept, Dismiss or Delete Selected job on the Mosaics page failed (section 12.17), one event per failed item, and the failed read that opens the Create mosaic dialog from the Target detail page (section 12.17), carrying that target's id | `{action, name, reason}`. `action` is `accept`, `dismiss`, `delete` or `create`; `name` is the suggestion's or the mosaic's name, or the target's name for `create`. |
| `enrichment` | `target_created` | info | A new target row is inserted | `{primary_name, catalog_id, source}`. Manual creation (section 9.7) adds `linked_frames` and `closed_candidates`: `linked_frames` is the count of LIGHT frames the retro-link moved onto the new target, and `closed_candidates` is the count of distinct unresolved `OBJECT` names it closed, not a count of `merge_candidates` rows (the member and key names were kept from an earlier design; the value they carry moved with the frame-driven retro-link of section 9.7 step 5). |
| `enrichment` | `target_merged` | info | A merge completes | `{winner, loser, moved_images}` |
| `enrichment` | `target_unmerged` | info | An unmerge completes | `{winner, loser}` |
| `enrichment` | `resolution_failed` | warning | A name resolved to nothing and was negative-cached | `{object_name}` |
| `thumbnail` | `reference_thumbnails` | info | The reference thumbnail pass finishes | `{generated, failed}` |
| `rebuild` | `rebuild_started` / `rebuild_complete` | info | A maintenance action runs | `{action, affected}` |
| `user_action` | `settings_changed` | info | Settings are saved | `{sections}` |
| `user_action` | `nina_send` | info on success, warning on failure | A "Send to NINA" item was chosen on the Target detail page (section 12.16) | `{instance, target_id, ok, rotation}`. `instance` is the instance name, never its URL. `rotation` is `sent`, `failed` or `none`: `none` when the target carries no position angle, `failed` when the coordinates landed and the rotation call did not. `reason` is added on failure and carries the exception's message. |
| `user_action` | `stellarium_send` | info on success, warning on failure | A "Slew Stellarium" item was chosen on the Target detail page (section 12.16) | `{instance, target_id, ok, focus}`. `focus` is `catalog_name`, `full_name` or `coordinates`, naming which of the three routes the slew actually used. `reason` is added on failure. |
| `user_action` | `astrobin_csv_copied` | info | The AstroBin CSV was copied to the clipboard (section 12.16) | `{target_id, nights, rows}`. `nights` is the number of checked nights the rows came from and `rows` the number of data rows, the header excluded. |
| `system` | `app_started` | info | Application start | `{version}` |
| `system` | `activity_pruned` | info | Activity retention pruning removed rows (application start and after every scan) | `{deleted_count, retention_days}` |
| `system` | `data_root_moved` | info | The application data root was relocated or adopted, written after the migration on the start that performed the move (section 17.2) | `{from, to, files_copied, bytes_copied}` |
| `system` | `update_available` | info | Velopack offers a version not offered before | `{version, channel, current_version}` |
| `system` | `update_applied` | info | Velopack is about to apply an update, written before the restart | `{version, channel, previous_version}` |

The three Phase 21 integration types are written by their own caller on a short-lived context,
like `settings_changed` and the maintenance events, because none of them runs inside a scan. None
carries a `parent_id`.

Every sub-event emitted during a scan carries `parent_id` set to the `scan_started` event's
id, so the activity feed can collapse a scan into one expandable entry. `activity_pruned` is
the one deliberate exception: it is housekeeping over the whole table, it also fires at
application start where no scan exists, and parenting it to a scan would make the feed report
the pruning of unrelated older rows as part of that scan.

The `rebuild` category's `action` value is the Maintenance action token of section 12.7:
`rebuild_targets`, `retry_unresolved`, `smart_rebuild`, `catalog_identity_backfill`,
`reference_thumbnails`, `frame_thumbnails`, `prune_activity`, `reset_database`. Every event
type, every action token and every key in every details payload in this table is snake_case, and
a new event added by a later phase follows the same rule.

All scan-time events are written by `ScanWriter` on the writer task, in sequence with the
record that produced them (section 10.6). Events raised outside a scan (`settings_changed`,
`app_started`, the update events, the maintenance events) are written by their own caller on
a short-lived context. There is no separate activity-writing task and no queue.

The `phd2_*` events raised during a scan are parented to that scan's `scan_started` event like
any other sub-event. They are **not** written by `ScanWriter` on the writer task: they are
emitted through the activity repository and parented to the scan's `scan_started` row, exactly
as the frame side's orphan events are, because the guide-log pass and the correlation run after
the writer has finished its record channel and are not sequenced with any record. The same event
types are raised outside a scan by the correlation re-run a settings save dispatches (section
7.6), and there they carry no `parent_id` and are written by their own caller, as
`settings_changed` is. `phd2_correlation_complete` with `trigger` `settings_change` is the event
that tells a reader their saved mapping, zone or site took effect.

**A failed correlation never fails the frame scan.** `phd2_correlation_failed` is the whole of
what a throw costs: the frame ingest of section 10.3 has already committed by the time the pass
runs, the scan finishes in state `complete` and writes `scan_complete` as usual, and the
registered `phd2_correlate` job of section 12 ends with outcome **failed** rather than
succeeded, carrying the same reason as its one-line summary. Exactly one of
`phd2_correlation_complete` and `phd2_correlation_failed` is written per pass that ran to an end,
**with one exception stated once here rather than at each rule above:** an **in-scan** pass with
no night to visit does not run, registers no job and writes nothing at all, which is the silence
a library with no guide logs is entitled to, while the **out-of-scan** re-run always writes
`phd2_correlation_complete` when it finishes, night or no night, because that row is the settings
save's own completion signal and has no other way to reach the reader. `phd2_correlation_failed`
is written on a failure whatever the count of nights and whichever path threw, because a throw is
always worth saying. **A cancelled pass writes neither**: cancellation is not a failure and a
half-visited set of nights is not a completion, so the job ends cancelled and the feed stays
silent about it. A
failure to write any of these events is logged at warning and never fails the scan, because by
then the guiding values are already committed and losing the note about them is not worth
losing the work.

---

## 11. Thumbnails and preview

### 11.1 Debayer

Port of `backend/app/services/thumbnail.py::debayer_superpixel`. Superpixel 2x2 binning: each
2x2 cell yields one red sample, one blue sample, and the mean of its two green samples,
producing a half-resolution `[3, H/2, W/2]` RGB image.

Pattern offsets, from `_BAYER_OFFSETS`, giving the (row, column) of the red sample within
each 2x2 cell:

| `BAYERPAT` | Red offset |
| --- | --- |
| `RGGB` | (0, 0) |
| `GRBG` | (0, 1) |
| `GBRG` | (1, 0) |
| `BGGR` | (1, 1) |

Blue sits at the diagonal opposite, `(1 - rRow, 1 - rCol)`. The two green samples are at the
off-diagonal corners, `(rRow, bCol)` and `(bRow, rCol)`.

Height and width are first truncated down to even values. The pattern is taken from the
`BAYERPAT` header keyword, trimmed and uppercased; a value not in the table means the frame
is treated as mono. For XISF, the `ColorFilterArray` element's `pattern` attribute is used
when `BAYERPAT` is absent.

Reading is done in horizontal strips of 512 rows so the full raw frame and the full
debayered result never coexist in memory. Strip height must be even so each strip starts on
a Bayer phase boundary, which makes strip-wise debayering byte-identical to whole-frame
debayering.

The strip rule applies to the FITS Bayer thumbnail read path and to that path only. Preview
mode debayers the whole frame, matching `generate_preview`, and the XISF path never strips
because `XisfDataBlock` decompresses a whole block before any pixel is read. Both are
deliberate, and both are part of the peak-memory figure in section 11.2.

`XBAYROFF` and `YBAYROFF` are not applied, matching the web application.

### 11.2 Stretch

Port of `backend/app/services/stretch.py`. This is the N.I.N.A. and PixInsight auto-STF
equivalent and must be ported arithmetically exactly; a rewrite that looks equivalent will
produce visibly different thumbnails.

Midtones transfer function:

```
mtf(x, m) = (m - 1) * x / ((2m - 1) * x - m)
```

Normalization to unit range, per channel, before anything else:

```
normalizeToUnit(data):
    dmin = min(data); dmax = max(data)
    if dmax > dmin:  return (data - dmin) / (dmax - dmin)
    else:            return all zeros
```

Per-channel stretch, operating on already-normalized data and returning bytes:

```
stretchChannel(data):                   # data in [0, 1]
    median = median(data)
    mad    = median(abs(data - median))

    midtone = 0.5
    shadows = 0.0

    if mad > 0:
        shadows = median - 2.8 * mad
        if shadows < 0.0:   shadows = 0.0
        if shadows >= 1.0:  shadows = 0.0

        scale = 1.0 - shadows
        if scale <= 0:  scale = 1.0
        medianNorm = clamp((median - shadows) / scale, 1e-6, 1.0 - 1e-6)

        target = 0.25
        denom  = 2.0 * target * medianNorm - target - medianNorm
        if abs(denom) > 1e-10:
            midtone = clamp(medianNorm * (target - 1.0) / denom, 0.001, 0.999)
        else:
            midtone = 0.5

    scale = 1.0 - shadows
    if scale <= 0:  scale = 1.0
    normed = clamp((data - shadows) / scale, 0.0, 1.0)

    if mad == 0:
        return a buffer filled with 128

    return (mtf(normed, midtone) * 255) as byte
```

Two details that are easy to lose and must not be:

- The `shadows >= 1.0` branch resets shadows to 0, it does not clamp to 1.
- The `mad == 0` early return to a flat 128 happens after the shadows and midtone
  computation, not before, and it returns a uniform grey rather than a black frame. A
  perfectly flat frame is a calibration artefact, not a black sky.

Colour data is stretched per channel independently and unlinked, matching
`generate_thumbnail`.

Resampling, from `stretch.resize_array`, applied to linear float data before the stretch,
never after:

1. If the width is already at or below the target, return unchanged.
2. `prefilter = width / targetWidth`, integer division. If it is 2 or more, crop height and
   width down to multiples of `prefilter` and mean-pool by that factor. This band-limits the
   input below the output Nyquist frequency and is what stops the subsequent stretch from
   amplifying aliasing on periodic patterns and noise.
3. If the width is now at or below the target, return.
4. Otherwise resample to exactly the target width, preserving aspect ratio, on float data.
   `SKBitmap.Resize` with `SKSamplingOptions(SKCubicResampler.Mitchell)` on an
   `SKColorType.RgbaF32` surface.

**The resampler is Mitchell cubic, not Lanczos, and this is a deliberate difference from the
web application.** PIL's `LANCZOS` has no SkiaSharp counterpart, and hand-writing a Lanczos
kernel to match PIL's windowing exactly would be a hundred lines of numerics serving a
thumbnail. Mitchell is a well-behaved cubic with mild ringing, applied to data the box
prefilter in step 2 has already band-limited, so the visible difference after the stretch is
below what a viewer can see at thumbnail scale.

Consequence for testing: there is **no** exactness assertion on resampling output. Section
18.1 tests resampling by shape (output dimensions, aspect ratio preserved, non-empty result,
brightness monotonic after stretch), and reserves arithmetic exactness for the MTF stretch
math, which is where a difference actually changes what the user reads off a frame.

Additional binning before resampling, from `thumbnail._read_binned`: for a 2D mono frame,
compute `step = max(1, max(height, width) / (targetWidth * 2))` and mean-pool by `step`
before the resize, leaving roughly twice the target width for the resampler. Block averaging
rather than strided subsampling integrates noise across each bin, giving square root of N
noise reduction per axis.

Pipeline order, from `generate_thumbnail`, and it is not interchangeable:

```
read -> block-bin -> normalize -> flip (FITS only) -> resize (linear) -> stretch -> encode
```

Peak memory. The normalize and the flip precede the resize, so a preview at native resolution
or at 2400 px holds full-resolution `float` buffers for as long as the pipeline runs, whatever
the output width is. For a 100 megapixel three-plane master that is roughly 3 GB of managed
heap, and roughly 6 GB at section 10.6's concurrency of 2, which is enforced for every caller
in the thumbnail cache. There is deliberately no pixel-count gate in v1: the only caps are the
FITS reader's maximum pixel-byte count and the XISF block's declared-size check, and a render
that still exhausts the heap is reported as a skip, not as an exception, so the frame falls
back to a placeholder. Adding a pixel-count gate is a change to this section, not a local
decision in the renderer.

### 11.3 Cache, keys, and formats

Cache root: `general.thumbnail_cache_dir`, defaulting to
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData\thumbnails`. User-configurable in Settings and in the setup
wizard. Changing it does not move existing files; the new location is populated on demand
and the old one is left alone, because the application does not move user-visible files.
Moving the **app data root** does copy the thumbnail cache when the cache sits at its default
location under that root, because the root move carries the database with it and a cache left
behind would be a cache the application no longer reads; the old root is still not deleted
(section 17.2).

Two sizes:

| Kind | Width | Format | Quality | Path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frame thumbnail | `general.thumbnail_width`, default 800 | JPEG | 85 | `frames/<key>.jpg` |
| Preview | `general.preview_resolution`, default 2400; 0 means native resolution | JPEG | 90 | `previews/<key>.jpg` |
| Reference thumbnail | 800 | JPEG | 85 | `reference/<target id>.jpg` |
| Sky view survey image | 1024 pixels square, as hips2fits serves it | JPEG as served | as served | `survey/<target id>/<key>.jpg` |

Cache key, per the decisions ("cached on disk keyed by path+size+mtime"):

```
key = lowercase hex of the first 16 bytes of SHA-256(
          fullPath + "|" + fileSize + "|" + mtimeUnixSeconds + "|" + width)
```

Including size and modification time means a re-saved or replaced frame produces a new key
rather than serving a stale image, and it means the cache never needs invalidation. Including
the width means changing the thumbnail width setting does not require a purge. The web
application's key is `md5(path)[:12]` plus the file stem, which does not react to file
changes; the port deliberately strengthens it.

Eviction: a least-recently-used sweep bounded by `max(general.preview_cache_mb, 100)` MB,
applied to the `previews` directory only, on application start and after each preview
generation. Frame thumbnails and reference thumbnails are not evicted; they are small and
regenerating them during scrolling would be visible. Sky view survey images are outside that
sweep and carry their own cap, 20 files per target folder, stated with the client below.

Least recently used is measured by last use inside the running process. An entry this process
has not touched sorts oldest, whatever its age on disk, so the first sweep after a start evicts
the previous session's files before anything this session has served; `LastWriteTimeUtc` breaks
ties, and the file path breaks a tie in that. The sweep never deletes a file the generation that
triggered it has just written, even when that one file is larger than the whole bound: the
caller is holding that path, and evicting it would hand back a path to a file that no longer
exists. It is counted against the bound regardless.

A reference thumbnail is keyed on the target, not on the frame, so `reference/<target id>.jpg`
is a stable path and an existing file is served as a hit. Regenerating one therefore means
replacing it: the caller asks for a forced render, which deletes the existing file and renders
again. Section 12.7's maintenance action is the only caller that does this.

**Sky view survey images** (Phase 22) are bytes a remote service returned, not thumbnails: no
frame of the reader's is read to produce one, and none is ever a reference thumbnail (section
11.4). They serve the Sky view window of section 12.4 and nothing else. One host, one endpoint:

`GET https://alasky.cds.unistra.fr/hips-image-services/hips2fits`, with exactly these parameters,
numbers formatted in the invariant culture:

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `hips` | The survey id, one of the five of section 12.4, sent as listed (`P/DSS2/red`, not `CDS/P/DSS2/red`) |
| `ra` | Centre right ascension in decimal degrees, 4 decimals, wrapped into 0 to 360 |
| `dec` | Centre declination in decimal degrees, 4 decimals, clamped to -90 and 90 |
| `fov` | The field in degrees, 4 decimals |
| `width` | `1024` |
| `height` | `1024` |
| `projection` | `TAN` |
| `format` | `jpg` |

No other parameter is sent: `coordsys` stays `icrs`, and `stretch`, `min_cut`, `max_cut` and
`cmap` stay at the service defaults. The CDS mirror `alaskybis.cds.unistra.fr` is not used. **The
DSS cutout is this client at `P/DSS2/red` and the target's default field**: there is no NASA
SkyView client and no second cache.

**The field rule**, one function for the default view and for every zoom:
`field = size_major * 1.5 / 60`, in degrees from the target's angular major axis in arcminutes,
clamped to 0.1 and 5.0, and `0.5` when `size_major` is null. A zoom multiplies or divides the
field by 1.5 and clamps it to the same 0.1 and 5.0.

**The cache.** An image is stored at `survey/<target id>/<key>.jpg` under the cache root, written
through `AppWriter` (section 2.1.1), where `key` is the lowercase hex of the first 16 bytes of
SHA-256(`hips + "|" + ra + "|" + dec + "|" + fov + "|" + width`), the four numbers as the request
formats them. One file per distinct survey, centre and field; a request whose key names an
existing file is served as a hit with no network call. After each write, when the target's folder
holds more than 20 files, the oldest by `LastWriteTimeUtc`, path breaking a tie, are deleted until
20 remain, never the file just written. The folder travels with the cache root as the rest of it
does (section 17.2); a merged-away target's folder is left in place and stays within its cap. A
refused cache write (the path resolves outside the cache root) is logged at Warning and the image
is still returned to the caller with nothing written; the target's own folder is never involved
in that refusal, only a path that failed to resolve under it.

**One fetch per view.** A view is one survey, centre and field. At most one request is in flight
for the window; starting a new view cancels the one in flight. A response that finished before
the cancel arrived is still a valid answer and is cached like any other, on disk under its own
key; the window itself has already moved on and does not draw it, and only a request actually
cancelled before it completed writes no file. A fetch is a registered job (section 12) of kind
`survey_image_fetch`, title "Sky view image", with a cancel delegate; a cache hit registers
nothing. The call uses the application's own `HttpClient` with a 15 second timeout. The web's
SkyView call allows 30 seconds because it runs in a worker with no reader in front of it; this
fetch has a window open in front of the reader, and 15 seconds is the bound every other outbound
call here uses. A failed, refused or timed-out fetch, a non-200 status, or a body whose content
type is not `image/jpeg`, writes no file and leaves no partial one, and the window shows its
error sentence. The switch of section 5.8.1 is read before every fetch, and a fetch is never
started while it is false.

The thumbnail cache directory is app data, so deleting files inside it is permitted by
section 2.1. Nothing outside it is ever deleted.

### 11.4 Generation timing

- **Frame thumbnails** are generated on demand, never during the header pass. A frame grid
  or a preview opening requests them; the request is queued to a bounded worker with the
  most recently requested item served first, so scrolling does not queue thousands of stale
  requests. Missing thumbnails render a placeholder that is replaced when generation
  completes. There are two on-demand requesters: the preview modal (section 11.5) and, from
  Phase 19A, the mosaic arranger (section 12.17), which asks for each panel's best frame below.
  There is no frame grid yet, and neither the dashboard nor the target detail page asks for one.
- **Reference thumbnails**, one per target, are generated in the background after the header
  pass, matching the decisions. The source frame is the target's most recent LIGHT frame
  that has a capture date and is not rejected for pixel reading. "Not rejected for pixel
  reading" is decided by attempting the render: a frame whose pixels do not decode produces no
  thumbnail, and the pass walks at most three of the target's frames, newest first, before it
  gives up and leaves the path null for the next run to retry. The pass processes targets
  that have no `reference_thumbnail_path`, or all targets when forced by the maintenance
  action; a forced run re-offers every target and asks for a forced render, which is what
  replaces the existing file rather than serving it as a hit (section 11.3). It is cancellable
  and commits every 10 targets so an interrupted run keeps what it produced.

**Best frame per panel** (Phase 19A, ruling R14). `Core/Mosaics/FrameScore.cs` scores a pool of
frames with the web's `score_frames` rule (`backend/app/services/mosaic_composite.py`), ported
exactly. Five metrics carry weights:

| Metric | Column | Weight | Better |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Detected stars | `detected_stars` | 0.35 | Higher |
| Median HFR | `median_hfr` | 0.30 | Lower |
| Eccentricity | `eccentricity` | 0.15 | Lower |
| Guiding RMS | `guiding_rms_arcsec` | 0.12 | Lower |
| FWHM | `fwhm` | 0.08 | Lower |

Each metric is min-max normalised within the pool over the values that are present and above
zero: a value v scores (v - min) / span for a higher-is-better metric and 1 minus that for a
lower-is-better one, the span being max minus min, or 1 when every such value is equal, so equal
values score 0 on detected stars and 1 on the other four, as on the web. A metric with fewer than
two such values scores 0.5 for every frame of the pool, and a frame whose value is null or not
above zero scores 0.5 on that metric. A frame's score is the weighted sum, from 0 to 1. A pool of
one frame scores 1.0 without normalising.

`Data/Queries/PanelFrameQuery.cs` has two reads. `PanelFrameQuery.ForMosaic(mosaicId)` returns,
in one read, the mosaic's available filters, its default filter and the best frame per panel per
filter. It builds one pool per panel per filter: the LIGHT frames the membership join of section
5.24 reaches for the panel whose canonical filter (section 5.8.4) is that filter. It returns the pool's top frame, ties going to the most recent `capture_date`, a null
date last, then to the ordinally first `file_path`, so the choice is stable across reads; a panel
with no frame in the filter has no best frame. The query also returns the mosaic's **available
filters**, the canonical filters of every panel's frames ordered by summed `exposure_time`
descending, ties by name, ordinal and case insensitive, frames with no filter excluded.
`PanelFrameQuery.ForSuggestionEntry(target, label, nights)` serves the suggestion preview of
section 12.17: one pool of the target's LIGHT frames on those nights whose stored `panel_label`
equals the label, compared case insensitively, over every filter, scored and tie-broken as above,
returning the top frame.

**The default filter** follows the web's `find_default_filter`. Each panel, in `sort_order`, is
scored on its own pool of every frame the join reaches for it in any available filter, and its
top frame is taken; the default filter is the filter of the best-scoring of those top frames, the
first panel in `sort_order` winning a tie. A panel with no frame takes no part. When no panel
yields a top frame the default is the first available filter, the most integrated (the web's
fallback); with no available filter there is no default. Section 12.17 ("The filter selector and the
thumbnails") states how the arranger uses all three.

Settled divergence from the web application: `reference_thumbnail_path` there holds a DSS
survey image fetched from NASA SkyView
(`worker/tasks_thumbnails.generate_reference_thumbnails`, "Fetch DSS reference thumbnails").
**No survey image is ever the reference thumbnail of this port**, and the Sky view window's images
(sections 11.3 and 12.4) are never read by this pass or written into `reference_thumbnail_path`.
The reference thumbnail is generated from the target's own most recent LIGHT frame, through the
same debayer, stretch, and resample pipeline as any other thumbnail. A target whose frames all
fail pixel reading has no reference thumbnail and renders a placeholder. Downloading survey
imagery for reference thumbnails is a non-goal
(section 19.2).

### 11.5 Preview modal

Port of `FilePreviewModal` and `backend/app/api/preview.py`.

| Interaction | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Open | Renders at `general.preview_resolution`, or native resolution when that is 0. Shows a spinner while generating. |
| Zoom | Mouse wheel, centred on the pointer. Range 0.1x to 8x fit. Below fit the image is centred and cannot be panned, because nothing lies outside the viewport to reach; fit is restored by double-click or the `0` key. |
| Pan | Left-button drag while zoomed. |
| Fit | Double-click, or the `0` key, resets to fit. |
| Next and previous frame | Right and left arrow keys, Down and Up as their aliases (P13 R10), and on-screen buttons.
