Navigation is within the frame list the modal was opened from, which is the current session in target detail. Navigation clamps at both ends: the first frame's previous is the first frame and the last frame's next is the last frame. There is no wrap-around. |
| Header panel | Toggled with `H`. Shows raw headers and, for each stored metric, its provenance string (section 7.3). |
| Reveal in Explorer | Button and `Ctrl+E`. Runs `explorer.exe /select,"<path>"`. |
| Open with default application | Button and `Ctrl+O`. `Process.Start` with `UseShellExecute = true`. |
| Copy path | `Ctrl+Shift+C`. |
| Metadata strip | A row of `Border.tag` badges under the frame's name line, rebuilt on every navigation step (PAR-011). Described below. |
| Render full preview on navigation | A checkbox beside the strip, bound to `general.preview_render_on_navigate` (section 5.8.1). Described below. |
| Close | `Escape`. |

The window focuses its image host, the `Viewport` border, on open, so the arrow keys and their
aliases fire at once rather than only after a Previous or Next button has been clicked (P13
R10, observed on the launched application: the headless test harness routes an unfocused key
press to the window regardless, so this mechanism is proven there, not reproduced). Left and
Right are window `KeyBinding`s. Up and Down are handled in code-behind behind the same guard
that keeps the header filter box usable: a window `KeyBinding` fires before the focused
control's own handler and without consulting `Handled`, and Up and Down are also a text box's
caret keys, so they are read in `OnKeyDown` rather than bound in markup. Left and Right still
fire while the header filter box has focus, a pre-existing limit R10 did not ask to fix.

**The metadata strip** (PAR-011) answers "what am I looking at" without opening the header panel.
It is one wrapping row of `Border.tag` badges under the path, each badge a label and a value, in
this fixed order: filter, exposure, HFR, eccentricity, FWHM, detected stars, guiding RMS. A badge
whose value is null is not drawn, so a frame with no guiding leaves no empty badge. The strip is
rebuilt on every navigation step, because it describes the frame on screen and not the frame the
modal opened at. It sits under the frame's name line: the modal's header shows the file name, not
the path, and the path is on the copy action and the reveal action rather than on the face.

The graded metrics carry the band ink section 12.4 defines. The modal does not grade anything
itself: the frame rows it was opened from already carry a band and a deviation sentence per cell,
and `PreviewFrameViewModel` is handed both. A badge in the watch or reject band additionally
renders its value in `metric-worst` and carries the same deviation sentence on its tooltip that
the frame table's cell carries, so the mark and its explanation are the same two facts in both
places. Where both marks land on one badge the band ink is what draws, because both styles are
application level and the band block is declared after `TextBlock.worse`; on a frame table cell
the opposite holds and the flag's `metric-worst` wins, because that view's own style host is
applied last (section 12.4's precedence sentence). The two orderings are deliberate and the
difference is not observable on the reject band, where `ColorMetricWorst` and `ColorErrorValue`
are the same colour in every theme.

A frame opened from a surface that has no grading, or a frame the grading left ungraded, shows the
value with no band and no tooltip rather than a neutral claim. In this port that surface is a
frame table row whose grading is null. A caller holding only an image id gets no strip at all
rather than an empty one, because it holds none of the formatted values the badges are made of,
so an absent strip there is the contract and not a defect. There is no verdict badge: the web's
verdict comes from its stacking-export gates, which this port does not ship.

**Render full preview on navigation** is a checkbox in the modal's own chrome, bound to
`general.preview_render_on_navigate`. On, the default, every step renders a fresh preview at
`general.preview_resolution` through the same path the modal's own open uses, one render per step,
each cancelled if the user steps again before it finishes. Off, a navigation step shows the cached
thumbnail for the new frame, which is what makes stepping through a few hundred frames usable.
Ticking the box renders the current frame at once rather than waiting for the next step. The
setting is read on each step rather than captured at open, so toggling it takes effect on the next
step without reopening. It changes no other behaviour: the zoom range, the fit gesture and the
cache in section 11.3 are unaffected.

Phase 8's ruling Q18 said both preview slots render on every navigation. That ruling is superseded
for the navigation case by this checkbox, which is what makes the thumbnail-per-step behaviour
reachable at all, and it is unchanged for the open case, where the modal always renders. The
default keeps Q18's shipped behaviour for a profile that never touches the box, so a reader
finding both rulings takes this one.

The preview is always autostretched. There are no manual stretch controls in v1.

---

## 12. Screens

**Terms:** a rig is the (telescope, camera) pair after equipment alias mapping (section
5.8.4). A rig-session is one (rig, target, session_date) group. Sections 12.4 and 12.5
both use this definition.

Shell: a single `MainWindow` with a left navigation rail (Dashboard, Mosaics, Statistics,
Analysis, Activity, Diagnostics, Settings; Mosaics from Phase 18, ruling R3), a content region, and a persistent status bar. The status bar shows
scan state, the progress envelope's message and percent, a cancel button while a scan runs,
and the update indicator.

`MainWindow` has a minimum size of 1280 by 720 (Phase 23 stage 1, spec C7 as reversed
2026-09-30), which supersedes the 1024 by 700 floor of Phase 14C, UI layout ruling 3. The
Dashboard filter panel needs no overlay drawer state because its 48 pixel collapsed strip is the
narrow answer at any width, and the window refuses to shrink past the floor. Every scrollbar in the
application, on every page, is the platform `ScrollBar` restyled to 8 pixels wide in the theme's
own inks (section 14); the platform theme itself is kept, so the bar collapses to a hairline at
rest and expands to the full 8 pixels under the pointer, exactly as it does outside this
application. It overlays its scroller's trailing edge and takes no layout space of its own, which
is the platform `ScrollViewer` theme's own behaviour and not something this application adds, so
no scroller's content is measured narrower for a bar that may or may not be drawn. A control
placed at a scroller's trailing edge keeps its own 8 pixels clear of the overlaid bar where that
matters.

**The job monitor and the job registry (PAR-015, ruling D1).** The status bar also carries a
running-job count and a flyout behind it. Every long-running action in the application registers
with one `JobRegistry` in `GalactiLog.App.Services`, and the registry is the only thing the
status bar reads for this. The guide-log pass of section 10.3 step 5 and the PHD2 correlation
re-run a settings save dispatches (section 12.7) are registered jobs like every other long
action (Phase 15A ruling F5): they are the tenth and eleventh members of the census test that
pins registration, and each is proven there behaviourally rather than by a declared list. Like
every other job they can end in any of the three outcomes: a correlation that throws ends
**failed** with the reason as its summary and does not fail the scan that hosted it, and a
cancelled one ends cancelled (section 10.9).

- A job registers with a stable snake_case kind token, a display title, and a cancel delegate or
  null when it cannot be cancelled. While it runs it reports a progress message and an optional
  percent; when it ends it reports an outcome, one of succeeded, failed or cancelled, with a
  one-line summary.
- The status bar shows the number of running jobs. The monitor button itself is offered whenever
  a job is running or the recent list holds a finished one; only the running-count text hides when
  that count is zero, because a button that hid the moment the last job finished would make the
  recent list it opens unreachable at the one instant a reader most wants it (coordinator ruling,
  Task 2 review escalation 1: the approved text read "shows nothing when that number is zero" and
  the user is told of the correction). The existing scan state line, its percent and its cancel
  button are unchanged: the scan is a registered job like any other, and `ScanStatusService` stays
  the scan's own surface, so the registry adds a second reader rather than a second source of
  truth.
- The flyout lists the running jobs first, each with its title, its progress message, its
  percent when it has one and its cancel button when it has one. Below them is the recent list:
  the most recently finished jobs with their outcome and summary kept after completion, and, when
  the job reported one, the last progress message it sent before finishing, newest first, capped
  at 10 entries. A finished entry stays until an eleventh newer one pushes it out. Nothing clears
  it on a timer, because an outcome nobody has looked at yet is the reason the list exists. Each
  section's own heading ("Running", "Recent") is shown only while that section's own list is
  non-empty, so the first flyout of a session, before anything has finished, carries no heading
  with nothing under it.
- Two or more jobs may run at once and are listed separately, each with its own progress. The
  registry serializes nothing and refuses nothing: an action that must not run beside another
  (a scan against the unresolved retry, section 9.7) refuses in its own service, where that rule
  already lives.
- The registry holds no database handle, writes no activity event and owns no thread. An action
  that wants an activity event emits its own (section 10.9); registering is how it becomes
  visible, not what it does.

Registration is a census rule of this specification, not a convention each action remembers: a
test enumerates every action that can run longer than a second without blocking the window and
asserts each one registers. In this phase that set is nine members: the scan and the eight
Maintenance actions of section 12.7, two of which are the reference thumbnail pass and the frame
thumbnail regeneration (they are not a tenth and eleventh member; naming them twice was a spec
contradiction the brief-writer recorded and the coordinator ruled at dispatch). Later phases add
their passes to the same registry and to the same census rather than growing a second status
surface. The spine is built here, at the second occurrence of the pattern, rather than at the
sixth. Phase 18 adds the four mosaic kinds (`mosaic_detection`, `mosaic_accept`, `mosaic_dismiss`
and `mosaic_delete`, section 12.17), which takes the set `JobRegistryCensusTest` declares to
nineteen members.

Target detail (section 12.4) is a screen that is not a rail destination, and from Phase 18 the
mosaic detail page is the second. It is a single
nullable overlay on the shell: the content region shows the open detail page when there is
one and the selected rail destination otherwise. The page's Back affordance closes it, and
clicking any rail entry closes it too, including the entry that is already selected, because
clicking a destination is a request to see that destination. At most one detail page is open,
and opening a second target closes the first. There is no navigation stack: a maximum depth
of one does not need one. From Phase 18 the overlay holds either a Target detail page or a mosaic
detail page (section 12.17), under the same rules: one detail page at a time, of either kind, and
opening a target from a mosaic page closes the mosaic page.

Every screen names the query it needs. Queries live in `GalactiLog.Data.Queries` and return
read models, never entities.

### 12.1 Setup wizard

Shown when `general.setup_complete` is false. Mirrors
`frontend/src/components/setup/SetupWizard.tsx`, which has steps
`["Environment", "Location", "Scan options", "First scan"]`. The port drops the Environment
step, which validates the container's mounted path, and adds a thumbnail location step the
decisions require.

| Step | Elements | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Scan folders | List of chosen folders with a remove button each. A folder picker button. A live count of supported files found in the chosen folders, computed by a shallow probe, not a full walk: the probe descends at most three directory levels below the chosen folder and stops counting at 1000, where it renders "1000 or more". The label reads "~N supported files found in M folders (estimate)." rather than a bare count, and the per-folder row reads "~N supported files", because a shallow probe undercounts a folder that nests its support files more than three levels down (fixer-list item 40: 254 reported against 570 on a deep real library), and the step must not read as a promise the first real scan then contradicts. The ceiling path takes the tilde too, so it reads "~1000 or more", which states the estimate twice rather than inventing a second phrasing. | Add folder, remove folder. Next is disabled until at least one folder is chosen. |
| 2. Storage locations | Data location path box, a folder picker, and the note that a change is applied the next time GalactiLog starts and deletes nothing from the current location. Below it, the thumbnail cache path box defaulting to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData\thumbnails`, a folder picker, and a free-space readout for the chosen volume. | Change either location. |
| 3. Observer location | Latitude and longitude numeric boxes with range validation (-90 to 90, -180 to 180), an IANA timezone combo box defaulting to the system zone, and an "imaging night grouping" checkbox defaulting to checked. Explanatory text stating that without a longitude, sessions group on UTC midnight. Each timezone entry reads its GMT offset first and a display name second, for example "GMT-08:00 Pacific Time (US & Canada)" or "GMT+05:30 Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai, New Delhi" (the platform's own zone names, provisional pending the user), the offset being the zone's standard offset so the list does not reorder when daylight saving starts, and the list runs negative offsets, then GMT, then positive offsets (Phase 14C, user ruling U4). | Save. |
| 4. Scan options | Auto-scan interval combo box with the same presets the web wizard uses: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 hours, default 4 hours. Watcher on/off checkbox, default on. Include calibration frames checkbox, default off. | Save. |
| 5. First scan | Progress envelope display, live counters, and a cancel button. On completion, a summary and a Finish button. | Run scan, cancel, finish. |

Finishing writes `setup_complete = true` and navigates to the Dashboard. Each step persists
its own settings before advancing, so a failure keeps the user on the step rather than
losing input. The wizard is also reachable from Settings as "Run setup again".

On a first run only, finishing also seeds five default folder-exclude rules: substring rules over
`masters`, `WBPP`, `calibrated`, `WORK_AREA` and `PixInsight`, each with the id
`setup-exclude-<name>` carrying the name verbatim, so they are identifiable and removable in the
Library tab's rule list. A re-run through "Run setup again" seeds nothing: the user may have tuned
the rules since, and a re-run exists to correct one field, not to restore defaults.

**The stepper is the shared wizard spine** (`ViewModels/Wizard/WizardStepViewModel.cs`,
`ViewModels/Wizard/WizardViewModel.cs`, `Controls/WizardFrame.axaml`). A step declares a title, a
help topic id, whether it can advance, an on-entered hook and a before-advance gate. The shell owns
the step order, the "Step n of m" header, the progress rail, Back and Next, a busy flag, a committed
flag after which Back and Next refuse, and an advancing hook, which this wizard uses to persist each
step before it moves on. The host window fills the frame's help slot with its own help glyph and
its footer slot with its own buttons, here Skip and Finish. The stacking export wizard (section
12.13) is the spine's second consumer.

### 12.2 Dashboard

Mirrors `frontend/src/pages/DashboardPage.tsx` with `Sidebar`, `TargetFeed`, `TargetTable`,
and `TargetRow`.

Layout: a collapsible left filter panel and a target list. The panel has two states (Phase
14C, UI layout ruling 4). Expanded, it is a column between 220 and 480 pixels wide, default
300, holding the summary strip and the seven collapsible sections below, plus the eighth,
"Custom" (section 12.15), which is drawn only while the library holds at least one custom
column; a `GridSplitter`
between the panel and the list drags a proxy and commits the width to
`display.dashboard.filter_panel_width` on release only, clamped 220 to 480 on write and again
on read, so the target list's shared-size spine (below) is not re-measured on every drag tick
(ruling E1). The panel's rendered width is bounded by what the list needs: the effective maximum
is the smaller of 480 and the page's width less the target list's own minimum, never below the
220 floor, and where even 220 would leave the list short the panel renders as its collapsed
strip; the bound is layout only and writes neither key, so widening the window gives the stored
width and state back. The bound governs what the application decides by itself, on load and on
resize, and an explicit gesture in the current window always wins: pressing the chevron or
clicking a strip label there opens the panel at its 220 floor, with the target list clipped at
its trailing edge as it was before the bound, a transient view state that is never persisted,
that a collapse or any change of window width clears, and during which a splitter drag is
bounded to that same 220 and commits no width. Collapsed,
it is a 48 pixel strip of one short label per filter section, sharing
the item template of the Target detail Nights ledger's own collapsed strip (section 12.4, P13
ruling R7, `DESIGN.md` section 6 "The collapsed vertical strip"): a chevron at the top reopens
the panel, and clicking a section's label expands the panel with that section already open,
the gesture the ledger strip's own dates already give a night. `display.dashboard.filter_panel_expanded`
and `filter_panel_width` (section 5.8.2) persist which state the panel is in and the committed
width, read at start-up per profile. This is a different persistence tier from the filter
values: every filter value persists for the running session only and is restored on return,
matching the web application's `sessionStorage` behavior (`DashboardPage.tsx`), while the
panel's own width and state persist across restarts, matching the web's separate
`localStorage` mechanism for the same two values (`components/sidebarLayout.ts`).

**Summary strip**, above the filter sections: Integration (formatted hours), Groups, Frames,
and a "filtered" marker when any filter is active. The Groups figure counts unresolved
`obj:` groups alongside resolved targets and is deliberately different from the Statistics
page's "resolved targets" count; both labels must stay distinct.

**Filter sections**, each collapsible, each showing an active marker when it holds a value:

| Section | Elements |
| --- | --- |
| Search | Text box with fuzzy, alias-aware matching. Results dropdown showing primary name, object type, and the matched alias. Selecting a result pins `target_id`. Unresolved `OBJECT` strings appear with their frame count and select as `obj:<name>`. |
| Object Type | Toggle pills, one per category from section 9.8: the nine SIMBAD-derived categories, the five solar system categories, `Other`, and `Unresolved`. Multi-select. |
| Date Range | Start and end date pickers over `session_date`, plus quick presets. |
| Filters | Toggle pills, one per canonical optical filter discovered in the library, each tinted with its configured colour. Multi-select. |
| Equipment | Camera combo box and telescope combo box, both listing canonical names. |
| Metrics Quality | Min and max numeric boxes per metric, grouped, labelled with the plain metric name (`HFR`, not `Avg HFR`). Groups, keys, and steps from `MetricFilters.tsx`: Quality (`hfr` step 0.1, `fwhm` step 0.1, `eccentricity` step 0.01, `stars` step 1 integer), Guiding (`guiding_rms` step 0.01), ADU (`adu_mean` step 1 integer), Focuser (`focuser_temp` step 0.1), Weather (`ambient_temp` step 0.1, `humidity` step 1 integer), Mount (`airmass` step 0.01). `fwhm` maps to the `fwhm` column, never `median_fwhm` (section 7.1.1). Semantics in 12.2.1. Inputs are debounced. |
| FITS Header Query | Rows of (key, operator, value). Key is a combo box populated from the distinct header keys present in the library. Operators: `=`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `contains`. Each existing row shows as `key op value` with a remove button. Enter in the value box adds the row. |
| Custom | One control per custom column (section 12.15), grouped by scope under a "Target", "Night" and "Rig" caption, each group in the column's own display order. A check-box column gives an Any, Yes, No segment; a text column a "Contains" box; a dropdown column a combo box whose first entry is "Any". The whole section is absent while the library holds no custom column. Semantics and the truth table in 12.15. |

A "Reset Filters" button clears everything.

**Target list columns**, from `TargetRow.tsx`: Name (with the common name), Designation
(monospace `catalog_id`), Palette (filter badges), Integration (right aligned), Equipment,
Last Session (right aligned), and a Sessions expander at the row's trailing end (Phase 14C,
user ruling U3). Clicking a row opens Target detail.
Column visibility is user-configurable and persists in `display.columns.dashboard`
(section 5.8.2) as the ordered list of visible column keys: `name`, `designation`, `palette`,
`integration`, `equipment`, `last_session`, and, after them, the `custom_`-prefixed slug of each
target-scope custom column the reader has switched on (sections 5.8.2 and 12.15). A custom column
is drawn after `last_session` and before the sessions expander, in the column's own display
order, and is off until its slug is added to that list; the column picker lists custom columns
under a "Custom" heading below the built-in ones, the way `ColumnPicker.tsx` does. A custom column
is also the first thing dropped when the row does not fit the width the list has, before the
Equipment column steps aside and without a built-in column or the Expand button being pushed out
(section 12.15). Sorting by name, integration, frames, sessions,
last session, or equipment, ascending or descending. Paged; the pager and its page-size select
are described below.

**Row shape (Phase 14C, UI layout ruling 6; amended Phase 14C, user ruling U3).** The list is
flat, rule-separated rows on one `Grid.IsSharedSizeScope` shared-size spine (`DESIGN.md`
section 6, "The aligned table"), the same idiom the Nights ledger and the session pane's own
tables already use: each column's `SharedSizeGroup` sets that column's width from its widest
cell, header included, and the per-row `Border` card and the seven fixed `TargetColumn*Width`
resources of the current build are retired. A row is carried by `Border.rule` (one bottom
edge, never doubled between two rows) rather than a bordered, padded, radiused card; the
header row carries the same `Border.rule` under it; the sessions expander opens inside the
row's own rule pair, under the row's cells and above its bottom edge, so an expanded row's
sessions read as part of the row rather than as a separate block. The expander block carries
no border of its own: the current build's 2 pixel left edge is retired, and indentation plus
the row's rule pair carry the containment (`DESIGN.md` section 8, nested bordered
containers). This closes the sixth two-worlds gap `DESIGN.md` section 4 named at the Phase 14B
close: the Dashboard's rows were the one page whose card chrome the web itself had already
left behind (layout assessment escalation 4).

**Row height and gutters (Phase 14C, user ruling U3).** A row is one line high. Figures: row
34 pixels, the Nights ledger's own night-row height; header row 30, the base control height
`Button.header-cell` already carries in the frame table; every rule 1 pixel in
`ColorBorderDefault`; cell gutter 8 left and 8 right on the header cell and on the row cell
alike (12 and 12 until the second fix pass), so adjacent columns sit 16 apart and a header label
starts at the same x as its own cells. The gutter is carried inside the cell, as padding rather
than as a margin, so a cap means the same number on a header cell and on a row cell; as a margin
it sat outside the cap and every capped row cell measured 16 wider than its header. No cell declares a `Width`.
Every column declares a `MaxWidth` on its cell, header cell and row cell alike, with
`TextTrimming="CharacterEllipsis"` on the text it carries, so one long value cannot set a
column's width for the whole page; the cap sits on the cell and not on the `ColumnDefinition`,
because a maximum on a column in a shared size group is reported by `ActualWidth` and then
ignored by the arrange, which drew a capped header cell 26 pixels past its own column (Phase 14C
Task 3 fix pass). A `MaxWidth` is not a fixed width and is the one size attribute the retirement
above leaves in place. Palette is the one column with no cap, for the reason its own paragraph
gives.

The list does not scroll sideways: its `ScrollViewer` disables the horizontal scroller rather
than hiding it, because a scroller that can scroll sideways measures its content at infinite
width and nothing inside it would ever give way. A row wider than the viewport is therefore
clipped at the viewport's trailing edge rather than carried past it, and the header row, which
sits outside the scroller, cannot drift out of line with the rows under a horizontal scroll that
no longer exists.

**Column order and alignment (Phase 14C, user ruling U3).** From `TargetTable.tsx`, in the
order `display.columns.dashboard` already defaults to: Name left, Designation left in
`TextBlock.mono`, Palette left, Integration right, Equipment left, Last Session right, then
the sessions control at the row's trailing end. The two right-aligned columns take
`Button.header-cell numeric` for their header cells and the rest take `Button.header-cell`, so
a header label is aligned exactly as its column's cells are. Header labels are sentence case
at weight SemiBold in the secondary ink, not the web's uppercase tracked tertiary, which
`DESIGN.md` section 8 refuses; the sort direction marker stays the one permitted text run.
Hiding a column removes its gutter with it: the gutter is carried on the cell, not as grid
column spacing, so a hidden column collapses to zero width in the header and in every row
together, and it leaves its shared size group at the same time, because a group in Avalonia only
ever grows and would otherwise keep reserving the width it last measured.

The header grid and every row grid declare one column set, the same seven definitions in the
same order: Name, the five remaining data columns, and the sessions column. Name is the one star
column and carries no `SharedSizeGroup`, with a floor of 120: it takes the remainder at a wide
window, as the web application's own name column does, and trims with an ellipsis down to its
floor. It still aligns with its cells because every row is drawn at the same width and every
other column is shared. A star column in Avalonia does not shrink below its own cell's desired
width, and a header cell holding the word "Name" desires far less than a row cell holding a
target name, so both cells are bounded by one width the view computes from the caps below; that
removes the flooring rather than compensating for it. Both grids carry the same trailing inset,
declared once, so the overlay scrollbar thumb cannot draw over the Expand button or the gear.

The header is drawn at a row's own width, not at a row's width less the page controls: the help
glyph and the column gear are drawn right aligned inside the header's own empty sessions cell
rather than in grid columns of their own, because a header measured narrower than a row puts
every column after the star out of line with its cells.

**Equipment leaves the row when it does not fit (Phase 14C, second fix pass, provisional pending
the user).** Below the width at which every shown column fits with Name at its floor, the
Equipment header cell and row cells collapse and leave their shared size group, exactly as a
user-hidden column does, and Designation, Integration and Last Session take a tighter cap. Above
it Equipment returns and every header label is whole with its sort mark. Below it a header label
may trim ("Last Ses..."): at the roughly 720 pixels the shipped 1280 by 800 window gives the
list, the six header labels with a sort mark need about 400 where the tighter caps leave 386, and
that trim is the accepted trade for keeping the Expand button on screen. The web application's
table has no equipment column at all, which is what makes it the one to give up; the alternative
is the sessions control off screen at the window the application ships in. It is a layout
suppression and nothing else: nothing is written to `display.columns.dashboard`, the column stays
shown in the picker with its box ticked, and a user who has hidden Equipment is unaffected
because the two gates are combined, and the tighter cap follows the width rule alone so unticking
Equipment in the picker never trims the other columns. The fit width is derived rather than
chosen, the way the session pane's breakpoint is derived from its tables' minimums: it is the sum
of the declared caps of the columns the user is showing, plus the sessions control and the
trailing inset, which is 1128 for the six default columns and falls as columns are hidden, so
hiding two columns brings Equipment back rather than leaving it suppressed under a figure
computed over columns that are not drawn. Every cap the sum is built from is applied by the
markup from that one declaration, and a case reads them back out of the markup and fails when one
moves without the sum.

**The Name cell (Phase 14C, user ruling U3).** One line: the name in the primary ink at weight
SemiBold, and the common name after it on the same baseline in the secondary ink, the common
name trimming first when the column is narrow. It is not a stacked subtitle, and the name
shares its baseline with the Designation cell beside it. The common name is drawn only when the
primary name does not already carry it, compared ordinally and case insensitively over trimmed
text, and a comma separated common name is matched on its first entry, so a row reads
"NGC 1909 - the Witch Head Nebula" rather than that name with "the Witch Head Nebula" printed
again beside it.

**The mosaic link (Phase 18, ruling R19).** A row whose target has at least one `included` row in
some panel of some mosaic (section 5.24) carries a mosaic link in its Name cell; a target with
`available` rows only carries none, because Add nights from any target (section 12.17) writes
`available` rows for every target the reader searches and must not decorate each of them. The
link sits straight after the name and before the common name: a `Button.quiet` holding a drawn 2 by 2 tile
glyph in the accent ink, the web's `TargetRow.tsx` glyph, with the tooltip "Mosaic: <name>" or,
for a target in several mosaics, "Mosaics: <name>, <name>", names in ordinal case-insensitive
order. Clicking it opens the mosaic detail page (section 12.17) of the first mosaic in that order
and does not open the row's Target detail. An unresolved `obj:` row never carries it, because it
has no target id to join. The set comes from step 6 of the query below, one extra read over
`mosaic_panel_sessions` joined to `mosaic_panels` and `mosaics` for the page's target ids, so the
link costs no round trip of its own. The web shows one mosaic per target and keeps whichever its
dictionary saw last; the port names them all and opens the first.

**The sessions control (Phase 14C, user ruling U3).** It sits in the row's trailing cell, after
Last Session, in the web's own form: a `Button.sm` reading Expand while the sessions are hidden
and Collapse while they show. The session count is that button's tooltip ("2 sessions"), not a
label beside the name, and there is no leading toggle cell. This supersedes the `Button.chevron`
form and the leading position the current build has. Deep dive inside the expander stays
`Button.sm`.

**The Palette cell and the Filters cell (Phase 14C, user ruling U3).** Both draw their badges
on one line, in a horizontal panel that does not wrap, in alphabetical order by canonical
filter name, compared ordinally and case insensitively. Alphabetical supersedes "in the order
the Filters tab stores them" for both cells, and it is applied in one place,
`TargetRowViewModel`, which is the one construction site of both badge lists;
`TargetListingQuery`'s own result order is a wire order, not a display order. A badge is
`Border.tag` (spec 14.5, `DESIGN.md` section 4) drawn in the web app's frosted-glass style
(user request, 2026-10-05, superseding the Phase 14C Task 3 fix pass that made the tint the 1
pixel outline and the label `ColorBadgeText`): the chrome stays `Border.tag`'s `ColorBadgeBg`
base at radius 3 with a 1 pixel edge, and the three figures the web's `utils/filterStyles.ts`
`frosted-glass` case derives from the filter colour are ported as they stand, the edge at 25%
of the tint, a wash at 18% of the tint inside the edge, an inset 6% white top highlight and a
soft drop shadow at 15% of the tint, with the label in the tint itself. Each is derived from the
tint in `PaletteBadgeViewModel`, so the template binds brushes and holds no literal. The earlier
contrast reservation (a stored `#4040FF` label measures about 1.5:1 on the dark themes, and Red
Light exists to emit nothing but red) stands as a known limit the user accepted for parity with
the web, and the filter panel's own pill keeps its outlined form. A badge carries the canonical
filter name alone
and its frame count moves to its tooltip, so the cell stays one line high whatever a target's
palette holds. The badge count is not capped and no `+n` fold is added: the column's shared size
is its widest cell, and it is the one column with no `MaxWidth`. A palette wide enough to push
the row past its viewport is clipped at the viewport rather than carried by a scroller, which is
the trade the paragraph above makes for every column.

**Pager (Phase 14C, UI layout ruling 5).** A numbered pager sits at the top of the list, above
the header row, where the count is read before the rows rather than at the bottom: previous
and next buttons, the page number buttons themselves, and a page-size select offering 25, 50,
100 and 250, writing `general.default_page_size` (section 5.8.1) on selection. The page button
set follows the web's own rule (`TargetFeed.tsx`'s `pageRange`): at 7 pages or fewer every page
number is shown; above 7, the set is page 1, an ellipsis once the current page is past 3, the
current page with one neighbour on each side, an ellipsis once the current page is more than
two short of the last page, and the last page. At 1 page the pager shows page 1 alone with
both Previous and Next disabled; at 5 pages it shows 1 2 3 4 5 with no ellipsis; at 40 pages,
on page 20 for instance, it shows 1 ... 19 20 21 ... 40, the ellipsis being three full stops in a
non-interactive label and not a button. This replaces the current build's bottom
Previous and Next pair, which carries no page numbers and no page-size control.

Beside the buttons the pager carries **the range alone**, "1 to 25 of 120", and "0 of 0" on an
empty result. It does not repeat the page number, because the numbered buttons already carry it
and a "Page 1 of 5, 120 groups" line trimmed against the page-size select at the shipped window.

**The refetch dim.** Changing a filter while a page of rows is already on screen keeps those
rows rendered, dimmed and input-disabled until the new page's response lands; nothing is
removed or replaced in the interval, and keyboard focus already on a row or a control inside
it survives the refetch rather than being dropped when the row it sat on is briefly gone. This
replaces the current build's behaviour of clearing and rebuilding the row list on every query,
matching `TargetFeed.tsx`'s dimmed, pointer-disabled treatment of the same interval.

Three mechanisms as built. The rows are made inert with `IsHitTestVisible`, not `IsEnabled`:
disabling the container drops keyboard focus permanently rather than for the length of the
refetch, so the pointer is blocked by hit testing and every keyboard-reachable path (opening a
target, toggling the sessions expander, the page commands) carries the refetch guard in its own
command body, which is the rule that a correctness guard lives in the body and not only in
`CanExecute`. The page buttons, Previous and Next are disabled for the same interval, so a click
during a refetch cannot queue a second page change. And the dim is not only a filter change: a
page change and a scan finishing while the page is open both go through the same flag, because
each replaces the whole page of rows.

**The sessions expander (PAR-010).** Expanding a row shows one line per session in that group,
newest first, as four columns: Date, Frames, Integration, Filters. Filters lists the canonical
optical filter names present in that night's LIGHT frames, deduplicated, in alphabetical order
(Phase 14C, user ruling U3, superseding the stored Filters tab order this clause named before),
drawn as the same `Border.tag` badges the Palette column uses under the Palette cell's own rule
above; a night whose frames carry no filter renders nothing rather than a placeholder. The names come from the same
second pass that builds the row's filter distribution (step 6 of the query below), grouped by
`session_date`, so the expander costs no extra round trip. Mirrors
`frontend/src/components/SessionTable.tsx`.

Each session line carries a Deep dive action, which calls the shell's
`OpenDetail(groupKey, sessionDate)` (section 12, and section 12.4 for what a deep link does on
arrival): Target detail opens for this group with that night already selected in the Nights
ledger and the session pane already on it. It passes the row's group key and the line's own date
and nothing else, so it works for an unresolved `obj:` group exactly as it does for a resolved
target.

**Session-scope custom columns on the expander (Phase 20).** The expander's night rows carry one
cell per session-scope custom column (section 12.15), in the column's own display order, after the
four columns above. They are not gated by a picker: the expander has no column picker and this
phase does not give it one. Each cell is the shared editor of section 12.15 and writes a value
keyed by this target and that night. The four columns above were built so that a fifth is an added
cell rather than a rewrite, and that is what this phase adds. The clause this paragraph replaces
named PAR-005 as the item these cells waited on; that was a misattribution. PAR-005 is the copy
list's per-filter row with the mapped filter id and the Bortle class, which still waits for Phase
21's filter id map and has nothing to do with custom columns.

**The column gear (PAR-010, ruling D4).** The target list header carries a gear button that
opens the dashboard column picker in a flyout. It is the same `ColumnPickerViewModel` the
Display tab renders (section 12.7), constructed once for the table id `dashboard` and shown in
two places, and both surfaces write `display.columns.dashboard` through `DisplayColumnWriter`
(section 5.8.2). Toggling a column in the flyout is reflected on the Display tab with no reload,
because there is one view-model and not two copies to keep in step. The Display tab keeps its
picker: the gear is the shortcut, not the replacement. The `name` column stays non-hideable in
both surfaces.

**The scan filter notice (PAR-014, placement corrected Phase 14C, fixer-list item 34).** A
`Border.callout` notice sits at the top of the target list column, above the toolbar row,
while the stored scan filters are still only what the setup wizard seeded: the five
`setup-exclude-*` name rules (section 12.1) and no others, with `include_paths` and
`exclude_paths` both empty. It states that GalactiLog is scanning everything under the
configured roots except those five folder patterns, and it carries one action, Review, which
opens Settings on the Library tab with the rule editor in view. It informs and never blocks: a
scan runs with the notice showing. It disappears as soon as the stored rules differ from the
seeded five in any way, a deletion included, and it returns if they are restored to exactly that
set. The same notice on the Library tab (section 12.7) is driven by the same condition computed
in one place, so the two surfaces cannot disagree. Mirrors
`frontend/src/components/ScanFiltersOnboarding.tsx` without its "use defaults" button: the
port's wizard has already written those defaults by the time this notice can show. It renders
in both filter panel states, because the target list column renders regardless of whether the
panel is expanded or the 48 pixel strip: its own condition is the only thing that governs
whether it shows, never the panel's. This is a placement fix, not new behaviour: the current
build nests the notice inside the collapsible left column, where it disappears the moment the
panel collapses, which the web itself does not do (`ScanFiltersOnboarding variant="global"`
renders in `<main>`, beside `<TargetFeed />`, never inside `<Sidebar>`).

**Query.** `TargetListingQuery.List(criteria)`, port of
`target_listing.list_targets_aggregated`. Shape:

1. Filter `images` to `image_type = 'LIGHT'` and to non-merged targets, then apply every
   criterion.
2. Group by the group key
   `coalesce(resolved_target_id, 'obj:' || coalesce(nullif(json_extract(raw_headers,'$.OBJECT'),''), '__uncategorized__'))`.
   The empty-string and missing `OBJECT` cases must collapse to the same key in both the
   listing and the detail phase or a frame lands in two different groups.
3. Aggregate per group: total integration (`sum(exposure_time)`), frame count, distinct
   session count, first and last session date.
4. Apply metric range filters per 12.2.1.
5. Compute the page slice and the overall aggregates in the same round trip.
6. Second pass over the page's groups only: filter distribution, equipment set, session
   summaries, aliases, and from Phase 18 the mosaics each target has an `included` night in (the mosaic link
   above).

Filter and equipment criteria are expanded through the alias map before matching, so
selecting canonical `OIII` matches stored `Oiii` and `O3`. Port of
`normalization.expand_canonical`. The reverse fold alone is not enough when both sides of
the comparison are user data written at different times.

The group key runs `json_extract` on every dashboard query and SQLite has no index that can
serve it, so the grouping step is a full scan of the LIGHT frames that survive the other
filters. Acceptable at the scale a single imaging PC produces. Known ceiling: if a dashboard
query exceeds 200 ms on a 50 000 frame library, the upgrade path is a stored generated column
holding the group key with an index on it, populated at ingest. Do not pre-build that; measure
first.

#### 12.2.1 Metric range filter semantics

A metric range filter is **per frame, and every frame must satisfy it**. A target group
passes the `hfr` filter with bounds `[lo, hi]` only when every LIGHT frame in the group whose
`median_hfr` is non-null satisfies `lo <= median_hfr <= hi`. Frames with a null value for
that metric are ignored by that metric's filter; they neither pass nor fail it, and a group
whose frames all have null values passes trivially.

In SQL, on the grouped query:

```
HAVING (min(<column>) >= :lo OR min(<column>) IS NULL)
   AND (max(<column>) <= :hi OR max(<column>) IS NULL)
```

`min` and `max` skip nulls in SQLite, and both return null when every value in the group is
null, which is what makes the null-tolerance fall out of the aggregate rather than needing a
separate `COUNT` term. Only the bound the user actually set contributes a clause.

Each metric is evaluated independently: a group passes when it passes every metric filter
that is set. A frame is not required to satisfy all filters simultaneously.

This is a deliberate departure from the web application, which uses
`HAVING avg(<column>) BETWEEN :lo AND :hi` and therefore lets a group containing one
excellent and one poor frame pass a tight filter on the average. "HFR max 3.0" here means no
frame in the group exceeds 3.0, which is what the label says.

Columns per metric key: `hfr` to `median_hfr`, `fwhm` to `fwhm`, `eccentricity` to
`eccentricity`, `stars` to `detected_stars`, `guiding_rms` to `guiding_rms_arcsec`,
`adu_mean` to `adu_mean`, `focuser_temp` to `focuser_temp`, `ambient_temp` to
`ambient_temp`, `humidity` to `humidity`, `airmass` to `airmass`.

### 12.3 FITS header query builder security

Ported from `target_listing.py` and mandatory even without authentication, because a header
key is user text reaching SQL:

- The key must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,20}$`. A key that does not match is dropped, not
  escaped.
- The key is passed as a bound parameter to `json_extract(raw_headers, '$.' || ?)`, never
  concatenated into the statement text.
- The value is always a bound parameter.
- For `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, the value must parse as a double or the clause is dropped
  entirely. The comparison casts the extracted text to `REAL`.
- For `contains`, the value is escaped for `LIKE` (`\`, `%`, `_` each prefixed with `\`) and
  the clause carries `ESCAPE '\'`.

### 12.4 Target detail

Mirrors `frontend/src/pages/TargetDetailPage.tsx` for its figures and its queries. The layout is
not the web page's: Phase 12 replaced the stack of session accordion cards with the Observing
Ledger workbench described below, and `DESIGN.md` at the repository root records the visual world
it is built from.

**Header block:** primary name with inline rename, aliases, object type and category,
constellation, RA and Dec, angular size, position angle, V magnitude, surface brightness,
SAC description and notes, catalog membership badges, and the reference thumbnail.

**Totals row:** total integration, total frames, session count, first and last session date,
average HFR (pixels and arcseconds), average eccentricity, average FWHM (the `fwhm`
column, arcseconds; see 7.1.1), average guiding
RMS, average detected stars, filters used, equipment used.

The arcsecond figures pool only frames that carry a plate scale; the count of frames
excluded for lack of one is shown. The eccentricity average pools only frames whose
`eccentricity_source` equals the target's modal source, and the excluded count is shown.
Both disclosures come from `target_detail.py` and exist because the underlying values are
not comparable across sources.

Section 7.2's pooling rule is applied per aggregate, not once for the target: the totals row
pools on the target's modal source, and each night pools on its own session's modal
source and reports the source it used. A night imaged entirely with one source therefore
reads correctly even when the library as a whole is dominated by another, and no figure on
this page ever mixes two sources.

A frame whose `DATE-OBS` did not parse has a null `capture_date` and therefore a null
`session_date` (section 7.1.2). Such a frame counts in every figure in the totals row,
because it is a real frame of the target and the dashboard counts it, but it appears in no
ledger row and moves no session count: session count is the number of dated sessions. The
consequence is deliberate and visible: the ledger's per-night frame counts can sum to less than
the target row's frame count. There is no "unknown" night.

**Actions:** rename and re-resolve, edit the object type (PAR-009), merge into another target
(section 12.9), unmerge from the merge history list, copy frame list to clipboard, export the
checked nights for stacking (section 12.13), copy the AstroBin CSV for the checked nights
(section 12.16), send the target's coordinates to a configured NINA instance, slew a configured
Stellarium instance to it (both section 12.16), reveal the target's folder in Explorer, and from
Phase 18 create a mosaic from the checked nights (section 12.17).

**Object type edit** (PAR-009). The Details panel renders the object type read-only beside a
pencil button. The row is drawn whenever the target can be given a type, not only when it has one,
because the `Other` category stores the empty string and a target sitting in it would otherwise
lose the affordance that put it there. The button swaps the value for a combo box listing section
9.8's display categories in that table's order, followed by `Other`; `Unresolved` is not offered,
because it describes a frame with no target rather than a target. The box opens unseeded with the
target's current category as its placeholder, so choosing the entry the target already shows is a
real selection that closes the editor, and the write below refuses it rather than recording a
change that did not happen. The pencil leaves the screen while its own editor is open. Choosing an
entry commits at once and the box swaps back to the read-only value; Escape cancels and leaves the
stored value alone.

The write goes through `TargetWriteRepository.SetObjectType`, which sets `targets.object_type` to
the chosen category's first SIMBAD code in one transaction and emits a `user_action` /
`target_object_type_changed` activity event carrying the target id, `previous_object_type`,
`previous_category`, `new_object_type` and `new_category`. It writes that one column: there is no
`targets.category` column, and the display category is derived at every read by
`ObjectTypeCategories.Categorize` over the stored code (section 9.8), so the category a surface
shows follows the code rather than being stored beside it. Nothing else is written: the catalogue
columns a re-resolve fills (section 9.7) are untouched, and a later re-resolve overwrites the
object type the same way it overwrites every other catalogue column, because a user's type choice
is not `name_locked`. The edit is offered on a resolved target only; a group row that is an
unresolved `OBJECT` string has no `targets` row to write and the pencil is absent. The dashboard's
Object Type filter and the target listing derive their category from the same
`ObjectTypeCategories` table, so a correction here moves the target on both at the next read. The
Statistics page has no object type breakdown to move: the section 12.5 table has no such section.
Phase 15B, which owns that page, adds a Guiding section to it and no object type breakdown, so
adding one remains unowned and is a decision of its own rather than a phase's leftover.

A target has no single folder: its frames can sit under several session directories, scan
roots and drives. "Reveal the target's folder" therefore resolves to the parent directory of
the most recent frame by capture date, revealed with section 11.5's
`explorer.exe /select,"<path>"` verb so the folder opens with a real file highlighted. It is
disabled when the target has no frame path.

**The Export flyout** (Phase 16) is one of the identity line's two frequent actions, in the place
the standing Copy frame list button held. Its entries are Copy frame list (below), Export for
stacking (section 12.13) and, from Phase 21, **AstroBin CSV**, which copies the acquisition rows
for the checked nights to the clipboard and writes no file (section 12.16). Every entry acts on
the nights the ledger's selection column has checked, appends that count to its own label once one
night is checked, and is disabled with the sentence "Select one or more nights first" while none
is. Only the entry point moved: the Copy Frame List command, its dialog and its behaviour below
are unchanged.

**Copy Frame List** (PAR-006) opens a dialog over the nights the ledger's selection column has
checked (below). It is a `ModalPageWindow` page, like the merge preview, and it writes the
clipboard and nothing else: no file is created, moved, renamed or deleted, and no script that
would do any of those is offered, because a move-or-delete affordance is a non-goal
(sections 2.1 and 19.2).

| Control | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Mode | A two-button segment, Good and Bad. Good lists the frames the grading did not reject; Bad lists the frames it rejected. Persisted in `display.target_page.frame_list_mode`. |
| Include unmeasured | A checkbox, offered in Good mode only and ignored in Bad mode. An unmeasured frame is one the grading left ungraded, for any of the reasons below. It is never bad, and it joins the good list only while this box is checked. Persisted in `display.target_page.frame_list_include_unmeasured`. |
| Tally | One line, live: "Good list: n of m frames. Graded g good, b bad, u unmeasured", with ", included" appended when Good mode is on, the box is checked and u is not zero. The tally counts the same verdicts the frame table's bands carry, so the dialog and the table cannot disagree. |
| Partial-load warning | When one or more checked nights failed to load, a `Border.callout warn` line naming how many of how many failed, which dates they were, and that the list below covers only the loaded nights. |
| Format | A combo box with the three formats below. Persisted in `display.target_page.frame_list_format`. |
| Copy | Writes the rendered list to the clipboard and closes. Disabled when the list is empty. |

A frame is bad when the grading put it in the reject band, good when it put it in the better or
neutral band, on the watch band's own side of the line stated below, and unmeasured when the
grading produced no score: its group held fewer than 8 frames, its group was uniform, or the
frame carried no value for any graded axis. The watch band counts as good: the band exists to be
looked at, not to be excluded, and a user who wants the watch frames out lowers nothing, because
this dialog has no thresholds of its own.

The three formats, exactly (PAR-006, ruling C6):

| Format | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `paths` | One absolute path per line, newline separated with a trailing newline, in the order the frame tables show the rows. The default, and byte for byte what the page copied before this dialog existed. |
| `names` | One bare file name per line, same order, same trailing newline. For a tool that works inside one folder. |
| `explorer` | Each bare file name wrapped in double quotes and joined with the literal ` OR `, one line, no trailing newline. Paste it into the Windows Explorer search box. A name containing a double quote is emitted as it is; Explorer's search box has no escape for one, and inventing one would produce a string that finds nothing. |

The frame table's own copies are unchanged by this dialog and take no dialog of their own: its
per-row "copy path" covers the single-file case, and its toolbar's "Copy paths (n)" writes the
selected rows in the order the table shows them, one absolute path per line with a trailing
newline, byte for byte the `paths` format above. An empty selection copies nothing. Neither
grades anything or writes to disk, and both stay inside section 2.1 for the same reason the
dialog does.

**Target notes:** a collapsible multi-line text box with autosave on a 1 second idle debounce
and a saving indicator.

**Cross-session metric chart:** section 13.

**Layout (Phase 23 stage 1, layout C, Question Modes).** The page never scrolls as a whole and
no region has two scroll bars, except in layout D, whose rows scroll as one column on a short
window (below). This paragraph and the ones after it describe layout C,
`TargetLayoutRegistry`'s key `modes`; layout A, Night Bench, key `bench` (stage 3), layout D,
Cascading Rows, key `rows` (stage 4), and the layout selector follow them. Across the top is the header. Its identity line holds Back, the primary name,
the other names, the object category, the two badges, Reveal folder, Sky view (Phase 22), the
overflow menu and the Details toggle. Its second line carries the totals as one sentence and the
hours of each filter as figures. The Export flyout sits in the Nights ledger's header row.

Under the header is the mode switch with three buttons: Night review, Compare nights and
Integration. A fresh mount is always Night review; the mode is a property of the layout view,
is never stored, and each button is a command.

Compare nights (Phase 23 stage 2) is the chart across nights (section 13) in a laned form, then
a table. The switch above it chooses All or Checked: Checked narrows both the lanes and the table
to the nights checked in the ledger, and is disabled while no night is checked. The chart draws
one lane per toggled metric. Each lane has its own labelled y axis (tick labels are numbers only;
the unit is in the lane's title, drawn horizontally at the lane's top left), and all lanes share
one plot left and right edge. Every frame of every plotted night is a small dot inside that
night's band, in capture order, and the night's median is a line drawn over the dots. The rig
pills draw a dashed line per rig. The overall pill draws the pooled dots and the pooled median
line; a filter pill draws that filter's dots over the pooled dots, in the filter's colour, with
that filter's median line. A filter pill turned off removes that filter's dots and line; the
overall pill turned off removes the pooled dots and line, so with overall on a filter pill off
hides no frame. A lane is at least 96 pixels tall, the lanes share the region's height and
scroll in `LanesScroll`, inside the chart view, so the help glyph and the pill rows stay put;
the wheel over the lanes scrolls them. The lanes' scroll bar is the application's thin auto-hide
bar. Below the lanes is the Compare table: one row per filter, one column group per night,
each group holding the night's five medians (HFR, eccentricity, FWHM, guiding RMS, stars) in
the ledger's column widths, in the lanes' order: the nights the chart plots, oldest at the left,
so a group sits under its night's band. The filter column is pinned at 110 pixels and the
groups scroll sideways inside the table. The table takes its natural height up to 40 percent of
the region and scrolls inside itself beyond that. A filter with no value for a metric shows an
empty cell, not zero.

Integration (Phase 23 stage 2) draws the per-filter hours as bars at full size, then two
tables, in one vertical scroll viewer with one scroll bar. Each bar is one row of 30 pixels
with a 14 pixel bar on a track that fills the width, every bar on the same scale (the longest
filter), cut into one segment per night in ledger order with a tooltip naming the night and its
hours. A hairline tick marks the goal and the text "short by 1.2 h" follows the hours. The goal
of a filter is the integration of the largest filter of its group, the group being SII, Ha and
OIII or R, G and B (`FilterCategory.Of`); L, a filter outside both groups, the largest filter
itself and a group of one have no goal and no short-by figure, and a short-by under 0.05 hours
is not shown. The first table is frame counts by exposure length (one row per length in
ascending order, one column per filter, with totals). The second is hours by night (one row per
night in ledger order, one column per filter, with a total column and a total row). Both use a
label column of at least 117 pixels, 64 pixel cells and one filter order, so their filter
columns line up. The label column is measured and is the same width in both tables.

The per-night, per-filter rows and the per-frame points that the Compare table, the Integration
tables, the bars and the lanes read come from the page's one query (`TargetDetailQuery`), as
`NightFilters` and `NightFrames` on `TargetDetail`: one row per night and canonical filter
(integration seconds, frame count, frame count per exposure length and the five medians) and one
point per dated frame (night, filter, capture time and the five metric values). Both are built
in memory from the rows the query already reads; there is no second SELECT and no migration.
The three tables are three presentations of one `NightFilterMatrixViewModel`. The registry
lists sixteen parts, adding `CompareTablePart` and `IntegrationTablesPart` to the fourteen of
stage 0, so each is on screen or one click away in every layout. Stage 2 added no stored key.

The left column is in every mode. It holds the Nights ledger, whose lit row opens into that
night's per-filter table in the ledger's own columns, then the Export actions with the checked
total, then the sharpest frame thumbnails, the comparison line, the ranges table and the night
notes. The column is the nights sidebar (Phase 24 R1): its width is the one the profile stores
(`sidebar_width`, dragged on the handle at its right edge or stepped by Left and Right, 24 pixels
a step) and its form follows that width alone, with no window-width breakpoint (`LedgerColumn`):
wide from 520 pixels, where Phase 20's rule holds that custom columns give way first; compact
from 472 up to 520, hiding the Frames and Filters columns and the custom columns, the aligned
per-filter rows hiding their frame count; collapsed below 472 or while `sidebar_collapsed` is
stored, which the ledger's chevron toggles back to the last open width. With nothing stored the
column takes the ledger's own width. The right region is a star column bounded by the window,
and the frames table's floor of 682 pixels is a minimum, not a desired width.

Night review places the night header, then the lanes region, then the frames region. The lanes
region is one scroll viewer with one scroll bar holding three lanes on one time axis: the night
strip (the timeline), the per-frame metrics chart in a fixed 180 pixel lane, and the Guiding
part with the guide graph. One `NightLaneAxis` per night gives the three the same time domain
(the earlier of the first frame and dusk to the later of the last frame and dawn, rounded to the
hour), a plot left edge of 76 pixels and a plot right edge of 52 pixels (21 before the stage 3
follow-up; 52 holds a five-digit count label). On this axis the per-frame chart's right axis
labels carry no unit and 2 pixels of side padding; on the left only px keeps its unit, arcsec and
count drop it; a count label is a whole number on every chart and both axes. The px unit stays
on a left axis that a unitless metric such as eccentricity shares ("0.00 px" to "2.00 px"),
accepted at the stage 4 look. The right axis is whole when a count shares it, and its floor is
zero, since every metric the night chart plots is non-negative. The per-frame chart
plots capture time, not frame index. In layout C the timeline carries the only clock labels; the
chart and the guide graph draw grid lines at the same ticks. The guide graph opens on the night's domain
and keeps its wheel zoom and drag, which take it off the shared axis until its reset. The
per-frame chart draws a ring around each outlier point, in the timeline's outlier ink. The
selected frame is marked at the shared x in the timeline, the chart and the guide graph, and the
timeline's view model is the single owner of the selection. A click on a timeline tick or on a
chart point selects that frame, scrolls the frames table to its row and opens the frame viewer,
the behaviour Phase 13 ruling R8 gave a tick click. The wheel over the per-frame chart scrolls
the lanes region.

The lanes floor is measured, not a constant: what sits above the chart (the night header, the
Night metrics header line and the timeline lane) plus the chart's 180 pixel default, so the chart
is whole at rest at 1280 by 720 and at 1600 by 900. The frames region takes the rest; a larger
text size grows the lanes and so may show fewer rows. At 1600 by 900 the frames table shows seven
rows; at 1280 by 720 with two rigs it shows about one and a half rows in the real font, the
accepted limit of the narrow form.

The frames chrome is two lines. In the wide form, line A is the Frames title and count, the rig
and outlier pills and, at the right, Copy paths, Reveal and Columns; line B is the grade tally
and, at the right, Compare to. Each line wraps rather than clips. The legend with its advisory
sentence is the table's own line under the toolbar and above the column header, in both forms,
so it sits with the rows it explains. In the narrow form, a right column under 800 pixels
(`FramesColumn`, the shared rule; since Phase 24 R22 that is 1280 by 720 with the compact
sidebar, and 1600 by 900 is wide), the part takes its compact form: one line holds the tally, the
rig and outlier pills take their own line under it, and the toolbar line holds the title, the
count, Compare to and the three buttons. The frames part takes the full width of the right column:
Phase 24 R22 removed the findings column that sat beside it, and the Filter segment's outlier
pills took its job. The `target.night-detail` help glyph sits in the night header.

**Layout A, Night Bench (Phase 23 stage 3).** Key `bench`, the second row of the registry. It
places the same sixteen parts and adds no content to any of them. The page never scrolls as a
whole and no region has two scroll bars: a table that scrolls sideways inside its part belongs to
the part, and the rule counts each region's own vertical bar.

Under the header is a row holding `IntegrationBarsPart` in its small form at the full width of
the page. The header part has no centre slot, and the small bars need 572 pixels for two filters
and wrap for seven, so they sit on their own row. Below that are three regions.

The left pane is 472 pixels wide, the compact width layout C uses, taken from one helper
(`LedgerColumn`) that both layouts call. It holds the Nights ledger in its compact form, then the
trend across nights in its laned form. The ledger takes its natural height up to half the pane
and scrolls inside itself beyond that. The per-filter table sits in the ledger's lit row, aligned
to the ledger's columns, as in layout C: the table is 682 pixels wide and does not fit the pane.
The trend's strips are at least 96 pixels tall and scroll in the trend's own scroll viewer.

The centre column holds the night header row, then the lanes region, the handle and the frames
table. The night header row sits above the lanes' scroll viewer, so the Night detail button never
scrolls away. The lanes region holds the night timeline, the per-frame metrics chart in its 180
pixel lane and the guide lane's night on one `NightLaneAxis`. The chart stays whole at rest and
the frames table gives way first. The frames part takes its compact form while the centre is
under 800 pixels wide. Measured on the launched application at text size Small, the table shows
2 to 3 whole rows at 1280 by 720 and 9 to 10 at 1600 by 900 (layout C shows 1 and 7); the handle
below lets the reader trade lane height for rows. With the rail expanded at 1280 the centre is
540 pixels and Compare to wraps to a second toolbar line.

Night Bench's right column and its Night detail drawer went with the layout at stage 6, and
their content is placed as the built layout places it (Phase 24 R1, R2, R3 and R22): the
sharpest frame thumbnails, the comparison line and the ranges table are in the Night metrics
section beside the per-filter table, the session notes are the Session notes box in the Details
drawer under the target notes, the guiding is the night chart's Guiding pill, the Compare table and the
Integration tables are their modes, and the findings column is gone, the frames taking the full
width of the right column with the outlier pills in their chrome.

The guide graph draws no clock labels of its own in Question Modes: since Phase 24 R3 it sits in
the night chart's slot under the timeline, which carries them (`GuideGraph.ShowsClockLabels` is
off there; on, the control labels the shared axis ticks itself, and a night whose domain holds
no even-hour mark, such as a one-hour night, has its two ends labelled with an end label that
would overlap the start label dropped). A guide session with no sample inside the night's domain
keeps the shared axis and is clipped outside the plot. Since stage 4 the night strip labels a
night with no even-hour mark at its two ends too; a label that would overlap the one before it is
dropped, and every label stays inside the control.

The shell builds no layout view until it is attached to the window, so the title and the night
heading take their text tier on the first load. The Compare to segment holds its own data
context from construction, so the stored baseline is lit after a layout switch. The ledger's
list is single-select while the page arrives and always-selected after, so a layout switch does
not select the newest night.

**Layout D, Cascading Rows (Phase 23 stage 4).** Key `rows`, the third row of the registry,
`Layouts/RowsLayoutView`. It places the same sixteen parts, all of them in the tree and none one
click away, and adds no content to any of them. Under the header are three full-width rows
divided by hairline rules, with no bordered panel.

Row 1, the target, holds the integration bars in their full form in a 240 pixel column, 30
pixels per filter, which scrolls inside itself past eight filters; the Nights ledger in its
compact form at the `LedgerColumn` width, with the per-filter table in the lit row as in the
other two layouts; and the trend across nights, overlaid, in the remaining width. Row 1 is 260
pixels, or taller by the trend's pill lines, so the trend's plot is never lower than the metrics
lane's plot; while the trend or the lane draws no plot, row 1 is 260. The trend opens on the
newest session, as in every layout (`default_chart_sessions`, section 5.8.3); "All sessions"
widens it. Question Modes alone sets all sessions when its Compare nights mode opens.

Row 2, the night, holds the night header, then the timeline and the per-frame metrics lane on
the night's `NightLaneAxis`, at the lane heights the other layouts use, about 302 pixels in all.
The lanes handle sits between rows 2 and 3.

Row 3, the frames, held a 440 pixel left column beside the frames table. The column and the
layout went at stage 6; the built layout places that content as the Night Bench paragraph above
states (Phase 24 R1, R2, R3 and R22), and the frames table is the full width of the right column,
in its compact form while that width is under 800 pixels (`FramesColumn`).

When the three rows do not fit the page height they scroll as one column under the fixed
header, and row 3 keeps its chrome plus six whole frame rows; this is the one layout whose page
scrolls. Each inner scroller passes the wheel on at its ends. Measured on the launched
application at text size Small, layout D shows six whole frame rows at 1280 by 720 and at 1600
by 900, the column scrolling at both, and 17 on a maximised 5120 by 1369 client. The compact
coordinates block of the drawing is not built; the Details drawer keeps the six fields.

Inside the column a bring-into-view raised in a row moves only that row's own scroller: a hover
on the timeline that brings a frame row into view scrolls the frames table, never the page
column. The column follows keyboard-gained focus only: a request reaches it when focus came by
Tab or an arrow key and the request's target holds the focused element, or when it comes from
inside a focused text box, so the caret of a growing night note stays in view. A row focused by
a mouse click does not move the column later.

**The layout selector and the stored keys (Phase 23 stage 3).** The page's layout is chosen in
two places that show the same state: a combo box named `LayoutSelector` in the header's action
row before Details, and a combo box named `TargetLayoutBox` in Settings, Display, in the idiom
of the theme box. Both list the registry's rows by display name (Question Modes, Night Bench and
Cascading Rows since stage 4) and both stay visible while the registry holds one row. The choice is stored per profile as `display.target_page.layout`, a
string, default `modes`. The registry's `Resolve` is the one place the string is read: a stored
value the build does not ship (`tracks` is not built yet, or any unknown or empty value) reads as `modes` and is not rewritten until the reader picks a layout. A pick on either
control writes the key once and moves the other control. A switch replaces the hosted layout
view and releases the old one first. The selected night, the selected frame, the grading
baseline and the metric toggles live on the page's view model and the two settings holders, so
they carry over a switch; layout C's mode does not, since it is never stored. Every open Target
page follows the same key. With the header's layout box focused, each Up or Down switches
layout at once and rebuilds the page.

`display.target_page.layouts.<key>.lanes_height` is the height of the lanes region for one
layout, in pixels, a number or null. Null, the value a fresh profile holds, is the automatic
rule above. The handle is a 12 pixel horizontal bar between the lanes and the frames table, in
every layout. A drag moves the split live and writes the value once, on release. Up and Down on
the focused handle move it by 24 pixels a step and write once, on release of the key; a key
press during a drag is ignored. A double click writes null. On load and on every size change
the value is clamped: the lanes keep at least the timeline lane and a 120 pixel chart, and the
frames region keeps its chrome and one row; when the window is too short for both, the lanes
minimum wins. The one handle sizes the chart and the frames together: the session chart takes
whatever the lanes height leaves under the timeline lane, 180 pixels with nothing stored, so
dragging the handle trades chart height for frame rows directly. In layout D
the lanes run from the timeline lane's bottom to their whole content and the page height bounds
nothing, since row 3's floor is held by the scrolling column. A clamp does not rewrite the stored
value. Each layout keeps its own value, and an unrecognized member of a
layout's object survives a write.
`display.target_page.layouts.<key>.chart_height` was the session chart's own height under a
second handle along the chart's bottom edge (Phase 24 R31). The night pane round retired that
handle: the key is no longer read and a stored value round-trips untouched.
`display.target_page.layouts.<key>.notes_open` was the Session notes section's disclosure and is
retired the same way, the notes having moved to the Details drawer.

A night keeps its own frame selection across a night switch: returning to a night shows the
frame picked there, and the table row, the timeline tick and the chart mark agree. A rescan
rebuilds the night's frame table and clears that selection.

The per-frame chart's rig pills offer only the rigs that shot the night on display, and a night
with one rig has no pill row. The cross-night trend chart keeps the union of rigs over all
nights. A rig turned off on one night stays off when the reader returns to it.

On a night that crosses a clock change, the guide lane places each guide sample through the same
`NightLaneAxis` fraction of its local clock time that the timeline and the chart use, so a
sample after the change sits at the same x as the frame beside it in all three lanes. The
earlier mapping placed samples at real elapsed seconds and put every sample after the change one
hour off. A skipped clock hour is an empty hour-wide stretch carrying the hour mark of a time
that never occurred; a repeated hour folds, so the data of its two passes overlap on one
stretch. Guide data outside the axis' domain falls outside the plot. A wheel zoom or drag takes
the graph off the shared axis, where it is linear in elapsed seconds as before, and the reset
returns it.

The retired arrangement is gone: the collapsed "Trend across nights" band, the collapsible
"Metrics over the night", "Night detail" and "Frames" sections, the splitter and its dragged
height, the ledger's 48 pixel strip form and the 1600 pixel three-way ledger rule. The five
stored keys that governed them and `graph.target_chart_expanded` are retired; an old profile that
holds them carries them through the extension data, written back unchanged.

At the shipped 1280x800 window with an 18 pixel root (the Large size), the identity line spends
what it has on the primary name and the two frequent actions: the other names trim to an ellipsis
and the object category is not drawn. Both live in the Details panel, which is where a reader goes
for them, so the line degrades by dropping the duplicated and the secondary rather than by wrapping.
It cannot wrap: the identity line sits above the workbench, the page has no scroll of its own, and
a second line costs the frame table its height. The narrow ledger's own header cells trim on the
same principle. The extra-large text size has not been verified against the narrow ledger.

**Header block, target notes and merge history** live in a Details panel, closed by default,
opened by the Details button or Ctrl+D. The panel carries the header block's fields verbatim,
including the target's mean HFR in arcseconds beside the plate scale that derives it, the target
notes box with its 1 second idle autosave and its saving indicator, and the merge history list
with its unmerge. The target's arcsecond mean lives here and in neither the ledger nor the log
line.

**The Sky view button and window** (Phase 22) port the web's Sky View section
(`TargetDetailPage.tsx`, `AladinViewer.tsx`) as a still-image viewer. The Details panel carries
no Sky view section, and no survey image is shown anywhere else in the application.

**The button.** A **Sky view** button sits in the identity line's action row, immediately after
Reveal folder and before the overflow menu. It is absent, not disabled, when the target has no RA
and Dec or no target id at all (a group row with no `targets` row to open), the condition the web
applies to its section. While `general.survey_downloads_enabled` (section 5.8.1) is false it is
drawn disabled and its tooltip, shown on the disabled button, reads "Turn on Survey downloads on
the General tab of Settings to use Sky view." Pressing it opens the window, owned by the main
window and modal to it.

**The window** uses the preview modal's shell (section 11.5): centred on its owner, resizable,
titled "Sky view: " followed by the target's primary name, Escape closes it, and the image
viewport takes keyboard focus on open. Its top row holds the title, the `page.sky-view` help
glyph, the survey combo over five entries, Reset and Refresh; its footer holds the hint "Drag to
pan, wheel or + and - to zoom", the credit caption "Image: CDS hips2fits, " followed by the
survey label, and Close (Esc).

| Label | Survey id |
| --- | --- |
| DSS2 Color | `P/DSS2/color` |
| DSS2 Red | `P/DSS2/red` |
| 2MASS Color | `P/2MASS/color` |
| PanSTARRS DR1 | `P/PanSTARRS/DR1/color-z-zg-g` |
| AllWISE Color | `P/allWISE/color` |

The window opens on the target's RA and Dec at the field of section 11.3's field rule, with the
survey `general.sky_view_survey` names. Choosing a survey writes that key and fetches the same
centre and field in the new survey; a null pushed through the combo's `TwoWay` binding (a
