transient state the binding can reach mid-rebind) restores the previously selected survey rather
than being held or read from, so `Caption` and `Reset` never dereference one.

**The image** is the JPEG section 11.3's client returns, decoded from bytes and drawn with Skia,
scaled uniformly to fit the viewport and centred. A drag moves the drawn image with the pointer
and, on release, fetches a new view centred where the drag left the sky, the offset converted
through the drawn image's own field and the cosine of the declination, floored at 0.01 so a
target near a pole does not divide by a number near zero. A wheel notch, or `+` or `-` on the
main row or the number pad, steps the drawn image's scale about the viewport centre by a factor
of 1.5; a touchpad's fractional notches accumulate instead of stepping on every event, and a step
is taken once the accumulated delta reaches a whole notch, with a direction reversal starting a
fresh count so a leftover part-notch cannot absorb the reverse notch. 400 ms after the last such
input, the window fetches the new field at the same centre. The drawn image stays up while its
replacement loads. **Reset** returns to the target's centre, default field and the current
survey. **Refresh** fetches the current view again without reading the cache; the fetch
overwrites the cached file only once it succeeds, and on any other outcome the existing file is
left in place and served again (section 11.3), so Refresh is the only caller that replaces a
cached image and the only one that can leave it exactly as it was.

**States.** A loading indicator over the viewport while a fetch runs, including the 400 ms zoom
settle before the fetch itself starts, the same indeterminate bar the preview modal shows. Two
fixed sentences, and the window shows at most one:

| State | Sentence |
| --- | --- |
| The switch is off when a fetch would start | "Sky view is off. Turn on Survey downloads on the General tab of Settings. Images are fetched from alasky.cds.unistra.fr." |
| The fetch failed, was refused or timed out | "The survey image did not load. Check the internet connection and press Refresh." |

With the switch off no cached image is drawn either (the approved answer to question 7). No
centre, field or pan state is persisted; the window opens on the target every time. No image is
saved, exported or copied from the window. Nothing in it writes a `targets` row.

**The nights ledger** is one aligned table, newest first, whose first row is the target itself.
Its columns are Night (the session date), integration hours, frame count, median HFR, median
eccentricity, median FWHM (`fwhm`), median guiding RMS, median detected stars and the filters
used, and the target row carries the same columns filled with the totals row's means. A night's
cell renders in `metric-worst` only when it is worse than the target's mean by more than one unit
of the last displayed decimal; better stays silent. Every one of the five quality column headers
carries the tooltip "Night medians against target means", because a night median against a target
mean is not a like-for-like comparison. Selection is a lit row: a lighter field, accent ink and a
2 pixel lit edge. Camera, telescope, the night's arcsecond HFR and the eccentricity source are on
the row's tooltip and in the session pane. The per-night rig count and the notes indicator are
retired from this page: the Details drawer, which holds the target notes and the lit night's
session notes, is the surface that answers both questions.

**Session-scope custom columns on the ledger (Phase 20, user ruling).** A session-scope custom
column (section 12.15) is drawn as one further column after Filters, carrying the shared cell
editor on every night row and nothing on the target row, which is not a night. They are governed
by `display.columns.ledger` (section 5.8.2) and are **off by default**: a newly created column
appears on no ledger until the reader switches it on in the Display tab's "Nights ledger columns"
picker. Below the 1600 pixel breakpoint the narrow ledger drops every custom column **before** it
drops the Filters column. The built-in columns, their minimums and their maximums are unchanged
whatever is switched on, and they are not in that list and are not hideable, so a ledger with no
custom column measures exactly as it does today.

**The wide ledger widens for them, and only for them (Phase 20, ruling C21).** The wide ledger has
three pixels of spare width, so a custom column cannot be fitted inside its 640 without taking the
date off the Night column, and no existing layout pin moves to make room. With nothing switched on
the ledger is 640 and the page is unchanged. With custom columns switched on the ledger grows by
the sum of their widths plus one 32 pixel gutter, to a ceiling of 208 extra pixels, and the starred
session pane column gives that space up; a column that does not fit under the ceiling is dropped
from the end of the list. The ceiling is the pane's own declared minimum read back: at the 1600
pixel breakpoint the workbench has 1558, spends 28 on its gutter and owes `SessionPane`'s
`FilterTableMinWidth` 682, which leaves the ledger 848, and 848 less 640 is 208. A ledger text cell
is 120 wide, which is what admits a check box column and a text column together under the ceiling.
The gutter is 32 rather than a smaller figure because the ledger's ten column definitions have
measured more than the ledger they sit in since Phase 12, 645 against 640 under the headless
harness's stub face and 669 against 640 at the shipped face and the default text size; that
overflow is pre-existing, is hidden today by the Filters cell's own margins, and is an accepted
limit rather than something this phase repairs.

**The night selection column** (PAR-006, ruling C5) is a check box in each night row's leading
gutter, and in the header row's leading gutter a tri-state box that selects all nights when it is
clear and clears them when any are checked. The column is 18 pixels, which is what an empty check
box measures, and the 16 it needed beyond the ledger's existing 2 came out of the cell gutter,
which went from 4 pixels a side to 2 across the eight drawn cells; the Night column's floor
followed its own two gutters from 108 to 104 and the date figure it is made of did not change. The
left inset was not the source: it held 2. The three clauses that held before hold unchanged: the
column adds no column to the ledger's declared set, drops none of the seven numeric columns, and
does not widen the 520 pixel narrow ledger or the 640 pixel wide one. The gutter change reaches
the wide ledger as well as the narrow one, deliberately, because an Avalonia shared size group
only ever grows and a wide ledger measured at the old gutter would hand its remembered widths back
to the narrow one and put the last cell outside the ledger again. The target row
carries no check box, because it is not a night. Checking a night does not select it: the lit row
still names the night the pane is showing, and the checks name the nights an action will act on,
which are two different questions and stay two different marks. The collapsed 48 pixel strip shows
no check boxes and keeps whatever is checked; expanding the ledger shows the same set. **Each
night's box carries a tooltip naming the Export actions rather than any one of them**, because the
check now feeds every entry of the Export flyout and naming one would be wrong the moment a second
consumer exists; it shipped in Phase 14A naming the frame list alone, when there was only one. The
sentence is "Include this night in the Export actions".

The checked set lives on `TargetDetailViewModel.SelectedNights`, an observable collection of
session dates in the ledger's own order, and it is the spine the later phases consume: Phase 16's
WBPP export, Phase 18's mosaic assembly and Phase 21's AstroBin CSV each read it rather than
growing a selection of their own. It is not persisted: a selection is a step inside one visit to
the page, and restoring yesterday's checks would act on nights the user has forgotten checking.
Opening a different target clears it. Its consumers are Copy Frame List and, from Phase 16,
Export for stacking (section 12.13); every one of them is disabled while nothing is checked.

From Phase 21 the AstroBin CSV is its third consumer, on the same terms: it reads `SelectedNights`
and grows no selection of its own, and it is disabled while nothing is checked. It needs each
checked night's per-filter figures, which the ledger row does not carry, so it loads the session
detail for any checked night the page has not already opened before it builds a row. A night whose
detail fails to load is named in the result and contributes no row, rather than failing the whole
copy: the shape Copy Frame List's partial-load warning already uses.

From Phase 18 the Create mosaic dialog (section 12.17) is its fourth consumer, on the same terms.

**Create mosaic from selected nights (Phase 18, ruling R12).** The overflow menu's standing entries
are Rename, Merge into another target and Re-resolve; Phase 18 adds a fourth after them, a
`MenuItem` reading "Create mosaic from selected nights", above the separator that leads to the two
submenus below. It reads `SelectedNights` and opens the Create mosaic dialog of section 12.17 over
the checked nights. While nothing is checked it is disabled, with "Select one or more nights first"
on its tooltip, the sentence the Export flyout's entries already use. It is drawn for a resolved
target only, because an unresolved `obj:` group has no target id for a panel night to name.

**The two submenus on the overflow menu (Phase 21, rulings B5 and B9).** Below the standing
entries, behind a `Separator`, the overflow menu carries two submenu items, "Send to NINA" and
"Slew Stellarium", each hidden while its own instance list is empty and both hidden together with
the separator when neither carries anything. "Send to NINA" lists one entry per offered NINA
instance and "Slew Stellarium" one per offered Stellarium instance, each entry reading the
instance's own trimmed name, in the order the External Tools tab stores them (section 12.7). An
instance is offered when it is enabled, its name is non-blank after trimming, and its URL passes
the rule of section 12.16, one predicate (`IntegrationInstance.IsOffered`) the tab's caption and
the menu's filter both read, so a menu with nothing configured looks exactly as it does today.
Every entry is disabled, with the reason on its tooltip, while the target carries no RA or no Dec,
because there is nothing to send; the tooltip sentence is "This target has no coordinates to
send." The coordinates are the header block's own RA and Dec in degrees, and the position angle is
the header block's position angle, which is the catalogue's value for the object and is absent on
most targets (section 12.16 says what is done when it is). **The two submenus rebuild the moment
an instance is disabled, deleted, renamed, added or edited while the target page stays open**,
because the page subscribes to `SettingsStore.GeneralChanged`, routed to the UI thread the way
`DisplayChanged` already is, and rebuilds both lists from the freshly saved document on every
fire, not only at construction or at the next scan or navigation (ruling B32).

**The night's content** is the ledger's lit night. The ledger has no collapsed form. The night
header carries the night title and a facts line: gain, the exposure times present, the first and
last frame time, the median airmass, the median ambient temperature and the median humidity. The
night strip (section 13) follows, then the metrics chart, whose Guiding pill draws the night's
guide trace in the chart's own slot (see "The Guiding pill" below). There is no findings part
(Phase 24 R22): the session insights reach no view, and the frames chrome's Filter segment
carries one outlier pill per metric the night has values for, in the column order HFR, Ecc, FWHM,
Stars and RMS, labelled "HFR outliers (n)" with n the frames the night's own rule flagged, disabled
while n is 0 and checked while that filter is on, beside the rig pills and Clear filters. The
sentence comparing the night with the target's averages sits under the same "night medians against
target means" note in the Night metrics section. The per-filter table joins the per-filter medians (HFR, eccentricity, FWHM,
guiding RMS and detected stars) and the per-filter detail rows (filter name, frame count,
integration, median HFR, median eccentricity, exposure time) by filter name, and in the ledger's
lit row it uses the ledger's columns. The ranges table carries the minimum, median and maximum of
HFR, eccentricity, FWHM, guiding RMS and sensor temperature. The session notes box autosaves. The
frames part holds, in order, the grading tally line with the "Compare to" baseline segment at its
right, the frame table's toolbar line with the Filter segment, the band legend with its advisory
sentence, and the frame table, which takes the remaining height in its own row below the chrome. A pill's count counts frames: every frame the
night's own outlier rule flagged on that metric, which is the per-frame verdict the frame table's
outlier filter reads; the HFR and eccentricity flags are also what the row ink and the night
strip's tall ticks read.

**The Guiding pill (Phase 15B, reshaped by Phase 24 R3).** The night's guiding is a "Guiding"
pill at the end of the night chart's pill row, present on the night chart only (never on the
trend chart) and disabled on a night with no guide log. On, the chart's plot slot draws the
guide trace instead of the metric dots, the metric pills dim and keep their set, the filter
pills give their slot to the five-layer legend, and one line of the night's figures sits under
the pill row; off restores the dots and the filter pills unchanged. The pill's state is
`graph.show_guiding`, stored beside `enabled_metrics` and `enabled_filters` (section 5.8.3)
through the same writer. It mirrors two web surfaces at once,
`frontend/src/components/Phd2GuidingPanel.tsx` (the night rollup) and `Phd2GuideGraph.tsx` (the
plot), which the web renders as two sibling collapsible panels; the separate Guiding section the
port carried from Phase 15B to Phase 23, with its session picker and its calibration chips, is
gone. The view-model behind the pill is still `GuidingSectionViewModel`, which the card builds
and the chart is handed.

**Nothing loads until it opens.** The pill is enabled whenever the library holds at least one
`phd2_logs` row, and disabled otherwise, so a library that has never seen a guide log carries no
dead affordance on every night. That test is one `EXISTS` issued with the page's own queries,
not with the section's. Opening the night issues `Phd2NightQuery` for it, narrowed to this card's
rig when the night carries one and unfiltered when it carries several, which is where the web
narrows it: the session list and the rollup are both that rig's. The graph's own
`Phd2FramesQuery` is issued after it, once per drawable session of the night and never for a
session the graph cannot draw; a session read once is not read again for that night. Selecting a
different night reissues the night query for that night. The graph's view-model is constructed
the moment the night publishes, in every state the table below lists that has a session at all;
only the frames reads wait for a drawable session with the night open. The section constructs the
graph itself; `AppHost` carries no factory for it.

**The help glyph** at the end of the pill row is the chart's one glyph: it reads
`target.session-metrics` while the dots show and `target.guiding` while the pill is on (section
12.12's bound-site form, the id set read from `SessionChartViewModel.HelpTopicIds`).

**The summary figures**, from `Phd2Metrics.AggregateNight`, which Phase 15A already built
(section 7.6) and which the section reads rather than recomputing. One line of labelled figures
under the pill row, drawn only while the pill is on and reporting the whole night, in this order,
each figure in the `MetricText` convention the pane already uses, two decimals with the unit
spelled out and an absent value drawn as nothing rather than as a dash:

| Figure | Reading | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RMS | `rms_total_arcsec` in arcseconds, in `ColorMetricGuiding` | Frame-count weighted over the night's sessions of at least `MinFrames` frames (section 7.6). |
| RA | `rms_ra_arcsec` in arcseconds | Same weighting. |
| Dec | `rms_dec_arcsec` in arcseconds | Same weighting. |
| Sessions | `session_count`, followed by "(n too short to grade)" when `gated_session_count` is above zero | The gate is `MinFrames`, 100 frames. The parenthetical is absent at zero rather than reading "0 too short". |
| Star lost | `drop_count`, followed by "(t unguided, longest run r)" when `drop_count` is above zero | `t` is `unguided_seconds` in the compact duration form below; `r` is `max_drop_run`, a frame count. |
| Dithers | `dither_count` | Always drawn, including at zero. |
| Settle | `settle_median_s` to one decimal with a trailing "s", followed by "n failed" in `ColorWarningValue` when `settle_failed_count` is above zero | A null median draws nothing where the figure would be. |

The compact duration form is the web's `formatSecondsShort`
(`frontend/src/utils/phd2Format.ts` lines 9 to 21): below 60 seconds the rounded whole seconds
with an "s"; below an hour the whole minutes, and the seconds after them when they are not zero;
otherwise the whole hours, and the minutes after them when they are not zero. The branch is on
the raw value and not the rounded one, so 59.6 seconds reads "60s" and not "1m". It is the
guiding readout's own format and does not replace the integration formatter, which pads to
hours and minutes because it totals a whole night.

**The calibration issues.** The calibration chips went with the separate section (Phase 24 R3);
nothing on the night draws `phd2_sessions.last_cal_issue`. The section view-model still carries
`AggregateNight`'s `CalIssues` list unfiltered (a null, an empty string and the literal `None` in
any casing are excluded in `AggregateNight` and in one place only), so a later surface for it
starts from the list rather than from a second filter.

**The guide graph** is `Controls/GuideGraph.cs`, a drawn control in `NightStrip`'s manner
(section 13): rendered in `Render`, every brush handed in by the host through `DynamicResource`,
no colour literal in the source, and a headless render tick in its tests. It is not LiveCharts.
The view-model is `GuideGraphViewModel`, and every gesture the control handles is a thin call
into a pure function on it, so the transform is testable without a routed input event.

What it draws, back to front:

1. The settle bands, one filled rectangle per settle window, spanning the plot's full height, in
   `ColorBgHover` for an ordinary settle and in `ColorMetricWorst` at 0.15 opacity for a settle
   that failed. Both are existing tokens (section 14.1) and no token is added for this; the
   failed band's opacity is applied to the bound brush the way `CalendarHeatmap` builds its ramp
   from two bound colours. A window narrower than 2 pixels is drawn 2 pixels wide, so a settle
   that lasted one frame is still visible. The bands are clipped to the plot rectangle, which is
   what stops a zoomed-in view painting over the axis labels.
2. The axis, the grid and the zero line, the zero line in `ColorBorderEmphasis`.
3. The RA trace in `ColorMetricGuiding` and the Dec trace in `ColorMetricFwhm`, 1 pixel wide,
   with no point markers and no gap spanning: a frame with a null value breaks the line rather
   than being interpolated across.
4. The star-lost points, one 2.5 pixel dot in `ColorMetricWorst` on the zero line at every frame
   whose `dropped` flag is set.
5. The dither lines, one 1 pixel dashed vertical line per `dither` event in
   `ColorMetricEccentricity`, dash pattern 3 on and 3 off, clipped to the plot rectangle.

The web's own colour choices are these five, from `Phd2GuideGraph.tsx` lines 58 to 61 and 436,
and the port keeps them rather than re-deciding a palette that already reads as one system.

**The settle windows** are derived from the session's stored `events` array by the same pairing
the web's `settleWindows` performs (`frontend/src/utils/phd2Guide.ts` lines 80 to 102): a
`settle_start` opens a window, the next `settle_done` or `settle_failed` closes it and decides
whether it is the failed form, a second `settle_start` with one already open closes the first as
an ordinary window at the second's time, a completion with no start is dropped, and a window
still open at the end is closed at the session's last frame time as an ordinary window. This is
a presentation window, drawn from the same `events` array section 7.6's metric window rule
reads; the two are deliberately different questions and the metric rule stays the one that
decides which frames an RMS counted.

**The transform.** Two windows on the view-model, a time window in elapsed seconds since the
earliest session's first frame and an arcsecond window, each applied in `Render` and each null
while it shows everything there is. On the night chart the time window at rest is the night's
shared axis, first frame to last (section 13's lane axis): every guide session of the night is
offset onto that one time base and drawn where its clock time falls, clipped outside the plot,
with the trace broken between sessions rather than joined across the gap. The figures are the
web's:

| Quantity | Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wheel step | 0.82 per notch, and its reciprocal outward | `Phd2GuideGraph.tsx` line 65 |
| Narrowest time window | 10 seconds | `phd2Guide.ts` line 126 |
| Narrowest arcsecond window | 0.1 arcseconds of total span | `phd2Guide.ts` line 138 |
| Arcsecond headroom at full zoom | 8 percent of the bound | `phd2Guide.ts` line 146 |
| Furthest the arcsecond axis zooms out | 10 times its own full width | `phd2Guide.ts` line 155 |
| Plotted points | at most 2,000 | `Phd2GuideGraph.tsx` line 63 |

The arcsecond axis is zero centred, its half-height being the largest absolute RA or Dec
excursion of the **whole** session rounded up to a tenth, with a floor of 1 arcsecond
(`phd2Guide.ts` lines 285 to 293), so panning the time axis never makes the vertical scale jump
and a spike stays visibly a spike. Zooming a window keeps the value under the pointer under the
pointer; a window is clamped to the data range without changing its width, so panning past
either end parks against the edge; and a window wider than the range, which only the arcsecond
axis can reach, is centred on the range instead.

**The gestures**, all on the control and all delegating to the view-model:

| Gesture | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl and wheel | Zooms the time axis about the pointer. A window back at the full width drops the override rather than being held at it. |
| Ctrl, Shift and wheel | Zooms the arcsecond axis about the pointer. Only a window back at the data's own width drops the override: wider than that is a zoomed-out reading of a calm night and is kept. |
| Left button drag | Pans whichever axis is zoomed. Dragging right moves the time window earlier, so the data follows the pointer; dragging down raises the arcsecond window, because pixels run down and arcseconds run up. A drag does nothing while both axes show everything, since there is no slack to take up. |
| Double click | Resets both axes. |
| Wheel | Scrolls the "Night detail" body under the pointer, as everywhere else in the application (section 5.1's wheel rule). The control leaves a plain wheel unhandled. |

A reload of the night clears both windows: they described the night the reader left. A zoom or a
drag takes the graph off the shared axis; the double click brings it back.

**Downsampling** runs over the visible window and not over the whole session, so zooming in
resolves a spike rather than magnifying the bucket average that survived a first pass. The
reduction is the web's min and max preserving bucket walk (`phd2Guide.ts` lines 31 to 73): the
bucket count is the point budget over three, and each bucket contributes the frame with the
largest absolute RA error, the frame with the largest absolute Dec error and its first dropped
frame, plus both endpoints so the time span never shrinks. A plain stride is refused, because it
erases exactly the excursions the graph exists to show. It runs once per session of the night,
because a bucket spanning two sessions would keep one frame of each and join them across the gap.

**The hover readout.** Pointing at the plot names the nearest frame on the time axis: its clock
time to the second as the heading, then one line per visible trace reading the trace's name and
its value in arcseconds, and the line "Star lost" alone for a dropped frame. It is the night
strip's hit test in another geometry, nearest on one axis and not requiring an intersection, and
it is the tooltip surface the drawn controls already share; a hidden trace contributes no line.

**The clock** of the hover readout is the **display** timezone (`general.timezone`), the same
setting the frame table and every other clock on the page read, so the readout and the timeline
above cannot disagree with one another. It is not the observer's zone: on a fresh profile, where
the display zone is still the machine's, a session PHD2 wrote at 21:59 local reads "8:29 AM",
which is correct by this rule and easy to misread as a bug until the display timezone is set to
match the observer's. The range caption of the separate section is not drawn on the chart: the
timeline carries the night's clock and the figures line carries the night's length in sessions.

**The slot** is the night chart's own, the lane under the timeline, 180 pixels by default and
sized by the lanes handle, which gives the chart whatever its height leaves under the timeline
(`lanes_height`, section 12.4);
the guide graph has no grip and no height key of its own, `guide_graph_height` having been
retired by polish wave 6.

**No session picker.** Every guide session of the night is drawn on the night axis at once, so
there is nothing to pick; `sessionOptionLabel` (`Phd2GuideGraph.tsx` lines 86 to 95) is kept on
the view-model and bound nowhere. A session that cannot be drawn (no frame, or no pixel scale)
is left out without a frames read, and a night of short sessions is still plotted, it simply has
no gradeable RMS behind it.

**The rig rule.** The night query selects the card's own rig's sessions through
`Phd2Metrics.SelectNightRows`, the one implementation of the mapped-or-sole-unmapped rule
section 7.6 states, and a card whose own night carries several rigs draws the whole night. A rig
label is the session's mapped `telescope`, falling back to its `equipment_profile` when the
profile is unmapped. The web panel's own rig filter combo box is not surfaced on the chart; its
local partition stays on the view-model unbound, and no second copy of `SelectNightRows`'s rule
is written for it.

**The legend** takes the filter pills' slot in the pill row while the pill is on: five entries in
this order, RA, Dec, Star lost, Dither and Settling, each a swatch and a label, each a toggle. A
hidden entry is struck through and its layer is not drawn at all rather than drawn dimmed, and
the entries keep their state while the pill is off and restore it when it comes back. The entries
are the same five layers the draw list above names, which is why Dither and Settling appear in a
legend although they are overlays rather than series.

**The states, and how they combine.** With the pill on, the line under the pill row and the slot
are decided in this order, first match winning, so a night that is several of these at once reads
as the most specific one:

| State | What the chart shows |
| --- | --- |
| The night is not open | Nothing is laid out and nothing is queried. |
| The night query is in flight | "Loading this night's guiding..." under the pill row, because the read is a SQLite call off the UI thread and the chart says so rather than rendering an empty slot while it runs, the same argument the empty and failed rows below make. |
| The night has no guiding session | "No PHD2 guide logs for this night." No figures, no plot. |
| Sessions exist, the first gradeable one has no frame | The figures, then "No guide frames for this session." under them. |
| Sessions exist, the first gradeable one has a null `pixel_scale_arcsec` | The figures, then "No pixel scale in this session's log header, so guiding error cannot be shown in arcseconds." under them. This is the ASIAIR case of section 7.6, and the notice is read off the session row, so no frame query is issued for it. |
| Sessions exist and one is drawable | Everything: the figures, the legend and the plot with every drawable session on the night axis. |
| Every session of the night is short | Everything, with "(n too short to grade)" on the Sessions figure and, when no session cleared the gate, no RMS figures at all, because a weighted RMS over an empty set is null and a null figure draws nothing. |
| The night query failed | One line in the warning ink under the pill row. The rest of the pane is unaffected: a guide-log failure never takes the night down. |

The empty and the failed cases say so under the pill row and leave the pill on, because a slot
that silently empties when its query returns nothing reads as one that is broken.

**Departures from the web, all deliberate.** The two web panels are one pill on the night chart
here, and the night is drawn whole rather than one picked session at a time (Phase 24 R3). The
plot is a drawn control rather than Chart.js with two hand-written plugins, and it has the
chart's slot rather than a height of its own. The no-pixel-scale notice is decided from the
session row rather than from a frames response that came back full of nulls, so the port issues
no query it already knows the answer to. The figures line prints the port's `MetricText` form,
two decimals and the word, rather than the web's double-prime glyph, which is the convention
every other arcsecond figure on this page already follows; the plot's hover readout keeps the
web's glyph, because it annotates a plot rather than stating a figure on the page. A null settle
median draws nothing where the web draws its missing glyph, which is this page's convention for
an absent figure. The web's range caption is not drawn.

**The night strip's active tick (Phase 14C, user ruling U1).** On a night with many close-set
ticks the one under the pointer is hard to place, so the strip marks which tick is active.
Active means the tick under the pointer and, at rest, the tick of the frame the table has
selected or the preview has open, so the strip and the table point at the same frame in both
directions; P13's R9 carried only the direction from the strip to the table, where a tick's
hover tints the matching frame row and scrolls it into view and a tick's click selects the
frame and opens the preview (`Controls/NightStrip.cs` already tracks the hovered frame index
through `SetHover` and `NightStripViewModel.HoverFrame`, and draws nothing for it). When
neither a hover, a table selection nor an open preview names a frame, nothing is drawn for
this: the strip degrades to its Phase 12 and 13 shape. The active tick draws taller than its
neighbours, past the band at both ends, at 2 pixels wide, in the primary ink, with a small
drawn caret on the axis beneath it; every other tick keeps its filter colour untouched, no
fill, no glow and no dimming of the rest, so `DESIGN.md` section 8's refusals of an accent hue
carrying state and of a second highlight layer both hold.

Three mechanisms as built. The hover wins over the resting selection while a pointer is on the
strip, and the strip repaints on both, so leaving the strip takes the mark with it. "The preview
has open" is reached **through the table's selection** rather than through a channel of its own:
every path that opens the preview from this pane also selects that frame in the frame table, and
the strip reads `FrameTableViewModel.SelectedCaptureIndex`, so the preview clause holds through
that proxy and no second wire exists. The active pass and its caret draw **after** the band's edge
labels, so an active first or last tick is not overpainted by a label; the labels themselves did
not move. And the ink is a bound brush with no fallback colour, so a host that binds nothing
degrades the active tick to its ordinary or outlier geometry rather than painting it invisible.

When the active frame is also an outlier frame, the primary ink the active tick draws in and
the worse ink an outlier tick draws in (`ColorMetricWorst`, the ink this section's "tall
ticks" already use) would otherwise land on the same tick. Active wins: the tick draws taller,
past the band, in the primary ink, with its caret, for as long as it is active, because the
height and the caret already say "this is the frame you are pointing at or have open"
independent of colour, and the frame's outlier status stays legible at the same moment on the
frame table's row ink and outlier filter and on the frames chrome's outlier pills, which
the paragraph above already states reads the same per-frame verdict the strip does. This priority
was put to the user at the 12.4 approval and the user named no ink, so the text stood and it is
what shipped (HANDOFF 5.1 item 9g). No new theme token was needed: the active tick's ink is
`ColorTextPrimary`, already declared (section 14.1).

The session insights are the same set the accordion card reported, relative to the session baseline
and to the rig baseline: three session-wide kinds in a fixed order, HFR outliers, eccentricity
outliers and eccentricity against the rig baseline, and then, on a night that more than one rig
imaged, the first two repeated per rig in rig order, which is first capture time within the night, and
prefixed with the rig's label. The
eccentricity-against-rig kind stays silent when the session's pooled source differs from the rig
baseline's, because the two scales are not comparable (section 7.2). Only the first line of each
outlier kind carries the frame-table filter, per ruling Q8: the per-frame flags carry the
session-wide rule only, so a rig line claiming the same filter would be a second answer about the
same rows.

A filter imaged at more than one exposure length is one medians row with a sub-row per exposure,
and that medians row's frame count and integration are the totals of its sub-rows.

**Per-night reference thumbnails** (PAR-008). The thumbnail strip is the first row of the "Night
detail" section, above that section's comparison sentence, holding one box per rig, which on the
ordinary single-rig night is one box. It is in that section rather than in the pane's fixed rows
(the user's ruling of 2026-09-18) because the section is closed by default: a fresh profile at
1280x800 keeps the "Night detail" band and the "Frames" band on screen at rest, and the thumbnails
appear when the reader opens the section that describes them.

**The box keeps the frame's aspect ratio and is never cropped.** It is bounded at 120 pixels high
and 240 pixels wide, and the image is fitted inside that bound with its own aspect preserved, the
`Uniform` stretch, which is what the web calls object-contain
(`frontend/src/components/ReferenceThumbnail.tsx`, whose fill mode is a maximum height with an
automatic width and whose card mode is object-contain under a maximum height; neither crops). A
3:2 landscape frame therefore renders 180 by 120, a 4:3 renders 160 by 120, a 3:2 portrait renders
80 by 120, and a frame wider than 2:1 is bounded by the width instead and falls below 120 high.
The 120 pixel bound is a 6.7 times reduction of the 800 pixel cached source
(`general.thumbnail_width`), which is enough to tell a galaxy from a nebula from an empty field,
and the 240 pixel width cap is what keeps a panorama from taking the row.

**Arrangement.** The boxes sit left aligned in rig order with an 8 pixel gap, on one line while
the row's width admits them all, wrapping to further lines in the same order when it does not.
That is one rule and it covers every case: at the shipped 1280 by 800 window the session pane is
about 490 pixels wide and two boxes at the 240 pixel cap plus the gap are 488, so a two-rig night
is side by side there and a narrower pane or a third rig stacks. Nothing is scaled down to force a
fit, because a thumbnail shrunk to fit answers the question less well than a thumbnail on the next
line.

**The source frame is ranked by quality**, not by recency. The candidate set is the LIGHT frames
of that night, and on a multi-rig night the LIGHT frames of that rig alone. The pick is the frame
with the lowest non-null, non-zero `median_hfr`, which is the same column the ledger, the frame
table and the grading read, so the sharpest frame of the night is the one the night shows. A tie
on that value goes to the newer capture time. When no frame of the set carries a `median_hfr` at
all, the set falls back to section 11.4's rule and takes the newest LIGHT frame with a capture
date, which is the case a night scanned before any metric was derived lands in.

The decode walk keeps 11.4's shape. At most three frames are tried, in the ranked order above,
and a frame whose pixels do not decode is skipped and the next candidate tried; after three
failures the box renders the "No thumbnail" placeholder. A frame skipped this way is not marked,
flagged or written to: the walk is a read that did not work, not a verdict about the file.

The walk is on demand, which is section 11.4's own rule for a frame thumbnail. It starts when the
"Night detail" section first opens, or at once when a night is loaded into an already open
section, and it is kept once started, so reopening the section costs nothing and a section the
reader never opens costs no render at all. A cache hit costs nothing either way.

The pick is made by `SessionDetailQuery`, which already returns the reference frame id per night
and per rig, so nothing on this page ranks frames a second time. `ThumbnailCache` generates the
file under `frames/`, keyed the way every frame thumbnail is keyed: by the content key
`ThumbnailKey.For` builds from the frame's full path, its length, its last write time and the
render width (section 11.3), not by the image id. That is what makes it the same file the frame
table's own preview of that frame would use, so no second cache directory appears and a re-saved
frame keys differently rather than serving a stale picture. The reference thumbnail of a target is
the one render keyed by a GUID, because it is keyed on the target rather than on a frame.

This selection differs from the web's and the difference is deliberate. The web picks the session
thumbnail as `images[0]`, the earliest frame of the night by capture date, and only when that
frame already has a cached `thumbnail_path`, otherwise it shows nothing
(`backend/app/services/target_detail.py`); its per-rig thumbnail is the first frame of that rig
that happens to have one (`backend/app/services/target_helpers.py`). Neither of those two ranks by
quality. The nearest web precedent is `select_best_frame` in
`backend/app/services/mosaic_composite.py`, which orders by lowest non-zero `median_hfr` exactly
as the rule above does, and which the web reaches for mosaic panels rather than for a session
thumbnail. The port takes that ranking and omits its second step, a fallback to the highest
`CENTALT`: altitude is not stored as a column for every frame, and a fallback that reads
`raw_headers` per candidate would make a thumbnail pick pay for a JSON parse it does not need. The
port's fallback is 11.4's newest rule instead. So where the web shows whichever frame happened to
be cached first, this page shows the sharpest frame it can decode, and it generates that
thumbnail rather than waiting for something else to have generated it, so a night always has a
picture and never a blank where a cache miss used to be.

A night, or a rig, whose frames all fail pixel reading renders a "No thumbnail" placeholder in the
same box at a 3:2 default aspect, 180 by 120, outlined, with the words in the tertiary ink; the
placeholder is not a failure message and carries no retry. Clicking a thumbnail opens the preview
modal (section 11.5) at that frame, inside the night's frame list, so the arrow keys step through
the night from there.

The target's own reference thumbnail, 128 pixels square in the header block and in the Details
panel, is unchanged by any of this: it answers what the target looks like, and these answer what
the night captured, which on a target imaged over two years are different pictures. It still
follows section 11.4's newest-decodable rule, and section 11.4 itself is unchanged by this phase;
ranking the target's own thumbnail by quality as well is a separate decision and is not taken
here.

The strip is laid out only while the "Night detail" section is open. It is inside the section's
body, which the height contract caps and scrolls inside, as every row of that section is, and it
reserves nothing at rest because a collapsed section is not laid out at all. Opening the section
lengthens the body by the strip and the rows below it, and the body scrolls past its cap, which
is the degradation that contract already specifies; the chart keeps its floor or collapses, as that
contract says, either way.

**A multi-rig night** (PAR-004) is a night whose frames carry more than one rig, a rig being the
(telescope, camera) pair after alias mapping, as this section's terms define it. The rigs are
ordered by first capture time within the night and labelled with the equipment's canonical names;
the label's index is the rig index every surface below reads. On such a night:

1. The facts line names the rigs, in that order, before the figures it already carries.
2. The per-filter table and the ranges table split per rig (ruling C4). Each rig's block opens
   with a rig label row, a full-width row in the table's own grid carrying the rig's label in the
   `section` type and its frame count, and the filter rows follow under it. The columns and their
   shared size groups are unchanged, so the two blocks stay aligned with each other. A
   single-rig night renders exactly as it does today: no label row, no block, one table.
   **Phase 20 adds the rig-scope custom column cells to that label row** (section 12.15), after
   the frame count, one cell per rig-scope column in display order, each preceded by a caption
   carrying its column's name and each writing a value keyed by this target, this night and that
   rig's label. The cells are drawn on the **per-filter** table's label row alone, the first table
   of the pane; the ranges table's own label row carries its label and its frame count and no
   cell, because two editors over one stored value fall out of step. While at least one rig-scope
   custom column exists, the label row is drawn on a **single-rig** night too, on both tables,
   carrying that rig's label, its frame count and, on the first table, the cells, because a rig
   column is otherwise unreachable on a one-telescope library; with no rig-scope column defined, a
   single-rig night renders exactly as the sentence above says.
3. The frame table gains a Rig column, placed after Time, and a row of rig pills in its toolbar
   that filters the rows to the checked rigs. The Rig column is not a `FrameColumns` entry and is
   not a `display.columns.frames` key, as the note at the end of this section's column table
   states: it is drawn only on a multi-rig night and it is not hideable. The pills are the
   `ToggleButton` style section 13 already uses for the chart toggles, all checked on open, and
   the last of them may be unchecked, which empties the table rather than being refused. The
   rig filter and the outlier filter compose: a row is shown when both admit it, and the toolbar's
   shown count reports the result. A single-rig night draws no Rig column and no pills.
4. Both charts gain rig toggles and one dash pattern per rig index (section 13).
5. The "Night detail" section's thumbnail strip carries one box per rig rather than one for the
   night, each the sharpest LIGHT frame of that rig's own frames by the ranking above, in rig
   order, each at its own aspect ratio and each with its own placeholder, laid out by the wrapping
   rule above.
6. The session insights already repeat their first two kinds per rig, prefixed with the rig's
   label, as this section states below. That behaviour is unchanged and is the model the rest of
   the split follows.

No figure on a multi-rig night pools two rigs silently. The ledger row and the log line still
report the night as one set, because they compare a night against the target and that is the
question they answer; every per-rig figure lives in the pane, where the rig it belongs to is named
beside it.

**Per-frame quality grading** (PAR-003) grades each metric cell of the frame table against a
robust baseline rather than a fixed threshold, in raw MAD units (ruling C2). The math is
`GalactiLog.Core.Metrics.FrameQuality`, which the session insights and the Statistics MADs already
read, so a sentence and a table on this page cannot contradict each other.

A baseline is a (telescope, camera, filter) group's median and median absolute deviation for one
metric, over the frames of that group. A frame's deviation is the signed quantity
`(value - median) / max(mad, 1e-9)`, with the sign flipped for a metric where a higher value is
better, so a positive number always means worse than the baseline. The deviation is null, and the
cell is ungraded, when the value is null, when the group holds fewer than 8 non-null values for
that metric (`FrameQuality.MinGroup`), or when the group is uniform and its MAD is 0. These are
raw MAD units, not sigma: there is no 1.4826 consistency scaling anywhere in this port or in the
web application, and one MAD unit is about 0.67 sigma on a normal sample. Every label, tooltip and
help paragraph in this port says "MAD units" and never says sigma, which corrects the web's own
wording in `SessionAccordionCard.tsx`.

| Band | Deviation z | Ink |
| --- | --- | --- |
| better | at or below -1.0 | `ColorSuccessValue` |
| neutral | above -1.0 and below 1.5, and every ungraded cell | `ColorTextPrimary`, which is to say no mark |
| watch | at or above 1.5 and below 3.0 | `ColorWarningValue` |
| reject | at or above 3.0 | `ColorErrorValue` |

The three inks are three of the four semantic `*Value` colours section 14 defines, so a theme
carries the bands with no new token. The table above names the colours; the markup binds
`ColorSuccess`, `ColorWarning` and `ColorError`, which are the `SolidColorBrush` resources built
from exactly those three colours, because a `Foreground` takes a brush and not a colour. The
colour and its brush are the same token. The band is carried by the cell's ink alone. No cell and
no row takes a tinted fill (ruling C3, and `DESIGN.md`'s refusal list).

Where a band and an outlier flag land on the same figure, the flag wins on a frame table cell and
the band wins on a preview badge. That is not two rules but one mechanism read twice: both marks
are style classes, Avalonia applies the nearest style host last, and the frame table declares its
cell inks in its own view while the band block lives in `Theme/Controls.axaml`, so on a cell the
view's flag ink outranks the application-level band, and on a preview badge, where both styles are
application level, the band block wins because it is declared after `TextBlock.worse`. Each
outcome is what its own section asks for: a flagged cell answers "this night's rules flagged this
frame" (below) and a graded badge answers "how far from the baseline this value sits" (section
11.5). The difference is unobservable on the reject band, where `ColorMetricWorst` and
`ColorErrorValue` are the same colour in every theme.

**Compare to** is a two-button segment in the Frames section's own header row, reading "This
session" and "This rig". This session builds the baselines from the selected night's own frames.
This rig builds them from every frame captured with the same telescope, camera and filter across
the library, whatever the target, served from `RigBaselinesCache`. The choice persists in
`display.target_page.grading_baseline` and applies to the whole page, so switching nights keeps
it. It governs the sharpness and roundness metrics only, which is HFR, eccentricity and FWHM. The
signal metrics, detected stars, median ADU and guiding RMS, are always graded against the night's
own baseline whichever way the toggle is set, because they drift with the sky and a catalogue-wide
baseline for them would grade the weather. The help paragraph for the section states this, so the
toggle never appears to be doing less than it is.

**The row score** is one number per frame, combining three axes: signal from detected stars
(higher is better), sharpness from HFR, roundness from eccentricity, weighted 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25.
An axis whose deviation is null is dropped and the remaining weights are renormalised to sum to 1;
a frame with no axis at all has no score. The weighted mean deviation is clamped to the range -3
to 3 and mapped to `50 - 16.7 * z`, giving a 0 to 100 figure where higher is better. The score's
own band is: 60 and above better, 45 to 60 neutral, 30 to 45 watch, below 30 reject, the same four
names the cells use.

The score is drawn as a 2 pixel rule down the row's leading edge in the band's ink, not as a fill
(ruling C3). A row with no score draws no rule. The rule sits in the row's own first column, the
way the lit row's selection edge does, so turning it on shifts no cell. A row the session's own
outlier rules flagged still lifts its whole line to the primary ink and renders the offending
figure in `metric-worst`, exactly as before this phase: that mark answers "this night's rules
flagged this frame" and the band answers "how far from the baseline this value sits", and the two
are deliberately different marks. The outlier filter, the pills' counts and the night strip's
tall ticks all keep reading the flags, not the bands.

**The tally** is one line above the frame table: the good, watch and reject counts of the loaded
night's frames by row-score band, each in its band's ink, followed by the mean score to the
nearest whole number. Better and neutral are counted together as good, which is what makes three
counts out of four bands. Frames with no score are in no count and the line states how many were
left ungraded when there are any. The line is recomputed when the baseline toggle flips.

**The cell tooltip** on a graded cell reads, for example: `HFR 2.80, 1.9 MAD units worse than the
session median 2.10`. The parts are the column's label, the value in the column's own format, the
absolute deviation to one decimal, the word worse or better, the baseline named by the toggle
("session" or "rig"), and the baseline's median in the same format. A cell whose deviation is
null, whose value is null, or whose baseline has no median carries no grading tooltip at all,
rather than one that says nothing: an empty claim reads as a claim.

**The legend** sits under the frames toolbar line, above the column header: two dots in the
watch and reject inks labelled watch and
reject (Phase 24 R23 dropped the better and neutral entries; a cell in either band carries no
mark), then the sentence "Grading is advisory. No frame is deleted or hidden." The sentence
is not optional chrome. This application writes no user file (section 2.1), and a page that
colours frames red owes the reader that statement where the colour is.

The session detail query is issued when a night is selected, not up front, and the page selects
the night it was constructed with, or the newest night when it was given none, so exactly one query runs
for the page's first paint. A night that has been selected once keeps its loaded detail, so moving
back to it is free.

**Opening the page** (PAR-018) is `MainWindowViewModel.OpenDetail(string groupKey, DateOnly?
sessionDate = null)`. The shell builds a new page per navigation, so the night is a construction
argument rather than a method on a live page: `TargetDetailViewModel` takes a trailing optional
`DateOnly? initialSessionDate`, the shell's page factory is
`Func<string, DateOnly?, TargetDetailViewModel>`, and `TargetDetailViewModel.LedgerScrollTarget`
is the seam the view reads to scroll the ledger to the chosen row. There is no
`TargetDetailViewModel.Open`.

A null date selects the newest night, which is every route that exists today and is unchanged
behaviour. A non-null date selects that night if the ledger holds it and scrolls the ledger to it;
a date the target has no night for falls back to the newest night rather than leaving the pane
empty, and no error is shown, because the caller is another surface of this same application and a
stale date there is not the user's mistake. Phase 14B's dashboard session rows are the first
caller to pass a date; later phases pass one from their own listings. There is no URL, no query
string and no navigation stack: the page is the shell's single overlay (section 12).

**Keyboard.** Ctrl+D toggles the Details panel, F2 begins a rename, Alt+Left goes Back, and Ctrl+C
inside the frame table copies the selected paths. Escape inside the frame table clears the outlier
filter, then the selection; with neither to clear it reaches the page, where it closes the Details
panel and otherwise goes Back. Escape while a text box has focus belongs to the box.

Escape while the object type editor is open cancels that edit, before the Details panel and before
Back, and it does so wherever the focus sits: opening the editor puts the keyboard on the combo
box, and a reader who clicks the pencil and then clicks elsewhere still cancels with Escape. There
is one mechanism for it, a tunnelling key handler on the page, and it has to be tunnelling: the
Details panel is a light-dismissable `SplitView` whose own handler closes the pane on Escape and
marks the key handled before the page's class handler runs, so a term added to the page's bubbling
handler never sees the key. The tunnelling handler consults `Handled`, fires only while the editor
is open, and carries the same text-editor guard the paragraph above describes. The combo box
declares no Escape handler of its own, so the edit has one cancel path and not two.

Known limit, and not to be re-litigated without reading the mechanism: the text-editor guard covers
Escape only. Ctrl+D, F2 and Alt+Left are `KeyBinding` shortcuts on the page, and Avalonia evaluates
a `KeyBinding` before the focused control's own key handler and without consulting `Handled`, so
neither a guard in the page's key handler nor a tunnelling handler that marks the key handled stops
them. F2 with the caret in the drawer's notes box or either session notes box therefore begins a
rename over the user's typing. Moving all three gestures into a guarded dispatch in the code-behind
fixes F2 and Ctrl+D and loses Alt+Left to the access-key path, which trades the defect for a
regression, so the markup bindings stand. A real fix needs Avalonia's Alt routing understood
first.

The view-model members that only the retired accordion card bound are deleted with it. From
`SessionCardViewModel`: `FilterMedians`, `FilterDetails`, `Insights`, `CameraText`, `TelescopeText`,
`EccentricitySourceText`, `HasEccentricitySource`, `HasDetail`, `HasMedianAirmass`,
`HasMedianAmbientTemp`, `HasMedianHumidity`, `ComparisonText`, `IsMultiRig`, `RigCount`,
`RigCountText`, `HasNotesIndicator` and `FiltersText`. From `TargetTotalsViewModel`:
`FilterDotsText`, `LogLineText`, the five `Avg*Text` figures, the five matching `Has*` flags,
`HasFilters`, `HasEquipment`, `EccentricityDisclosure`, `HasEccentricityDisclosure`,
`IntegrationText`, `SessionCountText`, `FirstSessionText`, `LastSessionText`, `FiltersText` and
`EquipmentText`. Three types went with them: `FilterMediansViewModel`, `FilterDetailRowViewModel`
and `SessionInsightViewModel`. The surfaces that survive are the ledger row, the session pane and
the log line, and the cases that pinned the deleted members were re-pointed onto those surfaces
rather than dropped.

**Frame table columns**, from the `SortHeader` list in the web `SessionAccordionCard.tsx`. Every
column is sortable ascending and descending. Visibility persists in
`display.columns.frames` (section 5.8.2) and is additionally governed by the display settings
metric groups, so a group turned off hides its columns everywhere.

Every column auto-fits the widest cell of the whole loaded night plus its header, measured
from every captured frame rather than from the filtered subset, so applying or clearing the
outlier filter never resizes it (P13 R6, generalised by P24 R5). It is recomputed when the
night's own frame set changes or a column is toggled, not on every sort or every filter change.
Each header cell carries a drag divider at its right edge: a drag sets that column's width live
and stores it per profile in `display.column_widths.frames` (section 5.8.2), where it wins over
the auto-fit on every later night until a double-click on the divider clears it and refits the
column; no drag goes under the 48 px floor. The file name column never trims: the full path is
on the cell's own tooltip, and a name wider than the pane widens the row, which the frame
table's existing horizontal scroll already covers.

Rows carry a multiple selection. The table's toolbar holds the shown and selected counts,
"Copy paths (n)", "Reveal", which is enabled at exactly one selected row because
`explorer.exe /select` highlights one file, and the column visibility picker. A row whose HFR or
eccentricity the session's own outlier rules flagged lifts its whole line to the primary ink and
renders the offending figure alone in `metric-worst`; nothing else about the row changes. The
outlier pills in the frames chrome filter the table to their own flagged rows, one filter at a
time, and the flagged row count equals the pill's count by construction, because
`SessionDetailQuery` returns the per-frame verdict it already computed rather than a count alone:
the HFR rule (the session median times 1.5) and the MAD rule (at or beyond 3 MAD on the bad side
of the group's session median) over eccentricity, FWHM, detected stars (few is bad) and guiding
RMS, as `IsHfrOutlier`, `IsEccentricityOutlier`, `IsFwhmOutlier`, `IsStarsOutlier` and
`IsGuidingRmsOutlier` on each frame row. The table's selected row is a lighter field
and a 2 pixel lit edge with no ink change, while the ledger's selected row adds the accent ink:
the ledger's selection names what the pane beside it is showing, the table's names what the next
action will copy.

A plain left click on a row selects that one row and opens the preview at it (P13 R8). Ctrl-click
and Shift-click extend the selection and open nothing. Keyboard navigation and Ctrl+A move or
extend the selection and open nothing, the same as before this phase. The row-end flyout's "Open
preview" item is unchanged and still opens the preview at that row regardless of the selection.

| Group | Columns (display key) |
| --- | --- |
| always | Time, File name, Filter (`filter_used`), Exp (`exposure_time`) |
| `quality` | HFR (`median_hfr`), Ecc (`eccentricity`), FWHM (`fwhm`), Stars (`detected_stars`) |
| `guiding` | RMS (`guiding_rms_arcsec`), RMS RA (`guiding_rms_ra_arcsec`), RMS Dec (`guiding_rms_dec_arcsec`) |
| `adu` | ADU Mean, ADU Med, ADU sigma, ADU Min, ADU Max |
| `focuser` | Focus (`focuser_position`), Focus Temp (`focuser_temp`) |
| `weather` | Amb Temp, Dew Pt, Humidity, Pressure, Wind, Wind Dir, Gust, Clouds, SQM |
| `mount` | Airmass, Pier, Rotator |
| always | Temp (`sensor_temp`), Gain |

**Guiding provenance (Phase 15A).** A guiding RMS cell whose row carries
`guiding_rms_source = 'phd2'` is followed by a dagger, U+2020, in the secondary ink at the
`t-label` scale, with no space before it. The glyph is present in all six embedded Atkinson
Hyperlegible Next and Mono faces under `src/GalactiLog.App/Assets/Fonts`, verified against the
font tables, so it renders in every theme and at every text size without a fallback face
(ruling F4). Were a future face to drop it, the replacement is a superscript `PHD2` tag in the
same ink, and nothing else about the rule changes.

**Alignment.** The dagger sits against the digits with no space, and it lives in **its own box
beside a right-aligned value box**, not inside the value box and not as a trailing character of
the formatted string. So a marked figure and an unmarked one in the same column share one right
edge: the digits line up and the dagger hangs outside them. This holds in the frame table and in
the ledger row alike, and it is why a column of mixed sources does not read as ragged. The mark
box reserves its width whether or not it draws, for the same reason.

**Accessibility.** The dagger is decorative to a screen reader and is excluded from the
accessible tree. The value's accessible name reads the figure first and then the sentence, in
that order, so a reader hears the number before its provenance. The visible tooltip carries the
same sentence.

The sentence is `from a PHD2 guide log`. A cell whose source is `csv` carries no glyph, because
the CSV sidecar is the frame's own file and needs no disclosure; the dagger marks the figure
that was measured somewhere other than beside the frame.

**The night-level summary.** The session pane carries the same mark and one sentence, computed
from the night's frames rather than from one frame, over the frames that **carry a guiding RMS**.
A frame with no RMS never counts towards the verdict either way: it has no source to disclose.
The unqualified sentence appears **only when every RMS-bearing frame of the night is `phd2`**.
Any RMS-bearing frame whose source is `csv`, is null, or holds a value this build does not
recognise makes the sentence the qualified one. A null source on a frame that carries an RMS
cannot occur under the invariant of section 5.2, and the qualified reading is what the summary
falls back to if one ever does, because claiming every frame came from a guide log when one
demonstrably did not is the worse failure.

**The pane's line carries no guiding figure.** Section 12.4's own session pane paragraph defines
the facts line as gain, the exposure times present, the first and last frame time, the median
airmass, the median ambient temperature and the median humidity: there is no guiding figure on
it, and Phase 15A does not add one, because the night's RMS is already in the ledger row beside
the pane. What ships is **the sentence alone, appended after the existing facts**, with the
dagger against it.

| Values present among the night's RMS-bearing frames | Pane's facts line gains | Dagger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `csv` only | Nothing | no |
| `phd2` only | "from a PHD2 guide log" | yes |
| `phd2` together with any `csv`, null or unrecognised source | "from a PHD2 guide log for some frames" | yes |
| no RMS-bearing frame at all | Nothing | no |

The last row adds nothing rather than an empty badge, which is the rule the night strip already
follows for a null metric. The same four-way summary is computed once, by `TargetDetailQuery`,
and read by both the pane and the ledger cells, so the two cannot disagree about a night.

The Rig column a multi-rig night adds (PAR-004) is not one of these columns and is not a
`display.columns.frames` key: it is drawn only when the night has more than one rig, it is not
hideable, and the 32 keys section 5.8.2 lists are unchanged. The same holds for the row-score rule
(PAR-003), which is the row's leading edge rather than a column. Adding either to the picker would
offer a control that does nothing on the single-rig nights that are most of a library.

Per-frame actions: open preview (section 11.5), reveal in Explorer, open with default
application, copy path, show raw headers.

**Raw header panel.** A per-frame expander listing every key in `raw_headers`, sorted, with
a filter box. `COMMENT` and `HISTORY` render as multi-line blocks, since they are stored as
arrays (section 6.1.2). Below it, a "Derived metrics" section listing each stored metric, its
value, and its provenance string from `images.provenance` (section 7.3), so the user can see
that a displayed HFR came from `csv:HFR` rather than the header. The panel renders inline under
its row with no bordered container of its own: the row's own indentation is the containment, and a
bordered box inside a bordered row was one level of nesting with nothing to do.

This panel is the only place `median_fwhm` appears. It is labelled "Header FWHM" with its
source keyword, adjacent to but visually separated from the `fwhm` row labelled "FWHM
(arcsec)", so the two are never read as one number (section 7.1.1).

**Queries.** `TargetDetailQuery.Get(groupKey)` returns the header block, the totals, and the
session overview list. `SessionDetailQuery.Get(groupKey, sessionDate)` returns one session's
ranges, per-filter details, insights, and frame rows, each frame row carrying the two outlier
verdicts the insight counts are built from. It additionally returns the night's rig groups
(PAR-004), the reference frame id per night and per rig (PAR-008), and, per frame row, the
deviation of each graded metric under both baselines (PAR-003), so flipping the "Compare to"
toggle re-reads a value the query already returned rather than issuing a second query. The rig
baselines come from `RigBaselinesCache`, the session baselines from the night's own frames.

**A merged night (Phase 25).** When several nights are reviewed together, `SessionDetailMerge.Merge` folds their loaded `SessionDetail` records, oldest first, into one detail whose `Nights` list carries one `NightSpan` per member over the concatenated `Frames`; a single night is one span. Every figure the query derives from frames is rebuilt over the union through the query's own builders: the five ranges, the arcsecond HFR median and its excluded count, the per-filter medians, details and acquisitions (split per rig and stamped with rig labels on the same rule a multi-rig night uses), the rig groups merged by label with summed counts and a reference ranked over the rig's union frames, and the median airmass, ambient temperature and humidity. `Gain` is the modal gain over the union, because a merged card has no one first frame. One modal `eccentricity_source` over the union decides every eccentricity figure on the merged card, and the excluded count is recounted against it, so a member pooled on another source contributes nothing to those figures. The per-frame outlier flags and grading are kept exactly as each night computed them against its own baselines and are not recomputed over the union. Insights are the members' lists concatenated, each message prefixed with its night's date as `yyyy-MM-dd: `. `Notes` is null; the per-night notes stay with the members. `SessionDetailMerge.Overview` builds the merged card's overview from the members' overviews alone: sums for counts and integration, the median of the members' medians per metric (an accepted ceiling, read only by the comparison ink), filters in first-appearance order, camera and telescope kept only when every member agrees, and a guiding provenance of `None`, the one agreed value, or `Mixed`.

Both take the dashboard row's group key, not a target id: a dashboard row is a group, either
a target GUID or `obj:<name>` including `obj:__uncategorized__` (section 12.2), and an
unresolved `OBJECT` string has no target id but is openable. The branch on the `obj:` prefix
lives in one shared SQL fragment so the listing and both detail queries name a group
identically.

**The parts and the shell (Phase 23, stage 0).** The page's markup lives in sixteen part views (fourteen in stage 0, two added in stage 2) under `Views/TargetDetail/Parts`: `TargetHeaderPart`, `IntegrationBarsPart`, `NightsLedgerPart`, `TrendChartPart`, `NightHeaderPart`, `NightMetricsPart`, `NightTimelinePart`, `SharpestFramePart`, `GuidingPart`, `FindingsPart`, `PerFilterTablePart`, `RangesTablePart`, `FramesPart` and `NightNotesPart` (stage 2 adds `CompareTablePart` and `IntegrationTablesPart`), with `FindingsSummary` and `CompareToSegment` as pieces inside two of them. `TargetDetailView` is now the page shell: it keeps the Details drawer and the keyboard shortcuts and hosts the chosen layout in a `LayoutHost`. `CurrentLayoutView` arranges the parts as the page shipped before, and `TargetLayoutRegistry` (both under `Views/TargetDetail/Layouts`) lists the layouts. Shared resources sit in `Theme/TargetParts.axaml` and `Parts/PartStyles.axaml`. Stage 0 changed nothing visible. A parity census over the registry checks, for every registered layout, that each part is on screen with nonzero bounds or reachable through one enabled opener, so a layout cannot drop a part silently. Stage 3 added `BenchLayoutView`, the base class `TargetLayoutView` that both layout views build on, the shared width helper `LedgerColumn` and the shared handle `LanesHandle`, all under `Views/TargetDetail/Layouts`, and a second registry row. Stage 4 added `RowsLayoutView`, the shared frames width rule `FramesColumn` and a third registry row; the selector and Settings, Display list three layouts and the census runs for all three. Phase 24 R3 deleted `GuidingPart`: its content is the night chart's Guiding pill, inside `NightMetricsPart`. Phase 24 R22 deleted `FindingsPart`: the outlier pills in `FramesPart`'s Filter segment replaced it, and the registry lists fourteen parts.

### 12.5 Statistics

Mirrors `frontend/src/pages/StatisticsPage.tsx`.

| Section | Contents | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overview tiles | Total Integration ("all LIGHT frames"), Total Frames ("all LIGHT frames"), Catalogued Size (subtitled "catalogued bytes, from the database", the figure being the sum of the recorded file sizes and not a measurement of the disk), Active Span (with first and last capture dates), Avg Rig-Session Length (with the rig-session count), Avg per Target (with the resolved target count). | `StatsOverview.tsx` |
| Equipment performance | One row per (telescope, camera) combination: frame count, total integration, average session length, median HFR, best HFR, median eccentricity, median FWHM (the `fwhm` column, already arcseconds), the count of frames carrying a `fwhm` value, MADs for HFR, eccentricity and FWHM, median guiding RMS (`guiding_rms_arcsec`), and an expandable per-filter breakdown. | `EquipmentPerformance.tsx` |
| Guiding | Two cards from the PHD2 tables: the per-rig scorecard and RMS by altitude band. Described in full below. Placed after Equipment performance, where the web places it. | `GuidingScorecard.tsx`, `GuidingAltitude.tsx`, `services/phd2_stats.py` |
| Equipment inventory | Cameras and telescopes, each with frame count, integration, nights, target count, median FWHM (the `fwhm` column), and median guiding RMS. A grouped marker when the name is a canonical grouping of aliases. | `EquipmentInventory.tsx` |
| Filter usage | Horizontal bars, one per canonical filter, tinted with the filter colour, labelled with formatted hours. | `FilterUsageChart.tsx` |
| Top targets | Ranked list with bars, integration hours per target. | `TopTargets.tsx` |
| Timeline or calendar | A toggle between the two. | `ImagingTimeline.tsx`, `ImagingCalendar.tsx` |
| Data quality | Average HFR, average eccentricity, best HFR, the pixel-domain HFR histogram, the arcsecond HFR histogram (0 to 8 in 0.5 steps plus an 8.0-plus overflow bucket), the count of frames with no derivable plate scale, and the eccentricity exclusion count. | `schemas/stats.py::DataQualityStats` |
| Storage | FITS bytes catalogued, thumbnail cache bytes, database bytes. There is no "FITS bytes on disk" figure: measuring it means walking every scan root on a page load, which the port refuses. | `StorageStats` |
| Ingest history | Files added per day: the sum of `new_files` per `date(started_at)` over `scan_runs` rows whose state is `complete`, the newest 30 dates, returned oldest first. `completed` is the wrong column here, it counts re-ingested changed files as additions. | `IngestEntry`, from `scan_runs` in this port. |

Timeline controls, from `ImagingTimeline.tsx`: granularity monthly, weekly, or daily; range
presets All, 1Y, Q, M, W; and a toggle between "Imaged only" and all periods in range.
Efficiency percentage labels appear above bars when observer coordinates are configured
(section 8.4) and are hidden otherwise.

Under the All preset the granularity selector offers Monthly and Weekly only, and selecting All
while Daily is chosen snaps the granularity to Weekly. All spans the whole library, and a daily
bar per day over a multi-year span is an unbounded category axis that renders as a solid block.
Choosing a preset also sets the granularity: All and 1Y select Monthly, Q selects Weekly, M and W
select Daily. The selector stays live afterwards, within the choices the preset allows.

**Wheel zoom and drag pan (Phase 14C, UI layout ruling 13).** Reverses Phase 9's Q15, which
shipped the timeline with the three explicit controls above and no wheel, drag or pinch,
citing a scroll-to-zoom chart inside a scrolling page as a known interaction trap. Ctrl with
the wheel or trackpad scroll now steps the granularity selector one notch per gesture, monthly to
weekly to daily and back, keeping the bar under the pointer in place rather than recentering
the axis. A left mouse button drag on the chart pans the visible date range along the axis
without changing granularity. Both act on the same three explicit granularity values the
selector already offers; the web's continuous zoom level (`ImagingTimeline.tsx`'s
`granularityForZoom`) and its pinch gesture are not ported, so there is no zoom state between the
three granularities and nothing to persist. The presets, the granularity selector, and the "Imaged
only" toggle are unchanged. A gesture with no vertical component steps nothing. Keeping the bar
under the pointer in place is approximate rather than exact: the bar pitch is the plot width over
the bar count and ignores the axis margin, so the anchor drifts about one bar, which is a named
ceiling in the source with its upgrade path stated there (read the chart's own scaler once a frame
has drawn).

Because the drag and the click share a button, the **click is deferred**. The chart library raises
its point-clicked command on pointer **down**, so a drag that begins on a bar would otherwise
navigate at the press: the press records a pending bar instead, a plain release commits it, and a
drag or a lost capture discards it. A release with no press commits nothing and a right-button
press records nothing.

Clicking a bar navigates to the Dashboard with its date range applied: a monthly bar gives the
first to the last day of the month, a weekly bar the ISO Monday to the following Sunday, a daily
bar the same day twice. The ISO week arithmetic follows the backend's definition, the one
section 8.4 states. The web frontend's `periodToDateRange` weekly branch is off by seven days
when 4 January falls on a Sunday; the port does not reproduce that.

**The Guiding section (Phase 15B).** Two cards over `phd2_sessions`, from `GuidingStatsQuery`,
which is the port of `backend/app/services/phd2_stats.py`. A rig here is the **telescope** the
PHD2 profile is mapped to, run through the equipment alias map, so two spellings of one scope
are one row and two cameras under one telescope share a row. A session whose `telescope` is null
belongs to no rig, is counted into the unmapped tally and appears in neither card.

**The scorecard** is one row per rig, rigs ordinally sorted by telescope name, each row followed
by a sub-row reading "Guide exposure: 1000, 2000 ms" over that rig's distinct guide exposures,
each rounded to the nearest whole millisecond and ascending, or nothing when no session carried
one. This departs from the web, which always draws the row: the web draws the row with its
missing glyph instead.

| Column | Figure | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rig | The canonical telescope | |
| Sessions | `session_count`, with "n too short to score" beside it when `gated_session_count` is above zero | The gate is `MinFrames`, 100 frames (section 7.6). |
| Hours | Guided hours to one decimal | The sum of `duration_s` over every session of the rig, short ones included, divided by 3600 and rounded to two decimals through `PythonNumerics.RoundLikePython`, then printed to one. |
| RMS Total | `rms_total_arcsec` to two decimals, graded | Frame-count weighted over the rig's sessions that clear the gate and carry a value, the same `WeightedRms` the night rollup uses, so a rig card and a night pane cannot disagree. |
| RMS RA | `rms_ra_arcsec` to two decimals, graded | Same weighting. |
| RMS Dec | `rms_dec_arcsec` to two decimals, graded | Same weighting. |
| Filtered | `rms_total_filtered_arcsec` to two decimals, never graded | The 5 sigma one-pass excursion figure of section 7.6. The gap to RMS Total is how much of the error is spikes. |
| Dec:RA | The ratio to two decimals, never graded | `rms_dec_arcsec` divided by `rms_ra_arcsec`, null when either is null and null when RA is zero. The column is labelled Dec:RA and the figure is Dec over RA; the web's field name reads the other way round and the label is what is true. |
| Settle s | The median to one decimal, never graded | The median of the rig's per-session `settle_median_s` values, a median of medians, over the sessions that have one. |

**The grading rule** is section 12.4's, unchanged and shared: `FrameQuality`'s median and median
absolute deviation, the signed deviation `(value - median) / max(mad, 1e-9)`, and the four bands
at -1.0, 1.5 and 3.0 in raw MAD units. What changes is the baseline. Here it is **the cross-rig
baseline**: for each of the three graded columns, the median and MAD of that column's value
across the rigs in the table, higher being worse. The consequence is stated plainly because it
is easy to misread as a defect: `FrameQuality.MinGroup` is 8, and a baseline built from fewer
than 8 values grades nothing, so **every cell is neutral until the library holds eight rigs with
a figure in that column**. One rig is therefore neutral, and so are seven. That is the web's own
behaviour, from the same shared utility, and the port keeps it rather than inventing a second
threshold for a table of three columns.

**The eight are eight rigs, not eight sessions**, and the help topic says so in plain words
rather than leaving a reader to infer it from a threshold shared with a table that counts
something else. The baseline this table grades against is built from one value per rig, the rig's
own weighted figure for that column, so the count the threshold tests is the number of rigs. The
frame table's grading counts differently: there a group is a rig and a filter and the eight are
eight frames. The help topic's own two load-bearing sentences, verbatim, from `stats.guiding`:

> The coloured cells compare each rig's figure against the middle of your rigs, and that
> comparison refuses to judge anything until it has at least eight values to compare. Here a
> value is one rig, so it means eight telescopes: a library with one, two or seven rigs sees
> plain uncoloured figures, and with one rig every cell is neutral.

The topic goes on to cover the unmapped tally, the alias folding, the altitude card's
independence from observer coordinates and the table view, none of which this quotation repeats.
