It exists so a reader does not wait for colour that a four-rig library will never show.

**The altitude card** is one sky arc per rig, laid out in a wrapping grid. Each arc is a quarter
dome with the observer at the lower left, the horizon to the right and the zenith at the top,
carrying three wedges in horizon-first order: below 30 degrees, 30 to 60, above 60. The band a
session falls in comes from `phd2_sessions.alt_deg`, the altitude PHD2 wrote on the session's own
pointing line, so the card needs no observer coordinates and works on a library that has
configured none; its help topic says that. A session with a null `alt_deg` is in no band and is
drawn in no wedge, while still counting on the scorecard row.

Each wedge prints its RMS total to two decimals, the ratio of that figure to the same rig's
above-60 figure as a times sign and two decimals, and the session count as "n 12". A wedge with
no session prints "no data" and takes the empty shade. This departs from the web, which prints
"no data" for any band with no RMS figure and so loses the session count of a band whose
sessions are all under the hundred-frame gate; the port prints the missing placeholder and its
`n` count and keeps the band's own shade. The ratio is absent when the rig has no
above-60 band or its figure is zero. Above the arc the card prints the rig's name and one line
reading the rig's own best to worst band figure, "0.62 to 1.04 arcsec", or the single figure
when they are equal, or "No RMS recorded", followed by the rig's total session count across its
bands.

**The shade is ranked inside one rig**, never across rigs: the rig's present band figures are
sorted and each wedge takes one of three steps by its rank, so a rig that guides badly stays
readable beside a rig that guides well. A rig with one band figure takes the middle step rather
than a false extreme. The three steps are the accent at three strengths over the card and the
empty step is the tertiary ink at the lightest, which is the ramp `CalendarHeatmap` already
builds from two bound colours; no token is added. A legend under the grid states the ranking and
that the times figure is the ratio to that rig's above-60 band.

**`Controls/AltitudeArc.cs`** draws one rig's arc, in the same drawn-control shape as the guide
graph (section 13). Hovering or keyboard-focusing a wedge opens a tooltip carrying the rig, the
band in words, RMS total, RMS RA, RMS Dec, the session count and the ratio to above 60. The
wedge is focusable and the tooltip answers focus as well as hover, because the figures behind a
shape have to be reachable without a pointer.

**The table view** is a disclosure under the arcs listing the same rows: rig, band, sessions,
RMS total, RMS RA, RMS Dec, one row per rig and band in rig order and then horizon-first band
order. It carries exactly the figures the wedges carry and no others, which is what makes it a
view of the same data rather than a second answer. The table view's columns carry no help of
their own, where the web gives each a popover: the section's one glyph covers them, because
every column is a column the scorecard above already explains.

**The empty notice** replaces both cards when no rig has a figure, and takes one of two forms.
With no unmapped session it reads "No PHD2 guide logs catalogued." followed by a link reading
"Enable guide log scanning", which opens Settings on the Library tab at the "Read PHD2 guide
logs" switch (section 12.7). With one or more unmapped sessions it reads "n guiding sessions
found but no PHD2 profile is mapped to a telescope." followed by a link reading "Map profiles",
which opens Settings on the Equipment tab at the PHD2 profiles panel (section 12.7). The second
form wins when both are true, because a library with logs and no mapping is one click from
working and should not be told to enable something it already enabled.

**Query.** `StatsQuery.Get()` returns the whole response in one call, matching the web
application's single `/api/stats` endpoint, and is cached in memory until the next scan
completes or settings change. `StatsQuery.Calendar(from, to)` is separate because the
calendar range is user-controlled. The guiding figures come from `GuidingStatsQuery` and are
returned inside that one response rather than from a second call: the web fetches
`/api/stats/guiding` separately and caches it separately, and this port has one page, one query
and one cache. The guiding cache is invalidated with the rest of the response, which includes
the settings saves that change the profile map, since a remapped profile moves a session from
one rig to another.

### 12.6 Activity

Mirrors `frontend/src/components/ActivityFeed.tsx`. A reverse-chronological list of
`activity_events`. Each row shows timestamp, severity, category, message, and duration.
Scan events expand to show their child events (`parent_id`). Details render as a key-value
table, falling back to formatted JSON.

Duration renders in one of three forms, chosen by magnitude: below one second, whole milliseconds
with a thousands separator ("847 ms"); from one second, seconds to one decimal ("4.2 s"); from one
minute, minutes and zero-padded seconds ("2:05"). The branch is taken on the rounded value, so a
duration that would render as "60.0 s" renders as "1:00" instead. A row with no duration renders
nothing rather than a zero.

Filters: severity, category, and a free-text search over the message. Actions: refresh, and
"prune now" which applies the retention window immediately.

**The seen marker (PAR-017).** `general.activity_seen_at` (section 5.8.1) holds the instant the
feed was last opened, or null on a profile that has never opened it. A row whose `timestamp` is
strictly newer than that instant is unseen: it carries a `Border.tag` reading "new" in its
leading cell, and the navigation rail's Activity entry carries the count of unseen rows while
that count is above zero.

The write happens on open, not on scroll and not per row. Navigating to the Activity destination
captures the current time, then, before writing the captured value through
`SettingsStore.MutateGeneral`, marks every row loaded on the page **in place** against the marker
stored before this open: the page's rail entry is memoized (Phase 9), so it is not rebuilt or
reloaded on a return visit, and a re-fetch would discard its scroll position and its loaded page
set. `ActivityRowViewModel.RefreshUnseen` recomputes `IsUnseen` for every loaded row, recursing
into a scan's already-expanded children, against the captured marker; a row that arrives through
later paging while the marker is still the one this open captured is built against that same
value. Reading before writing is what lets the first open show its markers at all. A row that
arrives while the feed is already open keeps its marker until the next open, because the stored
instant is already past it. (The approved text described a render against the stored value, which
reads as a re-fetch; the shipped mechanism is the in-place recomputation above, because the page
cannot re-fetch without losing state a reader is mid-way through using. Task 7 review escalation
1, a coordinator product correction.)

The truth table across opens, with one scan writing rows at T1 and a second writing rows at T3:

| Moment | `activity_seen_at` at render | Rows marked | `activity_seen_at` after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fresh profile, feed never opened | null | every row | null |
| First open, at T2 | null | the T1 rows | T2 |
| Still open when the T3 rows arrive | T2 | the T3 rows | T2 |
| Second open, at T4 | T2 | the T3 rows | T4 |
| Third open, at T5, nothing written since | T4 | none | T5 |

Mirrors `backend/app/api/activity.py` `POST /seen` and `ActivityFeed.tsx`, with the web
application's per-user column replaced by the one settings key, because this application has no
users (section 2.3). The marker is display state only: it filters nothing, it changes no query,
and retention pruning (section 5.12) ignores it. Pruning can therefore delete rows that were
never marked seen, which is correct: retention is about age, not about attention.

**Query.** `ActivityQuery.Page(filters, before, limit)` using keyset pagination on
`(timestamp, id)`.

### 12.7 Settings

Tabs, a reduced set of the web application's `ALL_TABS`. Dropped: Users, Account, API Keys,
API, Backup and Restore, Metrics. Custom Columns was on that list until Phase 20 built it (section
12.15), and External Tools until Phase 21 built it (section 12.16). The web application names that
tab AstroBin and puts the four groups below on it together with the WBPP library fields; this port
names the tab for what it holds rather than for one of the four things in it, and the WBPP fields
are on the Export for stacking page (section 12.13), where they are edited beside the thing they
act on.

| Tab | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Library | Scan roots list with add and remove. Include and exclude path lists. Name rule editor (section 10.2) with a rule list and a test-a-path box showing the verdict and the deciding rule ids. Include calibration frames checkbox. Auto-scan enabled checkbox and interval. Watcher enabled checkbox. Manual scan button with progress and cancel. A notice above the tab says when what is on screen is not what is stored, and it names which of the two reasons applies: the stored document changed elsewhere while the tab was open, or the first read landed after the user had started editing. Either way it offers Revert to load the stored values and states that saving keeps what is on screen. The scan control carries the run's scope as a radio pair, "All frames" against "Light frames only" (PAR-013), starting from the stored `general.include_calibration` and passed to `ScanCoordinator` as that run's argument without rewriting the stored value (section 10.3). Below the pair, a checkbox reading "Remove catalogue rows for missing files past the safety limit" (ruling D2), cleared on every visit to the tab rather than remembered, because it is a decision about one run. Its help paragraph is two sentences: "GalactiLog deletes database rows only. No file, folder or image on your disk is ever moved, renamed or deleted." followed by "Without this box, a scan that finds half or more of a root's catalogued files missing skips that root's cleanup and records it in the Activity feed, on the assumption that a drive or share is unreachable rather than that the frames are gone." Both sentences are honest but describe only section 10.3's guard 2, the partial-loss case: the paragraph is silent on guard 1 (zero discovery), which is the more common real shape of "a drive or share is unreachable" (the whole root discovers nothing rather than half of it) and which the checkbox can never override. A reader who ticks the box expecting it to force a cleanup of a vanished root is not told it will not; nothing in the shipped text is false, and verification found no launched-application defect here, so this is recorded as a documentation gap rather than a code change. The scan filter notice (PAR-014) shows above the rule list under exactly the condition section 12.2 states, from the same computed condition, and its Review action scrolls to this tab's rule editor rather than navigating. Below the calibration checkbox, a **"Read PHD2 guide logs"** checkbox writing `general.phd2_scan_enabled` (Phase 15A), on by default, with three sentences: "Guide logs named PHD2_GuideLog_*.txt found under your scan roots are read for guiding measurements.", "Turning this off stops future scans reading them and deletes nothing that has already been read.", and "While it is off, a frame that is scanned again loses the guiding figure that came from a guide log, and gets it back on the first scan after you switch this on." Clearing it stops the pass of section 10.3 step 5 from running; it drops no `phd2_*` row, which is why the second sentence says so, and the third sentence is the honest statement of section 5.2's ordering caveat, which a reader would otherwise meet as an unexplained blank cell. |
| General | Close to tray checkbox, on by default, carrying the sentence "Closing the window hides GalactiLog in the notification area. It keeps scanning." Minimize to tray checkbox. Start with Windows checkbox, disabled with the reason on a build the updater did not install. Start minimized checkbox. Scan completion notice checkbox. Below them, from Phase 22, its own **Survey downloads** section with a help glyph (topic `settings.general.survey-downloads`) and a **Fetch survey images for Sky view** checkbox writing `general.survey_downloads_enabled` (section 5.8.1), **on by default** since Phase 24 (a profile that stored off stays off), carrying two sentences beneath it: "Sky view on a target's page shows survey images of the sky around that target, fetched from the internet at alasky.cds.unistra.fr." and "While this is off, GalactiLog makes no request to that host, and nothing else in the application changes." The switch gates the Sky view window and nothing else: catalogue resolution (section 9.4) keeps the network behaviour it already has. Nothing else on the tab (sections 12.11 and 12.4). |
| Filters | Table of canonical filters, each with a colour swatch and an alias list editor. The swatch opens a colour picker with a hex field (P13 R2); choosing a colour on a grouped filter stores it on that group. A discovered list of filter names seen in the library with frame counts, and suggested groupings the user can accept or dismiss. Dismissed suggestions are remembered. Every ungrouped discovered filter carries a swatch too, seeded from the palette through the same resolution as the grouped rows (section 5.8.4); choosing a colour on one stores it as a one-name group with an empty alias list. A group created by the tab, grouped or ungrouped, stores no colour of its own: its category default resolves (section 5.8.4) until the user picks one. |
| Equipment | The same shape for cameras and telescopes: canonical name, aliases, discovered names with counts, suggested groupings, dismiss. Below them, the **PHD2 profiles** panel (Phase 15A), described under the table. |
| Location | Observer latitude, longitude, name, IANA timezone, imaging night grouping checkbox, 24-hour time checkbox. Saving a change to the timezone, the latitude or the longitude queues one PHD2 correlation re-run, described under the PHD2 profiles panel below the table (Phase 15A). Both the observer and the display timezone selectors read the offset first and a display name second, for example "GMT+00:00 Dublin, Edinburgh, Lisbon, London" (the platform's own zone names, provisional pending the user), the offset being the zone's standard offset so the list does not reorder when daylight saving starts, and the list runs negative offsets, then GMT, then positive offsets (Phase 14C, user ruling U4). |
| Display | Per metric group (Quality, Guiding, ADU, Focuser, Weather, Mount) an enabled checkbox and a per-field checkbox list, writing `display.groups` (5.8.2). A column picker per table, writing `display.columns`: the dashboard's, the frame table's and, from Phase 20, "Nights ledger columns", which lists the session-scope custom columns alone and is replaced by the sentence "No custom columns yet." while none exists (sections 5.8.2 and 12.15). The dashboard picker lists target-scope custom columns under a "Custom" heading below the built-in ones. Defaults from `schemas/settings.py::default_display_settings`: Quality and Guiding enabled, ADU, Focuser, Weather, and Mount disabled, all fields within each group checked. Also text size, content width, and the theme picker. |
| Custom Columns | Section 12.15. The create form (name, type, scope and, for a dropdown, its options) and the table of defined columns with order arrows, inline rename, options editing, a stored-value count and a delete that asks first. The tab is the only place a custom column is created, renamed, reordered or deleted; values are only ever edited on the surfaces that show them. |
| External Tools | Section 12.16. Four groups: the AstroBin filter id map, one numeric box per filter name the library knows; the Bortle class, one numeric box; the NINA instances list; and the Stellarium instances list. All four are described under the table. The tab is the only place any of the four keys is written. |
| Storage | Data location with a picker, the resolved path, where the value came from, the pending-move note naming both paths with a cancel action, and the previous-location note naming the folder that still holds a copy (section 17.2). Thumbnail cache path with a picker and free-space readout. Preview resolution. Preview cache size in megabytes. Thumbnail width. |
| Targets | Merge candidate list (section 12.9), merge history with undo, unresolved names with the retry action, and rename history. The rename history is read from `activity_events` (`user_action` / `target_renamed`, newest 50): there is no rename-history table, so the list is bounded by `general.activity_retention_days` like every other activity read, and a rename older than the retention window is gone. The tab header carries a **"New target"** button (Task 3 review, accepted; not "Create target", which is reserved for the row action below) that opens a form on this tab with six fields: primary name (required), object type, RA and Dec in degrees (both optional), catalog id (optional), and a comma-separated alias list. The object type control lists section 9.8's nine display categories, then its five solar system categories, then "Other", which reveals a free-text box; the empty choice leaves `object_type` null. Choosing a solar system category clears RA and Dec, because a fixed position is meaningless for a moving object, and sets the "user defined" checkbox, which otherwise ships checked and is the user's to clear. RA parses to 0 to 360 and Dec to -90 to 90 and both accept a blank; a value that is not a number or is out of range refuses the submit with the range in the message and writes nothing. Section 9.7 carries the rest: the alias construction, the two conflict refusals, the frame-driven retro-link, the created row being `name_locked` and `user_defined`, and the name-locked rule the created row lives under. Create target (PAR-001) also appears as a **"Create target"** row action on each unresolved name (section 12.8's Unresolved list is the read-only view of the same data): it opens the same form with the primary name pre-filled from that `OBJECT` string and that string already in the alias list, and on create it links every unresolved LIGHT frame whose normalized `OBJECT` matches the created name or an alias to the new target and closes a pending merge candidate for that name as accepted when one exists (section 9.7 step 5; a pending candidate is never required). Both entry points report what they did, in the form "Created <name>, linked <n> frames from <m> unresolved names", and a second create of the same name is refused with section 9.7's conflict sentence rather than creating a duplicate. |
| Maintenance | Rebuild targets, retry unresolved, regenerate reference thumbnails (missing or all), regenerate frame thumbnails (purge and regenerate), prune activity events, and reset database with a typed confirmation. Regenerating reference thumbnails for all targets must ask for a forced render, which replaces each existing `reference/<target id>.jpg` (section 11.3); without it the pass re-offers every target, the cache serves the existing file as a hit, and the action reports a generated count while producing no new pixels. Regenerating frame thumbnails has no row-level record to consult, because `images.thumbnail_path` is never written (section 5.2), so purge-and-regenerate deletes `frames/` under the cache root and lets on-demand generation refill it, and there is no missing-only variant to offer. Rebuild targets deletes no `targets` row: it clears `images.resolved_target_id` for LIGHT frames whose target is not `user_defined`, deletes every `merge_candidates` row, clears the negative resolver cache, and re-resolves each distinct unresolved `OBJECT` name in cache-only mode under the resolution lease. `TargetResolver` reuses existing target rows by identity (section 9.5), so the delete buys nothing, and deleting one would take the `merge_manifests` rows that record merges into it with it. Reset database clears `activity_events`, `merge_manifests`, `merge_candidates`, `session_notes`, `target_catalog_memberships`, `images`, `skipped_files` (section 5.21; it is scan output in the same sense `images` is, and a cleared `images` table with surviving skipped rows would be inconsistent), `targets`, `scan_runs`, `catalog_cache` (the positive rows included, which is the clearing section 9.6 refers to), `phd2_frames`, `phd2_sessions`, `phd2_calibrations` and `phd2_logs` (Phase 15A, cleared children first inside the same transaction; they are scan output in the same sense `images` is, and a reset that left them would keep a guiding history for frames that no longer exist), `custom_column_values` and `custom_columns` (Phase 20, children first for the same reason: values reference both their column and their target, so a reset that left them would keep values naming targets that no longer exist), `mosaic_panel_sessions`, `mosaic_panels`, `mosaics` and `mosaic_suggestions` (Phase 18, children first: a mosaic is built from catalogued nights, so a reset that left them would keep panels naming targets that no longer exist), keeps `user_settings` so the scan roots, observer location, thumbnail cache path and the five tray and startup residency keys (section 12.11) survive, and leaves the shipped `openngc_catalog` and `static_catalog_entries` rows in place because `CatalogSeeder.LoadIfNeeded` is guarded by `general.catalogs_loaded_version` and clearing them without that flag would leave the resolver with no catalogue. The typed confirmation itemizes exactly these three lists, with the four guide-log tables and the two custom column tables named among the cleared. **Every entry in that list is a sentence stating what the reader loses, not a noun phrase naming a table**, because the list is what is read before the confirmation is typed: the two custom column entries therefore say that every value filled into a column of the reader's own goes, and that the columns themselves go so each has to be created again. The two shipped sentences read "Every value you typed into a column of your own" and "Every
column you defined yourself, so each one has to be created again." The four mosaic sentences (Phase 18) read "Which nights you placed in each mosaic panel", "Every mosaic panel and its layout", "Every mosaic, with its notes" and "Mosaic suggestions, including the ones you dismissed, so a dismissed one can be suggested again". It is armed by typing the
literal phrase `RESET`, compared ordinally and case-sensitively. Smart rebuild (PAR-007, risk level Moderate, no confirm) repairs target data from the local database and the resolver cache with no network call at all, in six passes, each reporting its own count: frames pointing at a merged-away target are redirected to that merge's winner; unresolved LIGHT frames whose normalized `OBJECT` equals an alias of an active target are linked to it; every distinct normalized `OBJECT` seen on a target's own frames that is missing from that target's `aliases` is added to them; for each active target that is neither `name_locked` nor `user_defined` and that carries a `catalog_id` or a `common_name` (a target with neither is skipped, because `AliasCurator.BuildPrimaryName` answers "Unknown" for that pair and the unguarded pass would rename every uncatalogued target to it), a positive `catalog_cache` row keyed on the target's normalized `catalog_id` or, failing that, its normalized `primary_name` (never an alias, web parity) re-derives `catalog_id`, `common_name` and `primary_name` through the same curation a resolution uses (section 9.4.5); each remaining active target that is neither `name_locked` nor `user_defined` and whose `primary_name` disagrees with its `catalog_id` and `common_name` has its name rebuilt from them; and every `merge_candidates` row whose `suggested_target_id` names a row that is merged away, or is null with a `method` other than `orphan`, is deleted (a null `method` is spared by the same SQL `NOT IN` shape, and an `orphan` row is left for the Create target form to read). The six passes themselves create no `targets` row and delete none, for the reason rebuild targets deletes none; the action as a whole is not so scoped, because smart rebuild's own inline duplicate detection (below) orders itself at the end of the same action and can create a `targets` row when it reaches `DuplicateDetector` outcome 2, exactly as any other duplicate detection pass can (section 9.7). `Run_CreatesNoTargetRow` pins the six passes' own scope. Port of `backend/app/worker/tasks_target_rebuild.py::smart_rebuild_targets`, without that function's mosaic panel recomputation, because panel membership in this port is a join of target, night and frame label (section 5.24) and there is no stored membership to recompute, and without its queued follow-up tasks: duplicate detection (section 9.7) runs inline at the end of the same action instead. A resolver stub asserts the pass makes no network call. Catalog identity backfill (PAR-007, risk level Safe, no confirm) re-runs the identity matcher over unlinked frames: for each distinct `OBJECT` string carried by LIGHT frames with no `resolved_target_id`, most frames first, it resolves cache-only and, when the result matches an existing target by identity (section 9.5), links that name's unresolved LIGHT frames to it. A name that resolves to nothing, or to no existing target, is left orphaned for duplicate detection and the Create target form on the Targets tab. It reports linked names, linked frames and skipped names, creates no target, and is safely re-runnable. Port of `tasks_target_dedup.py::backfill_catalog_identity`, without that task's first phase, which repairs quote-corrupted cache rows from a data defect this port never had. Both actions take the resolution lease the way rebuild targets does and both refuse while a scan is running, per section 9.7's mutual exclusion. Every action on this tab registers with the job registry (section 12), so its progress and its outcome are in the status bar flyout as well as inline on the row, and the census test that pins registration counts the eight actions on this tab. |
| Diagnostics | Section 12.8. Also carries the `general.log_level` selector, which appears nowhere else: it is a troubleshooting control, not a preference, and it belongs beside the log viewer that shows its effect. Beside the level selector sit three retention editors (PAR-012), each a numeric box that validates its range before it writes and reverts to the stored value when it refuses: activity retention in days, `general.activity_retention_days`, 1 to 3650, which section 5.12 prunes against; application log retention in days, `general.app_log_retention_days`, 1 to 3650, which section 16.1 applies as the sink's retained file limit; and the log viewer row cap, `general.app_log_max_rows`, 1000 to 500000, which section 12.8 applies to the viewer and to its copy cap. Each writes through `SettingsStore.MutateGeneral`, and each states beside itself when it takes effect, because two are immediate and the log retention limit is not: it applies the next time GalactiLog starts, not at the next roll (section 16.1; the approved text read "next roll", corrected as a factual matter and the user is told). |
| About | Version, git SHA, release channel, update check button, release notes, log folder link. |

**The PHD2 profiles panel (Phase 15A).** Port of
`frontend/src/components/settings/Phd2ProfilePanel.tsx`. It lists the equipment profiles the
guide logs themselves named, read from `phd2_sessions` by `Phd2ProfilesQuery`, not a list the
user maintains. One row per distinct `equipment_profile`, ordered by last seen, newest first.

| Column | Source | Editable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profile name | `phd2_sessions.equipment_profile` | no |
| Guide camera | the most recent session's `guide_camera` | no |
| Focal length | the most recent session's `focal_length_mm`, millimetres | no |
| Pixel scale | the most recent session's `pixel_scale_arcsec`, arcseconds per pixel. Reads "not in the log" when it is null, which is the ASIAIR case of section 7.6 | no |
| Sessions | the count of `phd2_sessions` rows carrying the profile | no |
| First seen | the earliest `started_at_utc`, or the earliest `started_at_local` when no zone has resolved | no |
| Last seen | the latest of the same | no |
| Telescope | `phd2_profile_map[profile].telescope` | a picker over every telescope name the Equipment tab knows: each canonical name from the grouping editor above **and** each telescope name discovered in the library that belongs to no group, plus an empty choice meaning not mapped |
| Timezone | `phd2_profile_map[profile].timezone` | a picker **built by the same shared timezone builder** the Location tab's two selectors use, so all three read the offset first in negative, GMT, positive order (Phase 14C ruling U4), plus an empty choice reading "Use the observer timezone" |
| Latitude | `phd2_profile_map[profile].latitude` | a numeric box, -90 to 90, blank meaning inherit the site |
| Longitude | `phd2_profile_map[profile].longitude` | a numeric box, -180 to 180, blank meaning inherit the site |

First seen and last seen are shown in the display timezone (`general.timezone`) and in the
configured clock shape, the same way every other instant in the application is shown, when the
row that produced the value was itself a resolved instant; a session whose zone never resolved
shows the guide log's own wall clock, rendered as written and marked "(log clock, no timezone
set)". **The basis is decided per row, by what the query that built the row actually returned,
never by the panel's current zone resolution at render time.** A profile can take its earliest
seen value from an unzoned session and its latest from a zoned one, so the two markers are
independent. Because the basis travels with the row rather than being recomputed live, editing a
profile's zone and committing the edit does not itself change what first seen and last seen show:
the row still reports what the last read gave it until the panel next reloads, which is when a
value that just gained a zone stops carrying the log-clock marker.

**The Telescope picker offers the union, not the groups alone.** So a profile can be mapped on a
library where no alias group has ever been created, which is the common case of one physical
telescope carrying one name: `EquipmentTabViewModel.KnownTelescopes()` is the union of the
grouping editor's canonical names and its own discovered-but-ungrouped names, the same list the
"Ungrouped" column of the grouping editor above already shows. A grouped telescope appears once,
under its canonical name; a stored telescope the page no longer lists is still offered and shown
selected, marked "(not in the equipment list)" (the paragraph after the table above). A telescope
group the reader later deletes, whose canonical name is also a raw name the library still carries,
stays mapped, because it has become an ungrouped discovered name rather than an unlisted one; a
deleted group whose name the library does not carry becomes unmapped, exactly as before. This
mirrors the web, which reads the picker's options from the distinct telescope values of the images
table (`Phd2ProfilePanel.tsx:211`, `GET /api/targets/equipment`) rather than from an alias grouping
the web application does not even have; the port's picker previously offered only the grouping
editor's canonical names, which left a profile unmappable on any library with no alias group at
all, closed by `fix-p15b-e`.

Renaming a telescope's canonical name in the grouping editor above rewrites every
`phd2_profile_map` entry that named the old telescope to the new one, so a rig kept mapped through
a rename rather than reading as not mapped. The rewrite compares the saved map against a freshly
normalised one and writes only on a real difference (`Phd2Profiles.SameMap`), never on every save.
**The rewrite is a second write, not part of the same one.** The aliases move through the
equipment document's own save; the map moves through a separate write to the general document,
because the two live in different settings documents and no store method writes both at once. A
failure between the two is repaired at the next save of either; a crash between them leaves a map
entry naming a telescope no longer listed, which the picker then shows as not on the equipment
list rather than silently, so the gap is visible and one click to repair.

Each row shows, below its editors, the zone and the site that actually resolved for it and where
each came from, in the vocabulary of section 7.6: the profile's own value, the observer value,
or not set. A row whose zone resolves to nothing carries the same sentence the warning of
section 10.9 carries, so the fix is named where it is made.

Every write goes through `SettingsStore.MutateGeneral`, as every other settings view-model's
does, and each edit rewrites one profile's entry while leaving the other three fields of that
entry and every other entry intact (section 5.8.1). An out-of-range coordinate is refused before
it is stored and the box reverts to the stored value, the same shape the Diagnostics retention
editors use. Clearing the telescope of an entry that still carries a zone or a coordinate keeps
the entry; clearing it on an entry that carries nothing else removes the entry.

**A save re-runs the correlation.** A save that changes the map's **normalised** form dispatches
the correlation pass of section 7.6 over the nights that change invalidates, as a job registered
with the job registry (ruling F5, section 12), and the pass writes `phd2_correlation_complete`
with `trigger` `settings_change` when it finishes. The panel says a re-run has been queued rather
than blocking on it. A save that changes the normalised map in no way, which is what re-saving an
unchanged row does, queues nothing.

This queued pass is what the frame-level `images.guiding_*` columns wait on: only the correlation
re-run rewrites them. The night chart's Guiding pill and the Statistics
Guiding section do not wait on it, because `Phd2NightQuery` and `GuidingStatsQuery` resolve each
session's rig from the live `general.phd2_profile_map` on every call rather than from the stored
`phd2_sessions.telescope` column, so an unmapped or remapped profile changes what they report the
moment either query next reads, whether or not the queued pass has finished (section 5.16,
section 12.4, section 12.5).

The same save sets `general.phd2_correlation_pending` (section 5.8.1), which the completing pass
clears through the compare-and-clear door and a cancelled, failed or interrupted pass leaves set.
So a re-run queued here is not lost if the application is closed before it finishes: it is queued
again at the next GUI start, and the panel says a re-run is still owed while the flag is true
rather than reporting the work done, reading the flag itself at every load rather than only right
after a save. **Precedence: the queued sentence from this save wins over the owed sentence while
both could apply**, because the queued sentence names what the reader just did and is the newer
fact; the owed sentence returns the moment the queued one clears. **With `general.phd2_scan_enabled`
off, the owed sentence changes its wording rather than promising background work that cannot
happen**: `Phd2CorrelationRunner` refuses at the key gate before it registers anything, so a flag
left true while the key is off names the Library tab's switch and says the re-check resumes once
guide log reading is turned back on, instead of saying it is already under way.

**The Location tab dispatches the same re-run**, because its three fields feed the same
resolution. Saving a change to the observer timezone, latitude or longitude on that tab queues
one correlation re-run on exactly the terms section 7.6 states, one per save whatever the number
of changed fields, and the re-run begins with the session time re-derive of that section. It is
the same job, the same event and the same registry member as this panel's; there is not a second
pass and there is not a second control. A Location save that changes none of the three queues
nothing, and the tab's other fields (observer name, imaging night grouping, 24-hour time) never
queue it.

Renaming or regrouping a telescope in the editor above rewrites the map's `telescope` fields
onto the new canonical name in the same write, so a mapping never strands on an alias, and every
entry's timezone and site survive the rewrite (section 5.8.1).

The panel is empty until a scan has read a guide log. Its empty state says so and names the
Library tab's "Read PHD2 guide logs" checkbox, rather than offering a form for profiles that do
not exist yet.

**There is no WBPP export section on any tab either.** The four `wbpp_` keys of section 5.8.1 are
`general` keys like any other, but the only surface that reads or writes them is the Export for
stacking wizard (section 12.13): the staging folder and the exclusion patterns live on that
wizard's staging folder step, and the quality filter lives in its chips. `wbpp_default_os` is read
to preselect the flavour on that wizard's method step and is written by no surface at all, here or
there. Nothing on this page mirrors any of them, for the reason the object type has no tab either: a
setting edited beside the thing it acts on does not also belong in a list of settings, and two
editors for one key is how the two drift.

**The External Tools tab (Phase 21).** Port of
`frontend/src/components/settings/AstroBinTab.tsx`, without its PixInsight Export section, which
Phase 16 placed on the Export for stacking page instead. The tab is keyed `external-tools`, is the
thirteenth, and is placed after Custom Columns and before Storage, so the tabs that configure a
feature sit together ahead of the tabs that configure the installation. It holds four groups, each
a block in the shape the Custom Columns tab's two blocks use, each carrying its own help glyph
(section 12.12). Every write on the tab goes through `SettingsStore.MutateGeneral`, as every other
settings view-model's does, and each edit rewrites one key while leaving the other three intact.

**"AstroBin filter ids"**, the map. One row per filter name, each a label and a `TextBox`
watermarked "AstroBin id". The names are **the union of the Filters tab's canonical names and the
filter names discovered in the library that belong to no group**, sorted by an ordinal
case-insensitive comparison. That union is the same one, and for the same reason, the PHD2 panel's
Telescope picker offers above: a library where no filter group has ever been created is the common
case, and a map that offered canonical names alone would be empty on it. A filter name is matched
into the stored map case-insensitively (`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`), the same comparer
`FilterNameUnion` de-duplicates the tab's own names with, so two spellings differing only in case
read as one filter rather than as a second, silently unset row (ruling B11). It is
`FilterNameUnion.From`, one static declaration `FiltersTabViewModel.KnownFilters()` calls directly
and the External Tools tab calls through a `Func<IReadOnlyList<string>>` `AppHost` hands it, in
the shape `EquipmentTabViewModel.KnownTelescopes()` has; neither tab builds its own copy of the
union, so the two lists cannot drift (ruling B2). The tab rebuilds its rows from that union the
moment a filter group is renamed or added on the Filters tab, and the moment a scan discovers a
filter name no group has claimed, following `SettingsStore.AliasSourcesChanged` and the same
derived-data `Changed` signal Statistics and Analysis refresh on, so a stale union never strands an
edit against a row the reader can no longer see (ruling B32). A value is a positive integer; a
value that is not one is refused before it is stored and the box reverts to the stored value, the
shape the Diagnostics retention editors use. **Clearing a box removes that filter's key** rather
than storing zero, so a cleared row and a row never filled in leave the same stored document. A
filter the map names and the library no longer carries keeps its key and is not listed, for the
reason a stranded PHD2 map entry is kept: the tab deletes nothing the reader did not delete.

**"Bortle class"**, one row: a label and a `TextBox` watermarked "1 to 9", writing
`astrobin_bortle`. Blank clears the key. A value outside 1 to 9 is refused before it is stored and
the box reverts. The value is written into every row of the AstroBin CSV and is read nowhere else
in the application.

**"NINA instances"** and **"Stellarium instances"**, two lists of one shape, in the editable row
shape `ScanRootRowViewModel` already uses. One row per stored instance, carrying a `TextBox`
watermarked "Name", a `TextBox` watermarked "http://host:1888" on the NINA list and
"http://host:8090" on the Stellarium list, a `CheckBox` labelled "On", and a `Button.quiet`
"Remove" with the tooltip "Remove this instance". Below the rows an "Add instance" `Button.sm`
appends a row with an empty name, an empty URL and On checked, which is what the web does. A row
is written to the document on each committed edit, not on a save button: the tab has none, like
every other Settings tab.

**What the tab refuses and what it only marks.** A URL that fails the rule of section 12.16 is
refused before it is stored and the box reverts to the stored value, with the sentence "The
instance URL must start with http:// or https:// and name a host." An instance with a blank name
or a blank URL **is** stored, because a half-filled row is a row the reader is still filling in,
and that row carries the caption "Not offered on the target page until it has a name and a URL."
The target page's own filter (section 12.4) is the second half of the same rule: the menu builds
from enabled instances that have a name and a URL and from nothing else, so a half-filled row can
never produce a menu item whatever this tab did.

There is no object type editor on any tab. The object type is edited on the target it belongs to,
in the Details panel of section 12.4 (PAR-009), and the list that edit offers is section 9.8's
display category table in that table's order followed by `Other`, which is the same list the
dashboard's Object Type filter and the Statistics breakdowns group by. No tab holds a second copy
of it.

Settings write through `SettingsStore`, which validates before persisting and invalidates
the alias map cache on any change to `filters` or `equipment`. A view-model that writes the
general document takes `SettingsStore.MutateGeneral` as a delegate rather than the store
itself, and this now holds without exception: `LogViewerViewModel` was the last view-model
holding a store and takes the delegate too. The alias map is cached in
memory with a 30 second TTL as a backstop; explicit invalidation is the primary mechanism,
matching `normalization.invalidate_alias_cache`.

### 12.8 Diagnostics and log viewer

**Diagnostics page fields:**

| Group | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| Database | File path, file size, WAL size, page count, row counts for images, targets, session notes, activity events, catalog cache, merge candidates, and scan runs. Also (ruling F2) row counts for the four guide-log tables, `phd2_logs`, `phd2_sessions`, `phd2_frames` and `phd2_calibrations`, and one figure beside them, "PHD2 data size", the total bytes those four tables and their indexes occupy, read with SQLite's `dbstat` virtual table when the shipped library exposes it and estimated from the page count otherwise, with the field saying which of the two it is. `phd2_frames` is the volume table (section 5.17) and this is the field a reader checks before asking why the database grew. |
| Scan | Current state, current progress envelope, last run's trigger, start, finish, duration, and every counter. Watcher state per root, including whether the root is currently reachable. Next scheduled scan time. |
| Resolver | Catalog cache row counts split into positive and negative, hit and miss counters for the current process, and the count of negative rows that have expired. |
| Unresolved | Distinct unresolved `OBJECT` strings with frame counts, and a retry button. |
| Errors | The last 50 error-level and warning-level events. |
| Versions | Application version, git SHA, .NET runtime version, Avalonia version, SQLite library version, operating system version. |
| Paths | App data directory, then "Data location source" immediately after it, reading one of `default`, `pointer`, `environment` or `override`, then database path, log directory, thumbnail cache directory, catalog directory. The same value is a bundle field (section 16.3). Two fields close out the group: "Startup shortcut", reading one of `present`, `absent`, `not applicable` or `unknown` (a failed query on an installed build), and "Started minimized", reading `yes` or `no` (section 12.11). |

A resolver hit is a lookup answered from `catalog_cache` with no network call: a positive row,
or a negative row that has not expired. Every other lookup is a miss, including one that found
an expired negative row, which section 9.6 treats as a miss.

The diagnostics query opens the database read-only, on an unpooled connection that is closed with
the read, so a refresh never leaves a connection behind and is never the last handle on the file.

A stored `general` document that does not parse leaves the Scan group's watcher rows empty and
reports the failure in the Errors group instead of taking the page down. The bundle still
exports, with the unparseable document embedded verbatim under a `parse_error` key
(section 16.3).

**Export JSON bundle** writes one file containing every field above, the last 500 log lines,
the settings document (no redaction needed, there are no secrets), and the scan run history.
Section 16.3 defines the contents.

Write path, one of the two sanctioned writes outside app data (section 2.1.1; Save log as below
is the other and takes the same three steps):

1. The user picks a destination in the platform save dialog. The dialog is the only place a
   path outside app data can enter the application.
2. That path is handed to `AppWriter.BeginExport(path)`, which returns a scoped writer valid
   for this one operation and disposed when it ends.
3. The bundle is written as a **new file** at that path. The save dialog's own overwrite
   confirmation is the only way an existing file is replaced, and it is the operating
   system's prompt, not the application's. The application never overwrites a user file
   without that prompt and never chooses the path itself.

**Log viewer:** a virtualized list over the current Serilog file plus the retained rolled
files, all read through `UserFiles` in shared-read mode so the live sink is not disturbed.
Controls: minimum level filter (Verbose, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Fatal),
free-text search, a follow-tail toggle, copy selection, copy all, open log folder in
Explorer, Save log as, Clear log, and the `general.log_level` selector that sets what is captured
in the first place. Free-text search matches the message only, as a case-insensitive substring.
Copy all copies at most `min(50000, general.app_log_max_rows)` entries, newest first (ruling D3):
50,000 is the clipboard-shaped ceiling this port has always had, and a smaller row cap lowers it
so a copy never exceeds what the viewer itself is holding. The control's tooltip states the
effective cap, and the first copied line states it when the copy reached it. Follow-tail re-reads
every 2 seconds, one flush of headroom over the sink's `flushToDiskInterval` of 1 second
(section 16.1).

**The viewer cap (PAR-012).** `general.app_log_max_rows` (section 5.8.1, default 50000) bounds
how many lines the viewer holds at once: paging older stops when the loaded count reaches it and
the list says why rather than appearing to run out of log. The value takes effect on the next
load with no restart, and lowering it below the currently loaded count trims the oldest loaded
lines. It does not resize the 500 entry in-memory warning ring of section 16.1, which feeds the
Errors group above: that ring is a fixed diagnostic buffer, not a log store, and section 16.1
states its size.

**Save log as (PAR-016).** The viewer writes the log to a file the user picks, by the same three
steps the bundle above uses: the save dialog is the only place a path outside app data enters the
application, the path goes to `AppWriter.BeginExport(path)`, and the content is written as one
new file at that path. The content is the lines the viewer currently holds after the minimum
level filter and the search, oldest first so the file reads the way a log reads, bounded by the
viewer cap above. The save dialog's own overwrite confirmation is the only way an existing file
is replaced, and the application never picks the path. Port of `backend/app/api/logs.py`
`GET /download`.

**Clear log (PAR-016).** Deletes the rolled Serilog files under the app data log directory
through `AppWriter.Delete`, and nothing else. The file the sink currently holds open is not
deleted, not truncated and not touched: Serilog owns it, deleting a file out from under a live
sink is how a logging subsystem stops logging, and the live file is where the evidence of the
next problem goes. The action names what it will delete before it runs, reports the file count
and the bytes it removed, and reloads the viewer. It is permitted because the log directory is
app data, the same reason section 2.1 permits Serilog's own rolling to delete a retained file.
Port of `backend/app/api/logs.py` `DELETE`, whose database-backed log store has no counterpart
here.

### 12.9 Merge dialog

Mirrors `MergePreviewModal.tsx` and the merge flow in `TargetDetailPage.tsx`.

**Candidate list**, in Settings, Targets tab: one row per pending `merge_candidates` row
showing the source name, its frame count, the suggested target, the similarity score as a
percentage, the method (`simbad`, `trigram`, `duplicate`, `orphan`), and the reason text.
Actions per row: accept (opens the merge preview), dismiss (sets status `dismissed`), and edit
target (opens target search to choose a different winner). Edit target writes the chosen winner
to the candidate's `suggested_target_id` and leaves the row pending; it does not merge anything
and does not open the preview.

**Merge preview dialog**, opened from a candidate or from Target detail's merge action:

- A target search box with the same fuzzy, alias-aware search as the dashboard.
- Side-by-side comparison of winner and loser: primary name, catalog id, aliases, object
  type, RA and Dec, frame count, integration, session count, first and last session.
- A list of the session dates that will collide, with the note-merge behavior stated
  (section 9.7).
- Confirm and cancel. Confirm writes the manifest, moves the frames, and reports the counts.
  Cancel stays available while the preview is loading, which writes nothing and can be
  abandoned; it is disabled only while a confirm is writing, and so is the window's own close,
  because abandoning a dialog mid-transaction would report that nothing happened while the
  transaction commits.

**Merge history**, on Target detail and in Settings: one row per manifest, showing the loser
name, the merge time, the moved frame count, and an undo button. Undo consumes the manifest.
Both merge shapes appear: a target merge names the loser target, an unresolved-name merge names
the manifest's `source_name`. An undo whose manifest's winner has itself been merged away is
refused and the row says which merge to undo first (section 9.7).

### 12.10 Empty and error states

Every list has a defined empty state, because a fresh install shows all of them at once.

| Screen | Empty state |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard | "No frames catalogued yet" with a Run Scan button, or "No targets match these filters" with a Reset Filters button when filters are active. |
| Target detail | Not reachable empty: the Dashboard only offers rows that have frames. A stale group key is a separate state. |
| Statistics | "No data yet. Run a scan." |
| Activity | "No activity recorded." |
| Diagnostics | Always populated. |
| Log viewer | "No log entries at this level." |
| Log viewer, no log file | "No log files yet." |
| Log viewer, search matched nothing | "No entries match this search." |
| Merge candidates | "No duplicate suggestions." |
| Merge history | "No merges recorded.", in place of the rows, on both surfaces (Target detail and Settings). |
| Unresolved names | "Every OBJECT name resolved." |
| Rename history | "No renames recorded." |

A Targets tab list whose read fails renders one line in place of the list rather than an empty
state, because nothing was learned about whether it is empty: "Duplicate suggestions could not
be loaded.", "The merge history could not be loaded.", "The unresolved names could not be
loaded.", "The rename history could not be loaded.".

A scan root that is unreachable renders as a warning banner on the Dashboard naming the
path, not as a silent empty list.

Stale group key. A Dashboard page can sit on screen while a scan prunes a group's last frame,
or while a merge takes the target away, so a row click can name a group with no frames, a
`targets` row that no longer exists, or one whose `merged_into_id` is set.
`TargetDetailQuery.Get` returns null for the first two, and Target detail renders a one-line
callout naming the group key plus the Back affordance: never a blank page, and never an
exception on the UI thread.

A merged-away target is the third case and is no longer a stale key: the page opens and renders
a callout reading `This target was merged into "<winner>".` with an Open `<winner>` button that
navigates to the surviving target. There is no silent redirect: the user is told what happened
and chooses to follow it.

### 12.11 Tray residency and startup

The application can live in the Windows notification area. It keeps scanning while no window is
open, it can start with the machine, and it can start into the tray with no window at all. Every
behaviour here is off by default except where stated, and every one of them is a `general` key
(section 5.8.1).

1. **One instance.** A second GUI launch does not start a second application. It asks the running
   instance to show its window and exits 0 without opening the database, running a migration,
   writing a log line, or creating anything on disk. The claim is a named mutex plus a named
   auto-reset `EventWaitHandle`, not a file and not a socket; nothing in this application listens
   (section 19.2). A launch whose command line carries `--minimized` asks for nothing and exits 0
   silently, because it is the Startup shortcut firing while the user is already running the
   application. The switch is consumed only when it is the whole argument list; any other argument
   list, including one that also carries `--minimized`, reaches the CLI branch untouched
   (section 4.4).

2. **CLI verbs are unaffected.** `galactilog scan` beside a running GUI remains supported (section
   15). The single-instance claim is taken on the GUI path only.

3. **Activation.** The running instance shows its window, restores it if it was minimized, and
   activates it. The same action serves the tray menu's Open, a click on the tray icon, and a
   second launch.

4. **The tray icon.** The application shows one notification-area icon for its whole lifetime,
   carrying the program icon. Its tooltip reads the application name when idle and the scan state
   while a scan runs (section 10.4). Its menu holds four items in this order: Open, Scan now, Check
   for updates, a separator, Exit. Scan now and Check for updates are the same actions the status
   bar's Run scan button and the About tab's update button perform, with the same conditions on
   when they may be used. On a start into the tray (behaviour 9) the icon is the one route to the
   window and to Exit: no window and no taskbar button exist until it is used. Should the icon
   itself fail to appear, a second launch of the application with no `--minimized` argument is the
   fallback: it activates the running instance and shows its window (behaviour 3), the same escape
   hatch as an ordinary second launch. The icon is the application's own `Shell_NotifyIcon` on a
   message-only window, with a native `TrackPopupMenu` at the cursor, not Avalonia's `TrayIcon`:
   Avalonia 11.3's managed tray popup misplaces the menu under DPI scaling (Avalonia issue 8386).

5. **Close to tray** (`general.close_to_tray`). When it is on, closing the window hides it and the
   application keeps running, scanning and checking for updates. When it is off, closing the
   window ends the process. The application's own shutdown is never converted into a hide. It
   defaults to on, with no dialog and no separate key to remember one was shown: the General tab's
   control carries the sentence "Closing the window hides GalactiLog in the notification area. It
   keeps scanning."

6. **Minimize to tray** (`general.minimize_to_tray`). When it is on, minimizing the window hides
   it. Reopening restores it at the size it had.

7. **Exit.** The process ends through exactly one path: the tray menu's Exit, or a window close
   with close-to-tray off. Both run the same shutdown drain, with the same budget, as every other
   shutdown (section 10.5). There is one drain and one exit. Exit shows no confirmation while a
   scan is running: the drain cancels the scan and waits within its budget on this path exactly as
   it does on every other exit path.

8. **Start with Windows** (`general.start_with_windows`). When it is on, a shortcut in the user's
   Startup folder launches the install-root stub with `--minimized`, so the machine boots into the
   tray. When it is off, that shortcut is removed. The control is offered only on a build the
   updater installed, because the shortcut targets an install-root stub that no other build has;
   elsewhere it is disabled and the reason is on screen. The CLI never creates or removes it. The
   shortcut is the one file this application writes outside its data root and its export
   destination (section 2.1.1). The setting and the shortcut are not reconciled at start: if a user
   deletes the shortcut, or restores a profile that never had one, the setting is left as it is and
   Diagnostics (behaviour 11) is where the disagreement becomes visible. Whether the shortcut
   survives an uninstall is observed rather than assumed; the release checklist records what a
   verification run finds and the path to remove it by hand if it does not.

9. **Start minimized** (`general.start_minimized`, and the `--minimized` argument). The process
   starts into the tray with no window. The file watcher, the interval scheduler and the update
   check loop start exactly as they do on an ordinary start, so a machine that boots into the tray
   is scanning on its normal schedule with nothing on screen. The argument applies to one launch;
   the setting applies to every launch; the argument wins when they disagree. The setup wizard is
   not shown on a start into the tray: a first run has no scan roots for anything to act on, and
   the wizard appears the first time the user opens the window.

10. **Scan completion notice** (`general.notify_on_scan_complete`). When it is on and a scan
    finishes while no window is on screen, the tray tooltip carries the run's outcome and its
    non-zero counts until the next scan starts, requested through one notifier seam
    (`IScanCompletionNotifier`). The report is once per finished scan, and only while hidden. It
    adds no activity event: the `scan_finished` and `scan_failed` rows section 10.9 already defines
    are the durable record, and the Activity page (section 12.6) is where a user reads them. A
    Windows toast through a package is the documented upgrade path, carried as a backlog line
    rather than shipped now, because it costs a Windows-flavoured target framework, an Application
    User Model ID available only on an installed build, and the package itself. "No window is on
    screen" means hidden, not merely not-in-front: a window minimized to the taskbar with
    `minimize_to_tray` off counts as on screen, so a scan finishing then fires no notice. A user
    who wants minimizing to mean hidden turns on minimize to tray, and the notice then fires as
    behaviour 6 describes.

11. **Diagnostics.** Section 12.8 reports whether the Startup shortcut exists, as one of `present`,
    `absent`, `not applicable` or `unknown` (a failed query on an installed build), and whether
    this process started with no window. Both fields sit at the end of the Paths group. The JSON
    bundle carries both (section 16.3).

11a. **An owed PHD2 correlation is queued at GUI start** (Phase 15A). When
    `general.phd2_correlation_pending` reads true, the application queues one out-of-scan
    correlation re-run as it starts, as a registered job like any other (section 7.6). It is
    queued once per start, it does not block the window from appearing, and a start minimized
    queues it the same way: the obligation is about data, not about a window. The pass clears
    the key when it completes and leaves it set otherwise, so an application closed mid-pass
    queues it again at the next start. No CLI verb queues it; the CLI's own scan runs the pass
    inline as section 10.3 step 5 describes.

12. **Where the controls live.** A Settings **General** tab (section 12.7) carries all five
    controls and nothing else carries any of them. The setup wizard gains no step.

13. **Known ceiling.** A page that has been opened once keeps its subscription to the scan-finished
    event for the life of the process, so a scan that completes while the window is hidden still
    refreshes the Dashboard, the Statistics page, the Activity page and the Diagnostics page in
    memory. The work is bounded and runs off the UI thread. A session that has never opened a
    window has constructed none of those pages and pays none of it.

**Settings keys** (all of them `general`, all of them `bool`, all added to the table in section
5.8.1):

| Key | Type | Default | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `close_to_tray` | bool | `true` | 12.11 |
| `minimize_to_tray` | bool | `false` | 12.11 |
| `start_with_windows` | bool | `false` | 12.11, 12.8 |
| `start_minimized` | bool | `false` | 12.11, 12.8 |
| `notify_on_scan_complete` | bool | `false` | 12.11 |

A missing key reads as its default, so this version needs no migration (section 5.8).

### 12.12 Contextual help

Port of `frontend/src/components/HelpPopover.tsx` and its 83 placements across 27 files, and the
contract for PAR-002. Every page heading and every section heading in the application carries a
help glyph that opens a short paragraph saying what the surface shows, which baseline it grades
against where it grades anything, and what its figures do not mean. The port's 38 `ToolTip.Tip`
attributes stay where they are: a tooltip explains one cell, and a help paragraph explains a
section, and neither is the other's replacement.

**The spine.** One table, `GalactiLog.Core.Help.HelpTopics`, holding one record per topic: a topic
id, a title and a paragraph. It lives in Core, not in the application project, so the CLI and the
tests read it with no Avalonia dependency. It is a static table in source, not a resource file and
not a database table: the text ships with the build it describes, and a paragraph that disagrees
with the behaviour is a source change reviewed with the behaviour. Lookup is by ordinal id
comparison and a missing id throws rather than rendering an empty panel, because the census below
means a missing id cannot reach a build.

**The glyph.** `GalactiLog.App.Controls.HelpButton`, one control, one block in
`Theme/Controls.axaml`. The selector is `Button.help`, and the control carries `chevron` and
`help` together, so it takes `Button.chevron`'s shape and adds four setters of its own over it.
The selector is not `controls|HelpButton` and it cannot be: the control overrides
`StyleKeyOverride` to `typeof(Button)` so that it inherits the built-in `Button` theme, and an
Avalonia type selector matches on the style key, so a type selector for the subclass would never
match. The block is four selectors (`Button.help`, `Path.help-glyph`,
`Button.help:pointerover Path.help-glyph` and `TextBlock.help-paragraph`) plus two
`StreamGeometry` resources and one `DataTemplate`, not a single style.

Its content is a drawn `Path` pair: a ring with an `i` inside it, in one stroke weight. It is not
a Unicode glyph, per `DESIGN.md`'s refusal list, and no view declares its own version of the
style, which `ControlStyleScanTest` already enforces. It takes one property, the topic id, and
renders that topic's title and paragraph in a `Flyout`.

The flyout body is a keyed `DataTemplate`, `HelpTopicFlyoutTemplate` in `Theme/Controls.axaml`,
over `HelpTopic`; the control looks it up and builds its own `Flyout` from it, and only
`Placement` and `ShowMode` live in C#. It is not a `Setter`, and turning it into one would be
wrong twice: a setter's `Template` yields a `Control` rather than a `FlyoutBase`, and a `<Flyout>`
written in a setter would be one instance shared by all 81 glyphs.

Its behaviour is fixed and is narrower than the web's:

| Gesture | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Click, or Space or Enter while focused | Opens the flyout. |
| Click again, Escape, or a click outside | Closes it. |
| Hover | Nothing. The web opens on hover after 150 ms; the port does not (UI layout ruling 10). A reader moving the pointer across a page of headings would otherwise walk through a corridor of opening panels. |
| Tab | The button is a tab stop and the open flyout takes focus, so the paragraph is reachable and dismissable from the keyboard alone. The focus is a mechanism, not a side effect of opening: `FlyoutShowMode.Standard` governs light dismissal and moves the keyboard nowhere by itself, so the template's root is declared `Focusable` with `IsTabStop` off and the control focuses the popup host's first focusable element when the flyout raises `Opened`, posted at input priority because the host is open before its content has been through a layout pass. Removing the `Focusable` attribute as decoration breaks this row. |
| F1 | Nothing. There is no global help key and no docked help pane. |

The button carries the accessible name "About this section" followed by the topic's title, so a
screen reader distinguishes two glyphs on one page.

**Placement.** One glyph beside every page heading and every section heading, once each, on the
trailing side of the heading text, inside the heading's own row so it collapses with the heading.
A section behind a chevron band carries its glyph on the band, beside the title and before any
right-aligned summary, and the glyph is live whether the section is open or closed: a closed
section is exactly when a reader needs to know what is inside it. A glyph is never placed on a
column header, a field label, a button or a table cell.

A heading drawn inside a shared template gets its own heading row rather than a glyph inside the
template, because a glyph inside a shared template would give every instance the same topic id.
The Statistics page's bar chart template is the one case: it is a title over a body template, the
three cards that carry a topic (`stats.filter-usage`, `stats.top-targets` and `stats.ingest`) apply
the body template and draw their own title row beside the glyph, and the other three keep the full
template. The chart markup is written once either way. A surface with no heading element at all
takes the glyph on the row above the content, which is the overview tile row's case, rather than
gaining an invented heading.

Three surfaces are deliberately excluded and carry no glyph, so an implementer does not add one
and the census does not expect one:

- The Reset database confirmation window (section 12.7) and the update prompt (section 17.1),
  whose whole body is already the explanation.
- The frame table's own "Frames" label in `FrameTableView.axaml`, which is the same heading as the
  session pane's "Frames" band rendered inside it. The band carries the glyph.
- The navigation rail and the status bar, which have no headings.

**The census.** One test asserts three things: every `HelpButton` in every `.axaml` under
`src/GalactiLog.App` names a topic id that exists in `HelpTopics`; every topic id in `HelpTopics`
is named by exactly one `HelpButton`; and the set of topic ids equals the table below, row for
row. The count is placements in markup, not placements at run time: `DiagnosticsView` is hosted
both by the navigation rail and by the Settings Diagnostics tab and its glyphs are declared once.
Adding a page or a section to the application therefore fails the test until its topic is added
here and placed, which is the structural enforcement this document prefers to a convention
(`DESIGN.md`, and the same reason the theme token census exists).

A `HelpButton` whose `Topic` is bound rather than literal counts as the set of ids that binding
can produce, read from the view-model's own total switch, and it counts as one placement for each
of them. Four such sites ship: the Diagnostics group header, whose `DiagnosticsGroupViewModel`
switch produces the seven `diagnostics.*` group ids, the setup wizard's step header, whose
`SetupStepViewModel` switch produces the five `setup.*` ids, and the night chart's help glyph in
`NightMetricsPart.axaml`, whose `SessionChartViewModel.HelpTopicIds` switch produces
`target.session-metrics` and `target.guiding` (Phase 24 R3), and the stacking export wizard's step
glyph in `WbppExportWindow.axaml`'s header help slot, whose `WbppExportStepViewModel.HelpTopicIds`
list produces the six `export.*` step ids (section 12.13). The census resolves a bound site by
its markup file rather than by restating either list, so a bound site in a file the map does not
know carries its binding text into the failure instead of borrowing another site's ids.

**The topic table.** 113 topics, placed by 97 `HelpButton` elements across 41 markup files: 93
literal ids and the four bound sites above, which expand to the remaining 20. Phase 15A added one
topic, `settings.equipment.phd2-profiles`, beside one literal placement; Phase 15B added two more,
`target.guiding` and `stats.guiding`, each beside one literal placement (Phase 24 R3 moved
`target.guiding` and `target.session-metrics` onto the night chart's bound glyph and deleted
`GuidingPart.axaml`); Phase 16 added five,
`page.export-stacking` and the four `export.*` ids, all five placed in the one new markup file
`WbppExportWindow.axaml`, which is the twenty-seventh; Phase 17 added seven, `page.analysis`,
`analysis.filters` and the five `analysis.<tab>` ids, all seven placed in the one new markup file
`AnalysisView.axaml`, which is the twenty-eighth; Phase 20 added four, `dashboard.custom`,
`settings.display.ledger-columns` and the two `settings.custom-columns.*` ids, each beside one
literal placement, two of them in the one new markup file `CustomColumnsTabView.axaml`, which is
the twenty-ninth; Phase 21 added four, the four `settings.external-tools.*` ids, all four placed in
the one new markup file `ExternalToolsTabView.axaml`, which is the thirtieth; Phase 22 added two,
`page.sky-view` in the one new markup file `SurveyViewWindow.axaml`, which is the thirty-second,
and `settings.general.survey-downloads` beside one literal placement in the existing
`GeneralTabView.axaml`. Phase 21 placed no
help glyph on the Target detail page: the four items it adds to that page's two flyouts are menu
items, which carry no heading for a glyph to sit beside, and each is explained in the topic of the
group that configures it. Each carries a tooltip instead, the way the ledger's night check box
does. The stacking export wizard added four, `export.destination`, `export.method`,
`export.review` and `export.result`, and moved `export.folders` and `export.quality` from literal
headings onto the window's one bound step glyph, which places all six step ids; `export.settings`
and `export.script` stay literal, on the staging folder step and the result step. Phase 18 adds
nine, the four `mosaics.*` ids and the five `mosaic.*` ids, each beside one literal placement, in
three new markup files, `MosaicsView.axaml`, `MosaicDetailView.axaml` and
`CreateMosaicWindow.axaml`, which brings the table to 112 topics placed by 96 `HelpButton`
elements. Phase 19A adds one, `mosaic.arranger`, beside one literal placement in the one new markup
file `ArrangerView.axaml`, the forty-first, which brings the table to 113 topics placed by 97
`HelpButton` elements; the census test pins the new figures. The Source column
says where the paragraph came
from: a web file means the paragraph is that file's `HelpPopover` text, edited only for this
port's vocabulary, for the surfaces the port does not ship, and for MAD units in place of sigma;
`port-authored` means the web has no matching popover and the paragraph was written from this
document's own section for that surface.

| `page.dashboard` | Every target GalactiLog has catalogued, one row each, with the integration, frame count, filters and equipment it has recorded. The filter panel on the left narrows the list; the column picker chooses which figures the rows carry. Opening a row opens that target's detail page. |
| `page.statistics` | Aggregate figures across the whole library, in ten sections: overview, equipment performance, guiding, equipment inventory, filter usage, top targets, timeline or calendar, data quality, storage and ingest history. Open the glyph beside a section for what that section counts. |
| `page.analysis` | Explores relationships and trends across the frames GalactiLog has catalogued. Scope is set once in the Shared filters card, and four of the five tabs below are views of that one slice: Correlation as a scatter of two metrics, Distributions as a histogram or box plot of one, Time Series as a nightly median plotted over time, and Matrix as a grid of Pearson correlations between the X and Y metrics. Compare is the exception: it picks its own two groups and takes only the shared date range, which bounds the imaging night, then places them side by side. |
| `page.activity` | Everything the application did, newest first: scans, merges, renames, maintenance actions and their failures. A scan row expands to its child events. The list is bounded by the activity retention window, so an event older than that window is gone. |
| `page.diagnostics` | The state of this installation: the database, the last scan and the watchers, the resolver cache, unresolved names, recent errors, versions and paths. Nothing here changes anything. The Export JSON bundle button writes all of it to one file for a bug report. |
| `page.settings` | Settings configure how GalactiLog catalogues and displays your FITS data, and each tab covers one area. Open the glyph beside any section heading inside a tab for what that section does. Changes are written to this profile's settings document as you make them. |
| `page.target` | Everything GalactiLog knows about one imaging target: the identity line and the Details panel with the catalogue record, the log line with the totals, and the nights ledger. The page has three layouts, chosen from the layout box in the header or in Settings, under Display, and kept per profile; a change keeps the night, the frame, Compare to and the metric toggles. Question Modes has a mode switch under the header: Night review, Compare nights, for the trend across nights, and Integration, for the hours per filter against each goal. Night Bench shows the ledger and the trend strips at the left, the night's timeline, chart and frames in the centre, and the night's detail at the right on a wide window. Cascading Rows stacks the target, the night and the frames in three rows. In every layout, the lit ledger row opens into that night's per-filter figures. |
| `page.preview` | A rendered view of one frame, at the configured preview resolution. The wheel zooms, a drag pans, and a double-click or the 0 key fits. The left and right arrows step through the frames of the list this preview was opened from. The metadata strip under the frame name carries that frame's filter, exposure and graded metrics, and it updates on every step. Render full preview on navigation is on by default, so every step renders a fresh full-resolution preview; turned off, stepping shows each frame's cached thumbnail, which is faster across a few hundred frames. |
| `page.merge` | A preview of what merging two targets does before it does it: which target survives, which is merged away, and how many frames, sessions and aliases move. A merge is recorded and can be undone from the merge history. |
| `page.frame-list` | Copies the file list for the nights checked in the ledger. Good copies the frames the grading did not reject and Bad copies the frames it did. A frame with no recorded quality data counts as unmeasured: it is never bad, and it joins the good list only while Include unmeasured is checked. Absolute paths gives one full path per line, Names gives one bare file name per line, and Explorer search gives a string to paste into the Windows Explorer search box, which works best up to a few dozen files. This dialog writes the clipboard and nothing else; it moves, renames and deletes no file. |
| `setup.scan-folders` | The folders GalactiLog walks looking for FITS files. Each folder is its own boundary, so one folder may not sit inside another. The count beside the list is a shallow probe rather than a full walk, so it is an indication rather than a total. Folders to skip are configured later under Settings, Library, in the exclude paths and name rules. |
| `setup.storage` | Where this installation keeps its own files: the data location holds the database, the logs and the settings, and the thumbnail cache holds generated thumbnails and previews. A change to the data location takes effect the next time GalactiLog starts and deletes nothing from the old location. Neither path is inside your FITS library, and nothing is ever written there. |
| `setup.observer` | Your site latitude and longitude in decimal degrees, positive north and east, and the timezone your clock is set to. They are used as a fallback when a FITS header carries no site coordinates, to compute darkness hours and target altitude, and to compute the local noon boundary that imaging night grouping uses. Without a longitude that boundary falls back to UTC midnight, which splits most nights in two. |
| `setup.scan-options` | How often GalactiLog re-walks your library on its own, and whether it catalogues calibration frames alongside light frames. A shorter interval picks up new frames sooner at the cost of more disk activity; a large library on a network share is happier with a longer one. Each scan reads only files that are new or changed since the last run. |
| `setup.first-scan` | The first scan reads every file it finds, so it takes far longer than later scans, which pick up only new or changed files. Everything configured in this wizard is already saved, so starting the scan later from Settings loses nothing. |
| `dashboard.filters` | Narrows the target list.
