Text matches the name and the aliases; the date range matches the session dates; the metric ranges are applied per frame, so a target is shown only when it has a frame inside every range you set, not when its average falls inside them. Clearing a filter widens the list again; nothing is deleted. |
| `dashboard.targets` | One row per target, or per unresolved OBJECT name where no target could be resolved. Click a column header to sort by it, click again to reverse. The column picker chooses which figures the rows carry, and the Name column cannot be hidden. Expanding a row lists that target's nights. |
| `dashboard.custom` | Narrows the list by the values you have filled in yourself. Checkbox columns offer Any, Yes or No; text columns match anything containing what you type; list columns match one exact choice. Clearing a text value removes it entirely, and choosing "Not set" on a list column clears its value the same way, so a cleared value filters exactly like one that was never filled in. A column that belongs to a night or to a rig still shows the whole target: the answer is "this target has at least one night like that", and the list never hides part of a target. This block appears only once you have defined a column of your own. |
| `stats.overview` | Library-wide totals: integration time, frame count, catalogued bytes, the span between the first and last capture, the average rig-session length and the average integration per target. Catalogued bytes is the sum of the file sizes recorded in the database, not a measurement of your disk. |
| `stats.performance` | Metric summaries per telescope and camera combination, with a per-filter breakdown under each. HFR is measured in pixels and is comparable only within one optical train; use FWHM in arcseconds to compare across telescopes. The MAD columns state the spread, so a median with a wide MAD is a less settled figure than the same median with a narrow one. |
| `stats.guiding` | Each rig here is the telescope your PHD2 profile is mapped to, through the same equipment alias map the rest of the application uses, so two spellings of one scope become one row and two cameras sharing one telescope share that row too. A session whose profile is mapped to no telescope belongs to no rig: it is counted in the unmapped tally and appears on neither card. The coloured cells compare each rig's figure against the middle of your rigs, and that comparison refuses to judge anything until it has at least eight values to compare. Here a value is one rig, so it means eight telescopes: a library with one, two or seven rigs sees plain uncoloured figures, and with one rig every cell is neutral. The figures themselves are correct and comparable either way; only the colour is withheld. The frame table's own grading counts differently: there a group is a rig and a filter, a sample is a frame, and eight samples per group is enough. This table is not that table. The altitude card reads each session's altitude from the pointing line PHD2 wrote in its own log, so it needs no observer coordinates and works on a library that has configured none. The table beneath the arcs lists the same rows the arcs draw, one row per rig and altitude band, for a reader who wants the figures rather than the shapes. |
| `stats.inventory` | Every camera and telescope seen in the library, with the frames, nights, targets and integration recorded against each. A name marked as grouped is a canonical name standing for several raw header spellings, which are configured on the Equipment settings tab. |
| `stats.filter-usage` | Integration time per canonical filter, one bar each, tinted with that filter's configured colour. It counts light frames only, and an alias mapped to a canonical filter is counted under the canonical name. |
| `stats.top-targets` | The targets with the most integration time, ranked. It counts light frames only and it counts every night, so a target imaged briefly over many nights can outrank one imaged hard on a single night. |
| `stats.timeline` | When imaging happened. Timeline is a chronological bar per month, week or day; Calendar is a grid of nights shaded by integration. Clicking a bar opens the dashboard with that period's date range applied. The efficiency percentage above a bar is exposure time divided by astronomical dark hours, and it appears only when your observer coordinates are configured. |
| `stats.data-quality` | The distribution of HFR across the library, in pixels and in arcseconds, with the average and the best of both HFR and eccentricity. Frames with no derivable plate scale are outside the arcsecond figures and are counted separately, and so are the frames excluded from the eccentricity average for using a different source. |
| `stats.storage` | Three figures: the catalogued FITS bytes from the database, the thumbnail cache on disk and the database file itself. There is no total disk usage figure, because measuring it means walking every scan root on a page load. |
| `stats.ingest` | New files added per day over the last 30 days with a completed scan. It counts files added, not files read, so a scan that re-read a changed file adds nothing here. |
| `analysis.filters` | Five controls set the scope for the tabs below, though not every tab takes every one. Equipment picks one telescope and camera combination or all of them, Filter restricts to a single optical filter, Granularity switches between per frame and per session, and the date range bounds the imaging night. Granularity reaches only the Correlation tab and the Distributions histogram; every other tab, including the Distributions box plot, ignores it. A per-session point is one night and one target. A night on which two rigs imaged the same target still gives one point, not two, because the grouping key is the night and the target, never the rig. Compare ignores the equipment and filter controls entirely and reads only the date range, because its own two group pickers are the equipment or filter selection. Grouping two cameras together on the Equipment settings tab can fold two equipment combinations into one, merging two rigs whose plate scales differ, so this equipment list is only as separate as the alias groups you have configured. |
| `analysis.correlation` | A scatter of one X metric against one Y metric across the filtered frames, drawn with a trend line and a shaded confidence band. The trend, the band, the two stats cards and the point counts are all computed over every point that matches the filters. Hide Outliers removes only the points sitting outside 1.5 times the interquartile range on either axis from what is drawn, changing none of those figures. The band is a rough guide rather than a true 95 percent interval, and it is narrower than that interval on a small point set. When a PHD2 guiding metric is chosen on the X axis, its values are night-level figures joined by rig and imaging night, and a night with no mapped PHD2 profile is omitted rather than shown as a gap. Past 5,000 points the chart draws an even sample for speed, while the trend, the band and both stats cards still use every point that matched. |
| `analysis.distributions` | Histogram bins one metric across the filtered frames with a dashed line at the median; Box Plot draws one box per group, grouped By Filter, By Equipment, By Month or By Target. A group with fewer than four frames is not drawn at all, so a reader who filtered down to three frames per filter is not left thinking the chart failed. By Month groups by the calendar month of the exposure itself, while the shared date range still filters by imaging night, and the two are not the same day when a session crosses midnight. HFR is a per-train pixel figure: it is only comparable within one optical train, and FWHM in arcseconds is the metric to use across telescopes. |
| `analysis.timeseries` | One point per imaging night, always the median of that night's values across every target and rig the filters admit; the granularity segment does not reach this tab, so switching it between per frame and per session changes nothing here. The shaded band is the middle of your own nights plus or minus one MAD, and it needs at least eight nights before it is drawn. Both moving averages count points, meaning nights that have a frame, not calendar days, so a month's gap between two imaging nights does not widen the window. A night imaged under more than one target reads Mixed rather than naming one of them. |
| `analysis.matrix` | A grid of Pearson correlation coefficients for every pair of the ten metrics on the columns and the ten on the rows, always at frame granularity. A cell is blank, meaning no answer rather than an answer of zero, when the pair has fewer than 10 frames carrying both metrics or when one of the two never varies across those frames; otherwise it carries a figure. The printed figure carries the sign of the correlation; the cell's colour is only a reading aid, not a second source of information. Clicking a cell that carries a figure opens that pair on the Correlation tab; a blank cell cannot be clicked. |
| `analysis.compare` | Compares two groups you choose directly, either two equipment combinations or two filters, over one metric and the shared date range, which bounds the imaging night. The filter bar's own equipment and filter selections are ignored here, because applying them on top of two groups you already picked could ask you to compare two groups the bar had already emptied. When the metric is HFR, the verdict figure alone converts each frame to arcseconds through its own plate scale before comparing, because pixel HFR from two different optical trains is not the same unit; the box plot and both stats cards on this tab stay in pixels, as every other tab does. Each group needs at least four frames before a comparison is drawn. |
| `diagnostics.database` | The database file and its size, the write-ahead log, and the row count of each table. A WAL far larger than the database usually means a long-running reader is holding a checkpoint back, which the next clean shutdown clears. |
| `diagnostics.scan` | The current scan state and progress, the last run's trigger, timings and counters, one row per watched root with whether that root is reachable, and the next scheduled scan time. An unreachable root is skipped rather than treated as empty, so nothing is removed from the catalogue while a drive is offline. |
| `diagnostics.resolver` | The catalogue cache and how it is performing. A hit is a lookup answered from the cache with no network call, which includes a negative row that has not expired. A lookup that found an expired negative row counts as a miss. |
| `diagnostics.unresolved` | Every distinct OBJECT string in the library that no catalogue entry matched, with the frames behind each. The retry button re-runs the resolver over them. A name that never resolves is usually a comet, a sketch object or a field with no catalogue entry, and it still appears on the dashboard as its own row. |
| `diagnostics.errors` | The last 50 error and warning events, newest first. They are the same events the Activity page lists, narrowed to the two severities that need attention. |
| `diagnostics.versions` | The application version and git commit, and the runtime, toolkit, SQLite and operating system versions under it. Quote them when reporting a problem. |
| `diagnostics.paths` | Every directory this installation uses, and where the data location came from: a default, a pointer file, an environment variable or a command-line override. The last two fields state whether the Startup shortcut exists and whether this process started with no window. |
| `diagnostics.log-viewer` | The application's own log, newest first, read from the current file and the retained rolled files. The level filter shows the level you pick and everything more severe. The search box matches the message text only. Follow tail re-reads every two seconds. This filters what is displayed, not what was recorded. |
| `logviewer.show` | Narrows what the list displays: a minimum severity, a text match on the message, and whether the view follows the tail of the file. None of it changes what is being written. |
| `logviewer.capture` | Sets the minimum severity that gets written to the log in the first place. Leave it at Information for normal use and turn it up to Debug or Verbose only while you are chasing something, then turn it back down. It takes effect from the moment it is changed and needs no restart. |
| `settings.library.scan-roots` | The folders GalactiLog walks. Each is its own boundary and they may not be nested. Removing a root stops it being walked and removes nothing from the catalogue and nothing from disk. |
| `settings.library.include-paths` | Restricts the walk to paths containing one of these fragments. An empty list means every path under a scan root is eligible, which is the usual case. Include is applied before exclude. |
| `settings.library.exclude-paths` | Skips any path containing one of these fragments. This is where calibration masters, stacking work areas and processing output belong, so the walk never reads them. Exclude wins over include. |
| `settings.library.name-rules` | Rules matched against the file name rather than the path, each either a substring or a regular expression, and each either an include or an exclude. A first run seeds five exclude rules for the common processing folders, and they can be edited or removed like any other. |
| `settings.library.test-path` | Paste a path here to see whether the current rules would let the scanner read it, and which rule decided. It reads nothing and changes nothing; it answers the rules as they are configured right now. |
| `settings.library.scanning` | Whether GalactiLog re-walks the library on its own and how often, whether the file watcher picks up files as they land, and whether calibration frames are catalogued alongside light frames. A shorter interval picks up frames sooner at the cost of more disk activity. |
| `settings.library.manual-scan` | Runs one scan now, over the configured roots and with the configured rules, and reports its progress. It reads only files that are new or changed since the last run. It can be cancelled and it can be left running while you use the rest of the application. |
| `settings.library.setup` | Re-runs the first-run wizard so you can correct a setting from it. A re-run seeds no default rules: the five the first run added may have been tuned since, and a re-run exists to change one field rather than to restore defaults. |
| `settings.targets.duplicates` | Targets GalactiLog believes are the same object under two names, with the method and the score behind each suggestion. Accepting one opens the merge preview; dismissing one remembers the dismissal and does not offer it again. Nothing is merged until you accept a preview. |
| `settings.targets.unresolved` | OBJECT names from your headers that no catalogue matched. Retry re-runs the resolver over them, and assigning one to an existing target attaches its frames to that target. Frames of an unresolved name are still catalogued and still counted. |
| `settings.targets.rename-history` | The most recent target renames, read from the activity log. Because it is read from the activity log, it is bounded by the activity retention window, and a rename older than that window is gone. |
| `settings.targets.merge-history` | Every merge this installation performed, newest first, with what moved. Undo restores the merged-away target and moves its frames back. A merge that has been undone stays in the list as a record. |
| `settings.filters.groups` | Canonical filter names, the raw FILTER header spellings that map to each, and the colour used for that filter in badges, charts and the night strip. Grouping Ha, H-alpha and Halpha under one canonical name makes every page count them as the same filter. A filter with no colour of its own takes its category's default until you pick one. |
| `settings.equipment.cameras` | Canonical camera names and their aliases. An alias is the raw string as it appears in the INSTRUME header; the canonical name is what GalactiLog displays and groups by. Grouping two spellings of one camera is what makes per-camera statistics add up. |
| `settings.equipment.telescopes` | Canonical telescope names and their aliases from the TELESCOP header. Grouping consolidates spellings of one optical train into one entry, which keeps rig-level figures coherent across nights where the capture profile wrote the name differently. |
| `settings.maintenance` | Repair and rebuild actions over the catalogue. They run one at a time and none of them is available while a scan is running. None of them touches a file in your library: they rewrite database rows and the thumbnail cache only. Reset database asks you to type a confirmation and itemises exactly what it clears and what it keeps. |
| `settings.location.observer` | Your site latitude, longitude and name. They are used as a fallback when a FITS header carries no site coordinates, to compute darkness hours and target altitude, and to compute the local noon boundary that imaging night grouping uses. |
| `settings.location.grouping` | Imaging night grouping keeps a session that crosses midnight as one night, with the boundary at local noon computed from your longitude; without a longitude the boundary falls back to UTC midnight, which splits most nights in two. The display timezone and the 24-hour clock change only how already-recorded times are shown, never how they are stored and never which night a frame is grouped into. |
| `settings.display.appearance` | The theme, the text size and the content width. Text size scales every piece of text together, including table cells and chart labels. Content width caps how wide the content area grows on a large monitor. None of it changes any stored figure. |
| `settings.display.defaults` | Defaults the pages start from: the dashboard page size, the display timezone, the 24-hour clock, and how many nights the target chart pre-selects. Each page keeps its own choices afterwards. |
| `settings.display.metrics` | Which metric groups and which fields inside them appear on the target detail page. Turning a group off hides its columns everywhere, whatever the column picker says, so the group toggle wins. Hiding a metric hides the column; it does not stop the value being read or stored. |
| `settings.display.ledger-columns` | Chooses which of your own night columns appear on the Nights list of a target page. They start switched off, and when the window is narrow they are the first thing dropped, so the columns already on that list never lose room. The built-in columns are always shown and are not in this list. |
| `settings.custom-columns.add` | Creates a field of your own for something no camera or telescope records: whether a target has been processed, a note, a priority. Choose a checkbox, a text box or a pick-from-a-list, and choose whether it belongs to a target, to one night of a target, or to one telescope and camera pair on one night. The kind and what it belongs to are fixed once the column exists, because everything already filled in was entered under the old rule; to change either, make a new column. A second column with the same name is refused. A new Target column stays hidden on the dashboard until you switch it on in the column picker, and a new Night column stays hidden on the Nights list until you switch it on in Settings, under Display. Night columns appear in the dashboard's night expander and Rig columns appear on a night's rig lines straight away. |
| `settings.custom-columns.table` | Every column you have defined, with the number of values stored against it. The arrows change the order the columns appear in everywhere. Edit changes the name and, for a pick-from-a-list, the choices; removing a choice that values still use is refused and says how many. The first press of Delete arms it and states how many stored values will go with the column; the second press removes the column and every one of those values. |
| `settings.storage.data-location` | Where the database, the logs and this settings document live. A change takes effect the next time GalactiLog starts and copies rather than moves: the previous folder still holds a copy and is named here until you delete it yourself. The application never deletes it for you. |
| `settings.storage.thumbnail-cache` | Where generated thumbnails and previews are written, with the free space on that volume. Everything here is regenerable: deleting the cache costs rendering time and no data. It is never inside your FITS library. |
| `settings.storage.file-preview` | Preview resolution is the size a full preview is rendered at, with 0 meaning the frame's native resolution, and the cache size bounds how much of that rendering is kept on disk. A cache smaller than 100 MB is treated as 100 MB, because a smaller bound evicts each preview as it is written and turns the preview modal into a render loop. |
| `settings.storage.thumbnails` | The width thumbnails are generated at. Changing it does not regenerate what already exists; the Maintenance tab's regenerate action does that. |
| `settings.general.window` | What closing and minimising the window do. With close to tray on, closing hides GalactiLog in the notification area and it keeps scanning; the tray icon's Open brings it back and its Exit ends the process. With it off, closing ends the process. |
| `settings.general.startup` | Whether a shortcut in your Startup folder launches GalactiLog when you sign in, and whether it starts into the tray with no window. The control is offered only on a build the updater installed, because the shortcut targets an install-root stub that no other build has. |
| `settings.general.notifications` | Whether a finished scan reports its outcome on the tray icon's tooltip while no window is on screen. It is reported once per finished scan and only while hidden. It adds no activity event: the Activity page already records every scan. |
| `settings.about` | The version, commit and release channel of this build, the update check and its release notes, and a link to the log folder. Quote the version and the commit when reporting a problem. |
| `target.about` | The identity of this target as the catalogues describe it: names and aliases, object type and category, coordinates, angular size, magnitude and the catalogue notes. The object type can be corrected here with the pencil, which changes how the target groups under the dashboard's Object Type filter and in the target list. Correcting it changes no frame. |
| `target.notes` | Free-form notes about this target, saved a second after you stop typing. They are yours and nothing reads them: no figure on this page is derived from them. |
| `target.merge-history` | Every merge that produced this target, with what moved. Undo restores the merged-away target and moves its frames back. The list is the record; an undone merge stays in it. |
| `target.trend` | Each selected metric has its own lane. Every frame is a small dot inside its night's band and a line marks that night's median, so a slow drift across a season is visible where a single night is not. Nights with no value for a metric leave a gap rather than a joined line. The table under the lanes lists each filter's five medians for every plotted night, empty where a filter has no value. A per-rig or per-filter split plots only the nights whose detail has been loaded in this visit, so opening a night fills its points in. |
| `target.nights` | Every night this target was imaged, newest first, with that night's medians beside the target's own means in the top row. A night's figure is marked only when it is worse than the target mean by more than one unit of the last displayed decimal; better stays silent. A night median against a target mean is not a like-for-like comparison, which is why only the clearly worse figures are marked. The check box on a row selects that night for an action; the lit row is the night the pane beside it is showing, and the two are different marks. |
| `target.night` | This night's own facts: the gain, the exposure lengths present, the first and last frame times, and the median airmass, ambient temperature and humidity. |
| `target.session-metrics` | One point per frame across the night for each selected metric, in capture order, with a reference line at the night's median for the primary metric. It is where a focus drift, a guiding failure or a passing cloud shows as a shape rather than as a number. The Guiding pill at the end of the pill row swaps the dots for the night's guide trace on the same time axis; the metric pills keep their set while it is on. Drag the handle between the night charts and the frames table to trade chart height for frame rows; Up and Down move it from the keyboard, and a double click returns it to automatic. The height is kept per profile. |
| `target.guiding` | This night's guiding, read from the PHD2 guide log a scan catalogued for it and not from any frame's FITS headers, drawn in the night chart's slot while the Guiding pill is on. Nothing is read from the log until the night is opened. Every guide session of the night sits on the shared time axis, first frame to last, and the figures above the plot report the whole night; a session under 100 frames is too short to grade, so it counts in the totals and leaves no RMS figure. Five layers, back to front: the bands where guiding was settling, the axis grid, the RA and Dec error traces, the points marking a lost star, and the dither lines; a legend entry hides its layer. Four gestures: Ctrl with the wheel zooms time, Ctrl and Shift with the wheel zoom the arcsecond scale, a drag pans, and a double click resets both; a plain wheel scrolls the pane. |
| `target.night-detail` | It opens with this night's sharpest light frame, the one with the lowest recorded HFR, shown whole at the frame's own aspect ratio and never cropped, and on a night imaged by more than one rig there is one per rig; clicking one opens that frame in the preview. Then the per-filter figures for this night and the ranges across it. HFR and eccentricity in the per-filter table are graded against this rig overall, meaning every frame captured with the same telescope, camera and filter across your whole library, whatever the target. Integration, frame counts and exposure are not graded. On a night imaged by more than one rig the table splits per rig under a rig label row. This night's guiding is the Guiding pill on the night chart. |
| `target.frames` | Each frame is graded by how far its metrics sit from a typical baseline, not against a fixed threshold. Compare to picks it: This session is the other frames of the same night, and This rig is every frame captured with the same telescope, camera and filter across your whole library, whatever the target. Deviation is how many median absolute deviations a frame sits from its group's median, in raw MAD units and not sigma; one MAD unit is about 0.67 sigma, so they run smaller than a standard deviation score. Both ignore outliers, so a few bad frames cannot drag the baseline. A group under 8 frames, or one whose values are all identical, is left ungraded: there is no trustworthy spread to measure against. The colour states the verdict in both directions: better than typical, normal, watch, and likely reject. Signal metrics (star count, background ADU and guiding) are always compared within the same night whichever baseline is selected, because they drift with the sky. A Filter pill per measured metric shows only the frames the night's own outlier rule flagged on it, with their count; a pill at zero is disabled, and Clear filters restores every row. Grading is advisory. No frame is deleted or hidden. |
| `target.session-notes` | Notes about this night, saved a second after you stop typing. They are yours and nothing reads them: no figure on this page is derived from them. |
| `page.export-stacking` | Pick, for each checked night, which folder gets copied, then optionally filter which light frames go with it, choose the staging folder the copy lands in, and either let GalactiLog copy the folders now or generate a script and run it yourself. Nothing is written until you commit on the review step. GalactiLog only creates new files in the staging folder; nothing in your library is ever written, moved or deleted. |
| `export.folders` | The rows under a night are that night's own frames' folders, from the top of your library down to the folder the frames sit in, and one of them is copied whole. The default pick is the deepest folder that holds every one of that night's frames and drags nothing else along. A badge reading "+2 other nights" means that folder also holds frames from two other nights, which are copied too; it is advisory, and choosing such a folder is how you deliberately copy a date folder two targets share. The size figure counts every catalogued file in that folder, whatever target it belongs to and whatever kind of frame it is, because it answers how much the copy will move: it reads unknown rather than a partial total when any one file's size was never recorded, and sidecars and files GalactiLog never reads are copied too and are not counted. A night that says it has no folder to copy contributes nothing to the export. |
| `export.quality` | The chips are absolute limits you type, judged per frame on the metrics that frame actually carries. Type a limit with a decimal point, such as 3.5, whatever your regional number format is. A limit on a metric a frame does not carry is skipped, never failed, so a guiding limit does not silently drop every unguided frame. A frame carrying none of the limited metrics reads Unmeasured, and Unmeasured is not copied; the Copy box on its row is how you copy one anyway. The cell colours grade each frame against the baseline the segment chooses and decide nothing: the limits alone decide a verdict, and the colours are advisory. The limits are remembered per rig, so two rigs keep two sets, and the tally counts every light frame of the checked nights, a wider set than the totals the review step shows. |
| `export.settings` | The staging folder is where the copy lands. GalactiLog never picks one for you, because a folder the application chose would put a second copy of your frames somewhere you did not choose, and the copy is large. It is remembered the moment you choose it; you do not have to press Save as defaults for that. A folder inside your library, or one that contains it, is refused, because the next scan would catalogue the staged copy as a second set of frames. The folder patterns are the folder names the script skips inside each copied folder, one per line, matched against the path under the folder being copied and not against your whole library path. Save as defaults keeps the patterns for next time. |
| `export.script` | The script is a text file GalactiLog wrote once and never runs; you run it. It only copies: it contains no delete, no move and no rename, and it writes only under the staging folder. The run command beneath it is the line to paste; the PowerShell one unblocks the file first, which is harmless when the file was never marked. Copy script, Show script and the file all carry the same text. Starting another export withdraws this section, because it would otherwise describe a plan that is no longer on screen; the file already written is not touched. If a file of the same name is already in the staging folder, the script overwrites it; nothing in your library is ever overwritten, moved or deleted. GalactiLog counts a kilobyte as 1000 bytes and the script's own console counts it as 1024, so the two state slightly different totals for the same files. |
| `export.destination` | The folder the copy lands in, outside your library. With the subfolder box on, this export goes into a folder named after the target inside it, so exports of several targets can share one staging folder. The subfolder is created only when you commit on the review step, never when you open this step. |
| `export.method` | Copy now has GalactiLog copy the chosen folders itself, with a progress bar and a Cancel button. Generate script writes a PowerShell or Bash script that you run yourself, which suits a copy to another machine. Both write into the same staging folder and skip the same folders and frames. |
| `export.review` | What the commit will do, and nothing has been written yet. A destination inside your library, the top of a drive, or an export left with no frames blocks the commit. The warnings about free space, very long paths and files already in the destination do not. Once you commit, the wizard locks until the copy ends; only Cancel acts. |
| `export.result` | What the commit did. A file already in the staging folder is never overwritten: one of the same size is counted as already present, and one of a different size is listed by path. A cancelled or stopped copy lists the files it left part written. Running the same export again fills in only what is missing. Save report writes these lists to a text file. |
| `settings.external-tools.astrobin-filters` | AstroBin wants a number for each filter rather than its name, so a filter has to be matched to AstroBin's own equipment list once. Open the filter on AstroBin and read the number out of the address: Chroma LRGB L sits at app.astrobin.com/equipment/explorer/filter/4649, so its id is 4649. A filter you leave blank still gets its own row in the AstroBin CSV, with the filter cell empty, so you can fill the number in on AstroBin's side afterwards. The list shows every filter name this library has seen, grouped or not, and a number you enter against a group covers every name in it. |
| `settings.external-tools.bortle` | The Bortle class describes how dark your sky is, from 1 at a site with no light pollution to 9 in a city centre. It goes into every row of the AstroBin CSV, so an upload carries the sky it was shot under. It is one number for the whole library: if you image from two sites, set the one you use most and correct the other's rows on AstroBin. |
| `settings.external-tools.nina` | Each instance here is one copy of NINA on your network. Give it a name you will recognise in a menu and the address of its API, which is http:// then the machine and then the port the API is listening on, usually 1888. An instance that is switched on and has both a name and an address appears on a target's menu as "Send to NINA". Choosing it opens that target in NINA's framing assistant at the target's coordinates and, when the target has a known orientation, rotates the frame to it. Nothing listens on this machine: GalactiLog only ever makes the call. |
| `settings.external-tools.stellarium` | Each instance here is one copy of Stellarium running the Remote Control plugin. Its address is http:// then the machine and then the port the plugin is listening on, usually 8090. An instance that is switched on and has both a name and an address appears on a target's menu as "Slew Stellarium". Choosing it points Stellarium at the target by its catalogue name where Stellarium knows it, by its coordinates where it does not, and then sets the field of view to 20 degrees so the object is framed rather than filling the screen. |
| `mosaics.about` | A mosaic collects the panels of one large field, each panel a set of nights from any target. It totals the integration of each panel so you can see which one needs more time. Suggestions come from Run Detection and from every scan, and Create mosaic makes one by hand. Only light frames are counted. |
| `mosaics.keywords` | A keyword is a word that introduces a panel number in a target's name, such as Panel in "M 31 Panel 2" or P in "NGC 7000 P3". Detection reads these tokens to group targets into suggested mosaics, and the position tolerance sets how close two panels must sit on the sky. A change applies to your frames at the next Run Detection or scan, not at once. |
| `mosaics.suggestions` | Each suggestion is a group of targets that look like panels of one mosaic, found by name, by sky position or by both. High confidence means name and position agree; low means review the notes before accepting. The source badge says which signal found it. Accept creates the mosaic from the checked panels. Dismiss asks twice, and a dismissed suggestion comes back only when new nights of its panels are catalogued. |
| `mosaics.table` | Every mosaic with its panel count, integration, frames and date range, counting light frames only. A header click on a built-in column sorts by it and a second click reverses it, and the choice is kept for your next visit; a custom column's header does not sort. The column picker chooses which columns show, including your own mosaic columns. Expand renames the mosaic and edits its panels, and Delete asks twice before it removes the mosaic and its panels. No frame is ever touched. |
| `mosaic.about` | This mosaic's panels and the nights that count toward each. The summary line gives the panel count, the total integration and the total frames, and each panel row shows its own figures. The Deficit column shows how far a panel's integration is behind the leading panel, the one with the most, as a time such as 2h 10m behind. The figures count only included nights. |
| `mosaic.notes` | Free-form notes about this mosaic. They are saved a second after you stop typing, and an emptied box clears the note. They are yours, and no figure on this page is derived from them. |
| `mosaic.labels` | A panel label is the label carried by a target's frames, such as Panel 2. This banner lists labels found on this mosaic's targets that no panel of the mosaic has yet. Their frames count nowhere until you add a panel for the label. Add panel creates it and includes the nights that carry the label. |
| `mosaic.sessions` | Each panel counts a night as Included, and lists the other nights of its targets as Available. A night is one target, one date and one frame label, and that triple counts in only one panel of a mosaic. Include and Remove move a night between the two lists. As new panel moves an available night into a panel of its own, and Add nights from any target makes another target's nights available to include (it writes Available rows; Include still takes them). Delete panel asks twice and is enabled once the panel has no included night. |
| `mosaic.create` | Makes a new mosaic, or adds to an existing one, from the nights checked on this target. Rows given the same panel label combine into one panel, and the label starts as the frame label when the frames carry one. The name starts as the target's base name with the date range and stays until you edit it. Nothing is written until you press Create, and a refusal writes nothing. |
| `mosaic.arranger` | Each tile is one panel's best frame in the chosen filter, with its label, its integration and, when it trails the leading panel, a deficit badge: green under 20 percent behind, amber 20 to 60, red 60 or more. A panel with no frame in the filter reads No, the filter's name and frames, such as No Ha frames. Drag a tile to place it, or select one and use Rotate CW or Flip H, or right-click it. Fit, zoom and the wheel change the view, the Rotation slider turns the whole group, and Reset all clears every tile's rotation and flip and the group rotation, leaving positions as they are. Positions, rotation, flip and the group rotation are saved a moment after your last change, with Saving shown, and tile opacity, zoom, Labels and the filter are not. The layout is for the eye only and changes no figure and no composite. |

The nine stacking export rows above are transcribed from `HelpTopics.cs` character for character,
the four wizard rows and the corrected `page.export-stacking` and `export.settings` sentences
included, as the file stood after the wizard work. Before that, the five Phase 16 rows were
transcribed after every fixer that owns that file had landed: two sentences added to `export.script`, the overwrite
sentence and the kilobyte sentence, one added to `export.quality`, the decimal point, and one
corrected in `export.settings`, which had credited Save as defaults with keeping the staging folder
after that button stopped writing that key.

**The assertion behind this table now computes which rows it pins.** It takes the five longest
paragraphs from `HelpTopics.All` itself, longest first with ties broken by id, and compares each
against a transcription of that topic's row below. A paragraph that grows into the five with no
transcription fails by name, which is what keeps the pin from going stale the way a hand-written
list of five ids did between Phase 15B and Phase 16. Transcriptions for topics that have since
fallen out of the five are kept, because a pin that exists costs nothing.

Four paragraphs were shortened from their web originals for surfaces this port does not ship: the
Settings paragraph loses the tab list, which named seven tabs section 12.7 drops; the frame list
paragraph loses the move script and the browser move, which are excluded by decision
(section 19.2 and section 2.1); the log viewer paragraph loses the process source selector, which
has no meaning in a single-process application; and the per-frame grading paragraph loses the
PixInsight SubframeSelector comparison, which compares this port against a scale it does not use.
Every other edit is the sigma to MAD units correction and this document's vocabulary.

### 12.13 Export for stacking

Mirrors `WbppExportModal.tsx`, the four components under `frontend/src/components/wbpp/`,
`frontend/src/lib/wbppQualityFilter.ts`, `frontend/src/lib/wbppBrowserCopy.ts` and
`backend/app/services/wbpp_export.py`. It prepares the checked nights for PixInsight WBPP or SIRIL
in one of two ways the user chooses in the wizard: it copies the chosen folders into a staging
folder itself, or it writes one copy script, a PowerShell `.ps1` or a Bash `.sh`, to a path the
save dialog returned, for the user to run. One staging folder serves both routes.
**The application copies frames only into a staging folder the user picked in this wizard, creates new files only, and never overwrites, deletes, moves or renames anything on either side.**
The source side is read through `UserFiles` only, the destination side is written through the
staging writer of section 2.1.1, and nothing in this wizard writes, moves or deletes anything under
a scan root. In this section "the page" means the wizard.

**How it opens.** The target page's identity line carries an Export button whose flyout lists
Copy frame list and Export for stacking (section 12.4). Both entries act on the nights the
ledger's selection column has checked, read from `TargetDetailViewModel.SelectedNights` rather
than from a selection of this page's own. With no night checked both entries are disabled and
carry the sentence "Select one or more nights first"; the command body repeats the guard, so a
keyboard path to an enabled-looking entry still writes nothing. Export for stacking is the one
entry for both routes: the route is chosen inside the wizard, not in the flyout. The wizard is
`WbppExportWizardViewModel`, an `IModalPageViewModel` hosted on `WbppExportWindow`, a
`ModalPageWindow` that opens at 1000 by 780. `WbppExportViewModel` stays the one state owner, for
the levels, the quality filter, the staging folder, the totals, script generation and the copy, and
every step reads and writes that one model; it is no longer a modal page of its own.

**The wizard's steps**, in order, on the shared wizard spine (section 12.1). The header reads
"Step n of m: <title>" and carries the step's help glyph; the rail marks the current step.

| Step | Content | Next is available when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Folders to copy | The `Border.callout warn` empty-export line below, present only in the state it describes. Then one row per checked night: the date, that night's LIGHT frame count, the chosen folder's leading path in the secondary ink with its own name in the primary ink, and, only when this night's folder name was disambiguated, the name it will be copied under. The row expands into the level tree. The level, contamination, default-level and disambiguation rules below govern it unchanged. | The levels are read and at least one night has a chosen level. |
| 2. Quality filter (optional) | The chips toolbar, the tally and the verdict table below. With no limit set every frame is copied. | Always. |
| 3. Staging folder | The staging root with its picker, remembered the moment it is committed and by nothing else (as below); the excluded folder patterns, with Save as defaults, which keeps the patterns and never the staging root; and a checkbox, on by default, "Put this export in a subfolder named <name>", the name being the target's primary name sanitized by the rule of the Generate flow's step 2. The destination is the staging root, or that root plus the subfolder while the box is ticked, and it is the one destination for both routes: the copy writes into it, the script's staging root is it, and the review step shows it. The subfolder is created on the commit, never on entering the step, and the subfolder choice is never saved. | A staging folder is set and accepted. |
| 4. Copy or script | Copy now, the default, or Generate a script, with PowerShell (`.ps1`) or Shell (`.sh`) preselected from `general.wbpp_default_os`. Nothing is persisted, and the last choice is not remembered. | Always. |
| 5. Review | Summary lines for the nights, folders, frames, size or `unknown`, destination and method; the blocks and the warnings below; the file-safety sentence "GalactiLog creates new files in the staging folder only. It never overwrites, deletes, moves or renames anything, in your library or in the staging folder; a file already there is skipped."; the note on what the size counts; and the one commit button, labelled "Copy n folders (m frames)" for Copy now, n being the chosen folders and m the catalogued frame count, because the file count is unknown before the copy enumerates, or "Write script" for a script. **Nothing writes before that button.** | Never. The commit moves on. |
| 6. Result | For a copy: the outcome, the copied count and size, the skips by reason with every present-but-different-size path listed, the failures and the partial paths. For a script: the script path, Copy script, Show script and the run command. Then Open folder, which opens the destination in Explorer, Copy path, Start another export and Close, always, and Save report only while the skip count or the failure count is non-zero. | Last step. |

**The review step blocks the commit**, stating the reason on the step, when the destination lies
inside a scan root, when the destination is a drive root or a share root, and when no frame is
left after the quality filter. **It warns without blocking** when the destination drive's free
space is short of a known byte total, and is silent when the drive cannot be queried or the total
is `unknown`; when the longest destination path is 260 characters or more (the long-path warning
below); and when the destination already holds files, stating their count and that a file of the
same name is skipped and listed, never overwritten. No application manifest is added for long
paths.

**The commit locks the wizard.** The committed flag is set before the first write. From then on
Back, Next and Escape refuse; Close and the window's own close button refuse while the commit runs;
only Cancel acts. Cancel aborts the files in flight and leaves their partial contents on disk; the
result names every partial path, and the application never removes them (section 2.1.1). The copy
runs as a status-bar job titled "Copy for stacking: <target>" that reads "Copying n of m", the
review step shows the same progress, and a copy that copied at least one file records one activity
row. A script commit whose save dialog is cancelled, or whose write fails, wrote nothing: the lock
is released and the review step stays on screen, stating the failure when there was one. Start
another export returns to step 1 over the same nights, releases the lock and discards the result.
Save report writes the skips, the failures and the partial paths as one text file through
`AppWriter.BeginExport`, at a path a save dialog returned.

**The footer carries Back and Next, then Close, the commit button and Cancel**, each shown on the
steps where it applies. **Escape closes the wizard** until the commit, through the same close
command. **There is no default button** on any step: Enter inside the staging folder field, a
pattern or a threshold box never advances a step and never writes a file, and the one write is a
button the user presses on the review step.

**The scan root is the library root.** Every path on this page is native, so the web's
container-to-library translation and its `wbpp_library_root` field have no counterpart
(section 5.8.1). A night's ancestor chain is anchored at the scan root (section 10.1) that
contains the frame, resolved by the one function that answers which configured root a path lies
under (`Core/Io/PathConfinement.cs`) and never by a second string test. Three shapes leave a
night with no usable level, each named on the row and each contributing nothing to the export:
the night's frames sit directly in the scan root itself, so there is no folder under the root to
copy; the night's frames span several scan roots, so no one folder holds them; a frame lies under
no currently configured root, because the root was removed after the scan that catalogued it. The
first two are stated as such. In the third the night keeps whatever levels its remaining frames
produce and the row states how many frames those levels leave behind.

**The level rule.** For one night, take every LIGHT frame of this target with that session date,
and for each frame the chain of its ancestor folders from the first level under the scan root
down to the frame's own parent. The levels are the union of those chains, ordered by depth and
then by the folder path under `OrdinalIgnoreCase`. **The order is total.** A night whose frames
sit in sibling folders has several levels at one depth, and the tree draws them in that stated
order with each set of siblings under the parent they share. Each level carries:

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Path | The folder's own absolute path. |
| Depth | Its distance from the scan root, the first level under the root being 1. |
| Frame count | The night's own LIGHT frames under this folder: a frame whose path equals the folder or begins with the folder plus a separator. The test is at a path component boundary and never a bare substring, so `.../Ha_old` is not counted under `.../Ha`. |
| Other nights | The session dates, other than this one, of catalogued LIGHT frames anywhere under this folder, listed. |
| Other targets | The targets, other than this page's, of catalogued LIGHT frames anywhere under this folder, listed. |
| Contaminated | True when either list is non-empty. |
| Bytes | The rule below. |

**The contamination rule.** One query, read once when the page opens and off the UI thread,
returns `images.file_path` and `images.file_size` for every catalogued file, with
`images.session_date` and the frame's target identity for the LIGHT frames that carry a session
date. **That read is a full table scan of `images` and is accepted as one.** It carries no `WHERE`
clause, by the rule above that a level's bytes count every catalogued file under it, and it selects
six columns no index covers, so no index can serve it. It is issued once per page open, off the UI
thread, behind the loading line, which is the same shape the Statistics aggregate already reads
every LIGHT row with. Measured at the Phase 16 gate on a 200,000 row library whose rows carry a
realistic 3,126 byte `raw_headers`, 851 MiB on disk: 3,640 milliseconds warm for this read plus
three per-night reads, against 4,416 milliseconds with the statement's two `CASE` guards removed.
The recorded upgrade path, if a real library ever makes it felt, is a covering index on
`images(file_path, session_date, image_type, file_size, resolved_target_id)`, which makes it an
index-only scan for every row but an unresolved dated LIGHT one, whose group key needs
`raw_headers` and therefore still visits the table. It is not added in Phase 16.

**A catalogued row whose session date cannot be read contributes no night.** The statement reads
`images.session_date` as text, and a row holding an empty or malformed value answers no date rather
than throwing: such a row joins no night's other-nights list and is never an occupant, and it is
**not dropped**, because its `file_size` still counts toward every ancestor folder's byte total and
its path still counts toward the longest destination path. That is the shape this query has always
had for a row that can never be an occupant, a calibration row or an undated LIGHT row, and a row
whose date cannot be read joins it.
The read must not fail on one bad row,
because it has no `WHERE` clause and therefore meets every row in the library: a single malformed
date would otherwise open the page with no levels, no totals and no sentence. The other-night and other-target lists are computed over that LIGHT subset; the byte rule
below is computed over the whole of it. A level's cost is what it drags along, and it is stated
on the level row as "+n other nights" and "+n other targets", with the names themselves on the
row's tooltip. The cost is advisory: a contaminated level is selectable, and choosing one is how
a user deliberately copies a whole night folder that two targets share.

**The default level** is the deepest level that holds every one of the night's frames and drags
nothing along. When no uncontaminated level holds them all it is the deepest level holding the
most frames of any level and dragging nothing along, and when every such level is contaminated it
is the deepest level holding the most frames. A night with no usable level says so and
contributes nothing to the export.

**Staging name disambiguation.** Each chosen level is copied into the staging root under its own
folder name. When two of the chosen levels have the same folder name, every colliding entry is
prefixed with its session date and an underscore, `2025-03-20_LIGHT`. A name that collides with
nothing is left alone, and the rename is stated on the rows it happens to and on no others, with
the reason on the tooltip.

**The final names are distinct without regard to case, and the prefix alone does not guarantee
that.** Two comparisons are made, both under `OrdinalIgnoreCase`: the first decides which names
collide and therefore take a date prefix, and the second is made over the prefixed list, because a
prefix can collide too. A folder a capture program already named `2025-03-20_Ha`, which is a common
habit, produces exactly the same string as a folder named `Ha` on the night of 2025-03-20. While
any two final names are equal, the later ones in level order take `_2`, `_3` and so on, so the
list is distinct in every case. Without the second pass two copy operations write into one staging
folder, the second overwriting the first, while the page reports both.

**The date in a prefixed name is the night, not the folder.** It is the session date this page and
the ledger show, which is derived from the frames' capture times and the imaging-night boundary
(section 8.2), so on a capture tree whose own folders are named by the local calendar date it can
differ by one day from the `Date_` folder the frames sit in. The prefix names the night the frames
belong to, which is the identity the export is organised by.

**Byte totals measure the copy, not the night.** A level's byte total is the sum of
`images.file_size` over **every catalogued file under that folder**, whatever target it belongs
to, whatever its frame type, and whether or not it is one of the night's own frames. The figure
answers the question the user is about to act on, which is how much this copy will move, and a
figure scoped to the night's own LIGHT frames answers a different one: at a date folder two
targets share it understates by whatever else lives there. The review step states, once, that sidecar
files and files the catalogue never read are copied as well and are not in the figure, so the
total is a floor rather than a promise.

**The total is all or nothing.** It is unknown when any one contributing size is null. One
unknown size makes the level unknown, one unknown level makes the export total unknown, and an
unknown total is stated as `unknown` rather than rendered as a partial sum: a figure the user
acts on before committing to a copy must not understate by an unknown amount. A folder holding no
catalogued file totals zero, which is a known quantity. This holds whether the quality filter is
on or off: with it off nothing is subtracted, and an unknown level still makes the whole total
unknown.

#### The quality filter

Reuses `Core/Metrics/FrameQuality.cs` and the grades of section 12.4; it declares no band
threshold and no baseline rule of its own. Five metrics can be constrained:

| Chip | Column | Decimals | Better when | Default comparator |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HFR | `median_hfr` | 2 | low | at most |
| Ecc | `eccentricity` | 2 | low | at most |
| FWHM | `fwhm` (arcseconds, section 7.1.1) | 2 | low | at most |
| Stars | `detected_stars` | 0 | high | at least |
| RMS | `guiding_rms_arcsec` | 2 | low | at most |

An inactive chip is a ghost carrying a plus and the metric name; clicking it adds a constraint
with the comparator its polarity implies and no value. An active chip carries the metric name, a
comparator select of "at most" and "at least", a numeric threshold, and a button that disables
the constraint without deleting it: the chip drops back to a ghost that still shows its held
value, and clicking it again restores that value rather than starting over. Emptying the
threshold field returns the chip to valueless rather than pinning the last number typed. The
eccentricity chip alone carries three presets, Strict 0.55, Balanced 0.65 and Relaxed 0.75, each
setting the value and the comparator to "at most" and each lit while it is the current pair.
Eccentricity is the one constrained metric whose meaning is independent of the rig, which is why
it is the one with fixed presets; a preset seeded from the frames under judgment would pass most
of them and read as an authority it does not have. Pressing the preset that is already lit
publishes nothing: it is the value already in force, and republishing it would clear every row
override for no change.

**A threshold is typed with a decimal point**, whatever the machine's regional number format
writes. Every number this panel turns into text, and every number it parses back out of one, goes
through the invariant culture, so the figure the chip shows, the figure the settings document holds
and the figure the verdict is judged against are one string in every locale. An entry carrying a
comma decimal mark parses as no number and the field reverts to the value it held, with no sentence
beside it: this section's help paragraph says to type a decimal point, and a refusal message on a
field the user is still typing into would fire on every partial entry.

**Verdicts.** The constraints are an AND over the enabled ones that hold a value, judged per
frame on the metrics that frame carries:

- No enabled constraint with a value: every frame is Copy. An empty filter is no filter.
- A constraint the frame has no value for is skipped, never failed. Coverage is uneven across a
  library, and a constraint added for guided nights must not silently drop every unguided frame.
- Of the constrained metrics the frame does carry, all must pass: any failure is Exclude.
- A frame carrying none of the constrained metrics is Unmeasured.

Every enabled constraint the frame violated is recorded, in the user's own chip order, so a frame
failing two gates marks both of its cells. The failure sentence is the metric's short name, the
frame's value, the violated direction and the threshold, each number at the metric's own decimals:
`ecc 0.62 > 0.55` for an at-most gate and `stars 412 < 600` for an at-least gate.

**Unmeasured frames are not copied.** Unmeasured is a third verdict and not a pass: a frame with
no constrained metric recorded is excluded from the copy along with the failing frames, and is
distinguished from them by its own verdict, its own ink and its own count so that the exclusion is
visible rather than silent. The per-row override below is how a user copies one anyway.

**The verdict table** lists every LIGHT frame of the checked nights, sortable by any column and
chronological by capture time until a column is clicked. Its columns are Copy, Verdict, Filter,
the five metrics, File and Night. The Copy column is a check box carrying the per-row override:
it starts at the verdict's own answer and a click reverses it for that frame alone. **It works in
both directions**: a frame the filter passed is ticked off and is then not copied, and a frame the
filter excluded or left unmeasured is ticked on and is then copied. An override survives a
re-sort and is cleared when the constraint set changes, because a verdict the user reversed
against one filter says nothing about another. Turning the master Enable filters switch off and
on again preserves overrides, which are not a constraint, and so does changing a night's chosen
level, because an override is a property of a frame rather than of a folder. The Verdict column reads Copy, Unmeasured or
Exclude in the success, warning and error ink, with the tooltip "Copy", "Unmeasured: none of the
constrained metrics recorded" or "Exclude: " and the failure sentences joined by commas. A metric
cell that failed a gate is drawn in the error ink with a mark in a fixed trailing slot present on
every cell, so the digits keep one right edge whether a row failed or not, and the cell's tooltip
is that gate's failure sentence. Every other metric cell is coloured by the cell ladder of
section 12.4 against the selected baseline. The File column shows the file name with the full path
beneath it, because one name can live in several folders. Under the table: "Filters apply to light
frames only. All other files are copied unchanged."

**The Night column's floor is 112 pixels and the File column is what gives when the window is at
its minimum.** 112 is what a whole ISO date needs in the shipped face, 98.6 pixels for
`2025-03-20` plus the column's own 8 pixel trailing inset, with the same headroom the Nights
ledger's own Night column carries for the same string; below it every row reads `2025-03-...`,
which is what shipped before this was measured on a launched application. The nine fitted columns
therefore sum to 668, and at the window's 820 pixel body allotment the starred File column is 152
wide, of which the File cell occupies 148 because it carries a 4 pixel leading margin inside the
column. **That is deliberate.** A whole date beats eighteen pixels of a file name that already
trims at that width and that carries its full path on the line beneath it, so the File column's
floor is stated per width rather than as one figure for both: 170 at the 960 the window opens
with, and 146 at the 820 minimum, each measured cell origin to cell origin. One floor for both
widths would hide which of the two is binding. Nothing overflows at either width: the row lays out
inside its allotment and the row scroller's extent stays inside its viewport at both.

**The baseline toggle** is the two-button segment of section 12.4, This session and This rig, built
on the shipped segment idiom of that section. It colours cells and nothing else: the constraints
alone decide a verdict, and the toggle never moves a frame between Copy and Exclude. Detected
stars is always graded against the frame's own night whichever baseline is selected, because it
drifts with the sky, and guiding RMS has no baseline and is never coloured.

**The tally** is one line beside the chips: "n copy, n excluded, n unmeasured of N frames", with
", n overridden" appended when any row carries an override. It counts every LIGHT frame of the
checked nights, which is a wider set than the totals the review step shows. The first figure is what the
Copy column answers, overrides included. The second and the third split the frames that column
says no to, by each frame's **own** verdict, so a frame whose verdict is Copy and whose override
excludes it is counted as excluded; the three therefore always sum to the total. The overridden
count is reported beside them and is not part of the sum, because an override is a property of a
row rather than a fourth verdict.

**The filter is remembered per rig**, as the web application does, in
`general.wbpp_quality_by_rig` (section 5.8.1). The rig key is **the port's one rig label**, the
telescope or `Unknown`, a space, a slash, a space, then the camera or `Unknown`, taken from the
first frame of the selection in the ledger's order, the frames of a night being in capture order.
It is the same string `SessionDetailQuery` already composes for the frame table's Rig column, read
from there and never composed a second time, so the key the settings document holds is the label
the rest of the target page shows. That label is never empty: a frame carrying neither name reads
`Unknown / Unknown`, which is a legitimate key and gets its own entry like any other rig. The
literal `default` slot is therefore reached only by a selection that holds no frame at all. The
enabled flag, the
baseline and the constraint list are read from that key's entry when the page opens, and every
change to any of the three is written back to it, not held until Save as defaults: the writes go
through one queued `SettingsStore.MutateGeneral` per change, coalesced, so a threshold typed digit
by digit is one save and not four. The entry for one rig is replaced; every other rig's entry is
carried through untouched.

**The web application's rig-transition rule has no counterpart here.** There the modal can open
before a selected night's frames have arrived, so the rig resolves late and the stored state for
it would overwrite edits the user has already made; the web keeps a flag and lets in-session edits
win. This page opens over nights whose frames it reads before it draws a verdict, so the rig key
is known before the filter is first shown and never changes while the page is open. There is no
transition to arbitrate and no flag.

#### Totals, the warnings, and the staging folder

**The review step** states the frame count, the folder count and the byte total of what the copy
will write, then the destination on its own line. The frame count is this target's own LIGHT frames:
the sum of the chosen levels' frame counts less the excluded frames that lie **under those
levels**. Only excluded frames inside a chosen level are subtracted, because a frame outside it
was never going to be copied and contributed nothing to subtract from. This is why the review step and
the tally can disagree: a night split across two filter folders with one folder chosen has
failures in the other that the tally counts and the review step correctly ignores. The byte total is
the chosen levels' bytes, which count every catalogued file under those folders, less the sizes of
those same excluded frames, and is unknown when any contributing size is unknown. The two figures
therefore describe different sets on purpose. **The page and the script it writes count a kilobyte
differently, and the help topic says so.** The review step's size uses the application-wide byte
formatter, which counts 1000 bytes to the kilobyte; the PowerShell flavour's own console summary
counts 1024, because it is ported line by line from the web's own script and its output is pinned
by sixteen golden files. Both are correct arithmetic over the same bytes, and a reader who sees
the page and then the console sees two figures for one copy: 437,760 bytes reads 438 KB on the
page and 428 KB in the console. Neither side is changed here, because changing the script's side
moves sixteen goldens and changing the page's side moves a formatter the whole application uses;
one home for the rule is recorded rather than taken.

The review step states the two sets it describes in one line: "Frames counts
this target's light frames. The size counts every catalogued file in the chosen folders; sidecars
and files GalactiLog never read are copied too and are not counted." A contaminated level copies
more frames than the frame count states, which is what the level's own cost badge is for.

**The empty-export warning** is shown when the filter is on, the chosen levels hold frames, and
the filter leaves none of them: "The quality filter excludes every frame in the selected folders,
so this export would copy nothing. Loosen it below, or switch it off to copy everything." It sits
at the top of the body, above the parts it is about, because the one way a user must not learn
this is by opening an empty staging folder. A selection whose levels hold no frames at all is not
blamed on the filter and says so instead.

**The long-path warning.** The page computes the longest destination path this export would
create, which is the staging folder, a separator, the subfolder name and a separator while the
subfolder box is ticked, the longest staging entry name, a separator and the longest path relative
to its own level among the catalogued files under any chosen level. When that length reaches 260
characters the review step warns: "The longest file this export creates is n characters. The copy
succeeds, but PixInsight or a script may refuse to open files at 260 characters or more unless
long paths are enabled. A shorter staging folder avoids it." The warning does not block the
commit: the ceiling depends on a machine setting this application cannot read from here, and a
user who has enabled long paths is entitled to proceed. **The script is unchanged by this**, and
nothing in it works around the limit.

**The staging folder is chosen, never defaulted.** There is no default staging root anywhere in
this port: a folder the application picks on the user's behalf would put a second copy of their
frames somewhere they did not choose, and the copy is large. `general.wbpp_staging_path` null or
empty means unset. While it is unset, the staging folder step does not advance and states why,
"Choose a staging folder first", and the rest of the wizard works normally: the levels, the filter and the totals are all
readable before a folder exists. The field is filled either by typing a path or through a folder
picker beside it, and the picker starts at the current value when it names an existing folder and
at the user's Documents folder otherwise. It never starts at a scan root (section 12.8's same
rule). **The Browse button beside the field becomes available the moment the window installs the
picker**, which the window does after the page is constructed and after the button has already
read the command once: the seam therefore notifies when it is set, rather than relying on the
order the window happens to assign it in. Without that the button is drawn permanently disabled
and typing a path is the only route to a staging folder.

**The staging folder has a step of its own**, so no disclosure folds it away and nothing scrolls
to it.

**A chosen folder is remembered at once.** The first choice writes `wbpp_staging_path` in one
`SettingsStore.MutateGeneral` as soon as the field is committed, by the picker returning or by the
typed field losing focus, so that "remembered" is true without the user finding Save as defaults.
Every later edit of the field writes the same way. Save as defaults therefore adds nothing for
this key and exists for the exclusion patterns beside it. **Save as defaults must not write this
key at all**, because the field can be blank or standing refused while the button is pressed, and a
write from that state would clear a folder the user chose in an earlier visit with no sentence to
say so. The commit is this key's one writer and it never clears it.

**A staging folder inside the library is refused.** A folder that equals, lies under, or contains
any configured scan root is rejected when it is committed, with the sentence "That folder is
inside your library, so the next scan would catalogue the staged copy as a second set of frames.
Choose a folder outside every scan root." A folder that equals, lies under, or contains **any of
this export's chosen source folders** is rejected the same way and with the same consequence, with
the sentence "That folder is one of the folders this export copies from, so the copy would write
into its own source. Choose a folder outside every scan root." The refused value is not stored and
not used, the field keeps what the user typed so it can be corrected, and the step does not
advance.
The test is the containment test of `Core/Io/PathConfinement.cs` in both directions, made against
the scan roots as configured at the moment of the commit and against the levels chosen at that
moment.

**Both sides of that test are canonical full paths, computed without touching the disk.** The typed
value, every scan root and every chosen level go through `Path.GetFullPath` and the framework's own
trailing-separator trim before they are compared. That is a pure string operation: it resolves
forward slashes onto the platform separator, collapses `.` and `..` segments and normalises a
trailing separator, and it opens, probes and creates nothing, so the file-safety rule of section
2.1 is untouched. Without it a value typed with forward slashes, with a `..` segment or in a
different spelling passes a containment test it should fail, and the generator's own guard, which
compares the same strings, fails with it.

**Accepted limit: an 8.3 short name is not expanded.** Resolving `C:\ASTRO~1` to its long form needs
the file system, and this page reads no path from disk. A staging folder typed or picked in its
short form can therefore still lie inside a scan root spelled long, and the refusal will not fire.
The consequence is bounded and is not a mutation: the script would copy into the library, and the
next scan would catalogue the copies as a second set of frames. Nothing is overwritten, moved or
deleted by it. The upgrade path, if it is ever wanted, is a single expansion at the commit, which
is a disk read and therefore a decision about section 2.1 rather than a fix. Every source lies under a scan root, so the first rule implies the second on a settled
configuration; the second is stated and tested in its own right because a scan root removed after
a frame was catalogued leaves a source that no root covers, and because it is what makes the
script contract's "no source path is ever a destination" true rather than merely likely. The
generator repeats the check on the inputs it is handed and refuses a staging root equal to or
inside any source in them, so the guarantee does not rest on the page alone.

**The staging folder step** holds the staging folder above and the excluded folder patterns, one
per line, both seeded from `general` (section 5.8.1). A pattern edit applies to this export only
until Save as defaults is pressed, which writes the patterns in one `SettingsStore.MutateGeneral`
and writes nothing else: the staging folder is written by its own commit the moment it is accepted,
and the quality filter persists itself on every change, as below. A pattern containing any character of the one refused set (a double quote, a dollar
sign, a backtick, a backslash, a carriage return, a line feed, or U+2018 to U+201F) is refused as
it is entered, with the sentence "A folder pattern cannot contain a quote, a dollar sign, a
backtick or a line break", because a pattern reaches both scripts inside a quoted literal and those
are the characters a quoted literal cannot carry safely. The set is the script contract's own
`ScriptGenerator.IsRefusedPatternChar` and not a second, narrower copy written here; the script
contract below says what each character does.

#### The script contract

The script is a pure text value produced by `Core/Wbpp/ScriptGenerator`, which touches no file.
Both flavours:

- Copy only. They create the staging root and each destination folder, then copy files into them.
  Neither contains a delete, move or rename verb, and a test scans both generators' output on
  every golden input for one.
- Write only under the staging root. Every destination is the staging root joined with the copy
  operation's entry name, and no source path is ever a destination.
- Copy each chosen folder recursively, including the calibration files, sidecars and subfolders
  the catalogue never read, which is the point: WBPP wants the folder, not a file list.
- Skip any path whose **components** match an excluded pattern, anchored so that `finals` does not
  exclude `semifinals`. A `*` in a pattern matches any run of characters. The default patterns are,
  verbatim and in this order: `WBPP`, `PixInsight`, `finals`, `WORK_AREA`, `masters`, `Masters`,
  `MASTERS`, `*CALIBRATED`, `CALIBRATED`. The three spellings of masters are redundant in the
  PowerShell flavour, whose matching is case insensitive, and are not redundant in the Bash
  flavour, whose rsync patterns are case sensitive; the list is carried across unchanged so that
  one edited list serves both.
- **Match those patterns against the path under the chosen folder, never against the whole path.**
  The components above the chosen folder are the user's own library layout, which they did not
  choose for this feature and cannot edit from here: a library that happens to live under a folder
  named `masters` would otherwise exclude every file in every job and report success over an empty
  copy. Both flavours cut the path at the job's source root before testing it, which is the same
  domain the per-file exclusions below already use.
- Skip, per copy operation, the individual files the quality filter excluded from inside that
  operation's folder. An excluded frame is identified by its path relative to the scan root, mapped
  onto the chosen level whose own relative path is the longest matching component prefix, and
  re-expressed relative to that level; an excluded frame under no chosen level is dropped rather
  than emitted against the wrong folder. PowerShell carries them as an `ExcludeFiles` list per job,
  matched against the file's backslash-separated path relative to that job's source. Bash carries
  each as a `--exclude=/<relative path>` argument on that job's rsync, the leading slash anchoring
  it to that job's transfer root. With no per-file exclusions the output is byte for byte the
  folder-only script.
- Carry a header comment naming the target, the session dates joined by commas, how to run the
  script, and the staging root with the instruction to use WBPP's Add Directory on it.
- Quote every path and every name through one quoting function per flavour and never by
  interpolation: PowerShell single-quoted literals with an embedded apostrophe doubled, Bash
  single-quoted literals with an embedded apostrophe closed, escaped and reopened. **The quoter
  itself refuses a value containing a carriage return or a line feed**, throwing rather than
  emitting it, so no caller can reach the script text around the check; the page catches that,
  generates nothing and names the file it refused.
- **Overwrite inside the staging root only.** Where a file of the same name already sits in the
  staging folder, both flavours overwrite it: PowerShell's `Copy-Item -Force` replaces it and
