  `rsync -a` updates it. The web application's own scripts do the same. Nothing under a scan root
  is ever overwritten, moved or deleted, because the staging root is refused when it equals, lies
  under or contains a scan root or a chosen source folder, in both the page and the generator. A
  user who points the staging folder at a folder holding files of their own has those files
  replaced where the names collide; that is outside the library, and it is stated here, in the
  `export.script` help paragraph and by the review step's warning when the destination already
  holds files. **The in-app copy does not overwrite**: it skips an existing file (The in-app copy,
  below).

**The PowerShell quoter emits pure ASCII.** Windows PowerShell reads U+2018, U+2019, U+201A and
U+201B as single-quote characters, so a folder genuinely named with a typographic apostrophe, which
`Barnard's Loop` routinely is, closes a single-quoted literal and everything after it in that
folder name is parsed as code. Doubling the ASCII apostrophe does not reach that. The quoter
therefore **splices every non-ASCII character out of the literal by code point**: a character below
U+FFFF is emitted as `[char]0x<hex>`, a supplementary character as a `ConvertFromUtf32` term, and a
lone surrogate is refused outright. The quoted output is then pure ASCII and no code point in a
path can carry quoting power. A value that is one non-ASCII character alone is seeded with an empty
literal, because a bare `[char]` term evaluates to a `Char` and not a `String`. A value made only
of ASCII is emitted exactly as it was before the rule, so every golden file is byte identical
across it.

**One predicate refuses the characters a quoted literal cannot carry.** `ScriptGenerator`'s refused
set is the double quote, the dollar sign, the backtick, the backslash, the carriage return, the
line feed and U+2018 to U+201F. The double quote, the dollar sign and the backtick are what
PowerShell expands inside the double-quoted regions an exclusion pattern reaches; the backslash
ends an rsync `--exclude` literal, and two backslash-terminated patterns cancel every exclusion in
the Bash flavour silently; the two line-break characters end a line; and U+2018 to U+201F are the
Unicode quote characters, of which Windows PowerShell reads U+201C, U+201D and U+201E as a double
quote. U+201F measured inert on 5.1 and the range is kept whole, because one contiguous range is
cheaper to reason about than a list with a hole in it. **The same member is the whole rule in all
three places**: the generator refuses a pattern carrying one, the staging folder step refuses one
as it is typed, and the tolerant reader of `wbpp_exclusions` drops a stored entry carrying one
(section 5.8.1). No second, narrower copy of the set is written anywhere.

**The script file name is validated by allowlist, not by refusal.** It is the one value that reaches
text the user is told to paste into a shell, so it may hold only ASCII letters, digits, spaces,
dots, underscores, hyphens and parentheses; it may not begin with a dash or a dot; and it must end
in the flavour's own extension, `.ps1` or `.sh`. A refusal list is only ever as complete as the last
review of it. The name the save dialog's own suggestion produces is inside the set by construction
(the Generate flow below states how it is derived), so the allowlist is a boundary rather than a
constraint on ordinary use, and a name outside it refuses the generation and names the value.

The PowerShell flavour gathers the file list first so its progress bar can state an accurate
total, then copies with `Copy-Item`. The Bash flavour sets `set -euo pipefail` and copies each
folder with `rsync -a --copy-links --info=progress2`, with no `--delete` and no
`--remove-source-files`.

**Every path in the PowerShell flavour is passed as a literal.** `Get-ChildItem`, `Copy-Item` and
`Test-Path` each take `-LiteralPath`, at every one of the four sites that reads the file system.
`New-Item` keeps `-Path`, because **Windows PowerShell 5.1 gives `New-Item` no `-LiteralPath`
parameter at all**: a script that passed one would fail on its own first command, before it copied
anything. Its `-Path` is a path to create rather than a pattern to match, and creating a folder
whose name holds a bracket through `New-Item -Path` was proved on disk with a matching sibling
present. PowerShell's `-Path` parameter treats `[`, `]`, `*` and `?` as a wildcard pattern, and
a folder genuinely named `M31 [HaOIII]` or `Ha [reprocess]`, which is ordinary astronomical folder
naming, then matches nothing: the job copies no file, raises no error, and the script's own footer
reports a successful copy of zero files. Quoting cannot fix it, because a correctly quoted literal
is still expanded by `-Path`, and refusing those characters in a folder name would refuse real
folders. `-LiteralPath` is the whole fix.

**The Bash flavour cannot read a name as an option.** Every source and destination it passes is
an absolute path and therefore begins with a separator, and each command takes its paths after
the `--` end-of-options marker as well, so a folder whose name begins with a dash is a path in
every invocation and never a flag.

**The Bash flavour translates every Windows path it emits.** The paths this port holds are
Windows paths and the shell that runs a `.sh` is not a Windows shell, so a drive path
`D:\Astro\M 31` is written `/mnt/d/Astro/M 31`, lower casing the drive letter, and a UNC path
`\\nas\astro\M 31` is written `//nas/astro/M 31`; every separator becomes a forward slash. The
staging folder is translated the same way, so the sources and the destination agree. The header
comment states the assumption in one line and tells the reader to edit the `/mnt/` prefix if their
own mount differs, because WSL's default is not every distribution's and a mount point is the one
thing this application cannot know. Nothing else in the file is translated: the quoting, the
exclusions and the per-file excludes all run over the translated paths.

#### The Generate flow

The script route is chosen on the Copy or script step, PowerShell (`.ps1`) or Shell (`.sh`), with
the flavour `general.wbpp_default_os` names preselected. The review step's Write script button
runs the flow below; it cannot be reached while no staging folder is set.

1. The script text is built from the current levels, exclusions, destination and verdicts. Its
   staging root is the step 3 destination, the subfolder included while the box is ticked, so the
   script and the copy write into one folder.
2. A save dialog opens with the suggested file name `wbpp_<target>.ps1` or `wbpp_<target>.sh`,
   where `<target>` is the target's primary name with every run of characters outside
   `A-Za-z0-9._-` replaced by a single underscore and leading and trailing dots and underscores
   trimmed, falling back to `target` when nothing usable remains. The dialog starts at the staging
   folder when it exists on disk, and at the user's Documents folder otherwise. It never starts at
   a scan root.
3. A cancelled dialog writes nothing, releases the commit lock, leaves the review step on screen,
   and reports nothing.
4. A returned path is written as one new file through `AppWriter.BeginExport(path)`, whose scoped
   writer is disposed when the write ends and is not reused. The dialog's own overwrite prompt is
   the only way an existing file is replaced, and this is the only write the script route performs
   (section 2.1.1). **A `.ps1` is written with a byte order mark ahead of it and a `.sh` is not.**
   `ExportWriter.WriteAllText` encodes UTF-8 with no mark, and Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a
   mark-less file as the machine's ANSI code page, so every non-ASCII character in a path would be
   mojibake and the script would copy nothing on the very libraries the quoting rules above exist
   for. The page prepends U+FEFF to the PowerShell flavour's text and nothing to the Bash
   flavour's, which is a shell that reads UTF-8 and would carry a mark into its own first line.
   `AppWriter` is unchanged: the mark is the page's, on the one flavour that needs it. Copy script
   and Show script carry the same text without the mark, because a clipboard and a text panel are
   not a file.
5. **A write that fails is a sentence on the page, not a crash.** An `IOException` or an
   `UnauthorizedAccessException` out of the write is caught and stated on the review step, the
   commit lock is released, and the page
   re-checks that it has not been disposed after the dialog returns, so a page dismissed while the
   dialog was open writes nothing.
6. The result step then shows the script path, Copy script, which writes the same text to the
   clipboard, Show script, which reveals and hides it, and the run command. All three read the one
   string the file was written from, so the file, the clipboard and the shown text cannot
   disagree.

The run command is stated exactly. For PowerShell it is
`powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "Unblock-File -LiteralPath '.\<file>'; & '.\<file>'"`,
with any apostrophe in the file name doubled, and the same line appears in the script's own header
comment. For Bash it is `chmod +x <file> && ./<file>`. The unblock step is carried across from the
web application, where a downloaded script arrives marked; a script this application wrote
locally usually carries no such mark, and the step is harmless when it does not and correct when
the user has moved the file across a share.

After a commit no level, constraint, override, exclusion or staging folder can change, because the
wizard is locked. Start another export discards the result, so no script text outlives the plan it
was built from. The file already on disk is not touched: this application wrote it once and never
revisits it.

**The page writes one activity event, and only for a copy.** A copy that copied at least one file
records one activity row naming the count and the destination folder. Nothing else writes one: not
opening the wizard, not a script write, not Save as defaults, not a copy that copied nothing. A
settings write made here raises the `settings_changed` event every save raises and nothing of its
own.

#### The in-app copy

The copy engine is `Core/Wbpp/StagingCopier.cs`, reached from `WbppExportViewModel.RunCopyAsync`,
which opens `AppWriter.BeginStagingCopy(destination)` for the one run. It copies each chosen folder
whole and recursively, exactly as the script does: every file under the folder, including the
calibration files, sidecars and subfolders the catalogue never read, lands at
`<destination>\<staging entry name>\<path under the chosen folder>`. It leaves out every path one of
whose components matches an excluded pattern, **every component including the file name**, as the
PowerShell predicate and rsync both do, and every LIGHT frame the quality filter excluded. A
reparse-point directory under a source is not followed and is counted as skipped, as the scanner
does.

- **Pass 1** enumerates every source tree through `UserFiles`, so the file count and the byte total
  are known before the first byte moves, and decides every skip.
- **An existing destination file is skipped and never overwritten.** Equal in length to its source
  it is "already present"; different in length it is "present but different size" and is listed by
  path. A folder standing where a file would go fails that one file.
- **Pass 2** creates the directories, then copies the remaining files through a pool of 4, each
  through a 1 MB buffer, the source opened with `FileShare.ReadWrite` because N.I.N.A. may still
  hold a frame open and the destination with `FileMode.CreateNew`. Files are written in place, with
  no temporary name and no rename. Progress is reported after every file.
- **Disk full** (`ERROR_DISK_FULL`, `ERROR_HANDLE_DISK_FULL`), **a destination permission
  refusal**, and a destination the staging writer refuses **abort the run**: no file starts after
  the abort, the files in flight stop and are listed as partial, and the result states the reason.
  **Any other per-file error**, a refused source read included, is recorded against that file and
  the run continues.
- A staging entry name that is empty, `.` or `..`, or that carries a separator or a colon, aborts
  the run before any write.
- **A rerun into the same folder resumes** through the skip rule: a file copied whole is skipped as
  already present, and a partial file left by a cancel or an abort is skipped as present but
  different size and listed, for the user to deal with by hand.

#### States

| State | What the page does |
| --- | --- |
| No night checked | The Export flyout's entry is disabled and says to check a night first. The page cannot be opened. |
| Opening | The level rows are listed with a loading line, Next is unavailable, and no totals are stated until the levels are computed. |
| A night with no catalogued frame | The row reads "No frames found for this night", contributes no copy operation, and is excluded from the folder count. |
| A night's frames sit directly in the scan root | The row reads "These frames sit in the library root itself, so there is no folder to copy", offers no level tree, and contributes no copy operation. |
| A night's frames span several scan roots | The row reads "This night's frames are spread across more than one library folder, so no single folder holds them all", offers no level tree, and contributes no copy operation. |
| A frame lies under no configured scan root | That frame contributes no level. The night keeps the levels its remaining frames produce, and the row states how many frames those levels leave behind. A night whose every frame is in this state reads like the row above and contributes nothing. |
| Every level contaminated | The default is the deepest level holding the most frames, and its cost badge is shown on the chosen row as well as in the tree. |
| Two chosen folders share a name | Every colliding entry is prefixed with its date, and each affected row states the name it will be copied under. |
| A date prefix collides in its turn | The later names in level order take `_2`, `_3` and so on, so the final list is distinct without regard to case, and each affected row states its final name. |
| The longest destination path reaches 260 characters | The review step shows the long-path warning with the measured length. The commit stays available. |
| Any contributing file size null | The level's bytes and the review step's total read `unknown`. No partial sum is shown, and the free-space warning is silent. |
| No staging folder set | The staging folder step does not advance and says "Choose a staging folder first". Everything else in the wizard works. |
| A staging folder inside or containing a scan root | The value is refused and not stored, the field keeps what was typed, the step does not advance, and the sentence names the reason: the next scan would catalogue the staged copy as a second set of frames. |
| A staging folder inside, containing or equal to a chosen source folder | Refused the same way, with the sentence naming the reason: the copy would write into its own source. The generator refuses the same shape in the inputs it is handed. |
| A source folder or staging folder whose name holds a bracket or a wildcard character | Nothing special: every PowerShell path is a literal and every Bash path is guarded, so the copy proceeds normally. |
| A staging folder chosen for the first time | One `MutateGeneral` writes it at once; the user need not press Save as defaults for it to be remembered. |
| An exclusion pattern carrying a refused character | Refused as it is entered, with the reason; the list keeps its previous contents. |
| A threshold typed with a comma decimal mark | The entry parses as no number and the field reverts to the value it held. No sentence is shown. |
| Escape pressed | Before the commit the wizard closes; from the commit on, Escape does nothing. There is no default button, so Enter in a field does nothing of its own. |
| A catalogued row whose `session_date` cannot be read | It contributes no night and does not fail the read. The page opens normally. |
| A file of the same name already in the staging folder | The script overwrites it. The in-app copy skips it, as already present or as present but different size, and never overwrites it. Nothing under a scan root is ever overwritten. |
| A staging folder spelled as an 8.3 short name | The containment test compares canonical full paths without touching the disk, so a short name is not expanded and such a folder inside a scan root is not refused. An accepted limit, stated above. |
| The write to the dialog's path fails | The review step states the failure and the commit lock is released. The result step is not shown. |
| Filter on, frames not yet read | The verdict table shows a loading line and the tally counts nothing; the review step subtracts nothing until the verdicts exist. |
| Filter excludes every frame under the chosen levels | The empty-export warning is shown on the first step, and the review step blocks the commit: there is nothing to copy. |
| No LIGHT frame in the selection | The verdict table reads "No light frames in the selected nights" and the review step's frame count is zero. |
| Write script, dialog cancelled | Nothing is written, the commit lock is released, the review step stays, and no activity event is emitted. |
| Write script, path returned | One new file at that path, then the result step with the script. |
| Copy now committed | The wizard locks, the copy runs as a status-bar job with its progress on the review step, and the result step follows when it ends. |
| Copy cancelled | No new file starts, the files in flight stop with partial contents, and the result lists every partial path. Nothing is removed. |
| Disk full or a destination permission refusal during a copy | The run aborts, and the result states the reason and lists the partial paths. |
| Any other error on one file during a copy | That file is listed as failed and the run continues. Save report is offered. |
| A copy rerun into the same folder | Files already copied are skipped as already present; the run copies the rest. |
| Destination inside a scan root, or a drive or share root | The review step blocks the commit and states the reason. |
| Destination already holds files | The review step warns with the count. The commit stays available. |
| Free space short of the known total | The review step warns with both figures. The commit stays available. |
| A frame path containing a line break | The quoter throws, the script is not generated, and the page names the file and says the export cannot quote it. |
| A quality chip, its comparator, its value, the master switch or the baseline changes | One coalesced `MutateGeneral` writes this rig's entry in `wbpp_quality_by_rig`; other rigs' entries are untouched. |
| Save as defaults | One `MutateGeneral` over the exclusion patterns, and the button confirms for about a second. It never clears the remembered staging folder: that key has one writer, the commit above, which writes it on every accepted change and never clears it, so it is already current at every moment this button can be pressed. |

#### Departures from the web application

- **The in-application copy has one destination and creates new files only.** The web
  application's Chromium-only File System Access copy, its separate Copy to and Copy from folder
  pickers, its stored folder handles and its permission states have no counterpart. Here the copy
  writes into the one staging folder the script also uses, through the staging writer of section
  2.1.1, skips a file already present rather than replacing it, and runs as a status-bar job.
- **No file moves and no move script.** Neither flavour contains a move, a rename or a delete, and
  no option offers one (section 19.2).
- **No container path translation.** The port runs on the machine holding the files, so paths are
  already native. `translate_path` and `detect_os` have no counterpart, and the shell flavour is a
  stored preference rather than a guess read off a root string's shape.
- **No library root field.** `wbpp_library_root` is not ported; the scan root containing a frame
  is that frame's root (section 5.8.1).
- **No download.** The web application builds the script on the server and downloads it through
  the browser. Here the script is written once, to the save dialog's path, and Copy script and
  Show script read the same text.
- **No rescan control.** The web application's preview is a server round trip with a rescan icon.
  The levels here are computed from the catalogue when the page opens, and the page is closed and
  reopened to take a newer scan into account.
- **Unresolved names count towards contamination.** The web application's contamination query
  inner joins the targets table and therefore ignores every frame whose `OBJECT` name never
  resolved, so a folder holding only such frames reads as empty. Here they are counted under their
  own `OBJECT` string, because a folder full of them drags exactly as much into a copy.
- **The per-row override is offered here.** The web application wires its Copy column only into
  the Copy Frame List modal and not into this one, so a web user cannot reinstate one unmeasured
  frame. The column is the same control in both places here.
- **The baseline's second label reads This rig**, the label section 12.4's frame table already
  uses for the same baseline, in place of the web application's "Overall". The stored value is
  unchanged.
- **The quality filter persists per rig in the settings document**, not in browser storage. The
  web application keys the same state by the same rig and keeps it in `localStorage`, which loses
  it on another machine and cannot be backed up with the rest of the configuration; the five
  `wbpp_quality_*` keys its own settings document carries are written by no surface and read by
  nothing. Here the one key `wbpp_quality_by_rig` holds the map (section 5.8.1), written on every
  change exactly as the web writes its store.
- **The composite score mode is not ported.** The web application's settings document still
  carries `wbpp_quality_mode` and `wbpp_quality_score_threshold` from a scoring mode its own
  filter module records as removed. Neither is ported.
- **`adu_median` is not a constrained metric.** The web application's stored constraint schema
  lists six metrics and its filter offers five. The five are ported.
- **The staging folder is required and has no default.** The web application falls back to
  `<library root>/_WBPP_staging/<target>`, which writes a second copy of a night's frames inside
  the library that the next walk then catalogues. This port refuses to choose that folder: the
  user picks one, it is remembered on the first choice, and a folder inside or containing a scan
  root is refused with the reason.
- **The level order is total.** The Python sorts a set of ancestor paths by depth alone, so two
  folders at one depth come out in whatever order the interpreter's hash seed produced, which
  differs between runs. Here the order is depth and then the path under `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, which
  a night with frames in sibling folders needs in order to draw the same tree twice, and the
  default pick reads "holds every frame of the night" rather than "holds the most frames of any
  level" wherever such a level exists.
- **Folder exclusions are matched under the chosen folder.** The Python matches its patterns
  against the absolute path, so a library stored under a folder named `masters` has every file of
  every job excluded and the script then reports a successful copy of nothing. The patterns
  describe folders inside the copy, and that is the only place they are tested here.
- **The Bash flavour translates Windows paths.** The Python emits the same Windows paths into a
  POSIX script, producing a file whose `rsync` arguments mix separators and cannot resolve. Here a
  drive path becomes `/mnt/<drive letter>/...` and a UNC path `//server/share/...`, with the
  header comment naming the mount assumption. **The Bash flavour's own verification is narrower than
the PowerShell flavour's, and is stated as such.** The PowerShell flavour was executed on Windows
PowerShell 5.1 against a real folder tree inside `C:\tmp`, with the library hashed identical before
and after. Neither `pwsh` 7 nor `rsync` exists on the machine this port is built on, so the Bash
flavour is checked by `bash -n` for syntax and by an argument-printing stand-in for `rsync` that
records what each invocation would have been given. **It has never been run against a real
`rsync`**, and that is what the checks above cover rather than a claim of end-to-end behaviour.
- **The size figure counts the whole folder.** The Python totals only the night's own frames,
  which on a real library understated a shared date folder by a factor of 3.08. Here it totals
  every catalogued file under the chosen folder, and the review step says that sidecars and files the
  catalogue never read are copied as well and not counted.
- **The relaxation offer is not built.** `suggestRelaxation` in the web's filter module has no
  caller anywhere outside its own tests, so there is nothing to port and no surface it was removed
  from.
- **The PowerShell flavour addresses files literally.** The Python emits `-Path` at all five sites
  that reach the file system, so a folder named `M31 [HaOIII]` is read as a wildcard pattern, the
  job copies nothing and the script reports success. That is the same failure shape as the
  exclusion matching above, in a second place. Here every one of those sites takes `-LiteralPath`.
  The Bash flavour likewise guards its sources and destinations so that a name beginning with a
  dash is never read as an option, which the Python does not.
- **Staging entry names are distinct without regard to case.** The Python counts collisions over
  the unprefixed names only, and case sensitively, so two nights can end up with one staging folder
  name and merge into it silently, the second copy overwriting the first while the page reports
  both. Here the prefixed list is checked in its turn and a repeat takes `_2`, `_3` in level order.
- **The 260 character ceiling is stated.** The web application says nothing about it, and its
  PowerShell script stops at the first path it cannot create and leaves a partial copy. Here the
  page measures the longest destination path it would produce and warns when it reaches 260. The
  script is unchanged: the limit is the operating system's and a warning is what this page can
  honestly offer.
- **The staging folder may not be a source.** The web application has no such rule; its default
  staging root is inside the library, which is the shape the rule exists to refuse. Here the page
  refuses a staging folder that equals, lies under or contains a scan root or a chosen source
  folder, and the generator repeats the source half of the check on its own inputs.

---

### 12.14 Analysis

Mirrors `frontend/src/pages/AnalysisPage.tsx`, the ten components under
`frontend/src/components/analysis/`, `backend/app/api/analysis.py` (933 lines) and
`backend/app/schemas/analysis.py`. It is the **sixth** rail destination the port ships, placed
**after Statistics** and before Activity, so the rail reads Dashboard, Statistics, Analysis,
Activity, Diagnostics, Settings (section 12). The backlog calls it the fifth page, which predates
Diagnostics. The page reads and nothing else: every figure on it comes from `images`,
`targets` and `phd2_sessions` through `Data/Queries/AnalysisQuery.cs`, and the only thing it
writes is the four `display.analysis` keys of section 5.8.2.

**The page's parts**, top to bottom:

| Part | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Heading | "Analysis" with the `page.analysis` help glyph. |
| Shared filters | One card holding the five filter controls below, the date range error sentence, and the tab strip. Its own heading carries the `analysis.filters` glyph. |
| Tab strip | Five buttons: Correlation, Distributions, Time Series, Matrix, Compare. Each is a plain `Button.sm` and the current one takes the `Button.page.current` form over it (`DESIGN.md` section 4), which is already a horizontal row of small buttons with a current state and needs no change to any shared class. |
| Tab body | The current tab's controls, its chart or table, and its stats cards. Each tab's heading carries its own glyph. |

#### The filter bar

| Control | Values | Default | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment combination | "All equipment" plus one entry per (telescope, camera) combination, labelled "telescope + camera" and carrying the grouped marker below when the combination folds two or more raw names. | All equipment | `AnalysisPage.tsx` lines 93 to 102, over the Statistics equipment performance rows. |
| Filter | "All filters" plus every distinct non-null `images.filter_used` over LIGHT frames, ordinally ascending. | All filters | `analysis.py` lines 335 to 348, the `/filters` endpoint. |
| Granularity | Per Frame or Per Session, a two-button segment. | Per Frame | `AnalysisPage.tsx` lines 202 to 209. |
| Date from | A date, or empty. | empty | `AnalysisPage.tsx` lines 211 to 227. |
| Date to | A date, or empty. | empty | Same. |

**The grouped marker** is the same mark the Statistics equipment inventory already uses for a
canonical name that folds aliases (section 12.5), and the combination is marked when either of
its two names folds more than one raw name (`backend/app/api/stats.py` line 844). The list itself
is not a second query: the equipment performance rows `StatsQuery.Get()` already returns carry
the pair and the grouped flag, and the page reads them from there.

**The date range error.** When both dates are set and From is later than To, the page shows
the sentence **"From date must be on or before To date."** under the two fields, marks both in
the error ink, and **runs nothing**: no tab issues a query while the range is reversed. This
mirrors the web, which passes `undefined` for both dates rather than firing an empty query
(`AnalysisPage.tsx` lines 51 to 58 and 88 to 90). A range with only one end set is legal and
is applied as a one-sided bound.

**Where the filters apply.** Not every tab takes every filter, and the differences are the web's
own, not an oversight to be tidied:

| Tab | Equipment | Filter | Granularity | Dates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Correlation | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Distributions, histogram | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Distributions, box plot | yes | yes | **no** | yes |
| Time Series | yes | yes | **no**, always per night | yes |
| Matrix | yes | yes | **no**, always per frame | yes |
| Compare | **no** | **no** | **no** | yes |

Compare takes neither the equipment combination nor the filter because its two groups **are**
the equipment or filter selection (`analysis.py` lines 846 to 877): applying the bar's selection
on top of them would let a reader compare two groups the bar had already emptied. The spec says
so rather than leaving it to read as a defect, and the tab's help topic says so too.

**Every query additionally requires** `image_type = 'LIGHT'`, a non-null `capture_date`, and a
non-null value in each metric column it reads. The equipment filter expands the chosen canonical
telescope and camera to their alias variants through `Core.Aliases.AliasMap` and matches
`images.telescope` and `images.camera` against those variants, which is the port of
`expand_canonical` (`analysis.py` lines 156 to 163). The filter selection matches
`images.filter_used` **exactly**, with no alias folding, which is what the web does
(line 165); the box plot's own "By Filter" grouping does fold aliases, and the two are
deliberately different, as the web is.

**The date bounds are applied to `images.session_date`**, not to `capture_date`
(`analysis.py` lines 166 to 169). The web's help text calls the range "capture date"; the port's
help topic calls it the imaging night, which is what it filters. A row whose `session_date`
cannot be read answers null through `SqlReaders.ReadDate` and is skipped rather than thrown on
(ruling A11).

#### The metric vocabulary

Twenty metrics, one table, one key each. The key is the persisted spelling. Every column named
is an `images` column (section 5.2). The label and unit are `metricLabels.ts`'s, which is the
one place the web defines them and the one place the port does.

| Key | Label | Unit suffix | Source column | X | Y |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `humidity` | Humidity (%) | `%` | `humidity` | yes | no |
| `wind_speed` | Wind Speed | none | `wind_speed` | yes | no |
| `ambient_temp` | Ambient Temp (C) | `C` | `ambient_temp` | yes | no |
| `dew_point` | Dew Point (C) | `C` | `dew_point` | yes | no |
| `pressure` | Pressure (hPa) | ` hPa` | `pressure` | yes | no |
| `cloud_cover` | Cloud Cover (%) | `%` | `cloud_cover` | yes | no |
| `sky_quality` | Sky Quality (SQM) | none | `sky_quality` | yes | no |
| `focuser_temp` | Focuser Temp (C) | `C` | `focuser_temp` | yes | no |
| `airmass` | Airmass | none | `airmass` | yes | no |
| `sensor_temp` | Sensor Temp (C) | `C` | `sensor_temp` | yes | no |
| `hfr` | HFR (px) | ` px` | `median_hfr` | no | yes |
| `fwhm` | FWHM (arcsec) | arcsec | `fwhm` | no | yes |
| `eccentricity` | Eccentricity | none | `eccentricity` | no | yes |
| `guiding_rms` | Guiding RMS (arcsec) | arcsec | `guiding_rms_arcsec` | no | yes |
| `guiding_rms_ra` | Guiding RA RMS (arcsec) | arcsec | `guiding_rms_ra_arcsec` | no | yes |
| `guiding_rms_dec` | Guiding DEC RMS (arcsec) | arcsec | `guiding_rms_dec_arcsec` | no | yes |
| `detected_stars` | Detected Stars | none | `detected_stars` | no | yes |
| `adu_mean` | ADU Mean | none | `adu_mean` | no | yes |
| `adu_median` | ADU Median | none | `adu_median` | no | yes |
| `adu_stdev` | ADU StDev | none | `adu_stdev` | no | yes |

The X column marks the ten the Correlation X picker and the Matrix columns offer; the Y column
marks the ten the Correlation Y picker, the box plot metric picker and the Compare metric picker
offer. The Distributions histogram and the Time Series metric picker offer **all twenty**, in the
order above (`DistributionsTab.tsx` lines 12 to 17, `TimeSeriesTab.tsx` lines 35 to 40).

**Every label and unit above ships as the word `arcsec` and never as the double-prime glyph**
(ruling B15). `metricLabels.ts` writes U+2033 in both places, and the Phase 17 core half read the
six embedded font faces with `fontTools`: U+2033 is in none of them, and neither is U+2032, so a
glyph there would render as a missing-glyph box on the reader's screen. `C` is U+00B0 followed by
C, as `metricLabels.ts` writes it, and the degree sign is in all six faces.
`AnalysisMetricLabelsTests` asserts the rule by code point in both directions, so a later phase
cannot reintroduce either absent mark.

`fwhm` reads the `fwhm` column and never `median_fwhm`, the rule section 7.1.1 already fixes.
It is **already in arcseconds**, from the N.I.N.A. Session Metadata CSV, which is why it is never
plate-scaled (`analysis.py` lines 76 to 80). Its unit suffix ` arcsec` is a departure: the pinned
`metricLabels.ts` gives `fwhm` an empty unit, so the web prints an FWHM figure bare wherever a
suffix is appended. The port follows this table, because a figure whose unit is stated only in its
picker label is the one a reader misreads beside a pixel HFR on the same page.

**The five PHD2 night metrics** are X only and **Correlation only**. They are not in the metric
map, so every other tab rejects them, and they are not in the X list, so the Matrix does not try
them (`analysis.py` lines 91 to 98). They are rendered as their own group, "Guiding (PHD2)",
under the ten above in the X picker.

| Key | Label | Unit | Figure over one (rig, night) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `phd2_rms_total` | PHD2 RMS Total (arcsec) | arcsec | The frame-count weighted RMS of `phd2_sessions.rms_total_arcsec`. |
| `phd2_rms_ra` | PHD2 RMS RA (arcsec) | arcsec | The same weighting over `rms_ra_arcsec`. |
| `phd2_rms_dec` | PHD2 RMS Dec (arcsec) | arcsec | The same weighting over `rms_dec_arcsec`. |
| `phd2_star_lost_pct` | PHD2 Star Lost (%) | `%` | `100 * sum(drop_count) / sum(frame_count)` over **every** session of the night, gated or not. |
| `phd2_snr_mean` | PHD2 Guide SNR | none | `sum(snr_mean * frame_count) / sum(frame_count)` over the sessions carrying an SNR, gated or not. |

**The weighted RMS** is `sqrt(sum(v * v * frame_count) / sum(frame_count))` over the night's
sessions that carry a value **and** whose `frame_count` is at least `MinFrames`, 100 frames
(section 7.6), so a two minute test run cannot drag a night's figure around
(`analysis.py` lines 113 to 118). A denominator of zero answers null, and a night with no eligible
session carries a null for that metric.

**These figures are not rounded.** `phd2_night_subquery` rounds nothing, and the night figure is
consumed unrounded by the trend, by Pearson, by Spearman and by the summary stats, so rounding it
to 6 as the night pane's and the Statistics scorecard's figures are rounded would move the answer:
measured over the user's own library, rounding the three RMS columns moves the trend slope from
-0.826913 to -0.826918 and the intercept from 2.239317 to 2.23932, and 47 of that library's 50
PHD2 night rows carry more than six decimals. There is nonetheless **one weighted-RMS algorithm
and no second implementation**: `Phd2Metrics` holds one unrounded core, `Phd2Metrics.WeightedRms`
is a wrapper that applies its 6 decimal round for the existing callers of sections 12.4 and 12.5,
and the Analysis query calls the core directly. One algorithm, two entry points. The accumulation
is the plain loop of the bullet below, not the wrapper's own shape.

**The join.** The night rows are joined to frames on **strict equality** of `images.session_date`
with `phd2_sessions.session_date` **and** equality of the rig. There is no tolerance and no
overlap test: a session filed one calendar day off its frames joins nothing. A frame whose (rig,
night) has no PHD2 night row carries a null X and is dropped from the plot, which the web
achieves with an outer join plus its `x IS NOT NULL` filter (`analysis.py` lines 395 to 407).
**When nothing joins, every row is dropped and the tab shows the ordinary no-rows state**, with
the PHD2 note above it; there is no error and no separate empty message, so a reader sees the
same empty chart whether the library has no guide logs, no mapped profile, or a profile whose
sessions land on the wrong night.

**That last case is why section 8.3's longitude split is closed in this phase.** A frame resolves
its own longitude from its own header, so it is always filed on the right night; a guiding session
has no header and, before this phase, resolved to no longitude at all when none was configured,
fell back to UTC-midnight grouping, and filed an evening session under the **next** date. On the
user's own library that would have joined zero of five PHD2 nights and drawn an empty chart with
no error on every PHD2 correlation. Sections 7.6 and 8.3 now give the guide-log side the same
resolution order the frame side has, the timezone guess included, so the two sides agree on the
calendar date of one evening. **The rig is
resolved through the live `Phd2Profiles.EffectiveTelescope`, never through the stored
`phd2_sessions.telescope` column** (ruling A10, and the rule section 12.5 already states for the
Statistics guiding cards), so remapping a profile in Settings moves a night's figures at once. A
session whose profile maps to no telescope belongs to no rig and joins no frame. The web reads
the stored column through its alias map instead; the port's rule is the one already shipped for
every other PHD2 surface, and having two would be worse than departing from the web here.

The Correlation tab shows the sentence **"Night-level PHD2 figures joined by rig and imaging
night; nights with no mapped PHD2 profile are omitted."** under the pickers whenever the chosen
X metric is one of the five (`metricLabels.ts`, `PHD2_METRIC_NOTE`).

#### Frame against session granularity

Per Frame plots one point per catalogued frame. **Per Session groups by `(session_date,
resolved_target_id)` and takes the median of each group.** The grouping key is the night and the
resolved target, **not** the night and the rig: `analysis.py` line 421 builds the key as
`(str(r.night), r.resolved_target_id)` and line 523 builds the distribution's the same way. A
night on which two rigs imaged one target therefore yields **one** point, not two. The port
copies that key exactly. A frame with no resolved target groups under a null identity, which is
one group per night for all such frames.

**The aggregate is the median, not the mean**, at every place the web aggregates a group: the
correlation's X and Y (`analysis.py` line 430), the distribution's values (line 524) and the time
series' nightly value (line 716) are each `statistics.median` over the group. The port takes
`Core.Metrics.Statistics.Median`, the one median in the application (ruling A5), which already
answers Python's rule: the middle value for an odd count and the arithmetic mean of the two
middle values for an even one.

Per Session changes only what a point is. Every filter, every statistic and every rounding below
is applied to the resulting value set unchanged.

#### The statistics

Every figure on this page is one of the following, each stated with its formula and the
`analysis.py` line it ports. The port's implementations are pure functions on the one static class
`GalactiLog.Core.Metrics.Analysis`, which is **partial across three files**, `Analysis.cs`,
`Analysis.Correlation.cs` and `Analysis.Distribution.cs`. One class, three files, so that two
implementers could write it at once; a caller sees one type.

**Summary stats** (`_compute_summary_stats`, lines 183 to 197). Null when fewer than two values.
Otherwise, over the values **sorted ascending**:

- `count` = n.
- `min` = the first value, `max` = the last.
- `mean` = `sum(sorted) / n`.
- `median` = the median rule above.
- `std_dev` = `sqrt(sum((v - mean)^2 for v in sorted) / (n - 1))`, the **sample** standard
  deviation.

The sort is load bearing for parity: the mean sums the sorted list, so the summation order is
the sorted order and not the query's. Each of the six fields is rounded to **6** decimals.

**Pearson r** (`_pearson_r`, lines 239 to 250). Zero when n is below 3. Otherwise
`sum((x - mx)(y - my)) / (sqrt(sum((x - mx)^2)) * sqrt(sum((y - my)^2)))`, with `mx = sum(xs)/n`
and `my = sum(ys)/n`. When either root is below `1e-12` the answer is **0.0**, not null.
Rounded to **4** decimals where it is reported.

**Spearman rho** (`_spearman_rho`, lines 253 to 274). Zero when n is below 3. Otherwise Pearson r
over the two rank vectors. **The tie rule** is the average rank, computed by the web's own walk:
sort the indices by value; scan runs of exactly equal values; a run spanning positions i to j
(zero based) gives every member the rank `(i + j) / 2.0 + 1`. Rounded to **4** decimals.

**The trend line** (`_compute_trend`, lines 277 to 330). Null when fewer than 3 points.
Ordinary least squares over the full point set:

- `denom = n * sum(x^2) - sum(x)^2`. When `abs(denom) < 1e-12` the whole trend is **null**,
  and the chart draws no line, no band and no stats line.
- `slope = (n * sum(xy) - sum(x) * sum(y)) / denom`, rounded to **6**.
- `intercept = (sum(y) - slope * sum(x)) / n`, rounded to **6**.
- `ss_tot = sum((y - mean_y)^2)`, `ss_res = sum((y - (slope * x + intercept))^2)`.
- `r_squared = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot` when `ss_tot > 0`, else **0.0**. Rounded to **4**.
- `pearson_r` and `spearman_rho` as above, over the same full set, each rounded to 4.

**The confidence band** (lines 302 to 320). `se = sqrt(ss_res / (n - 2))` when n is above 2 and
`ss_res` is above 0, else **0**. The multiplier is **`1.96` when n is above 30 and `2.0`
otherwise**. The band is evaluated at `n_band = min(50, n)` evenly spaced X values from the
smallest X to the largest, with step `(x_max - x_min) / max(n_band - 1, 1)`. At each such `bx`,
with `sx2 = sum((x - mean_x)^2)`:

```
y_hat  = slope * bx + intercept
h      = 1/n + (bx - mean_x)^2 / sx2   (or 1/n when sx2 is 0)
margin = t * se * sqrt(h)
```

The upper point is `y_hat + margin` and the lower is `y_hat - margin`; each X and each Y is
rounded to **6**. **The multiplier is not a t distribution quantile and the band is narrower
than a true 95 percent interval at small n.** The port reproduces it exactly, because ruling A4
makes every figure on this page match the web with no tolerance, and correcting it would make
every band in the application disagree with the source it is a port of. The label on the chart
reads "95% CI" as the web's does; the tab's help topic says the interval is indicative.

**The IQR outlier rule** (`_is_outlier_iqr`, lines 226 to 236). A correlation point is an outlier
when it lies outside the fences on **either** axis. Per axis, over the axis's full sorted value
set of length n:

```
q1 = median(s[0 .. n/2))            (the first floor(n/2) values)
q3 = median(s[(n + 1)/2 .. n))      (the last floor(n/2) values)
iqr = q3 - q1
outlier when value < q1 - 1.5 * iqr  or  value > q3 + 1.5 * iqr
```

This is the **exclusive** quartile method: for an odd n the middle value belongs to neither half.
It is the same rule the box plot uses. **Outlier flags are computed only when the point set has
at least 4 points**; below that every point is flagged false (line 446).

The web recomputes both halves' quartiles inside the per-point loop, which sorts both axes once
per point. The port computes the four fences **once** for the whole set and tests each point
against them. The flags are identical, by construction: the quartiles do not depend on the point
being tested. The difference is that the web's shape is quadratic in the point count and this
page routinely holds tens of thousands of points.

**The box plot** (`_compute_box_plot`, lines 200 to 223). Null, so the group is **dropped**,
when the group holds fewer than 4 values. Otherwise, over the sorted values:

- `q1` and `q3` by the exclusive rule above, `median` by the median rule.
- `lower_fence = q1 - 1.5 * iqr`, `upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * iqr`.
- **`min`** is the smallest value at or above the lower fence and **`max`** is the largest value
  at or below the upper fence. These two fields are the **whisker ends**, not the extremes of
  the data; the chart and its tooltip label them as the range the whiskers cover.
- `outliers` is every value below the lower fence or above the upper fence, in ascending order.
- `count` is n, the **whole** group including its outliers.

`min`, `q1`, `median`, `q3`, `max` and every outlier are rounded to **6**.

**Histogram binning** (lines 533 to 543). The bin count is **Sturges' rule**,
`max(1, ceil(log2(n) + 1))`. The width is `(max - min) / bins`, or **1.0** when every value is
equal. Bin i covers `[min + i * width, min + (i + 1) * width)`, half open. `bin_start` and
`bin_end` are each rounded to **6**; the count is an integer.

**When `v_max` is greater than `v_min`, the last bin's upper edge is `v_max`, and every value is
counted, so the bin counts sum to n. This is a departure from the web, ruled by the user (choice
19).** The web accumulates the last
edge as `v_min + (bins - 1) * width + width` and then admits a value at exactly that edge with
`i == n_bins - 1 and v == b_end` (line 542). In binary floating point the accumulated edge is not
`v_max`, so the equality fails for the single frame at the maximum and that frame falls in no bin
at all. Measured on the user's own library, 416 LIGHT frames of `median_hfr`: `v_min` 0.0,
`v_max` 2.6245, 10 bins, width 0.26244999999999996, last edge 2.6244999999999994, **and the bin
counts sum to 415 of 416** with the last bin reading 0 where it should read 1. The port sets the
last bin's `bin_end` to `v_max` and admits `b_start <= v <= b_end` there, which restores the
value the Python's own arithmetic dropped and agrees with the Python on every input where the
Python's own stated property holds. The verification bar's "the histogram bins sum to the frame
count" is therefore a property of this port and not of the web.

**The qualifier is load bearing, and the degenerate branch keeps the Python's own shape.** When
every value in the selection is equal, `v_max` equals `v_min`, the width is the fixed `1.0` above,
and the last bin's accumulated start is already above `v_max`: over ten copies of 3.5 the rule
gives five bins of width 1.0 whose last bin starts at 7.5, so forcing its end to 3.5 would invert
it. On that branch the end stays the accumulated `start + width`. Nothing is lost by it: every
value falls in bin 0 under the half-open rule, the counts already sum to n, and the shape is the
Python's unchanged. A metric that is constant across a selection is ordinary, a cloud cover of
zero or a fixed sensor set point, so this is a branch real data reaches and not a corner.

**Skewness** (lines 545 to 552). The Fisher adjusted sample skewness:

```
skew = n / ((n - 1) * (n - 2)) * sum(((v - mean) / std)^3)
```

Zero when `std` is not above zero or n is not above 2. Rounded to **4**. **The `mean` and `std`
it uses are the already-rounded summary fields**, the 6 decimal `stats.mean` and `stats.std_dev`
above, not the unrounded values. The port rounds first and then computes the skewness, which is
what the web does and what parity requires.

**The moving average** (`_moving_avg`, lines 723 to 733). Two series, a **7** night and a **30**
night window, both computed over the nightly values in date order. **The input is the nightly
median already rounded to 6**, the value the point carries, not the unrounded median behind it:
line 721 builds the list from `p.value`, which line 716 rounded. Passing the unrounded medians
produces a different sixth decimal on every average point, which ruling A4 forbids. For index i
the window is the
values at `max(0, i - window + 1)` through i inclusive; a point is emitted **only when the window
is full**, so the first `window - 1` nights carry no average and the 30 night series is empty on a
library with fewer than 30 imaged nights. The value is the arithmetic mean of the window,
rounded to **6**. The window counts **points**, which are nights that have a frame, not calendar
days: a gap of a month between two nights does not widen the window.

**The matrix cell** (lines 776 to 815). One cell per (X metric, Y metric) pair, 10 by 10, so
**100** cells, X outer and Y inner. `n_points` is the count of frames where **both** columns are
non-null under the shared filters. **A cell carries an r only when `n_points` is at least 10**;
below that the r is null and the cell renders as no data. The r is Pearson's, rounded to **4**.

The web computes this with PostgreSQL's `corr(Y, X)` aggregate in one statement. SQLite has no
`corr()`, so the port makes one pass over the filtered rows in C# and accumulates all 100 pairs
together, which is the shape `AnalysisQuery` uses. **The formula is the mean-centred one, Sxx,
Syy and Sxy about each axis's own mean, which is what current PostgreSQL computes**, and not the
uncentred computational form: the two agree to 4 decimals on every cell of the user's own library
but disagree unrounded on 89 of its 90 non-null cells, worst 7.0e-10, so only the centred form
can be asserted exactly against the oracle. Two behaviours of `corr()` are matched deliberately:
it excludes a row where either argument is null, which is what `n_points` counts; and it answers
**null** when either column has no variation, where the Python `_pearson_r` would answer 0.0.
**The port answers null in that case**, because the cell the user sees comes from `corr()` in the
web and a spurious 0.00 in a coloured cell reads as a measured result rather than as an absent
one.

**The no-variation test is `min == max` on that axis, taken over the pair's own rows and
evaluated before any arithmetic.** It is not a threshold on the accumulated variance term. The
streaming pass already visits every value, so each pair carries a running minimum and maximum per
axis and the gate reads them directly. Testing the cancellation residue instead does not work and
the failure is not rare: over 400 identical values the residue is frequently **positive**, at
5.4e-07 for 12.7 and 4.8e-08 for 3.14159, so the null never fires and the cell prints `0.00` in a
coloured square, which is exactly the reading this section says must not ship. Whether it fires at
all would depend on which literal the constant happens to be, which is not a rule. A cell is
therefore blank when either axis has no variation, or when `n_points` is below 10, and carries an
r otherwise. The matrix is always at frame granularity.

**The point cap** (lines 44 to 47 and 457 to 468). The Correlation scatter draws at most
**5,000** points. The web caps for payload size, which this port does not have; the port keeps
the same number for parity, and the reason it needs **a** cap is drawing cost, measured by the
Phase 17 chart spike at 900 by 420 with animations off: 18.9 milliseconds a frame at 5,000
points, 38.2 at 10,000, 71.3 at 20,000 and 201.9 at 50,000, with one data replacement rising from
2.5 milliseconds at 5,000 to 982 at 50,000. **5,000 points do not themselves need the cap**, at
40 to 50 frames a second and an imperceptible replacement; the knee where the chart stops feeling
live is near 20,000 and 50,000 is unusable. The number is kept because the two applications
should draw the same picture, not because 5,000 is where the cost bites. When the full set is
larger it is downsampled by an even stride:
`step = total / 5000` as a real number, and the returned points are `points[floor(i * step)]`
for i from 0 to 4,999. **The trend, the confidence band, the outlier flags and both stats cards
are computed over the full set, before any downsampling.** When the set was sampled the tab
shows the sentence "Showing S of T frames (sampled for display; trend and statistics use all
frames)" above the chart, with both counts group-separated (`CorrelationTab.tsx` lines 99 to
108).

**Every rounding on this page**, with its digit count, so no implementer has to infer one:

| Figure | Digits | Line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SummaryStats` min, max, mean, median, std_dev | 6 | 191 to 196 |
| Trend slope, intercept | 6 | 323 to 324 |
| Trend r_squared, pearson_r, spearman_rho | 4 | 325 to 327 |
| Confidence band x and y | 6 | 319 to 320 |
| Box plot min, q1, median, q3, max, each outlier | 6 | 216 to 221 |
| Histogram bin_start, bin_end | 6 | 543 |
| Skewness | 4 | 558 |
| Time series point value | 6 | 716 |
| Moving average value | 6 | 731 |
| Matrix cell pearson_r | 4 | 811 |
| Compare arcsecond medians | 3 | 911 to 912 |
| Compare verdict percentage | 0, as a formatted string | 898 to 900 |

Every one of them goes through `PythonNumerics.RoundLikePython`, which is Python's round-half-to-
even on the decimal expansion, and never through `Math.Round`'s default. The verdict percentage
is formatted, not rounded, and Python's `format(x, '.0f')` is also half-to-even, so it takes the
same helper.

**The accumulation rules** (ruling A4). `analysis.py` accumulates in exactly two ways and the
port must not blur them:

- Every `sum(...)` in the file is CPython's **builtin** `sum()` over floats, which since 3.12
  uses Neumaier compensated summation. The backend requires 3.12 (`backend/pyproject.toml`), so
  every one of them ports to `CompensatedSum`. That covers the summary mean and variance, both
  Pearson sums, all four regression sums, `ss_tot`, `ss_res`, `sx2`, the skewness sum and the
  moving average's window sum.
- **The five PHD2 night figures are not on that list.** `phd2_night_subquery` lines 113 to 135
  are SQL aggregates, executed by the database, with no Python `sum()` anywhere behind them, so
  they port as a **plain left-to-right accumulation loop**, which is what the database did. This
  is the third of the three rules section 7.6 names, not the first.
- `sum(1 for v in values if ...)`, the histogram's bin count, is an **integer** sum and is exact.

`math.fsum` and `statistics.fmean` do **not** appear in this file, so `ExactSum` and `ExactMean`
have no caller here; using one of them where the Python uses the builtin would produce a
different last digit.

**The shared home is `GalactiLog.Core.Metrics.PythonNumerics`, in
`Core/Metrics/PythonNumerics.cs`.** The four members that reproduce a CPython rule,
`RoundLikePython`, `ExactSum`, `ExactMean` and `CompensatedSum`, live there and nowhere else.
They arrived in `Phd2Metrics` because PHD2 was the first port that needed them; Task 2 is their
second consumer, which is where the spine is built rather than copied (design lesson 1).
`Phd2Metrics` calls them at their new home and keeps no copy, and `Analysis.cs` reaches for them
there rather than into the `Phd2` namespace. Every figure in the rounding table above and every
accumulation in this section resolves to that one file.

#### Correlation

Controls, in order: a row of six **presets**, the X picker, the Y picker, and a **Hide Outliers**
toggle. The presets are `CorrelationTab.tsx` lines 34 to 41 and set both pickers at once:

| Preset | X | Y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Humidity vs HFR | `humidity` | `hfr` |
| Airmass vs FWHM | `airmass` | `fwhm` |
| Wind vs Guiding | `wind_speed` | `guiding_rms` |
| Temp vs Eccentricity | `ambient_temp` | `eccentricity` |
| Sky Quality vs Stars | `sky_quality` | `detected_stars` |
| Guiding vs FWHM | `phd2_rms_total` | `fwhm` |

A preset whose pair is the current pair is drawn selected. The X picker offers the ten X metrics
and then the "Guiding (PHD2)" group of five; the Y picker offers the ten Y metrics.

**Hide Outliers** removes the flagged points from the drawn series and from nothing else: the
trend, the band, the two stats cards and the counts are unchanged, because they were computed
before the toggle was read (`CorrelationTab.tsx` lines 89 to 94). The button's label states the
action it will perform, "Hide Outliers" while they are shown and "Show Outliers" while they are
hidden, which is the web's wording.

The chart is a scatter with four layers, drawn in this order: the confidence band, which is an
upper-bound area and an opaque mask over the lower bound rather than a band series (section 13);
the ordinary points as filled dots; the outlier points as hollow rings in `metric-worst`; and the
trend line from the smallest plotted X to the largest. A
session-granularity point is drawn larger than a frame one, as the web draws it. Hovering a point
names its target, its night and its two values.

**Three of the five layers answer no hover and two do.** The band, the mask and the trend line are
not hoverable; the ordinary points and the outlier rings are, because an outlier **is** a point
and a reader who wants to know which frame was flagged has nowhere else to ask.

**The chart declares its finding strategy as `CompareOnlyXTakeClosest`.** Left at the library's
Automatic, rc5.4 resolves a chart holding a scatter to `CompareAllTakeClosest`, and a scatter's
hover area is its geometry box, 4 pixels square at frame granularity and 6 at session: a reader
had to land the pointer within 2 pixels of a dot's centre **in both axes** before any tooltip
appeared, which on a chart of this height with the points near the trend meant that none ever did.
Under the X strategy the pointer has to be inside the hover area in X alone, so a point answers
anywhere in a vertical strip over it, at any height of the chart. The trend line is marked not
hoverable in the same breath, because under the X strategy a line series' hover area is a full
axis unit wide and the trend carries no tooltip formatters, so it would otherwise answer a bare
default tooltip near either end.

Under the chart, **the verdict sentence**, ported from `describeCorrelation`
(`CorrelationChart.tsx` lines 34 to 67). It is built from `r_squared` in four bands, below 0.05,
below 0.15, below 0.4 and above, reading "No meaningful correlation", "Weak correlation",
"Moderate correlation" or "Strong correlation", followed by
`(R2=x.xx, Pearson r=x.xx, Spearman rho=x.xx)` and a plain-language line. With no trend, or
fewer than 3 points, it reads "Not enough data to determine a pattern (n points)."

**The point count follows the verdict on the same line**, as the string `(n points)` in
`text-tertiary`, which is the pinned `CorrelationChart.tsx`'s own `opacity-60` span. Two text runs
in one block and not two blocks: the web draws the count on the verdict's own line, and a second
line costs the chart height at 1280 by 800. **The count is the full point set's and never the
drawn one**, so Hide Outliers does not move it, which is the clause above promising that the
counts are unchanged. **The verdict sentence takes `text-primary` explicitly.** It carries no state
colour and no band-dependent colour: the four band names describe the data and do not judge it,
which is the same reason the two stronger bands are direction neutral. It is one of the few text
blocks on the page that names its own ink rather than taking it from a class, because a launched
look found it drawing pure white on `red-light`, the brightest thing on a night-vision page; the
application now also declares an inherited default text ink (section 14.6), which would answer it
in any case, and the explicit ink is kept beside that so this sentence cannot be moved into an
unclassed context and lose it.

**The chart is bound to the page viewport less a named fixed spend, floored at 280 pixels.** It
measures 280 at 1024 by 700 and at 1280 by 800, where the subtraction lands under the floor, and
460 at 1920 by 1080, where it does not. 280 is the smallest of its peers on the page, the
histogram, the box plot, the time series and the matrix standing at 280 to 460; the floor was 180
until a launched look measured what 180 gives a reader, which is two tick labels on the value
axis, a confidence band that cannot be told from the trend line it surrounds, and 59 points
collapsed into a strip a few pixels thick. **No rule in this document ever required the stats
cards to sit above the fold**, and the page scrolls: at 1280 by 800 the chart's own bottom 25
pixels, the row carrying its X axis title, sit just under the fold before the reader scrolls, and
one page down brings the chart, the verdict, the disclaimer and both cards on screen together.

**The web's wording for the two stronger bands assumes that a lower Y is better**: it says a
rising slope is a "negative impact" and a falling one "improves". That is wrong for
`detected_stars`, where more is better, and it is a statement about the user's data, not a colour.
`detected_stars` is the example because it is a **Y** metric: the verdict reads the Y axis, and
`sky_quality`, the other higher-is-better metric on the page, is X only and can never reach this
sentence. **The port's sentence is direction neutral**: it names which way Y moves with
X and leaves the judgement to the reader. The four band names and the three figures are
unchanged, so the only difference is the trailing clause.

Under the sentence, the fixed disclaimer **"Correlations show statistical associations, not
causation. Many factors affect image quality simultaneously."**

Below it, **two stats cards**, one for X and one for Y, each labelled with its axis and its
metric label and each showing the six summary fields as N, Min, Max, Mean, Median and StDev.
The card is one control, `StatsCardViewModel`, used by this tab and by Compare (ruling A7).
Its number format is `StatsCard.tsx` lines 12 to 16: no decimals at 1000 and above, one decimal
at 10 and above, two decimals below 10, with the metric's unit suffix appended. Absent stats
hide the cards rather than showing zeroes.

**The Correlation tab has no CSV export.** The web offers one (`CorrelationTab.tsx` lines 110 to
126). This port writes a file only through `AppWriter` with a save dialog and a named
`FileSafetyTest` allowlist entry (section 2.1.1), which is a decision of its own and not part of
a read-only page; Copy Frame List and Export for stacking are where that machinery lives today.

#### Distributions

A two-button segment selects **Histogram** or **Box Plot**; both keep their own controls and
their own last result.

**Histogram.** One metric picker over all twenty metrics, defaulting to `hfr`. The chart is a
column histogram over the bins, with a dashed vertical reference
line at the distribution's own median. The count axis is titled **"Frames"**; the bin axis takes
the metric's full label, so the metric's own unit is stated there and not on the count axis, which
counts frames and has no unit. Below it, one stats card labelled
"<metric label> (skewness: x.xx)".

**The chart has one convention and all three of its parts obey it: bin-edge space.** The bin axis
is numeric, not categorical: bin i spans i to i + 1, its bar's point sits at i + 0.5, and the bars
are drawn **edge to edge** with no gap. One tick stands on every integer, so a tick sits at each
bar's left edge and names that bin's lower edge, with one further tick at the last bin's upper
edge, which under user ruling U1 is the distribution's own maximum and is the one edge no bin's
lower edge names. The median line falls **inside the bar of the bin that holds it**, at its
proportional position within that bin, and is lifted over the bars so the bar it stands in does
not paint over it.

**Why this is stated at all.** The three parts had three conventions and only a launched look
could see it: the ticks stood at bin edges, the bars were centred on those ticks at a third of
their slot's width, and the median was placed at its proportional position within the **slot**, so
the line landed in the empty gap between two bars and a reader could not tell which bin the median
belonged to. The pinned `HistogramChart.tsx` has two of the three, the median inside its bar and
lower-edge labels, and puts its label at the bar's centre, which a category axis forces; the
numeric axis is what lets the port put the label where the edge is.

**One consequence for the reader, and it is parity.** The tick labels print to one decimal, as the
pinned web prints them, so over a narrow range two neighbouring edges can round to the same text
and the axis reads 2.0, 2.1, 2.1, 2.2, 2.2, 2.3, 2.3, 2.4.

**The bin tooltip, verbatim**, with both edges to two decimals and the frame word singular at a
count of one:

> x.xx to y.yy), n frames

**The closing bracket is the only visible trace of user ruling U1.** It is `)` on every bin but the
last of a ranged distribution, whose upper edge is inclusive and which therefore closes with `]`.
The pinned `HistogramChart.tsx` writes the two edges around an en dash with no bracket at all,
which this document's own prose rules forbid, so both strings are written here rather than
transcribed.

**When the filters leave fewer than two values the tab draws nothing and says, verbatim:**

> The current filters leave too few frames to bin. Widen them in the filter bar above.

**Box Plot.** A metric picker over the ten Y metrics, defaulting to `hfr`, and a **Group by**
picker with four values: By Filter, By Equipment, By Month, By Target. The chart is one
**vertical** box per group on a category X axis, groups in ascending ordinal order of their name,
each drawing the whisker range, the interquartile box, the median mark and the outlier rings.
Vertical because rc5.4 offers no horizontal box series at all; section 13 states the shape.

**The median mark's ink is chosen per group by contrast against the box fill**, through the same
shared rule the matrix cell labels use, and **not** the flat `text-primary` an earlier ruling gave
it. That ruling is refuted in the three dark themes measured, on the declared tokens and confirmed
on the rendered pixels:

| Theme | Box fill | `text-primary` against it | Elevated background, opaque, against it | Chosen |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `deep-sky` | `2DD4BF` | 1.51 to 1 | 9.22 to 1 | the elevated background |
| `luminance` | `4F9FA5` | 2.44 to 1 | 4.93 to 1 | the elevated background |
| `red-light` | `D24C33` | 1.04 to 1 | 4.30 to 1 | the elevated background |

On `red-light` the mark at `text-primary` measured 1.13 to 1 on screen and the box read as one
solid block, so the reader had to open the tooltip to learn the median at all.

**The mark is a third series, not the box series' stroke.** One `BoxSeries` paints the whiskers,
the box outline and the median mark from one `Stroke`, and the contrast rule picks the elevated
background in all three themes measured, each of them dark, so re-inking that one stroke would have
rescued the median by putting the whiskers, which stand on the page and not on the box, within
about 1.3 to 1 of the page they stand on. The mark is therefore drawn again over the box as its
own scatter, sized under the box series' own pinned bar width so it marks the box rather than
overhanging it, not hoverable and not in the legend.

The grouping key per mode (`analysis.py` lines 613 to 646):

| Group by | Key | Rows with no key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| By Filter | The canonical filter name, folded through the filter alias map, falling back to the raw name. | Dropped. |
| By Equipment | "telescope + camera" over both canonical names, each folded through its alias map and falling back to the raw name. | Dropped when either name is absent. |
| By Month | `capture_date` formatted `YYYY-MM`. | Dropped. |
| By Target | The resolved target's primary name. Two target ids resolving to one name merge into one group. | Dropped when there is no resolved target. |

**By Month reads `capture_date`, while the date range filter reads `session_date`.** That is the
web's own asymmetry (line 597 against line 167) and the port keeps it, so a frame taken after
midnight can sit in the month after its night. The help topic says the month is the calendar
month of the exposure.

**A group with fewer than 4 values is dropped silently**, with no row and no notice, which is
what `_compute_box_plot` returning null does. The port keeps the drop and states it in the tab's
help topic, so a reader who filtered down to three frames per filter is not left thinking the
chart failed.

**When every group is dropped that way the tab says so, in its own sentence, verbatim:**

> No group has enough frames. Group by something coarser, or narrow the dates to a period with
> more frames per group.

The first clause is this section's own, the second is the port's. It is a **different state** from
"no row matches the filters" and needs a different sentence, which is why the box plot result
carries `RowCount`, the count of the rows the query read after its filters and before any grouping
key: with rows read and no group left, widening the filters is the one action that makes the
reading worse, and grouping more coarsely is the one that helps. The pinned web has no counterpart
at all and shows the empty chart.

**One tooltip per box, carrying both of the web's two hover strings.** `BoxPlotChart.tsx` draws
two hover regions over one box, a quartile region and a whisker region, each with its own string.
rc5.4's `BoxSeries` has one point per group and two label formatters on it, so the port attaches
the quartile string to one and the whisker string to the other and both appear together on one
hover. Every figure the web shows is still shown; what changes is that they arrive at once rather
than by pointing at the right part of the box. The two strings, verbatim, with the en dash the
port's prose rules forbid replaced by the word "to":

> Q1: x.xx, Median: y.yy, Q3: z.zz (N=n)

> Range: x.xx to y.yy

`Range` names the **whisker ends** and not the group's extremes, which is what the `min` and `max`
fields above hold.

**The pixel-domain note.** Whenever the chosen metric is `hfr` and the scope can span more than
one optical train, the tab shows "Values are per-train pixel-domain units, not comparable across
optical trains. HFR is measured in pixels and is only comparable within a single optical train.
Use FWHM in arcseconds for cross-telescope comparison." The scope can span more than one train
when the filter bar has not selected both a telescope and a camera, or when the box plot is
grouped By Equipment (`DistributionsTab.tsx` lines 82 to 87).

#### Time Series

One metric picker over all twenty metrics, defaulting to `hfr`, and a three-button segment,
**Raw**, **7-Night MA**, **30-Night MA**.

The points are one per imaged night, in ascending date order, each the **median** of that night's
values across every target and rig the filters admit, with the night's frame count carried for
the tooltip. The moving average draws as a line over the points when its segment is selected; Raw
draws the points alone. There is **no confidence band on the moving average**.

**The band on this chart is a robust baseline band**, computed by the view over the plotted
nightly values, not by the query (`TimeSeriesTab.tsx` lines 22 to 33 and
`TimeSeriesChart.tsx` lines 49 to 96). It is `Core.Metrics.FrameQuality`'s own median and median
absolute deviation, the same pair section 12.4 grades frames with, and it is absent when fewer
than `FrameQuality.MinGroup` (8) nights are plotted or when the MAD is zero. When present the
chart draws, behind the points: a filled band between `median - MAD` and `median + MAD`, the
median line, and a dashed bound at `median + 3 * MAD`, mirrored to `median - 3 * MAD` for the
two higher-is-better metrics `detected_stars` and `sky_quality`. Each point is tinted by its own
band through `FrameQuality`'s existing thresholds: the warning ink for watch, the error ink for
reject, the ordinary series ink otherwise. **The moving average line is drawn in `accent`**, not
in a metric token: section 13 states why, and the short reason is that the token an earlier draft
gave it is the same hex as the warning ink in one shipped theme, which would have painted a watch
point and the average alike.

**Both axes are titled**, as the pinned `TimeSeriesChart.tsx` titles them: the value axis takes the
chosen metric's full label from the metric table above, unit parenthetical included, and the time
axis is titled "Date". The tick labels on the value axis carry **no** unit suffix, so the unit is
stated once per axis rather than on every tick, which is what the other three charts on this page
do. Section 13 says what paints an axis title.

The X axis is a date axis. Hovering a point reads "<target name>: value (n frames)", or "Mixed"
in place of a name.

**The web picks that name non-deterministically.** It collects the night's target ids into a set
and takes `list(...)[0]` (`analysis.py` lines 712 to 713), so on a night with two targets the
name shown is whichever the set happened to order first, and it can differ between two runs of
the same query. **The port names the target only when the night has exactly one**, and shows
"Mixed" otherwise, which is the reading the chart already gives an absent name. No figure
changes; only a label that was arbitrary becomes true.

#### Matrix

No controls of its own. A 10 by 10 grid, Y metrics down the rows and X metrics across the
columns, drawn with the short labels `MatrixTab.tsx` lines 9 to 19 give. They are a third label
per metric, shorter than the picker label of the metric table above, and they live in
`AnalysisMetricLabels` beside the other two:

| Column (X), left to right | Row (Y), top to bottom |
| --- | --- |
| `Humid.` | `HFR` |
| `Wind` | `FWHM` |
| `Temp` | `Ecc.` |
| `Dew Pt` | `Guide` |
| `Press.` | `Guide RA` |
| `Cloud` | `Guide DEC` |
| `SQM` | `Stars` |
| `Focus T` | `ADU` followed by U+03BC |
| `Airm.` | `ADU med` |
| `Sensor T` | `ADU sigma` |

Two rows carry the glyph rule of the metric table above. `ADU` plus U+03BC ships as the glyph,
because the mu is in all six embedded faces and `MatrixTab.tsx` line 18 writes it. The row beside
it ships the word `ADU sigma`, because `MatrixTab.tsx` writes U+03C3 there and no embedded face
draws it. `FWHM` carries no unit here: the grid is ten labels wide and the short label's job is to
fit, which the picker label's `(arcsec)` does not.

Each cell that has an r prints it to
two decimals; **a cell with no r is omitted from the series entirely and is blank**, because a
cell drawn with no value takes the ramp's neutral ink and prints `0.00`, which a reader cannot
tell from a measured zero.

The cell's ink comes from a diverging ramp **pinned to the range -1 to 1**, so a matrix whose
strongest correlation is weak does not render that cell as though it were perfect. Section 13
names the three tokens. **The printed figure carries the sign and the ramp is decoration**: on
red-light every ink on this page is a shade of one red, and the sign of r has nowhere else to go.
A legend in markup beside the grid names the two ends and the blank cell, because a heat series
draws no colour bar of its own. Its three entries, verbatim, the first two beside a swatch in the
ramp's own end token and the third with no swatch because a blank cell draws nothing:

> r = -1: the two move in opposite directions

> r = +1: the two move together

> Blank: no value for that pair

Hovering a cell reads `r=x.xxx (N=n)`, built as `r={r to three decimals} (N={count})`. **A blank cell cannot be
hovered**, because nothing is drawn there, so the web's "Insufficient data (N=n)" hover has no
counterpart: the caption below states the minimum instead, and the pair's own point count is
reachable by choosing it on the Correlation tab.

**A wholly blank column or row is still drawn, with its label**, because both category axes are
pinned to all ten categories whatever the data holds (section 13). An axis left to fit itself to
the points it has drops a category no point sits in, and the grid then showed nine columns and
nine labels while the keyboard still walked into the tenth and announced it, so a keyboard reader
could reach a column a pointer reader could not see.

**The keyboard layer is laid out over the chart's own draw margin**, not over the whole control.
The painted grid reserves a gutter on the left for the row labels and lays its columns out after
it; a layer covering the whole control puts every cell's reported screen rectangle a gutter-width
to the left of the cell it names, which is what a screen reader or a magnifier is pointed at. The
layer reads the draw margin from the chart at the moment the margin becomes known and follows a
resize. **The cell buttons draw no focus adorner of their own**, through an empty adorner
template: the chart's own focus rectangle is the grid's one focus affordance, and the platform's
default adorner is a plain white rectangle, white on `red-light` too.

**Clicking a cell that has an r opens the Correlation tab with that pair selected.** A cell with
no r is not clickable. The navigation is a single call on the page view-model, not a window-level
event as the web uses.

A caption above the grid reads "Pearson r for all metric pairs. A pair needs at least 10 frames
carrying both metrics; below that the cell is blank. Click a cell to explore in the Correlation
tab." The web's caption is the first and last sentences; the middle one is added because the port
removed the hover that carried it.

#### Compare

Controls: a two-button segment, **Equipment** or **Filter**; a metric picker over the ten Y
metrics, defaulting to `hfr`; and two group pickers, A and B, each offering the equipment
combinations or the filters of the filter bar's own lists depending on the segment. Switching the
segment clears both groups.
