**Nothing is queried until two different groups are chosen.** With fewer than two, or with the
same group twice, the tab reads "Select two different groups to compare." (`CompareTab.tsx`
line 34 and lines 127 to 131).

On a result: one box plot holding both groups' boxes, the verdict sentence, and two stats cards,
one per group, each labelled with its group's name.

**Every user-visible place shows the group's display label, never the persisted key.** A group's
identity is a wire value, and in Equipment mode that value joins the telescope and the camera with
a three-character separator, so a reader who is shown the identity is shown `Telescope|||Camera`.
The display label is the text the picker draws for that same row, `<telescope> + <camera>` or the
filter's name, with the grouped marker where the picker shows one. **Eight places take it**: the
box plot's two category labels, the verdict sentence twice, the two stats card headings, and three
of the four too-few sentences above. The two tooltips carry quartiles and counts and never a name.

**The verdict is rebuilt in the tab, through the same one builder, and never by string surgery.**
The query builds the sentence itself from the two wire values, so the key is baked into one
preformatted string and cannot be edited out of it: a canonical telescope or camera name may hold
any text, including the substring of another group's name. The tab calls the same
`Analysis.CompareVerdict` with the two display labels and the result's own figures, which are the
very values the query handed the builder and not a rounded copy. **The query and its cache key are
untouched**, so the display names never reach what is memoised and a grouped marker cannot change
which entry an earlier read is served.

**The two labels are captured when the query goes out, beside the wire values of that instant, not
when the result lands.** A bar re-read can withdraw a chosen group while that group's query is in
flight, and the in-flight result still publishes; reading the labels at draw time would find a
null selection and print nothing at all where the group's name belongs. **A vanished group prints
the name it was queried under**, which makes the drawn result self-consistent: its figures and its
two names come from the same instant.

**The verdict** (`_pct_verdict`, lines 890 to 901) names the group with the lower median and by
how much: "<name> has P% lower median than <other> (N=a vs N=b)", as a percentage with no
decimals. When the medians are equal it reads "Both groups have identical median values (N=a vs
N=b)".

**P is the absolute difference of the two medians over the absolute value of the larger of them.
This is a departure from the web, ruled by the user (choice 20).** The web divides by the
absolute value of the **first** median whenever it is non-zero, falling back to the second and
then to zero (lines 890 to 896), while the sentence it builds always names the **smaller** group
first and phrases it as lower than the larger. When the smaller median is less than half the
larger, the sentence therefore reads above 100 percent lower, which is not a quantity that can
exist. All three comparisons available on the user's own library print one: the two rigs read
"126% lower median (arcsec)" at 1.772 against 3.997 where the honest figure is 56, the two
filters read "100% lower" at 1.944 against 3.879, and the FWHM comparison reads "111% lower".
Dividing by the larger median is dividing by the one the sentence says the smaller is lower than,
so the figure and the words agree and the percentage cannot pass 100. When both medians are zero
the difference is zero and no percentage is shown, which is the equal-medians sentence above.

**HFR to arcseconds through plate scale.** `hfr` is the one metric measured in pixels, and two
optical trains cannot be compared in pixels: the same star measures a different pixel HFR at a
different focal length or pixel size. **On this tab only**, and only when the metric is `hfr`,
each frame's value is additionally multiplied by its own `images.arcsec_per_pixel`, the
materialised plate scale (section 7.1), and the verdict runs on the **medians of those
arcsecond values**, rounded to **3** decimals, with the unit " (arcsec)" in the sentence. A frame
with a null plate scale contributes to the pixel box plot and the pixel stats card but not to the
arcsecond comparison (`analysis.py` lines 836 to 877 and 903 to 920).

When either group has fewer than 4 plate-scaled frames the two groups are declared **not
comparable**: no percentage is shown and the tab reads, in the secondary ink, **"Different
optical trains: pixel HFR is not comparable between these groups, and arcsecond data is
unavailable (plate scale unknown). No improvement figure is shown."**

**That is the only not-comparable sentence, and the port builds no other.** The web's
`CompareTab.tsx` (lines 57 to 66) carries a second one, "Comparing in arcseconds instead: <A>
median x.xx arcsec vs <B> median y.yy arcsec", for the case where the groups are not comparable
and both arcsecond medians exist. **No input can reach it.** The two medians are set only inside
the branch that also keeps `comparable` true (`analysis.py` lines 910 to 913); the branch that
sets `comparable` false leaves both null, so "not comparable" and "both medians present" cannot
hold at once. Building the branch would be building a state no library can produce and no case
can cover.

**No other tab converts HFR to arcseconds.** The Correlation scatter, the histogram, the box plot
and the time series all plot the raw `median_hfr` column in pixels, with the pixel-domain note
above as the disclosure. That is what `analysis.py` does: `_PIXEL_METRICS` is read at line 843
and nowhere else.

**Both groups need at least 4 values** or the tab shows the too-few-points state below rather
than a chart, **naming which group is short**. That sentence needs two figures the result has to
carry: the query answers the **two raw value counts** alongside its data, so the tab can say
"Group A" or "Group B" or both, and can tell this state apart from "no row matches the filters",
which is its own row in the states table. A bare null cannot do either.

**The three sentences, verbatim.** Each names the group by its own name and not merely by its
letter, and each prints the raw count the result carries:

> Group A, <name>, has too few frames to compare (n values).

> Group B, <name>, has too few frames to compare (n values).

> Both groups have too few frames to compare: <name A> (a values) and <name B> (b values).

#### The mixed plate scale warning

**Pixels stay on the four tabs, and a tab whose own frames span more than one optical train says
so where a reader cannot miss it.** This is an addition to the web, ruled by the user (choice
21).

**The condition.** It is the number of **distinct non-null `images.arcsec_per_pixel` values among
the rows the tab actually read**, not a guess from the filter bar. Nulls are ignored entirely: a
frame whose headers gave no derivable plate scale neither raises the warning nor suppresses it.
Two or more distinct values raises it; one, or none, does not. **All five of the pixel tabs' query
results carry that count** as one integer field beside their data, computed in the same pass that
builds the result, so no second query runs and the count is over exactly the rows the chart drew.
The five are the four tabs' results with Distributions counted twice, because its two modes are
two queries: the correlation result, the distribution result, the box plot result, **the time
series result** and the matrix result. The time series one is named because it is the one an
implementer drops: four of the tabs are easy to list and the fifth result is the second half of
one of them, and a result that carries the field but never populates it leaves the warning
silently dead on exactly the two-rig library it exists for. On the Correlation tab the count is
over the rows behind the **full** point set, before the 5,000 point cap, because the cap is a
drawing decision and the warning is a statement about the data.

**When it is shown.** Only for a pixel-domain metric, which is `hfr` and only `hfr`, the web's
own `_PIXEL_METRICS` set. On the Correlation tab that means the Y metric is `hfr`; on the
histogram, the box plot and the Time Series it means the chosen metric is `hfr`; on the Matrix it
means the grid's `hfr` row, which is present whenever the grid is. Compare is not in this list:
it converts to arcseconds and carries its own not-comparable sentence above.

**What it looks like.** The warning callout composite of the control vocabulary,
`Border.callout warn` (`DESIGN.md` section 4), above the chart and inside the tab body. **Not a
caption and not tertiary ink**: the figure it warns about is wrong by a factor of three on the
user's own library, and a reader who misses the warning reads the two rigs backwards.

**The sentence, verbatim:**

> This selection mixes optical trains with different plate scales. HFR is measured in pixels, so
> these figures are not comparable across them. Choose one equipment combination in the filter
> bar.

**The web's existing note stays** and is not replaced by this. `DistributionsTab.tsx`'s
cross-train note is shown by its own rule, which is about what the scope *could* span rather than
what it does: it appears whenever the metric is `hfr` and the filter bar has not selected both a
telescope and a camera, or the box plot is grouped By Equipment. The two are different statements
and both are useful. The note says HFR is a per-train unit; the warning says this particular
selection is currently mixing two of them. When both apply, both are shown, the warning above the
note.

**Why the threshold is the plate scale and not the equipment combination.** Two combinations can
share one plate scale, in which case their pixel figures are comparable and no warning is owed,
and one combination can carry two plate scales across a focal reducer change, in which case a
warning is owed although the filter bar shows one rig. Measured on the user's own library: 416
frames, every one carrying a plate scale, taking exactly two distinct values, 0.9892 and 2.9377,
one per rig, a factor of three apart. Raw HFR makes the second rig look the better one, median
1.3607 against 1.7913 pixels, and the arcsecond conversion says the opposite, 3.997 against
1.772. That inversion is what this warning exists to catch.

#### Caching and invalidation

`Data/Queries/AnalysisCache.cs` follows `StatsCache` (section 12.5). It holds one entry per
**filter key**, the tuple of the endpoint, its own controls, and the five shared filter values,
which is the port of the web's cache key strings (`analysis.py` lines 369 to 374 and the
matching blocks in each endpoint). All six queries are cached, including Compare, which the web
leaves uncached.

**There is no time-to-live.** The web expires an entry after 5 minutes because its cache is
shared between processes and it cannot see an ingest; this application can. Instead there are
**four explicit triggers, and the memo and the open page follow all four**:

| Trigger | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `GeneralChanged` | A general settings save, through the one `AppHost` staleness handler, which fails closed against its named inert key list (ruling A6, HANDOFF 5.1 item 12d). The alias maps, the filter map, the PHD2 profile map and the observer location all live there and all feed these queries. |
| `Phd2CorrelationRunner.PassCompleted` | A correlation pass rewrote the guiding nights the PHD2 X metrics join. |
| `ScanStatusService.ScanFinished` | A scan catalogued frames. This is the commonest event there is. |
| `SettingsStore.AliasSourcesChanged` | An alias group was renamed or refolded, so the equipment combinations and the box plot's By Filter and By Equipment groups are different groups. |

The first two arrive as the one process-level derived-data notification the Statistics page
already follows; the last two are subscribed beside it. **All four drop the Statistics memo and
the Analysis memo through one shared handler**, not two handlers per event, so a fifth trigger
cannot reach one page's memo and be forgotten on the other (design lesson 2). Dropping the memo
is only half of it: **the page itself is a singleton and follows the same four**, because a
reader who scans a night with a second rig, or renames an alias group, and comes back to a page
that never heard about it has no control on the page that can recover either.

**A refresh re-reads the filter bar's two option lists and applies them in place.** The equipment
combination list and the filter list are read once at construction and again on every refresh, and
the answer is applied to the two existing collections rather than replacing them, because both are
bound under a live two-way selection. **The reader's selection is carried across that apply by
identity, captured before it and reassigned after it**, with both selection setters silenced for
the duration and one change raised at the end. This is not a precaution: Avalonia writes `null`
back through a two-way `SelectedItem` when the row at the bound picker's selected index is
replaced, and the equipment list is ordered by frame count first, so a scan that adds frames
carries one rig past another with no row added or removed. Compare's two group pickers are built
on the same lists and carry their two selections the same way.

**The page's own `display.analysis` save must not invalidate the cache.** It lives in the
display document, which the general-document staleness handler does not read, so a tab switch
does not discard every cached result. The implementation proves that rather than assuming it.

#### Persistence

`display.analysis`, four keys, section 5.8.2. Everything else on the page is per visit: the
Correlation outlier toggle, the Distributions mode, metric and grouping, the Time Series metric
and smoothing, the Compare mode, metric and two groups, and **the date range** are not stored.
A date range is a question, not a preference, and a stored one would silently narrow the page on
the next launch.

#### Tab behaviour

The five tabs are one pattern five times and are built on one base (ruling A7). A tab is created
**lazily**, on its first selection, and is kept afterwards with its controls and its last result.
A tab issues a query only while it is **visible**: a filter change marks a hidden tab stale and
the tab refreshes when it is next selected, so switching the equipment combination does not fire
five queries. While a refresh is in flight the tab keeps its last drawn result rather than
blanking, which is the web's `keepPreviousData`.

**The controls stay live in every state and only the result is hidden.** The base carries one
member, `ShowsResult`, true in the Ready and Refreshing states and false in every other, and each
of the five tab body views carries exactly one element named `ResultRegion` whose visibility is
bound to it. **The chart and the stats cards go inside that region; every picker, segment, toggle
and legend stays outside it.** Hiding the whole body instead would strand a reader on a metric
with no data, because the picker that would move them off it would be hidden too, and it would
make Compare unreachable, since its groups start empty and the pickers that fill them are the
only way out. A source census over `Views/Analysis/*TabView.axaml` fails a tab view that declares
no `ResultRegion`, or more than one, so a sixth tab cannot forget it (design lesson 2).

**Four sentences are the base's and are written once for all five tabs**, verbatim, because a
wording edit that lands in four of five makes the page say two different things about one state
(design lesson 1):

> No frames match the current filters. Widen them in the filter bar above.

> The figures could not be read.

> Loading...

> From date must be on or before To date.

The first is the no-rows state and stays overridable, so a tab that later needs its own sentence
can still say so; the Distributions half above is the one tab that does. The second sits beside
the Retry button. The third is every tab's first-result line but the Matrix's, which says
"Computing correlations...". **The fourth is the filter bar's date range error, reused as a tab's
own status line**: a tab first selected while the range is reversed has no last result to keep, so
it carries that sentence rather than standing blank and silent.

**A reversed range reads the same whichever route reached it**, which is the rule the fourth
sentence serves. What the reader sees depends on the state and never on the route:

- A tab, or a Distributions half, that holds a **drawn result** stays drawn, stays Ready and
  carries no sentence at all. That is what reversing the range without touching anything else
  already shows on all five tabs, and it is this section's "the last drawn result stays on
  screen". The date error is the filter bar's to show, in its own error ink.
- A tab, or a half, that holds **nothing**, whether it loaded no rows or was never loaded at all,
  closes its result region and carries the reversed-range sentence.
- **The no-rows sentence and the too-few sentences never appear while the range is reversed.**
  Both send the reader to widen or regroup filters that are not the problem.

`IsEmpty`, a member of three of the four data chart view-models, is **not** the empty-state gate
and no view binds it: `ShowsResult` on the result region is the mechanism a reader sees. It is
recorded here so a later phase does not read it as one.

#### States

| State | What the page does |
| --- | --- |
| A tab not yet visited | Nothing is created and nothing is queried. |
| Loading, first result | The tab's body is replaced by a loading line. The Matrix reads "Computing correlations..." |
| Loading, refresh | The last result stays drawn and the controls stay live. |
| No row matches the filters | The tab states that no frames match the current filters and names the filter bar as where to widen them. No chart is drawn. |
| Correlation with 1 or 2 points | The points are drawn. There is no trend, no band and no verdict; the sentence reads "Not enough data to determine a pattern (n points)." The stats cards are hidden below 2 points. |
| Correlation with 3 points | Trend, band and verdict appear. Outlier flags stay false until there are 4. |
| Distributions with fewer than 2 values | The histogram states that the current filters leave too few frames to bin, and draws nothing. The web answers HTTP 400 here; a page state is the port's equivalent. |
| A box plot group with fewer than 4 values | The group is not drawn. The tab's help topic says a group needs 4. |
| Box plot with no group left | Rows were read and every group was dropped at the four-value gate. The tab shows the no-group-left sentence above, verbatim, and draws no chart. Distinct from the no-rows row, which is why the result carries `RowCount`. |
| Time Series with fewer than 8 nights, or a zero MAD | The points and any full-window average are drawn; the baseline band, the median line and the 3 MAD bound are absent. |
| Time Series with fewer than 7 nights | The 7 night average is empty and its segment draws no line. The same holds for 30. |
| Matrix with every cell below 10 points | The grid draws its two axes and its labels with no cell in it, because a cell with no r is omitted from the series. Nothing is clickable and nothing is hoverable; the caption states the minimum. |
| Any chart with no data at all | The chart still publishes one axis per side. An empty axis array throws at rc5.4 (section 13), so no empty state may leave the axes off. |
| Compare with fewer than two groups chosen, or the same group twice | "Select two different groups to compare." Nothing is queried. |
| Compare with fewer than 4 values in either group | The tab names which group is short, from the two raw value counts the result carries, and draws no chart. Distinct from the no-rows row above, which is why the counts are carried rather than a null returned. |
| Compare on HFR across two optical trains | The percentage verdict is suppressed and one of the two arcsecond sentences above is shown. |
| An HFR chart whose own rows carry two or more distinct plate scales | The `Border.callout warn` mixed plate scale warning above the chart, with its sentence verbatim. The chart still draws, in pixels. The count is over the rows the tab read, nulls ignored, and on Correlation over the full set before the cap. |
| An HFR chart whose rows carry one plate scale, or none at all | No warning. A frame with no derivable plate scale neither raises it nor suppresses it. |
| Reversed date range, on a tab or half holding a drawn result | The sentence "From date must be on or before To date." under the two fields, both fields in the error ink, and **no query on any tab**. The tab stays Ready, the last drawn result stays on screen and the tab itself carries no sentence. |
| Reversed date range, on a tab or half holding nothing | The same filter bar sentence and the same absence of any query, and the tab closes its result region and carries that sentence as its own status line. This covers a tab first selected under a reversed range, a tab that loaded no rows, and a Distributions half switched to under a reversed range. The no-rows and too-few sentences never appear here. |
| A query fails | The tab states that the figures could not be read and offers a Retry. The other tabs are unaffected; a failure is per tab, not per page. |
| Correlation over more than 5,000 points | The sampling sentence above the chart. Every figure is still over the full set. |
| PHD2 X metric with no mapped profile | The X values are all null, so no frame survives, and the tab shows the no-rows state with the PHD2 note above it. |

#### Help topics

Seven topics, placed one per heading, one placement each: `page.analysis` on the page heading,
`analysis.filters` on the Shared filters heading, and `analysis.correlation`,
`analysis.distributions`, `analysis.timeseries`, `analysis.matrix` and `analysis.compare` on the
five tab headings. All seven placements live in the one new markup file `AnalysisView.axaml`, so
section 12.12's census grows by seven topics and seven placements and its file count by one. Each
topic is written from the web's
own popover text (`AnalysisPage.tsx` lines 135 to 147, 153 to 164, and one per tab), with three
corrections the port makes rather than copies:

- **The Matrix popover in the web describes a different feature.** It says "Heatmap grid of one
  metric across two categorical axes" and gives "integration time per channel" and "telescope by
  filter" as examples. The tab is a Pearson correlation matrix over metric pairs and has neither
  categorical axis. The port's topic describes what the tab does.
- The Time Series popover says the metric can be aggregated "per frame or by session or night".
  It is always per night; the granularity segment does not reach this tab. The port's topic says
  so.
- Every topic that mentions the date range calls it the imaging night, not the capture date,
  because that is the column it filters.

The three figures a reader is most likely to misread are stated in the topics in plain words:
that a per-session point is a night and a target rather than a night and a rig, that the matrix
refuses to answer below 10 paired frames, and that the confidence band is indicative rather than
a t interval.

#### Departures from the web, in one place

1. **The PHD2 rig is the live mapped telescope**, not the stored `phd2_sessions.telescope`
   column. The rule this port already applies everywhere else (ruling A10, section 12.5).
2. **The matrix answers null, not 0.00, for a zero-variance pair**, matching PostgreSQL `corr()`
   rather than the Python helper the web does not use there.
3. **A matrix cell with no r is blank and cannot be hovered**, where the web draws a grey cell
   carrying the missing-value placeholder and an "Insufficient data (N=n)" hover. The heat series
   has no way to draw a cell without giving it a value, and a cell given one prints `0.00`, which
   a reader cannot tell from a measured zero; the caption carries the 10 point minimum in its
   place.
4. **The box plot is vertical**, where the web draws it horizontal. rc5.4 has no horizontal box
   series and a drawn control would buy nothing (section 13).
5. **The outlier quartiles are computed once** rather than once per point. Identical flags,
   linear instead of quadratic.
6. **A night's target name is shown only when the night has one target.** The web shows an
   arbitrary one.
7. **The correlation verdict's strongest two bands are direction neutral.** The web's wording is
   wrong for the two higher-is-better metrics.
8. **The three corrected help topics** above.
9. **No CSV export** on the Correlation tab.
10. **No cache time-to-live**; invalidation on scan completion and settings change instead.
11. **All six queries are cached**, where the web leaves Compare uncached.
12. **Compare is the only tab that converts HFR to arcseconds**, which is also what the web does;
    it is listed here because the roadmap's Phase 17 section says the conversion happens on the
    correlation endpoint, and it does not.
13. **The histogram's last bin ends at `v_max` and counts every value** (user choice 19). The
    web's accumulated edge loses the single frame at the maximum; measured at 415 of 416 on the
    user's own library.
14. **The Compare percentage divides by the larger of the two medians** (user choice 20). The web
    divides by the first, which prints above 100 percent on all three comparisons the user's own
    library offers.
15. **An HFR chart whose own rows span two or more plate scales carries a visible warning
    callout** (user choice 21). The web has only its standing per-train note, which says what HFR
    is rather than what this selection is currently doing.
16. **A guiding session with no longitude of its own falls back to the observer timezone**, as a
    frame already did (user choice 22, sections 7.6 and 8.3). The web has the same split and keeps
    it; without this the PHD2 X metrics join nothing on a library with a zone set and no longitude
    configured, and do it silently.
17. **The confidence band is refused below 3 points**, where the pinned `CorrelationChart.tsx`
    draws it whenever bounds arrive. The two agree on every input the port can produce, because
    the trend is null below 3 points and a null trend carries no bounds, so this is a second gate
    on the same state rather than a different answer. It is listed because it is a rule the port
    states and the web does not, and because the States table above promises it in words.
18. **One tooltip per box, carrying both of the web's two hover strings**, where the web draws two
    hover regions over one box. Every figure is still shown; they arrive together.
19. **`fwhm` carries the unit suffix ` arcsec`**, where the pinned `metricLabels.ts` gives it no
    unit at all and prints the figure bare.

Everything else on this page, every figure and every threshold, is the web's, matched exactly
with no tolerance (ruling A4). **Items 13, 14, 15 and 16 are the user's own rulings at the
approval gate**, each taken on a defect the real-data pass found by running the web's own code
over the user's own nights; the rest are the port's, listed in `work/phase17/task1-report.md`
section 3 and approved with them. **Items 17, 18 and 19 were found after that gate**, by the
per-task and phase reviews reading the shipped code against the pinned web, and each is recorded
here rather than corrected: none of them changes a figure and each of them is the smaller
surprise.

**One departure an earlier draft of this list carried is withdrawn and must not be reinstated:**
the Time Series tab does **not** drop the pinned web's two axis titles. It titles both, as the
Time Series section above states. The reason the drop was first recorded, that an axis title needs
a `NamePaint` no axis in the application sets, was wrong on a matter of fact and is answered in
section 13.

### 12.15 Custom columns

Mirrors `frontend/src/components/CustomColumnsTab.tsx`, `InlineEditCell.tsx`,
`CustomColumnFilters.tsx`, `ColumnPicker.tsx`, the custom-column parts of `TargetRow.tsx`,
`SessionTable.tsx` and `SessionAccordionCard.tsx`, and `backend/app/api/custom_columns.py` with
the custom-column half of `backend/app/services/target_listing.py`.

A custom column is a field the user defines and fills in by hand, for what no FITS header carries:
whether a target has been processed, a note tag, a priority. It has one of three **types** and one
of four **scopes**, and the two are fixed at creation.

| Type | Stored values | Editor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `boolean` | `true` or `false` | A check box. |
| `text` | any text, 1 to 500 characters after trimming | A text box. |
| `dropdown` | one of the column's own options | A combo box with an empty first entry. |

| Scope | What one value belongs to | Where it is edited |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | one target | The dashboard target row. |
| `session` | one night of one target | The dashboard night expander, and the Nights ledger row on the Target detail page. |
| `rig` | one rig of one night of one target | The rig label row of the Target detail page's session pane. |
| `mosaic` | one mosaic (Phase 18) | The mosaics table row and the mosaic detail page's header (section 12.17). |

The first three shipped in Phase 20; the fourth arrived with mosaics in Phase 18. **The mosaic scope** is below.

#### The Custom Columns tab

Settings gains a **"Custom Columns"** tab (section 12.7), the twelfth, keyed `custom-columns`,
placed after Display and before Storage, so the three tabs that decide what a table shows sit
together. The tab holds two blocks, each carrying its own help glyph (section 12.12).

**"Add column"**, the create form, one row of controls:

| Control | Shape | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Name" | `TextBox`, watermark "For example, Processed" | Required. Trimmed. 1 to 60 characters. |
| "Type" | `ComboBox`: "Checkbox", "Text", "Dropdown" | Defaults to "Checkbox". |
| "Applies to" | `ComboBox`: "Target", "Night", "Rig", "Mosaic" | Defaults to "Target". |
| "Options" | Revealed only while Type is "Dropdown". A wrap panel of `Border.tag` chips, each with a remove glyph, over a `TextBox` watermarked "Type an option and press Enter" and an "Add" `Button.sm`. | At least one option is required before the column can be added. |
| "Add column" | `Button.primary` | Disabled while the form cannot be submitted, with the reason on its tooltip. |

**"Columns"**, the table, one aligned table (`DESIGN.md` section 6) with a header row and one row
per column in `display_order`:

| Column | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Order | Two `Button.quiet` arrows, "Move up" and "Move down" on their tooltips. The first row's up arrow and the last row's down arrow are disabled. |
| Name | The name, or a `TextBox` over it while the row is being edited. |
| Type | "Checkbox", "Text" or "Dropdown". |
| Applies to | "Target", "Night", "Rig" or "Mosaic". |
| Options | The dropdown options as `Border.tag` chips, or the options editor while the row is being edited. Empty for the other two types. |
| Values | The number of stored values for this column, so a delete states what it is about to take. |
| Actions | "Edit", which turns into "Save" and "Cancel"; then "Delete". |

The table's empty state is the sentence **"No custom columns yet."**

**Reordering swaps.** "Move up" exchanges the row's `display_order` with the row above it and
writes both rows in one transaction; "Move down" does the same downward. A first row moving up and
a last row moving down write nothing. The orders stay dense and distinct. This is a departure,
numbered below: the web writes `display_order + 1` on the moved row alone, so two columns can come
to hold the same order and the arrows then stop moving anything.

**Editing a row changes the name and, on a dropdown, the options.** The type and the scope are
fixed at creation: changing either would leave every stored value under a rule it was not written
to, and the honest repair is a new column. The row states so on the two disabled controls'
tooltips: **"Type and scope are fixed when the column is created."**

**Removing a dropdown option that values still use** is refused while any value holds it, with the
sentence **"n values still use this option. Change them first, or delete the column."**, and at
exactly one value with **"1 value still uses this option. Change it first, or delete the
column."**, so the refusal reads properly at one. The web lets the option go and leaves those
values unmatched by its own validator.

**Delete asks first**, with the two-press inline confirm the Settings Maintenance cards already
use (section 12.7): the first press arms the row and shows **"Delete this column and all n of its
values? This cannot be undone."** with "Confirm" and "Cancel" beside it; the second press deletes.
The sentence has three branches, for the same reason C14 gave the option refusal two: a column with
no values at all is the commonest delete, a column created by mistake, and "all 0 of its values"
and "all 1 of its values" both read as a defect. At zero it names no count; at one it says "and its
one value"; at two or more it is the sentence above.
Shipped: at zero, "Delete this column? This cannot be undone."; at one, "Delete this column and
its one value? This cannot be undone."
The delete cascades to `custom_column_values` (section 5.20) and removes the column's slug from
every `display.columns` list on the next write of that list. The repository writes no settings
document: an inert slug is `DisplayColumnWriter`'s business, and it costs nothing until then.

**A definition change reaches the open surfaces.** Creating, renaming, reordering or deleting a
column tells the pages that draw its cells, its filter control and its pickers, so a column defined
in Settings appears without a sort click, a page change or a restart. It is one mechanism and not one
per surface: the repository raises a single event after a **definition** write and never after a
value write, which would reload a page under the reader's own keystroke, and the application shell
routes it into the staleness handler the open pages already follow. Reset database raises the same
notification, because it truncates both tables without passing through the repository. Three rules
bound it. The route posts to the UI thread, because the write runs on a thread-pool thread and the
collections the surfaces rebuild are bound to the interface. It does **not** invalidate the derived
data caches: renaming a custom column must not make the Statistics and the Analysis pages re-run a
full library pass for data neither of them reads. And a Settings tab that has never been opened
subscribes nothing and is never built by the handler, because building it reads four settings
documents.
The event is `CustomColumnRepository.Changed`, an `EventHandler` raised by the repository's own
private `NotifyDefinitionsChanged()` after every definition write (create, rename or options,
reorder, delete) and, separately, by a completed database reset, because a reset truncates both
tables without passing through the repository. `AppHost` subscribes it, in the block built only at
GUI startup, to post through `UiPost.Default` to `DashboardViewModel.RefreshCustomColumns()`, which
reloads the filter panel's Custom section (`Filters.Reload()`) and requests a fresh listing query
(`RequestQuery()`), so the dashboard's cells, its gear picker and its filter section all pick up the
new definition list on their next query, with no scan and no restart. The Settings Display tab
(`DisplayTabViewModel`) takes a subscribe and unsubscribe delegate pair in its own constructor
(`subscribeCustomColumnsChanged` and `unsubscribeCustomColumnsChanged`) rather than reading the
repository directly, so a tab that has never been opened subscribes nothing and is never built by
the handler; while built, its handler (`OnCustomColumnsChanged`) re-reads the definition list off
the UI thread and rebuilds its Nights ledger column picker. Both column pickers, the Display tab's
dashboard picker and the gear flyout (`ColumnPickerViewModel.Groups`), list custom columns under a
"Custom" heading below the built-in ones, hidden while only one group exists
(`ShowGroupHeadings`).

#### The cell editor

One control, `Controls/CustomCellEditor.axaml`, serves every surface. It chooses its kind from the
column's type and nothing else, which is what keeps the four surfaces from drifting apart.

| Type | Control | Unset renders as | Commits on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `boolean` | `CheckBox` with no content | Cleared, which is the same as `false` | Every toggle, at once. |
| `text` | `TextBox` watermarked with the column's name in the tertiary ink | The watermark | One second of idle typing, Enter, and losing focus. |
| `dropdown` | `ComboBox` whose first entry is **"Not set"** and whose remaining entries are the column's options in order | "Not set" | Every selection, at once. |

**A check box has no third state.** A target that has never been touched and a target explicitly
set to `false` both render as cleared and both filter as No, because clearing the box stores
`false` rather than deleting the row. That is the web's behaviour and it is stated here so a reader
of the filter truth table below does not expect an "unset" case the editor cannot produce.

**An empty text value deletes its row.** Clearing a text box, or typing only whitespace into it,
removes the value rather than storing an empty string, so an emptied cell and a never-filled cell
are the same state on every surface and in the filter. The web stores the empty string.

**Selecting "Not set" clears a dropdown value**, deleting the row. The web's select refuses to save
its own empty choice (`InlineEditCell.tsx` line 101 guards on `if (val)`), so a dropdown value once
set can never be removed there.

**The text kind writes through `AutosaveField`** (the one debounced write spine, section 12.4's
notes boxes), not through a click-to-edit state machine. The window is the same one second, the
writes are chained so two cells cannot interleave into a lost update, and a refresh of the page
never clobbers text the user has typed and not yet saved. This is design lesson 1 applied at the
second occurrence rather than the sixth: the web hand-rolls a confirm-then-commit dance per cell
and carries two comments explaining the two bugs it grew (`InlineEditCell.tsx` lines 18 to 27 and
77 to 82).

**A refused write keeps the stored value.** The editor reverts to what is stored, takes the error
ink, and carries the refusal sentence on its tooltip until the next successful write. Nothing on a
table row opens a dialog and nothing pushes a toast: a cell that cannot be written is the cell that
has to say so. A write that throws rather than being refused shows **"The value could not be saved.
Try again."**, never the exception's own message, and the exception goes to the log.

**Keyboard.** Tab reaches every editor in the row's own column order, after the row's own content
and before the row's trailing control.

| Key | Check box | Text box | Combo box |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Space | Toggles and writes | Types a space | Opens the list |
| Enter | Nothing, and stops at the cell | Commits and keeps focus | Commits the highlighted entry and closes |
| Escape | Nothing | Drops an unsaved edit and closes an open idle window; a write already sent is not recalled | Closes without changing |
| Tab | Moves on | Commits, then moves on | Commits, then moves on |
| Up, Down | Nothing | Nothing | Move through the entries |

Two of those rows are rules rather than defaults, and both are stated because a plausible
implementation gets them wrong:

- **Space must reach a text cell as a character.** The editor marks Space handled for the check box
  and the list and never for the text box. The Windows backend drops the character message that
  follows a key down the application has handled, so swallowing Space in the text box swallowed the
  space itself and "ab cd" was typed in as "abcd". A headless case cannot show this, because a case
  that supplies both the key press and the text input supplies the half the platform was dropping;
  the proof is a look at the running application.
- **Escape reverts without leaving a pending write behind, and it does not recall a write already
  sent.** Cancelling the edit cancels the open idle window, restores the value and clears the dirty
  flag together, in one operation on the write spine. Reverting the text alone leaves a live window
  that fires a second later and writes the old value over a newer one. What Escape cannot do is
  unsend: once the idle window has elapsed the write is attached to the chain and is going to land,
  so Escape between that moment and the write's own completion puts the pre-edit value on screen
  while the store takes the typed one, and the next load of the page shows the typed one. Under a
  database held by a scan that window is seconds rather than milliseconds. The write cannot be
  recalled, so the rule is stated as what it is rather than promised as a revert.

**Screen reader.** Each editor carries `AutomationProperties.Name` built from the column's name and
its subject, so an unlabelled control never reaches a reader: "Priority, NGC 7000" on a target row,
"Priority, 2026-03-14" on a night row, "Done, 2026-03-14, Askar FMA180 / ASI2600MC" on a rig row.
The refusal sentence is also the editor's `AutomationProperties.HelpText` while it is refused, so
it is announced rather than only drawn. The check box announces its own checked state; nothing
overrides it with a word of its own.

**Clicking an editor does not open the row.** The editor swallows the click on every surface whose
row is itself clickable, which is the dashboard target row and the ledger night row.

#### Where the cells appear

| Surface | Scope | Which columns | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dashboard target row (section 12.2) | `target` | Every target-scope column whose slug is in `display.columns.dashboard`, in `display_order`, after `last_session` and before the sessions expander | The dashboard column picker, which lists custom columns under a "Custom" heading below the built-in ones. Off by default: a new column's slug is not added to any stored list. |
| Dashboard night expander (section 12.2) | `session` | Every session-scope column, in `display_order`, after the expander's own columns | None. The expander has no picker today and this phase does not give it one. |
| Nights ledger row (section 12.4) | `session` | Every session-scope column whose slug is in `display.columns.ledger`, in `display_order`, after the Filters column | A "Nights ledger columns" picker on the Display tab. **Off by default**, and the narrow ledger below the 1600 pixel breakpoint drops them before it drops the Filters column. |
| Session pane rig label row (section 12.4) | `rig` | Every rig-scope column, in `display_order`, on the **first** table of the pane only | None. |

**A custom column is the first thing to give way, on both pages.** Neither page takes room from a
built-in column to draw one. Where the row or the ledger cannot hold everything, custom columns are
dropped from the end of the list, one at a time, until what is left fits, and folding the filter
panel or widening the window brings them straight back with nothing reloaded and nothing re-read.
The two pages apply that one principle to two different constraints, below.

**The dashboard row drops custom columns before anything else.** With a check box column and a text
column switched on, the row wants more width than the list has at the shipped 1280 by 800, and the
Expand button would be drawn past the list's trailing edge. The drop runs inside the one place the
taken column set is computed, immediately before the Equipment step-aside it shares that method
with, so it is the same width rule and not a second one: the trailing custom column leaves while
the row fits neither the wide layout nor the narrow one, and only then is the Equipment column
stepped aside exactly as before. No built-in column and never the Expand button is pushed out by a
custom column. One figure drives the header strip and every row's cells, so the two cannot
disagree. A drawing of a dashboard custom cell therefore needs a wide window or a folded filter
panel; at the window minimum with the panel open the row may draw none.

**A custom strip never tightens a built-in column.** The row's own tight cap, the per-column text cap
that applies once the row can no longer draw every shown column whole, is the same figure whether a
custom strip is drawn or not. A Last Session date is not shortened to make room for a column the
reader added: the row drops the custom column instead, by the rule above.

**A custom column's header entry is as wide as its own name, not as wide as its editor.** A check box
cell measures 36 and a name like "Processed" needs more than twice that, so sizing the header from the
editor drew every heading as an ellipsis and two check box columns side by side read as two identical
dots with nothing on screen saying which was which. The entry's width is therefore the greater of the
editor's width and the heading's measured width, capped at the dropdown cell's 120, and the heading is
measured at the rendered view's own type size and family, the way the frame table's file name column
already is, so a root text size change re-measures both strips together. Above the cap the heading
trims and the whole name is on the entry's tooltip and in its automation name. **The Nights ledger
cannot widen its heading**, because ruling C21 fixes its allowance at 208 and the session pane's own
minimum bounds it, so the ledger heading trims and carries the full name on its tooltip and in its
automation name instead. A reader and a screen reader can recover the name on both surfaces.

**A ledger text cell draws no watermark.** The dashboard row and the rig label row have no heading
above their cells, so the column name in the watermark is the only label there and earns its place.
The ledger has a heading directly above every cell, so a watermark there repeats the same word on
every night row.
It is turned off by one `ShowWatermark` styled property on `Controls/CustomCellEditor`, default
true, assigned from the code behind rather than bound in markup because the control declares no
style element of its own; the ledger's row strip is the one instance that sets it false. The
dashboard target row, the dashboard night expander and the session pane's rig line leave it at its
default and show the column's name as the watermark. The screen reader name is unchanged on all
four surfaces: it still names the column and the subject whether the watermark is drawn or not.

**The per-kind cell width table has one home**, read by the dashboard and the Nights ledger alike, so
the two surfaces cannot come to disagree about what a check box, a dropdown or a text cell measures.
A text cell is 120.

**A library with no custom column pays nothing.** The value reads are skipped entirely while the
definition list is empty, on the dashboard query and on the Target page load, so a reader who never
defines a column issues no extra statement for this feature.

**The ledger widens for custom columns, and only for them.** The wide Nights ledger has three
pixels of spare width, so a custom column cannot be fitted inside its 640 without taking the date
off the Night column. No existing layout pin moves. With no custom column switched on the ledger is
640 wide, exactly as it has always been, and nothing on the page moves. When custom columns are
switched on, the ledger grows by the sum of the switched-on columns' widths plus one gutter and the
starred session pane column gives that space up, to a ceiling of **208 pixels** including a **32
pixel** gutter; a column that does not fit under the ceiling is dropped from the end of the list,
the same drop the narrow ledger applies to all of them. A text cell on the ledger is 120 pixels
wide, which is what keeps a check box column and a text column both drawable under the ceiling.

The ceiling is measured rather than chosen. At the page's own 1600 pixel breakpoint the workbench
has 1558 pixels and spends 28 on its gutter, and `SessionPane.FilterTableMinWidth` claims 682,
which is the pane's only declared minimum; 1558 less 28 less 682 leaves the ledger 848, and 848
less the wide ledger's own 640 is 208. The gutter is 32 rather than a smaller figure because the
ledger's ten column definitions have measured more than the ledger they sit in since Phase 12: 645
against 640 under the headless harness's stub face, and 669 against 640 at the shipped face and the
default text size. That overflow is pre-existing, is hidden today by the Filters cell's own
margins, and is recorded as an accepted limit rather than repaired by this phase.

**Rig cells are drawn on the first table's rig label row only, with their column name beside them.**
A rig label row carries no header row, so a bare editor on it has no visible name: each rig cell is
therefore preceded by a caption carrying its column's name, in the secondary ink at the same size
as the frame count beside it. And the cells are drawn on the rig label row of the **first** table
of the pane, the per-filter table, never repeated on the ranges table's own rig label row, because
two editors over one stored value fall out of step with each other. The ranges table's rig label
row keeps its label and its frame count and carries no cell.

**Rig rows are drawn for a single-rig night too, while any rig-scope column exists.** Section 12.4's
rig label row is a multi-rig shape: on a single-rig night the pane draws no such row at all, so
rig-scope cells would be unreachable on the common one-telescope library. While at least one
rig-scope column exists, the pane therefore draws one rig row on every night, carrying the rig's
label, its frame count and the rig cells, and on a single-rig night that row carries the cells and
nothing the pane does not already state. A library with no rig-scope column draws exactly what it
draws today, so the existing layout pins are unchanged on every night that has no such column.

**One night value has two editors, and the stale one is refreshed rather than guarded against.** A
session-scope value is drawn both on the dashboard's night expander and on the Nights ledger row of
the same night, and it is the only scope drawn on two surfaces. Two rules close the reachable case:
the expander re-reads its night values on **every** expand rather than once per row, and the shell's
close-detail path re-reads the values of every expanded row, so a value edited on the Target page is
current when the reader returns to the dashboard. A refresh never touches a cell that is dirty or
focused, so it cannot take text out from under the reader. What is deliberately **not** built is an
expected-previous-value check inside the write: this is a one-user desktop application, and one
stored value with two editors does not justify a compare-and-set on every write path. The upgrade
path is recorded rather than built, in HANDOFF section 7, for the day a third editor of one value
appears.

**A page change inside the idle window can redraw the pre-flush value once.** Typing into a text cell
and paging away before the one second window elapses does not lose the value: the pending text is
attached to the write chain before the row goes. But the next page's values are read before the rows
are rebuilt, so an immediate return to the first page can issue its read before the attached write
has landed and draw the pre-edit value once. The catalogue holds the new value and the next query
corrects the screen. Accepted rather than repaired: awaiting the flush would block a page change on a
database write.

**The night expander's session cells are the port's own.** The web renders session custom columns
in `SessionTable.tsx` as a literal `-` and has never populated them (591234b lines 70 to 72, whose
own comment records it). The port shows and writes the real value, which is what the column picker,
the filter and the ledger all already imply.

#### The dashboard filter section

The filter panel (section 12.2) gains an eighth section, **"Custom"**, placed after "FITS Header
Query", with the collapsed strip label **"Cust"**. **The section is absent entirely while the
library holds no custom column**, so a user who never defines one sees seven sections exactly as
today.

Inside, the columns are grouped by scope, each group under a `TextBlock.t-caption` heading,
**"Target"**, **"Night"** then **"Rig"**, and within a group they are in `display_order`. A group
with no column is not drawn. Each column contributes one control labelled with the column's name.

**The truth table.** Every custom filter is combined with `AND`, with each other and with every
other filter section. A filter is applied as one `EXISTS` over `custom_column_values` for that
column and that target.

| Type | Control | Choices | A target passes when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `boolean` | Three buttons in one segment, the `Button.pill` shape the Object Type pills already use | "Any", "Yes", "No" | **Any**: always, the filter contributes no clause. **Yes**: a matching value row exists whose `value` is exactly `true`. **No**: a matching value row exists whose `value` is exactly `false`. A target with no value row at all fails both Yes and No. |
| `text` | `TextBox`, watermarked "Contains", debounced on the panel's own window | free text | **Empty or whitespace**: no clause. **Otherwise**: a matching value row exists whose `value` contains the trimmed text, case insensitive. |
| `dropdown` | `ComboBox` whose first entry is "Any" | "Any", then each option | **Any**: no clause. **Otherwise**: a matching value row exists whose `value` equals the chosen option exactly, case sensitive. |

"A matching value row" means a row with that `column_id` and that `target_id`, and additionally:

| The column's scope | The matching row must also have |
| --- | --- |
| `target` | `session_date` null and `rig_label` null |
| `session` | `session_date` not null |
| `rig` | `rig_label` not null |

**Every custom filter is target level, whatever the column's scope.** A night-scope filter says
"this target has at least one night with this value", not "show me only those nights": the
dashboard's unit is a target, and the rows it returns are unchanged. The web does the same
(`target_listing.py` lines 381 to 400), and this is the user's ruling.

**The dashboard reports no matched-night count for a custom filter.** The web adjusts its "n of m
sessions" marker from a second pre-fetch that requires a non-null `session_date` and reads every
column rather than the filtered ones (`target_listing.py` lines 894 to 972), so the count and the
row set can disagree for a rig-scope filter. The port leaves the marker to the metric filters,
which is the only filter that narrows a night set.

**The text clause is `LIKE` with an explicit escape.** The typed text has `\`, `%` and `_` each
prefixed with `\` and the clause carries `ESCAPE '\'`, the same rule section 12.3 already fixes for
the header query's `contains`, through the same widened `HeaderQueryBuilder` helper rather than a
copy of it. SQLite's `LIKE` is case insensitive for ASCII by default, which is the case folding the
table above promises; the web reaches the same answer with `ILIKE`, and appends no `ESCAPE` clause
at all (`target_listing.py` line 376). Every value, slug, column id and `LIKE` pattern reaches the
statement as a bound parameter.

**A stranded value satisfies a custom filter.** The scope predicate tests only whether
`session_date` or `rig_label` is set; it never joins the night or the rig back to anything that still
exists. So a target can be returned for a value whose night, target assignment or rig label has
moved, which reads as a wrong result rather than a stale one. It is the filter side of "a value is
keyed, never owned" above, and it is an accepted limit of this phase.

**A filter naming a column that no longer exists is dropped**, silently, the way an unknown metric
key already is (section 12.2.1), and it is dropped before any text is composed. A dropdown filter
holding an option the column no longer offers is kept and applied, and matches nothing until the
reader changes it, because dropping it would silently widen the result.

**Custom filter values live in the per-visit tier**, with every other filter value (section 12.2):
they are restored on a return to the page inside one run and are not persisted across restarts.
"Reset Filters" clears them with the rest.

#### Validation, quoted

The repository refuses each of these and writes nothing. The sentence is what the surface shows,
verbatim, and the repository is the only place any of them is composed.

| Refused | Sentence |
| --- | --- |
| A create or rename with an empty name | "Enter a name for the column." |
| A name longer than 60 characters after trimming | "Keep the column name to 60 characters or fewer." |
| A name another column already carries, compared case insensitively after trimming | "A column named \"<name>\" already exists." |
| A dropdown created with no options | "Add at least one option before adding a dropdown column." |
| An option the column already carries | "\"<option>\" is already an option." |
| Removing an option that stored values still use, at two or more | "n values still use this option. Change them first, or delete the column." |
| Removing an option that exactly one stored value still uses | "1 value still uses this option. Change it first, or delete the column." |
| A boolean value that is not `true` or `false` | "A checkbox column stores only yes or no." |
| A dropdown value that is not one of the column's options | "\"<value>\" is not one of this column's options." |
| A dropdown value on a column with no options at all | "This column has no options yet. Add one on the Custom Columns tab." |
| A text value longer than 500 characters after trimming | "Keep the value to 500 characters or fewer." |
| A scope other than target, session, rig or mosaic | "This column scope is not available yet." |
| A write that threw rather than being refused | "The value could not be saved. Try again." |

The scope sentence cannot be reached from any surface: every scope the picker offers is accepted.
It is stated because the repository is the choke point, and a stored `applies_to` this build does
not know is refused there rather than at each caller (design lesson 2). Phase 18's mosaic scope
arrived at that one entry point, which is all it changed there. The last sentence is the view
side's, not a validation: it is what a cell shows when the write throws, and it is the only one of
the thirteen a reader can see without the repository having judged anything.

Two refusals carry no sentence at all, because neither is a user path: a value written against a
column id that does not exist, and a key whose shape disagrees with its column's scope (section
5.20). Both are programming errors, and a surface that builds its key through the four key
factories cannot reach the second.

**The boolean and dropdown sentences are the port's wording of the web's two.** The web answers
`Boolean columns require 'true' or 'false'` and
`Value must be one of: ['A', 'B']` (`custom_columns.py` lines 153 and 155), both of which print a
Python literal at a user.

#### The slug rule

A column's `slug` is derived from its name once, at creation, and never again:

1. Lower-case the trimmed name with the invariant culture.
2. Replace every run of characters outside `a` to `z` and `0` to `9` with a single `_`.
3. Trim leading and trailing `_`.
4. If nothing is left, use `column`.
5. Prefix `custom_`.
6. If that slug is taken, append `_2`, then `_3`, and so on until it is free.

So "Processed" gives `custom_processed`, "Notes tag" gives `custom_notes_tag`, and a second column
also named "Priority" would give `custom_priority_2`, except that a duplicate name is refused
before it gets there.

**The prefix is mandatory and is the whole point.** A column named "Name" slugs to `custom_name`
and cannot collide with the dashboard's built-in `name` key, with any of the 32 frame-table keys of
section 5.8.2, or with a key a later phase adds. The web has no such rule: its `_slugify` would
produce the bare `name` and the collision would be silent in every column-visibility document.

**An inert slug after a reset is never cleaned up, and that is harmless.** Reset database clears both
tables and keeps `user_settings` (section 12.7), so `display.columns.dashboard` and
`display.columns.ledger` still hold `custom_` slugs for definitions that are gone. Every surface
builds its cells from the definition list, so the slugs draw nothing; the rule that an inert slug is
dropped on the next write of that list still holds, but after a reset there is no picker entry left
to toggle, so that write may never come and the slugs persist. Stated so a reader of a settings
document is not surprised by them.

**The slug never changes on a rename.** The web re-slugs on every rename
(`custom_columns.py` line 106), which orphans that column's entry in every stored
`display.columns` list and every restored filter at once, with nothing to say it happened. In the
port, renaming a column changes what is drawn and nothing that is stored by key.

#### What happens to values

| Event | Values |
| --- | --- |
| A column is deleted | Every value of that column is deleted, by the `column_id` cascade of section 5.20. |
| A target is deleted | Every value naming it is deleted, by the `target_id` cascade. |
| Two targets are merged | The loser's values move to the winner where the winner has no value in the same slot, a slot being (`column_id`, `session_date`, `rig_label`). A conflicting value stays on the loser, so the winner's own value is never overwritten. The moved ids are recorded in the merge's `merge_manifests` row, and an unmerge moves them back. An edit made to a moved value while the targets are merged belongs to the moved row itself, not to a copy of it, so an unmerge carries that edit back to the loser with the row. Ported from `target_merge.py` lines 77 to 99. |
| A night's date changes | Nothing. See "A value is keyed, never owned" below, which is the one rule every such event falls under. |
| A telescope or camera is renamed in the Equipment tab | Every `custom_column_values.rig_label` built from the old canonical name is rewritten to the new one, in one catalogue transaction, issued from the same save that already rewrites `general.phd2_profile_map` (section 12.7). |
| A telescope or camera alias group is regrouped, or a group is deleted | The same rewrite. A raw header name moved into another group, or a group removed outright, changes the canonical name the frames resolve to and therefore the composed rig label, exactly as a rename does, so the rewrite takes its pairs from the alias table rather than from the changed-canonical list alone. A **filter** group has no part in a rig label, which is composed from the telescope and the camera and nothing else. |
| Two equipment names are folded into one | The rewrite lands two values on one slot. Inside the same transaction the row with the latest `updated_at` stays and the others are deleted; at an equal instant the row with the higher id stays, so the answer never depends on the order the rows were read. See below. |
| Scan, rescan, cleanup, rebuild targets, smart rebuild | Nothing. No scan path reads or writes either table. |
| Reset database | Both tables are cleared with the rest of the scan output, and the typed confirmation names them. |

**A value is keyed, never owned.** A value row survives everything except the deletion of its column
or of its target. It is found by its key, and nothing re-keys it when what that key names moves out
from under it. Four paths move one:

| Path | What moves |
| --- | --- |
| A night's date is re-derived (sections 8.2 and 8.3) | The night. The value stays on the old date. The date moves only when the observer's longitude or timezone changes. |
| The orphan prune (section 10.3) | The night, or every night: it deletes `images` rows, so a night can cease to exist entirely. |
| Rebuild targets (section 12.7) | The target's frames. It clears `images.resolved_target_id`, so a target can be left with no frames and no row on the dashboard while keeping every value. |
| Smart rebuild with its inline duplicate detection (sections 9.7 and 12.7) | The target. Frames can move to another target row. |

A value whose key no longer names anything reachable is **stranded**: nothing prunes it, no surface
draws it, every count the application shows includes it, and the dashboard filter matches it. That
last one is the consequence worth stating plainly: a target can be returned for a custom filter
because of a stranded value that no cell on that target's own page draws. The data layer cannot tell
a reachable value from a stranded one without the listing query's own group set, so this is one
stated rule rather than a guard in four places, and the option-removal refusal can therefore name a
count the reader cannot act on. Recorded as an accepted limit in HANDOFF section 7 with that
sentence, and the question of whether the refusal needs a way out, a "clear this column's values"
action or a reachable-only count, is the user's rather than this phase's.
They remain counted. Excluding a stranded value from `ValueCount` and from the option-in-use census
turned out not to be one predicate in one place, and no existing predicate was reusable: a
session-scope value whose night is gone is one SQL `EXISTS` clause, but a rig-scope value whose
label is gone needs the equipment alias document, which this repository does not take and should
not, and a target-scope value whose target keeps no frame after a rebuild is a third shape again.
Three shapes across two layers is not one predicate, so nothing was added and the accepted limit
above stands as written.

**The fold rule is code rather than a caught constraint violation.** Renaming two telescopes, or
two cameras, into one name folds two rigs into one, and any values those two rigs held for the same
column on the same night then belong to the same rig. Letting `uq_custom_column_value` throw is not
a one-time failure: the rename pairs are rebuilt from the loaded names on every save, so the same
collision would be retried and would fail again on every later save of that tab, the whole rewrite
would roll back each time, and those values would never reach a surface again. The rewrite reads
every row carrying a label that moves **and** every row already carrying a label something else
moves onto, flushes the deletes first inside the one transaction so no surviving row is moved onto
a slot the row it replaces still occupies, and looks each row's new label up by its original label,
so a rename chain and a swap each land once per row.

**The rig rewrite is a third write and is not atomic with the other two.** The equipment aliases
live in the equipment settings document, the profile map in the general document and these labels
in the catalogue, and no one call writes all three (section 12.7 already states the first half of
this). A failure after the equipment save leaves rig labels on the old canonical name; the pairs
are rebuilt from the loaded names on each save, so the next save of the same rename repairs it, and
until then those values render under a rig row the pane no longer draws rather than under the wrong
rig. That is the same accepted shape the profile map already lives with.

**A value written against a merged-away target is a stated ceiling.** `SetValue` does not refuse
one. Such a value can occupy a slot an unmerge is about to restore into, which throws
`uq_custom_column_value` out of the unmerge; that transaction rolls back, so nothing is corrupted,
and no surface this phase ships reaches a merged-away target's cells.

#### The mosaic scope

Phase 18 offers the fourth `applies_to` value, `mosaic` (ruling R2). It is the fourth entry of the
"Applies to" picker, reading "Mosaic", and the Columns table shows it the same way. A mosaic-scope
value belongs to one mosaic: its key sets `mosaic_id` alone (section 5.20), built through
`CustomValueKey.ForMosaic`, and `CustomColumnRepository.SetValue` accepts it under the same key
shape check as the other three scopes, so the scope arrives at the one write path and nowhere else.
Its cells are the shared cell editor above, on two surfaces: the mosaics table, one cell per
column after the built-in columns, shown only while its slug is in `display.columns.mosaics`
(section 5.8.2) and off by default; and inline in the mosaic detail page's header, every
mosaic-scope column in display order with its name as a caption, ungated by any picker (section
12.17). The foreign key from `custom_column_values.mosaic_id` to `mosaics.id` carries the cascade,
so deleting a mosaic deletes its values. No column and no index was added for it: the Phase 20
migration had already created both.

A mosaic-scope column has no place on the dashboard: the target row, the night expander, the
Nights ledger and the rig label row draw only their own scopes, and the dashboard filter's Custom
section lists target, night and rig columns only, because a target row cannot answer a question
about a mosaic. A merge moves no mosaic value, because a mosaic value names no target. Values are
counted in the Columns table's Values cell like any other, and the delete prompt counts them.

#### Nothing here writes a user file

Every write in this section is a row in `custom_columns`, a row in `custom_column_values` or a key
in `user_settings`. No surface here reads, writes, moves, renames or deletes a file on disk
(section 2.1).

#### Departures from the web, in one place

1. **The slug carries a `custom_` prefix and never changes after creation.** The web re-slugs on
   rename and emits bare slugs, so a column named "Name" shadows the built-in `name` key and every
   rename orphans that column's stored visibility and filter entries.
2. **Reordering swaps two rows in one transaction.** The web writes `display_order + 1` on the
   moved row alone, so two columns can come to hold the same order and the arrows then stop moving
   anything.
3. **A dropdown value can be cleared**, through the "Not set" entry. The web's select guards on a
   truthy value, so a dropdown value once set can never be removed.
4. **A dropdown with no options refuses every value.** The web skips its own membership check when
   the option list is empty (`custom_columns.py` line 154 requires `col.dropdown_options` to be
   truthy) and stores anything sent.
5. **Session-scope columns show real values on the dashboard night expander.** The web renders them
   as a literal `-` and has never populated them.
6. **An empty text value deletes its row** rather than storing an empty string, so an emptied cell
   and a never-filled cell are one state everywhere, the filter included.
7. **The text editor is a plain text box on a one second idle autosave**, through the existing
   `AutosaveField`, not the web's per-cell click-to-edit with its own confirm-then-commit.
8. **A duplicate column name is refused** with a sentence. The web silently creates a second column
   with a suffixed slug and two identical labels in every picker.
9. **A column's type and scope are fixed at creation**, and the two controls say so. The web's PATCH
   accepts neither, so the restriction is the same; the port states it where the reader meets it
   instead of leaving the controls unexplained.
10. **Removing a dropdown option that stored values still use is refused.** The web removes it and
    leaves those values outside their own column's option set.
11. **Deleting a column asks first**, with the inline two-press confirm every destructive Settings
    action already uses, and the prompt states how many values go with it.
12. **The name is bounded at 60 characters and a text value at 500.** The web bounds the name at
    255 and the value not at all.
13. **No `created_by` and no `updated_by`** (section 2.3). The web's own baseline already makes both
    nullable against its model.
14. **`dropdown_options` is one JSON TEXT column**, not a Postgres string array.
15. **Rig values survive an equipment rename**, rewritten from the same pairs the profile map
    rewrite already uses. The web has no alias grouping at all, so it has nothing to rename.
16. **Merged values move to the winner and are recorded in the merge manifest**, so an unmerge puts
    them back. This is the web's behaviour, listed because it is a rule the port has to build rather
    than inherit.
17. **The text filter clause carries an explicit `ESCAPE`.** The web escapes the three wildcard
    characters and then omits the `ESCAPE` clause, which leaves the escaping meaningful only because
    of a server default.
18. **No matched-night count is adjusted by a custom filter.** The web's count comes from a second
    pre-fetch that requires a non-null session date and reads every column rather than the filtered
    ones, so it can disagree with the rows it labels.
19. **The mosaic scope was held back until Phase 18** (the user's ruling of 2026-09-21), and was
    refused by the repository until then. From Phase 18 it matches the web: the fourth choice,
    cells on the mosaics table and the mosaic detail header, and a cascading foreign key (ruling
    R2).
20. **A rig row is drawn on a single-rig night while any rig-scope column exists**, so a rig column
    is usable on a one-telescope library.
21. **The key's shape is checked against its column's scope at the one write path**, and a
    disagreement writes nothing. The web's endpoint accepts whatever key parts the caller sends.
22. **A rig cell carries its column's name as a caption and is drawn on one table only.** The web
    draws rig cells under a header row, which the port's rig label row does not have, and it has no
    second table to repeat them on.
23. **Custom columns give way before built-in ones**, on the dashboard row and on the Nights ledger
    alike, and the ledger widens rather than taking room from a built-in column. The web's tables
    scroll horizontally instead, so nothing there ever has to give way.
24. **Folding two equipment names keeps the newest of the colliding values** rather than failing the
    save. The web has no alias grouping and therefore no fold.
25. **A definition change reaches every open surface through one event**, posted to the interface
    thread, which does not invalidate the derived data caches and never builds an unvisited Settings
    tab. The web refetches on navigation and has no equivalent.
26. **A stranded value is stated as a rule rather than pruned.** The web strands values on the same
    paths and says nothing about it either, so this is a departure in the spec rather than in the
    code: the rule is written down here.

Everything else here is the web's, matched exactly.

---

### 12.16 Integrations

Port of `backend/app/api/integrations.py` and the integration half of
`frontend/src/components/SessionAccordionCard.tsx` and
`frontend/src/pages/TargetDetailPage.tsx`. Three things live here: the NINA framing call, the
Stellarium slew, and the AstroBin acquisition CSV. They share one settings tab (section 12.7), one
page of entry points (section 12.4) and one rule about what a URL may be.

Nothing in this section opens a listening socket and nothing in it writes a file. The CSV goes to
the clipboard; the two protocols make outbound HTTP calls and read the responses. There is no
`AppWriter` caller anywhere in the section, so nothing here is on section 2.1.1's allowlist and
nothing here has to be.

#### The URL rule

One method, `IntegrationUrl.TryParse`, is the only place a stored instance URL becomes a base
address. It accepts a URL when, and only when:

| Condition | Why |
| --- | --- |
| It parses as an absolute URI | A relative address has no host to call. |
| Its scheme is `http` or `https`, compared ordinally and case-insensitively | Web parity. `file`, `ftp` and the rest are refused. |
| Its host is present and not empty | Web parity. |

Everything else is accepted, **loopback and the private ranges included**. This is the one place
the port departs from the web's own validation, and it departs deliberately. The web refuses
`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `169.254.0.0/16` and their IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms, and resolves a hostname
before calling it, because there a browser persuades a **server** to make a call the browser could
not make itself, which is the server-side request forgery the web's own comments name. This
application is the reader's own desktop process, the URL comes out of the reader's own settings
document, and the ordinary configuration is NINA on the same machine at `http://localhost:1888`:
refusing loopback here would refuse the common case to defend a boundary that does not exist. The
web's optional `GALACTILOG_INTEGRATION_ALLOWED_HOSTS` allowlist is not ported for the same reason,
and neither is its DNS pre-resolution probe, which is a check the outbound call itself performs a
moment later.

The rule is enforced at two points and at no third: the External Tools tab refuses a URL before it
is stored (section 12.7), and each client calls `TryParse` before it builds a request, refusing a
stored URL that reached the document some other way. The second is the fail-closed one: a client
that cannot parse its URL makes no call at all and reports the refusal sentence below.

The third condition, a non-empty host, is written for completeness but is never independently
observable under a mutation of just that check: .NET's `Uri` parser refuses every hostless `http`
or `https` URL at the first condition, before the third has anything left to test (ruling B12). It
stays as one fail-closed line rather than as a line proven red on its own, because the parser's own
refusal is not a reason to drop a rule this method states.

The base address is the accepted URL with every trailing `/` trimmed, so `http://host:1888/` and
`http://host:1888` build the same request.

#### The timeout

Every request either client makes is bounded at **5 seconds**, web parity. The bound is imposed per
request through a `CancellationTokenSource` linked to the caller's own token, **never by setting
`HttpClient.Timeout`**: the two clients share one `HttpClient` that `AppHost` builds for them
alone, over the same `httpHandlerOverride` mechanism the catalogue clients use so tests can stub
it, and neither client ever touches its `Timeout` (rulings B1, B19). That client is owned by a
typed `IntegrationHttpClient` singleton the container disposes with the host; nothing registers
the bare `HttpClient` type, so nothing else can resolve it and rewrite the timeout for both
clients' whole life. Its handler refuses a redirect (`IntegrationHttp.NewHandler()`,
`AllowAutoRedirect = false`): a 302 from a configured instance is a failure with the fixed sentence
below rather than a second call to a host the reader never configured (ruling B28); the two
catalogue clients keep their own standing handler and still follow one. The bound covers one
request; a Stellarium slew that tries two focus names, a coordinate fallback and a field of view
call can therefore run longer than 5 seconds in total, which is the right bound, because each leg
is a separate thing that can hang.
