That theme declares every metric token as a shade of one red by design, and the spike measured
every pair that meets on one Analysis chart there: the widest separation between two series
tokens is deltaE 28.3 and the narrowest 6.9, and `accent` is itself deltaE 8.0 from `warning`, so
no token swap opens a gap. Every one of them is clear of the surface at contrast 4.57 or better,
so lightness carries even where hue does not. The encodings the Analysis rows below are built on
are therefore the encodings, in every theme: **a filled dot for the data, a hollow ring for the
outlier, a 2 pixel line for a derived overlay, and a fill at `0x40` alpha for a band.** The
matrix is the one row where that is not enough, because the sign of r has nowhere else to go:
**there the printed r carries the sign and the colour ramp is decoration.**

**Which makes the matrix's printed figure the one text on an Analysis chart that has to be
readable on every cell of its own ramp, and one fixed ink cannot be.** On red-light
`text-primary` is `E0442E` at luminance 0.202 and the ramp's negative end is at 0.182, a contrast
of about 1.08: the figure carrying the sign is close to invisible on a strongly negative cell.
The rule is therefore the per-cell choice the matrix row below states, in **every** theme and not
only in red-light.

**What it still does not reach on red-light, measured on the running application and not
sampled.** The figures below were read off the rendered pixels of the launched page, cell by cell,
and they supersede an earlier set taken at r of minus 1, 0 and plus 1 only, which missed the part
of the ramp that is worst:

| r on the cell | Contrast of the printed figure against that cell |
| --- | --- |
| -0.47 | **2.54 to 1** |
| 0.47 | **2.70 to 1** |
| -0.30 | **3.26 to 1** |
| 0.01 | 4.48 to 1 |
| -0.00 | 4.49 to 1 |
| 0.92 | 6.96 to 1 |
| 1.00 | 8.14 to 1 |

**The mid band is the part that misses 4.5 to 1, not the extremes**, which are comfortable, and
the two neutral cells land a hundredth under the bar. Every figure is legible to a reader with
good sight; the mid band is what would not survive a contrast audit. The cause is the theme, not
the rule: every token of red-light is a shade of one red, so the ramp spans the theme's whole
luminance range and both candidate inks lie inside it. The rule promises the better of the two
inks there and its case asserts exactly that. AA everywhere on red-light needs a token off that
theme's red ramp, which is a section 14 change and a later phase's. Alpha is ignored in the
contrast arithmetic, which changes no choice on any measured cell.

**The contrast rule is one shared static, `InkContrast`, not a member of either chart.** It holds
`Choose`, `Contrast` and `RelativeLuminance`, and it has two users: the matrix cell labels and the
box plot's median mark. It was extracted at the second occurrence rather than copied (design
lesson 1).

The focus box the Matrix draws around the keyboard-focused cell takes `accent` for the same
family of reasons: on red-light no opaque token separates from the ramp by lightness, and the two
pixel stroke reads because it sits in the four pixel gutter the series' own point padding leaves,
over the chart background, at about 6.3 to 1.

Each cell prints its r to two decimals as a data label, and that printed figure, not the ramp, is what carries the sign, so the ink it is printed in is load bearing: **each cell's label ink is chosen per cell by contrast** through the shared `InkContrast`, between `text-primary` and `bg-elevated` forced opaque, against that cell's own colour on the ramp, the better ratio winning. The web application uses Chart.js for the two metric charts (`SessionMetricsChart.tsx`,
`TargetMetricsChart.tsx`) and hand-rolled markup for the rest. The port moves everything to
one library, which is the shared spine for the third occurrence of "draw a chart".

Four of the graphics above are drawn controls rather than LiveCharts series: the night strip,
the imaging calendar, the guide graph and the guiding altitude arc, in that order of arrival.
The reason is the same each time and is worth stating once. A chart library earns its keep on a
series of values against two axes with ticks, a legend and a tooltip; it earns nothing on a
graphic whose marks are its content, where every mark would become a visual and a binding, and
it cannot express a mark the library has no series type for at all, which the settle band, the
dither line and the altitude wedge each are. The web reaches the same conclusion from the other
side: its guide graph disables Chart.js's own legend and draws the settle bands and dither
lines in a hand-written plugin rather than add `chartjs-plugin-annotation`, and it hand-wires
zoom and pan onto the canvas rather than add `chartjs-plugin-zoom`
(`frontend/src/components/Phd2GuideGraph.tsx` lines 53 to 57). The four share the shape
`DESIGN.md` section 7 records: rendered in `Render`, every brush handed in by the host, no
colour literal in the source, hover through a hit test, and a headless render tick in the
tests. What two of the four would otherwise duplicate is extracted when the second of them
needs it, and not before.

**Phase 19A's mosaic arranger (section 12.17) is a composed control and adds no drawn control**,
so the four drawn controls above are still the four. It is a `Canvas` of templated tile
`ContentControl`s under one `RotateTransform` for the global rotation and one `MatrixTransform` for
zoom and pan, each tile's rotation and flip a `LayoutTransformControl` around its `Image`, and the
tiles' overlays ordinary `TextBlock`s on `Border`s, so the theme, the style census and the
no-colour-literal rule reach every part of it. It is not drawn because its marks are controls, not
data: a tile is a pressable, draggable, selectable box holding an image and text, and drawing it
would re-implement the hit testing, pointer capture, text layout, automation names and theming
that `Canvas` and a template give for nothing (ruling R18). The chart table above lists charts and
gains no row for it.

Chart metric and filter selections persist in `user_settings.graph`, matching
`schemas/settings.py::GraphSettings`: `enabled_metrics` defaulting to
`["hfr", "eccentricity", "fwhm", "guiding_rms"]`, `enabled_filters` defaulting to
`["overall"]`, plus the two retired expanded-state flags, `default_chart_sessions` and the
port's own `show_guiding`, the night chart's Guiding pill (section 12.4).

Both Target detail charts render their metric toggles and their filter toggles as one row of
pills, each carrying a 7 pixel filled dot in its series colour rather than a tinted border, and
neither chart draws a legend: the pills are the legend and the box under the chart repeated them.
`LegendPosition` is `Hidden` on both. The pill row wraps rather than clipping when the pane is
narrow, because a clipped pill hides a toggle the reader cannot then find. The collapse state
still writes through the two `graph` flags; what carries the toggle is the band's own disclosure
rather than an expander around the chart.

**Rig series** (PAR-004). On a target imaged by more than one rig, and on a night imaged by more
than one rig, both Target detail charts draw one series per rig per metric and give each rig a
dash pattern taken by its rig index, from this fixed table, which repeats from the top when a
target has more than five rigs:

| Rig index | Dash pattern |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | solid |
| 1 | 6, 3 |
| 2 | 2, 2 |
| 3 | 8, 3, 2, 3 |
| 4 | 1, 3 |

The two charts read that table from different rows, and the reason is the data each has. The
per-night chart has every rig of the night loaded by construction, so a split is a partition of
what it already plots: it splits each metric into one series per rig and takes the table as
written, rig 0 solid. The cross-session chart does not. A per-rig figure is taken over a night's
own frames, which only a night whose detail has been loaded in this visit has, while the unsplit
whole-night value comes from the session overview, which every night carries. So the cross-session
chart keeps its unsplit whole-night series always, one point per night, and draws the per-rig
series beside it for the nights whose detail is loaded. Because the whole-night line is the solid
one there, its rig series take rows 1 to 5 of the table, the rig index plus one and repeating past
five, on the series and on the pills alike so the legend cannot disagree with the lines it labels.
Replacing the whole-night series with the split, which an earlier draft of this rule implied,
turned a season trend into one marker per opened night the moment a second rig was offered.

While the cross-session chart is split per rig, the unsplit series is a whole-night figure and
nothing else: it plots the night's own value from the overview and carries no per-filter split of
its own, while the per-rig series carry the per-filter split and, like the rig split, plot only the
nights whose detail has been loaded in this visit. The reason is in the query. On a multi-rig night
`SessionDetailQuery` builds the per-filter block per rig and stamps every row with its rig's label,
so there is no night-level per-filter median to plot, and drawing one under the night's name would
state one rig's median as the night's. On a single-rig target the question does not arise: the
per-filter rows are the night's own, so the unsplit series draws its per-filter lines there exactly
as it did before this phase.

The colour still comes from the metric, never from the rig: one hue per metric is the mapping this
section fixes so the user learns it, and a second encoding on the same line would break it. The
dash pattern is the rig's only mark, which is also why the first rig is solid on the per-night
chart, so a single-rig target and a single-rig night draw exactly what they drew before this
phase.

The web application's equivalent table has six rows and differs at index 4, where it uses `[1, 2]`
against this port's `1, 3`, and it carries a sixth, `[10, 4, 2, 4]`, which this port does not. One
pixel of gap at index 4, and a sixth rig on one target is an unusual library; the difference is
recorded rather than reconciled.

The rigs are offered in one order, first capture time within the night, which is the order the
rig labels, the per-rig insight lines, the rig label rows and the dash indices all read. The dash
index comes from the full offered list rather than from the enabled subset, so unchecking rig 1
does not re-pattern rig 2 and a rig keeps its pattern on both charts.

A row of rig pills sits beside the existing metric and filter pill rows on both charts, one
`ToggleButton` per rig carrying the rig's label, all checked on open. Unchecking a rig removes its
series from the chart, and the last one may be unchecked, which leaves the cross-session chart its
whole-night line and the per-night chart nothing. The state is per visit and is not persisted: it
names which of tonight's rigs the reader is looking at, which is not a preference. The frame table's own rig pills
(section 12.4) are a separate filter over rows and the two do not drive each other: one hides a
line, the other hides a row, and a reader who wanted both unchecks both. The charts draw no
legend, as stated above; the pills are the legend, and a rig pill carries its dash pattern as a
short drawn line rather than the 7 pixel dot a metric pill carries.

The primary metric, for both Target detail charts, is the first entry of the section 13
series order (`median_hfr`, `eccentricity`, `fwhm`, `guiding_rms_arcsec`, `detected_stars`)
that is currently enabled and has at least one value in the data being plotted. When none
qualifies there is no reference line and no left-axis scaling decision to make. Defining it
by the fixed series order rather than by the stored order of `enabled_metrics` is what makes
the phrase mean one thing on both charts: the stored order follows the order the user clicked
toggles, which is not a property a user can reason about.

Axis sides follow from that: the left axis carries the primary metric's unit, and the right
axis carries the other units among the plotted metrics. Both Target detail charts use the
same rule, so a metric does not change sides between them.

Two known limitations of the two-axis plan, both accepted:

- Three or more distinct units cannot each get their own axis. A two-axis chart has one left
  unit and one right side, so a right axis carrying more than one unit is labelled without a
  unit suffix rather than with a wrong one. The shipped default selection reaches this: HFR
  (pixels), eccentricity (a ratio), FWHM (arcseconds) and guiding RMS (arcseconds) already
  span three units. The upgrade path, if it ever matters, is one axis per distinct unit with
  the third and later axes stacked on the right, which LiveCharts supports and which no
  screen currently needs.
- A per-filter or per-rig split on the cross-session chart plots a point only for sessions whose
  detail has been loaded, because a per-filter or per-rig session figure comes from
  `SessionDetailQuery` (section 12.4) and the session overview does not carry one. Sessions that
  have not been selected at least once in this visit leave a gap in the split series, which is the
  same rendering this section already specifies for missing data; the unsplit whole-night series
  beside them plots every night regardless, which is what keeps the season trend readable while a
  split is on. Adding per-filter medians to the session overview would make every Target detail
  load pay for a feature that is off by default; a third query returning per-filter session medians
  for the whole target is the upgrade path if the feature turns out to matter.

---

## 14. Theme

Six themes ship since polish wave 6 (user ruling 2026-09-24), four dark and two light.
`civil-dusk` ("Civil Dusk") is the default: a dome interior at civil dusk, cool concrete and
painted steel with one amber accent. `luminance` ("Luminance", shipped as `observing-ledger`
before this wave) is neutral luminance greys with no blue cast, colour spent only on data and
light spent only on state. `red-light` is that world re-tinted through one more dictionary for
dark adaptation at the telescope. `deep-sky` ("Deep Sky", shipped as `glass-void` before this
wave) is the web's own theme, kept and selectable. `atlas` ("Atlas") and `logbook` ("Logbook")
are light: printed star atlas stock with the grid in print blue, and the ruled greige of an
observing logbook written in blue-black ink. A theme's variant is a column of `ThemeManager`'s
table, not something its dictionary declares: the two light rows carry `ThemeVariant.Light`, so
the platform controls follow the light variant while every application ink still comes from the
theme's own tokens; section 19.1's deferral of a light theme ends with
them. Tokens live in `GalactiLog.App/Theme/Themes/CivilDusk.axaml`, `Luminance.axaml`,
`RedLight.axaml`, `DeepSky.axaml`, `Atlas.axaml` and `Logbook.axaml`, one `ResourceDictionary`
each, merged into `App.Resources` one at a time by `ThemeManager`. Adding a
theme means adding one dictionary carrying the same 41 brush tokens (38 through Phase 14B, plus
the three thin-scrollbar tokens Phase 14C adds below), the eight callout composites,
the four semantic `*Value` colours the composites derive from, the two gradient stops with
their `BrushPageBackground`, and the six platform scrollbar aliases the thin scrollbar paragraph
below names, which is 62 `x:Key` entries in total (56 through the Phase 14C task waves; the six
aliases arrived with the phase fixer's withdrawal of the hand-written control theme), plus one
entry in `ThemeManager`'s private table; no other file changes. A dictionary that omits the gradient stops
paints no window background and fails `WindowBackgroundsTest`, and one that omits any key fails
`ThemeResourceTest`, which asserts both the full census and that the six key sets are identical.
The theme picker exists in Settings and lists `ThemeManager.Available`, which is a derived
projection of that table and is not edited by hand. A stored `general.theme` that this build does not
ship falls back to the first entry, and an existing install keeps the theme its user chose: the
default applies where nothing is stored.

`red-light` does not reach the craft floor's 4.5:1 body contrast, and ships that way by decision.
A single red hue over a near-black red surface has 4.77:1 of headroom at the primary ink, so the
two ink tiers below it measure 3.50:1 and 2.51:1; lifting them further pushes the ink toward
orange, which is what the mode exists to avoid. Dark adaptation outranks the contrast bar for that
theme and for no other.

Resource key convention: the web CSS variable `--color-<token>` becomes the Avalonia key
`Color<PascalCase token>`, with each hyphen-separated segment capitalized. Every key is a
`SolidColorBrush`. Where Avalonia needs a `Color` rather than an `IBrush`, the theme uses the
suffix `Value` on the few keys that need it (the gradient stops and the four semantic
colours, for example `ColorSuccessValue` and `ColorGradientFromValue`), and everything else
reads the brush resource and takes its `Color`. Chart paints do exactly that, through one
helper on `ChartTheme`, so every token works with no dictionary change and each of the six
shipped dictionaries reproduces the same key set and no more.

**Thin scrollbar tokens (Phase 14C; ruling E3 reversed by the phase fixer).** Every scrollbar is
the platform Fluent `ScrollBar`, restyled through the resource keys that theme already reads.
Ruling E3's hand-written control theme is withdrawn: written from a blank page it cost an
inverted vertical axis, with the thumb at the bottom of its track at offset zero and a downward
drag scrolling up, and the loss of the platform's collapsed and expanded states, which left a
full strength 8 pixel thumb drawn permanently over the trailing content of every scroller.
Neither was visible to the suite. Restyling keeps the direction, the paging, the line buttons and
the two states by construction, and no view and no theme file declares a `ScrollBar` style or
control theme anywhere.

What ships. `ScrollBarSize` is overridden to 8 in `Theme/Controls.axaml`, so the bar is 8 pixels
wide in either orientation. At rest the thumb is the platform's hairline in `ColorScrollbarThumb`
over a transparent track; with the pointer over it the bar expands to the full 8 pixels with the
platform's own two line buttons, and the thumb takes `ColorScrollbarThumbHover` under the pointer
and while dragging. There is no third colour: the platform's pressed fill is aliased to the hover
token, which keeps the web's own two states through a theme that does declare a pressed rule. The
bar overlays its scroller's trailing edge and takes no layout space, which is the platform
`ScrollViewer` theme's `AllowAutoHide` behaviour rather than anything this application declares.
Because the platform theme is keyed by type, this applies equally to the ScrollBar inside a
ListBox's, a ComboBox popup's or a multi-line TextBox's own template as to one a view declares in
its own markup.

Three keys carry the colour, each starting equal to an existing token so a later theme can
diverge from that starting point without a control change: `ColorScrollbarThumb` (the thumb,
equal to that theme's `ColorBorderEmphasis` at ship), `ColorScrollbarThumbHover` (the thumb under
the pointer or while dragging, equal to that theme's `ColorTextTertiary` at ship) and
`ColorScrollbarTrack` (`#00000000` in all six, matching the web's transparent track). Each of
the six shipped dictionaries also aliases the six platform keys the restyle works through
(`ScrollBarPanningThumbBackground`, `ScrollBarThumbBackgroundColor`,
`ScrollBarThumbFillPointerOver`, `ScrollBarThumbFillPressed`, `ScrollBarTrackFill` and
`ScrollBarTrackFillPointerOver`) to those three, as `StaticResource` entries beside them, the same
shape the callout composites use. The alias lives in the dictionary and not in
`Theme/Controls.axaml` because that file is parsed once at startup, so a `StaticResource` there
would freeze on whichever theme was merged at the time and a theme swap would leave the bar
behind; the six are additional resources and are not counted among the 41 tokens. None of the
three tokens has a web `ThemeTokens` counterpart, the same standing `ColorAccentPressed` already
has, because the web reaches its scrollbar colours through a raw CSS variable
(`frontend/src/index.css`) rather than through its typed token interface.

`red-light` as shipped, `deep-sky`, which is verbatim from `frontend/src/themes.ts`, and the two
light themes, `atlas` and `logbook`. The count and the grouping are the same for all six: 5
surface, 2 border, 3 text, 3 accent,

`ColorBadgeBg` is fully transparent in every theme but `deep-sky` by design: a badge is a 1 pixel
outlined run of tertiary text (`Border.tag`), not a filled pill.

Two `luminance` values differ from the approved comp, both lifted for contrast, which the
phase's inputs allow and require to be reported: `ColorTextTertiary` and `ColorBadgeText` move from
`#FF77746E`, which measures 3.85:1 against `ColorBgSurface`, to `#FF8A867F`, which measures 4.95:1.
Three `red-light` values move for the same reason and still fall short: `ColorTextSecondary` from
`#FFA8372A` to `#FFB73C2E` (3.07:1 to 3.50:1) and `ColorTextTertiary` with `ColorBadgeText` from
`#FF7A2A20` to `#FF903126` (2.06:1 to 2.51:1). Section 14's opening states why that theme ships
below the bar.

### 14.2 Page background

Each theme declares a `GradientFrom` and a `GradientTo`: `civil-dusk` `#FF131619` to
`#FF1B1E22`, `luminance` `#0F0F0F` to `#171717`, `red-light` `#120303` to `#170404`, `deep-sky`
`#0a0c14` to `#0f1320`, `atlas` `#FFFFFFFF` to `#FFFAFAF9`, `logbook` `#FFF7F3EF` to `#FFEFEBE7`.
For the three polish wave 6 themes the pair is derived rather than lifted from a comp:
`GradientTo` equals `ColorBgSurface`, and `GradientFrom` is 8 per channel, Luminance's own gap
between `GradientFrom` and `GradientTo`, darker than it on a dark theme and lighter on a light
one; `atlas` clamps at white. The gradient
brush is kept, per the decisions, and `MainWindow` still paints a `LinearGradientBrush` at 135
degrees between them as `BrushPageBackground`. `ColorBgBase` stays fully transparent so panels
composite over the gradient exactly as they do on the web. On every theme but `deep-sky`
the two stops are close enough that the page reads as one flat field, which is the direction's own
choice and not a loss of the mechanism.

Every `Window` root in the application paints `BrushPageBackground`. `ColorBgBase` is
transparent by design and must not be used on a window root, which has nothing behind it, so a
window painted with it shows the desktop. `WindowBackgroundsTest` enforces both halves.

### 14.3 What is dropped

| Web feature | Disposition |
| --- | --- |
| `backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.0)` | Dropped. Avalonia has no cross-platform backdrop blur and the decisions rule it out. Surface tokens are used at their declared alpha over the gradient, which on `deep-sky` is already near-opaque (0.85 and 0.90), so the visual difference is minimal. |
| The two orb radial gradients | Dropped by the decisions. |
| The glass-only forced `border-color: rgba(255,255,255,0.10)` override | Dropped with the blur; `border-default` is used as declared. |
| The glass-only inset highlight and heavy drop shadow on surfaces | Dropped. The theme-independent shadow scale below applies instead. |
| `.glass-popover` `color-mix` background | Replaced by `ColorBgElevated` at full opacity. |
| `data-theme-mode` and `data-theme-style` root attributes | Not needed; a theme dictionary declares whether it is light or dark directly. |
| The card shadow on a page region | Dropped on Target detail. The page's containment is alignment and a 1 pixel rule; `ShadowSm` survives in `Scales.axaml` for the surfaces that still use it. |

### 14.4 Theme-independent scales

These are not per-theme and must not be redeclared in a theme dictionary. They live in
`Theme/Scales.axaml`.

Radius, as `CornerRadius` resources:

| Key | Value | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RadiusSm` | 6 | Buttons, badges, small containers, focus ring corners, compact stat cards. |
| `RadiusMd` | 8 | Cards, panels, modals, toasts, popovers. |
| `RadiusLg` | 12 | Large primary containers. |

Shadow, as `BoxShadows` resources:

| Key | Value | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ShadowSm` | `0 1 2 #4D000000` | Cards. |
| `ShadowMd` | `0 4 12 #66000000` | Popovers. |
| `ShadowLg` | `0 8 24 #80000000` | Modals, floating menus. |

Typography. Interface font Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, monospace Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono, both
SIL Open Font License 1.1, both embedded as application resources under
`GalactiLog.App/Assets/Fonts` with their licence file, reached through the `FontSans` and `FontMono`
resource keys. Fallbacks `Segoe UI, sans-serif` and `Cascadia Code, Consolas, monospace`. The
family was chosen for the subject: catalogue designations and figures are read at low brightness at
night, and it was drawn to keep 0 and O, and 1, l and I, apart. Six static weight instances are
embedded rather than the variable files (Next at 400, 500, 600 and 700, Mono at 400 and 500),
because Avalonia does not support variable fonts. That mapping is asserted by file census only:
`FontResourceTest` proves the six files are present, are TrueType, carry no `fvar` axis table and
resolve as resources, and no headless test can prove that `FontWeight` Medium, SemiBold and Bold
select the three Next instances rather than one synthetic bold, because the headless platform does
not shape text. The verification agent settled it on the launched application on 2026-09-17: the
interface renders in Atkinson Hyperlegible Next at visibly distinct weights with no synthetic bold,
and the mono columns render in Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono rather than Cascadia Code.

The interface face is applied by a `Window` style in `Theme/Controls.axaml` rather than by an
attribute each window sets, so a new dialog cannot forget it. Root font size is user-selectable:
Small 14 (the default since polish wave 6), Medium 16, Large 18, Extra large 20, set as
`MainWindow.FontSize` so every relative size scales.

| Key | Ratio to root | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FontSizeMicro` | 0.500 | Minimal labels. |
| `FontSizeTiny` | 0.643 | Small metadata. |
| `FontSizeCaption` | 0.714 | Badge labels, chevrons. |
| `FontSizeLabel` | 0.786 | Form labels, section headers. |

The four `FontSize*` keys are ratios and never bind to a `FontSize` directly; `MultiplyConverter`
over `$parent[Window].FontSize` is the only sanctioned form, and `FontSizeTokenTest` fails the
build on any other.

Above these four tiers, use the root size and the standard scale. Headings use weight 600.
Section headers are label size, medium weight, uppercase, letter-spaced, in
`ColorTextTertiary`. Numeric columns use tabular figures
(`<FontFeatures>tnum=1</FontFeatures>`) so figures align.

The Target detail page is the one exception to the section-header rule, and the rule stays
app-wide everywhere else: that page's own section labels (Nights, Frames) are sentence case at
weight 600 in `ColorTextPrimary`, through the `section` class, and the page carries no tracked text
at all, because a tracked uppercase label beside a figure competes with the figure.

One family throughout; weight and ink carry the hierarchy. The tiers, as the style classes in
`Theme/Controls.axaml`, which carry the ratio themselves so no call site on the Target detail page
repeats a `FontSize` attribute. One site elsewhere still carries the converter form inline,
`Views/Settings/DisplayTabView.axaml`'s text-size preview, which is a size the user is choosing
rather than a tier:

| Class | Ratio to root | Weight | Ink | Role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `t-hero` | 1.5 | 700 | primary | The page title |
| `t-stat` | 1.2 | 700 | primary | A night header |
| `figure` | 1.0 | 600 | primary | A figure in prose, tabular |
| (none) | 1.0 | 400 | primary, secondary for text columns | Body, and a summary table's cells |
| `t-label` | 0.786 | 500 | secondary | Table headers, facts lines, buttons, frame cells |
| `t-caption` | 0.714 | 400 | tertiary | Stat labels, tags, disclosures, deltas |

Control geometry that is not a token: shared controls carry `CornerRadius` 3 as a literal in
`Theme/Controls.axaml`, not `RadiusSm`. The radius scale above is theme-independent and must not be
redeclared per theme, so the comp's 3 pixel controls are a control decision inside one style file
rather than a new token.

`Theme/Controls.axaml` is the whole shared control vocabulary and is the only file that declares
one. Besides the four type tiers and the button and badge shapes named in 14.5, it carries
`Button.pill` (the selectable filter pill, a 1 pixel outline with no dot, lifted out of the three
views that each had their own copy), `Button.header-cell` with its `.numeric` variant (the frame
table's sortable header cell, two alignment setters and no chrome), `Border.tag` (the outlined
badge) and a `ToggleButton` default (the chart pill rows, which a `Button` style cannot reach
because a `ToggleButton` is not a `Button`). `ControlStyleScanTest` needles `Button`,
`ToggleButton`, `Border.tag` and `Border.callout`, so a view that declares a style for any of the
four fails the build.

Motion: page enter 200 ms ease-out (opacity plus a 6 pixel rise); tab switch 150 ms; toast
200 ms slide; hover and colour transitions 150 ms; expander collapse 200 ms. Themes add no
motion.

### 14.5 Role rules

- Style with token resources, never a literal colour. A literal `#RRGGBB` anywhere outside a
  theme dictionary is a review finding.
- `ColorBgBase` is the page. `ColorBgSurface` is a top-level card, table, or panel.
  `ColorBgElevated` is a nested panel, dropdown, popover, or selected state, and must read
  as lighter than surface.
- `ColorBgHover` is row and button hover fill. `ColorBgInput` is text boxes, combo boxes,
  and text areas.
- A button is a 1 pixel outline over a transparent fill, with `ColorBgHover` behind it on hover
  and `ColorBgElevated` while pressed. No tinted fill, no gradient, no shadow. Exactly one button
  in the application is filled: Run scan in the status bar carries `Button.primary`, which is
  `ColorAccent` at full strength with `ColorBgSurface` as its ink, a flat outlined disabled form,
  and `ColorAccentPressed` while pressed. The accent is a three-rung ramp, `ColorAccentHover` above
  the rest value and `ColorAccentPressed` below it, so a keyboard activation, which raises
  `:pressed` without `:pointerover`, still changes the fill;
  `ButtonStateStyleTest.AKeyboardPressOnThePrimaryButton_ChangesTheFillWithNoPointerOver` pins it.
  A second filled button is a review finding.
  `ControlStyleScanTest` fails the build on a `Button` style that carries a gradient or a
  semi-transparent tinted fill, and on a view that declares a style of its own for any of the four
  needled selectors, `Button`, `ToggleButton`, `Border.tag` or `Border.callout`, instead of using
  the shared ones.
- Colour is spent on data and light is spent on state. The metric tokens and the filter tokens
  identify series; `ColorMetricWorst` is the one evaluative ink and it marks a figure, never a
  fill, never a row and never a left edge. Selection is a lighter field with accent ink and a
  2 pixel lit edge, so no hue on a page ever means "selected".
- Icons are drawn paths in one stroke weight. A Unicode glyph standing in for an icon is a review
  finding. The sort direction marker in a table header is the one exception already in the tree
  and is a text run, not an icon.
- Callouts, which survive as the one tinted surface: semantic colour at 20 percent fill,
  50 percent border, full-strength text.
- Focus ring: 2 pixel `ColorAccent` outline at 2 pixel offset with `RadiusSm`, applied
  globally through a `:focus-visible` style, not per control.
- `Border.tag` for a badge: a 1 pixel `ColorBorderDefault` outline over `ColorBadgeBg`, which the
  two new themes declare transparent, with `ColorBadgeText` ink. Not a filled pill.
- Modals use an opaque surface: `ColorBgSurface` composited over the gradient's `from`
  colour, so a table behind the modal does not bleed through.
- Metric colours are a data-series palette, one stable hue per metric in every theme. Never
  reassign them per chart. `metric-best` equals `success` and `metric-worst` equals `error`
  by definition; `metric-temp` intentionally equals `metric-fwhm`.
- Semantic colours are status signals, not brand. Do not restyle them per theme.
- Filter tokens are the fallback palette. Runtime filter colours come from
  `user_settings.filters`, resolved through section 5.8.4's four-step order rather than through
  a single stored-or-default read. `GalactiLog.Core.Aliases.FilterCategory`, which holds the
  seeded default palette and the category name fold, is the second documented exception to this
  rule's "never a literal colour outside a theme dictionary", beside `FilterColor.Fallback`: a
  filter's tint is user data, not a theme token, and `GalactiLog.Core` references no UI type.
- A view-model that holds a brush holds an `ImmutableSolidColorBrush`, never a
  `SolidColorBrush`. `SolidColorBrush`'s constructor calls `VerifyAccess` once a dispatcher
  exists, so constructing one on a background thread throws; a view-model builds its brushes
  wherever its data arrives, which is not always the UI thread. An immutable brush has no
  dispatcher affinity and cannot be mutated behind the binding either.

### 14.6 The inherited default text ink, and the platform control inks

**The application declares one default text ink, and it is the theme's own.** `Foreground` is set
as a `DynamicResource` of `ColorTextPrimary` on the one `Window` style in `Theme/Controls.axaml`,
beside the `FontFamily` that was already there. Inheritance is the lowest priority there is, so
every control that gives its own content an ink keeps it: a filled button's label, a badge's text,
a callout's text and all seven inked text classes are unaffected.

**It is a `Window` style and never a `TextBlock` selector.** A type selector on `TextBlock` would
outrank the ink a control hands its own content, and the one filled button in the application
would then draw its label in the page ink over its accent fill. An Avalonia type selector matches
on the control's style key, which `Window` fixes for its subclasses, so the one style reaches all
eight shipped windows; the `FontFamily` beside it has always worked the same way. It does **not**
reach a popup top level: a drop-down, a tooltip and a flyout presenter are their own roots.

**Until Phase 17 there was no such declaration at all.** A `TextBlock` carrying neither an inked
class nor its own `Foreground` inherited the Fluent theme's Dark default, pure white, a colour no
theme dictionary here declares. On the two dark-neutral themes that reads as a small shift from
the primary ink; on `red-light`, whose whole purpose is to preserve dark adaptation, it made every
such figure the brightest thing on the page. It reached 99 text blocks in 27 files, every `num`
figure among them, so every tabular figure in the application drew white. A launched look measured
1,749 pure white pixels on one `red-light` page and 0 after the one setter.

**The platform's own combo box and date picker inks are aliased, not inherited.** Those controls
take their ink from Fluent resource keys rather than from inheritance, so each theme dictionary
aliases ten of them to its own two text tokens, the same mechanism the scrollbar aliases already
used: `ComboBoxForeground`, `ComboBoxForegroundFocused`, `ComboBoxForegroundFocusedPressed` and
`DatePickerButtonForeground`, `DatePickerButtonForegroundPressed` to `ColorTextPrimary`;
`ComboBoxForegroundDisabled`, `ComboBoxPlaceHolderForeground`,
`ComboBoxPlaceHolderForegroundFocusedPressed`, `DatePickerButtonForegroundDisabled` and
`TextControlPlaceholderForeground` to `ColorTextTertiary`. The key set is identical in all six
dictionaries and a census case asserts that. `TextControlPlaceholderForeground` is the platform's
single placeholder ink, shared with every text box watermark, which therefore also moves to the
tertiary token; that is deliberate rather than a side effect.

**Three families of platform ink are not aliased and still draw the platform's own colours**, each
because it pairs with a background this rule does not touch: the open drop-down's rows
(`ComboBoxItemForeground` and its seven state siblings), `ToolTipForeground`, and
`ExpanderChevronForeground` and its siblings, which is what leaves the `red-light` Dashboard's
seven filter-card chevrons white. HANDOFF section 7 carries them.

---

## 15. CLI

`galactilog.exe` dispatches to the CLI when `args.Length > 0` and `args[0]` is a known verb.
Otherwise it starts the GUI. The CLI shares `GalactiLog.Core` and `GalactiLog.Data` with the
GUI and uses the same database and settings.

Global options, accepted by every command:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--json` | Emit machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of text. |
| `--quiet` | Suppress progress output; results and errors only. |

| Command | Arguments | Behavior | Text output | JSON output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `scan` | `<path>...` optional. Each must be a fully qualified path to an existing directory; a relative path such as `.` exits 2 and a path that is not there exits 3. No path means every configured scan root. | Runs a full scan against the given paths, writing to the database. Honors scan filters. Ctrl+C cancels cooperatively. | Progress lines `<task> <step>/<total> <message>`, then a summary. The summary prints the same six guide-log figures on one line. | The `scan_runs` record as an object, plus the guide-log pass's own tally as the members `phd2_skipped_unchanged`, `phd2_empty` and `phd2_removed`, which are read from the pass result in memory and are not `scan_runs` columns. With them the pass reconciles: `phd2_found` equals `phd2_ingested` plus `phd2_skipped_unchanged` plus `phd2_empty` plus `phd2_failed`, for a pass that ran to completion. Without them it does not, because a log recorded `empty` (section 5.15) is neither ingested nor failed, and a log the delta skip passed over is neither. On a cancelled pass the identity does not hold even with them: `phd2_found` is the full candidate count the walk discovered, while the four outcomes cover only the candidates the pass reached before it stopped. |
| `resolve` | `<name>` | Runs the resolution pipeline for one name and prints what it found. Read-only with respect to targets: it never creates one. It does write resolver cache rows, since that is what the pipeline does and the cache is app data. | `primary_name`, `catalog_id`, `common_name`, RA, Dec, object type, aliases, and which stage resolved it (`cache`, `offline`, `simbad`, `sesame`, or `unresolved`). | The resolved identity object plus a `source` field. |
| `inspect` | `<file>` | Reads one FITS or XISF file and prints the extracted metadata with provenance. | One `field = value  (provenance)` line per stored field. | The `ExtractedMetadata` record plus the `provenance` map. |
| `dump-headers` | `<file>` | Prints every raw header card. | One `KEY = value` line per card, in file order. | The `raw_headers` object. |

Exit codes:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Success. Includes a `scan` that found nothing new, which is the normal result of a scheduled scan and is not a failure. It also includes a `scan` that rejected one or more files during ingest (section 10.3 step 3): the failed count rides `scan_runs.failed` and the text and JSON summaries, not the exit code. For `resolve`, a name that resolved. |
| 1 | The operation ran and produced no result where one was expected: `resolve` found nothing. Never returned by `scan`. |
| 2 | Invalid arguments, an unknown verb, or a scan filter configuration that fails validation. Usage is printed on stderr for an argument error; a filter error names the offending entry. |
| 3 | Input error: file not found, not readable, or rejected by the reader rules in section 6. |
| 4 | Database error: the database could not be opened, migrations failed, or a database write failed during a scan. |
| 5 | Cancelled by the user. |
| 6 | The data location named by the pointer is not available. The application did not start and created nothing, so that no second, empty library is created beside the user's own (section 17.2). |
| 70 | Unhandled internal error. The exception is logged and its message is printed on stderr. |

Errors always go to stderr. Results always go to stdout, so `galactilog inspect x.fits --json | jq`
works.

Piped output works because `Program.Main` calls `AttachConsole(ATTACH_PARENT_PROCESS)`
before dispatch (section 4.4). When no parent console exists, the verb still runs and
its output is discarded, with the exit code preserved.

The CLI never starts the watcher or the scheduler and never writes UI state.

There is no option to point the CLI at a different database, and no option to create a target
from `resolve`. The CLI opens the same app data database the GUI does, through the same
`AppWriter`-resolved path (section 2.1.2). A `--db` switch would put an arbitrary user path
into a write handle, which section 2.1 forbids; running against a copy is done by copying the
application's data directory, not by aiming the application at a file.

## 16. Diagnostics and logging

### 16.1 Serilog configuration

Configured in `AppHost` before anything else runs, so a startup failure is still logged.

| Sink | Destination | Level | Format |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rolling file | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData\logs\galactilog-.log`, under the resolved app data root (section 17.2) | From `general.log_level`, default `Information` | `{Timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff zzz} [{Level:u3}] {SourceContext} {Message:lj}{NewLine}{Exception}` |
| Console | stderr | `Information` | Compact, CLI mode only. Every level goes to stderr, never stdout, so a verb's `--json` stdout contract stays exactly one JSON object (section 15). |
| In-memory ring | 500 entries | `Warning` | Structured, feeds the Diagnostics "last errors" panel |

Rolling policy: daily roll, `retainedFileCountLimit` from `general.app_log_retention_days`
(section 5.8.1, default 14, range 1 to 3650), `fileSizeLimitBytes: 33554432` (32 MB) with
`rollOnFileSizeLimit: true`, `shared: false`, `flushToDiskInterval: 1 second`. The default of
fourteen matches the web application's `app_log_retention_days` default.

The retained file limit is fixed when the sink is configured, so a change to
`app_log_retention_days` on the Diagnostics tab (section 12.7) applies **the next time GalactiLog
starts**, not at the next roll: `AppHost` reads the stored value once, before `Log.Logger` exists,
and passes it to Serilog as `retainedFileCountLimit`, a constructor argument the sink cannot be
told to change while it runs, and the application does not rebuild the sink to force it. The
approved text of this paragraph read "applies at the next roll rather than at once"; that was
wrong as a factual matter, not as a ruling, because Serilog bakes the limit into the sink at
construction rather than re-reading it on each roll, and the user is told of the correction. The
read is a tolerant pre-logger read through `DatabasePaths.TryReadStoredGeneralJson`, not through
`SettingsStore.GetGeneral`, because `SettingsStore` is not yet constructed at that point in
startup; it returns the compile-time default 14 on a missing database, a missing table, an
unparsed document or a value outside the key's own 1 to 3650 range, and clamps any in-range,
in-`Int32` value read from the document to that same range, so no value this function reads can
throw out of it or reach Serilog out of range. The editor says so beside itself, which is why that
field states a delay and the other two do not: `log_level` reaches a live `LoggingLevelSwitch` and
`app_log_max_rows` bounds the viewer's own paging, both read on demand rather than baked in. The
roll is daily and the limit counts files, so one unit of this key is one day until a 32 MB size
roll produces a second file for the same day; it is a file count with a day-shaped name, inherited
from the web application, and the spec states which it is so nobody reads a retention guarantee
into it. The in-memory ring above stays 500 entries at `Warning` and is not governed by
`app_log_max_rows`, which bounds the log viewer (section 12.8).

The sink's path is not a literal. `AppHost` composes it from
`DiagnosticsService.LogDirectoryName + "/" + DiagnosticsService.LogFileNamePrefix + ".log"`,
handed to `AppWriter.ResolveAppDataPath`, so Serilog can only ever write and roll inside the app
data directory (section 2.1.2). The table's `logs/galactilog-.log` above is illustrative of the
result, not a literal the code contains. The log directory is app data, so Serilog deleting a
rolled file is permitted by section 2.1.

`general.log_level` sets the minimum level for the file sink through a
`LoggingLevelSwitch`, so changing it on the Diagnostics tab takes effect immediately with no
restart. Default `Information`. It appears only on that tab (section 12.7).

Levels:

| Level | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Verbose | Per-card FITS parsing detail. Never enabled by default. |
| Debug | Per-file ingest decisions, cache hits and misses, filter verdicts. |
| Information | Scan lifecycle, target creation, settings changes, updates, degraded-but-handled cases such as an unsupported sample format. |
| Warning | A skipped or rejected file including a compressed FITS, an unreachable scan root, an unparseable `DATE-OBS`, the imaging-night longitude fallback, a resolver network failure that was retried. |
| Error | An operation that failed and lost work: a scan that aborted, a migration failure, a write failure. |
| Fatal | Startup failure. |

Every log line written during a scan carries the scan run id as a Serilog property so a run
can be isolated with a text search.

Rate limiting: the imaging-night fallback warning is emitted once per scan run, never once
per frame (section 8.3). The same rule applies to any warning whose condition is per-frame
and library-wide: emit once per run with a count in the message.

### 16.2 Diagnostics page

Fields listed in section 12.8.

### 16.3 JSON bundle

`DiagnosticsService.ExportBundle(destination)` writes one UTF-8 JSON file:

```
{
  "generated_at":  ISO-8601,
  "app":           { version, git_sha, channel, dotnet, avalonia, sqlite, os },
  "paths":         { app_data, database, logs, thumbnails, catalogs, startup_shortcut, started_minimized },
  "database":      { file_bytes, wal_bytes, page_count, row_counts: { ... }, phd2_bytes, phd2_bytes_method },
  "settings":      the full settings document,
  "scan":          { current_state, current_progress, watcher_states, next_scheduled },
  "scan_runs":     the last 50 scan_runs rows (Phase 15A adds phd2_found, phd2_ingested, phd2_failed to each),
  "resolver":      { cache_positive, cache_negative, cache_expired, hits, misses },
  "unresolved":    [ { object_name, frame_count } ],
  "recent_events": the last 200 activity_events rows,
  "log_tail":      the last 500 log lines as strings
}
```

There is nothing to redact: the application holds no credentials, no tokens, and no account
data. File paths are included because they are the point of the bundle.

`DiagnosticsService.ExportBundle(destination)` writes through the scoped writer returned by
`AppWriter.BeginExport(destination)`, where `destination` came from a save dialog and from
nowhere else. It creates a new file at that path; the dialog's own overwrite confirmation is
the only path by which an existing file is replaced (section 12.8). This is the sole
sanctioned write outside app data in the whole application.

## 17. Packaging and update

### 17.1 Velopack

- Packaged with `vpk pack` from a `dotnet publish -r win-x64 --self-contained` output.
- Package id `GalactiLog`, application name `GalactiLog`, main executable
  `GalactiLog.exe`.
- Update feed: GitHub Releases on this repository, via `vpk upload github`.
- Channels map to branches (section 17.4). The installed application checks its own channel
  only, so a stable install never offers itself a prerelease.
- `VelopackApp.Build().Run()` is the first statement in `Program.Main`, before any Avalonia
  or Serilog initialization, because Velopack's hooks must run and exit during install,
  update, and uninstall. CLI verb dispatch comes second and Avalonia startup comes third
  (section 4.4).
- Update flow: `UpdateManager.CheckForUpdatesAsync` on start and every 6 hours;
  `DownloadUpdatesAsync` with progress into the status bar; the user is prompted, and
  `ApplyUpdatesAndRestart` runs on confirmation. Nothing is applied silently while the user
  is mid-scan.
- While a downloaded update waits for the user's confirmation, no further check runs. The
  About tab's check button starts no check until the prompt is answered, and the status line
  reads that the update is ready to install.
- Delta packages are enabled, which is the reason for the dependency. `vpk pack` emits a delta
  only when the channel's previous full package is in its output directory, so `release.yml`
  runs `vpk download github` before it (17.5 step 7); a channel's first release is full only.
- Applying a confirmed update restarts the process through Velopack's `ApplyAndRestart`, which
  ends this process without the shutdown drain (section 10.5): the thumbnail worker is not
  cancelled, the single-instance listener is not stopped, and Serilog is not flushed. Spec 12.11
  behaviour 7's "one drain and one exit" names the one exit this application performs on its own;
  an update restart is the updater's exit. The planned fix is a `drainForRestart` seam on
  `UpdateService`, bound to the same shutdown expression `App.axaml.cs`'s `ShutdownRequested`
  handler uses and invoked immediately before the restart call, which also closes the mid-scan
  check-then-act window between reading the scan state and ending the process. Not built this
  phase; carried as a Phase 12 backlog line.

### 17.2 Paths and first run

| Purpose | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Application binaries | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLog\current` (Velopack layout) |
| Database | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData\galactilog.db` |
| Database write-ahead log and shared-memory file | beside the database |
| Settings document (`user_settings`) | inside the database, so it moves with it |
| Logs | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData\logs` |
| Thumbnail cache | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData\thumbnails`, user-relocatable |
| Data location pointer | `%APPDATA%\GalactiLog\datapath.json` |
| Bundled catalogs | alongside the binaries, in `Catalogs` |

Every path in that table except the bundled catalogs and the pointer is produced by `AppWriter`
(section 2.1.2). The catalogs directory sits with the binaries and is read-only, opened
through `UserFiles`. The pointer is `AppWriter`'s one authorized file (section 2.1.1).

The data root is a sibling of the install root, not a directory inside it. A Velopack uninstall
removes `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLog` in full, which from this version holds the binaries,
`current\` and Velopack's own files and nothing else. The database, the settings, the logs and
the thumbnail cache sit at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData`, or wherever the pointer names, and
the uninstall does not touch them. This is why the root moved: on 2026-09-15 an uninstall of
1.0.0-alpha.1, whose data root was still inside the install root, removed that directory in
full, the database, the logs and the thumbnail cache with it, along with the Start menu entry
and the HKCU uninstall entry.

The root is resolved in `AppHost.Build`, before the database is opened and before Serilog is
configured, and the GUI and every CLI verb reach it through that one method. The order:

1. The test-only explicit override parameter.
2. `GALACTILOG_APPDATA`, when it names a fully qualified directory that is not a drive or share
   root.
3. The pointer's `data_root`, when it is usable and the directory exists.
4. `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData`.

When 1 or 2 supplies the root, the pointer is neither read nor written and no relocation runs,
so a test run and a packaging verification run never touch a real library. A pointer that is
malformed, empty or names an unusable path is treated as absent: the default applies and the
reason is logged once at warning, rather than failing the start.

The pointer document is UTF-8 with no byte order mark, one JSON object with the snake_case keys
`data_root`, `pending_root`, `previous_root` and `updated_at`. Unknown keys are preserved on
write, which is the rule section 5.8 states for the settings document. The file sits outside the
install root, so an uninstall does not reach it, and outside the data root, so it survives a
move.

It is written through a sibling staging file that is then moved over it, so a process killed
during the write leaves the old document or the new one and never a truncated one. A pointer that
exists and cannot be read is left exactly where it is and is never rewritten with the default
root: the application runs on the default root and names the file on the Storage tab, so the user
repairs or removes the document rather than finding it silently replaced.

Moving the data root: the user picks a folder in the setup wizard or on the Settings Storage
tab, which writes `pending_root` and changes nothing else, and the running session stays on the
current root. The next start copies the database, its write-ahead log, `logs\` and
`thumbnails\` to the destination, verifies every copied file's length, and only then promotes
the pointer, so a half-copied destination is never opened. The write-ahead log is part of the
copy because it can still hold most of the catalogue after a clean exit; the shared-memory file
is deliberately left behind, because SQLite rebuilds it from the log and a stale one beside a
fresh database is worse than none. A hand-made backup of a data root is the same set taken with
the application closed: `galactilog.db`, `galactilog.db-wal` and `galactilog.db-shm` together.
That session continues on the new
root. A failed copy leaves `data_root` unchanged, keeps `pending_root` so the next start
retries, and shows the reason with a cancel action. **The old root is never deleted**, on any
path: the user removes it by hand. This is a deliberate divergence from section 11.3, where
relocating the thumbnail cache moves nothing at all. The cache is derived data that regenerates
on demand; the database is not.

Three rules guard the copy, and none of them deletes anything. It is refused before anything is
copied when another GalactiLog process still holds `galactilog.db`, with the message "GalactiLog
is already running; the move will be performed the next time it starts alone." It writes the
state file `.galactilog-relocation` into the destination before it copies anything and rewrites
it once every copied length has been verified, and that file is what tells an aborted copy of
GalactiLog's own apart from somebody else's library; it is never deleted. And the copy skips
reparse points, so a junction or a symlink under `logs\` or `thumbnails\` is neither followed nor
copied.

A destination that already holds a `galactilog.db` is refused, with the message chosen by that
state file. An unfinished marker means an earlier move of this application's own:

> '<folder>' holds an incomplete copy from an earlier move that did not finish. Nothing was
> deleted. Empty that folder yourself, or choose a different one.

No marker, or a finished one, means a library that is not this one:

> '<folder>' already holds a galactilog.db, and two catalogues are never merged.

Adopting an existing library: on the first start after this version, when no pointer exists, the
default root holds no database and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLog` holds one, the same copy runs
from that legacy root into the default root. It copies that file set and nothing else, because
the source is the Velopack install root and `current\`, `packages\` and Velopack's own files
must stay where they are. It refuses when the destination already holds a database, and it
deletes nothing.

When the pointer names a folder that is not available, the application refuses to start: it
reports the folder, the reason and the pointer path, creates nothing, and exits 6 (section 15).
The rule that refusal enforces is that the application never silently creates a second, empty
catalogue beside the user's own, because a pointer naming a missing folder is a disconnected
drive far more often than it is a deleted library. A root that exists but cannot be written is
the same refusal when the root came from the pointer; a default root that cannot be written
stays exit 4, because that is a broken profile rather than a data location problem.

The app data root is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GalactiLogData` unless the environment variable
`GALACTILOG_APPDATA` names an absolute directory, in which case `AppHost.Build` uses that
directory instead, creating it if missing through `AppWriter`. The override exists for CLI
verification and CI against a fresh root and is honored identically by the GUI and every CLI
verb. It never changes which directories are user files: `AppWriter`'s authorized roots are
computed from the resolved app data root. The override is honored only when it is a fully qualified path that is not a drive root; a relative or empty value falls back to the default. The app does not check the app data root against the configured scan roots: placing it inside a scan root is allowed but unsupported, since the walker would enumerate the database, logs, and thumbnail cache (none match a supported extension, so nothing is ingested).

First run: create the resolved app data directory, create the database, apply migrations, load the
bundled catalogs into `openngc_catalog` and `static_catalog_entries`, set
`general.catalogs_loaded_version`, then show the setup wizard. Loading roughly 14 000 OpenNGC
rows plus the static catalogs takes a few seconds and runs behind a progress dialog. The
wizard finishing sets `general.setup_complete`.

A migration on an existing database runs at startup before any window is shown. A migration
failure is fatal, logged, and reported in a dialog naming the log file; the application does
not start with a half-migrated database.

### 17.3 Branches

Three branches, created locally: `main`, `dev`, `snd`. All work happens on `snd`. The
merge direction is one-way: `snd` to `dev` to `main`.

### 17.4 Version scheme

Mirrors the web repository's `build-deploy.yml`, whose derivation is purely from existing
git tags with no VERSION file, no date component, and no run number.

| Branch | Channel | Version form | Derivation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `snd` | `alpha` | `X.Y.Z-alpha.N` | Base `X.Y.Z` is the newest stable tag with its patch incremented, or `1.0.0` when no stable tag exists. `N` is one more than the highest existing `X.Y.Z-alpha.*` tag on that base, or 1. |
| `dev` | `rc` | `X.Y.Z-rc.N` | Identical derivation with `rc` in place of `alpha`. This is exactly the web repository's `dev` logic. |
| `main` | `stable` | `X.Y.Z` | The newest stable tag with its patch incremented, or `1.0.0` when none exists. |

Derivation details carried over verbatim:

- The newest stable tag is `git tag -l | grep -E '^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$' | sort -V | tail -n 1`.
  The anchored pattern excludes prerelease tags.
- Only the patch segment is auto-incremented. Major and minor move only by a manually
  created tag.
- The prerelease counter restarts at 1 whenever the base changes, that is, after a stable
  release lands on `main`.
- Because `main` derives the same base that `dev` has been building against, `1.4.1-rc.N`
  graduates to stable `1.4.1`.
- Both the patch increment and the prerelease counter force base-10 arithmetic, so a
  hand-created zero-padded tag such as `1.4.1-alpha.08` is read as eight rather than failing
  the release job as an invalid octal literal.
- The derived base is escaped before it is interpolated into the prerelease tag pattern, so
  base `1.4.1` matches `1.4.1-alpha.N` and not a tag such as `1x4x1-alpha.5`, which an
  unescaped `.` would match as a wildcard.

Divergence from the web repository, and the reason: the web `snd` branch builds a mutable
`snd` Docker tag with the literal version string `snd` and creates no tag and no release
(`build-snd.yml`). A desktop installer cannot use a mutable version, because Velopack needs
a monotonically increasing semantic version to decide whether an update applies. `snd`
therefore gets a real `alpha` prerelease line here.

### 17.5 CI workflows

Four files under `.github/workflows`, all on the self-hosted Windows runner
(`runs-on: [self-hosted, Windows, X64]`); there is no macOS or Linux target. The runner
account's PowerShell execution policy is Restricted, so run steps use `cmd` or Git Bash, never
`powershell`. One runner serializes every job, so the suite runs once per push: every push
runs `release.yml`, whose Test step is the gate; `build-test.yml` runs for pull requests only.

Two steps call the Gemini API: the release notes step of `release.yml` and the one step of
`pr-description.yml`. Both run as `actions/github-script@v7` steps whose script lives under
`.github/scripts`, so the runner's bundled node makes the call; the Windows runner needs no
python, jq or curl. `.github/scripts/gemini.js` holds the one HTTP call, the shared writing
rules every prompt carries, and the delimiter parser. Both steps read the `GEMINI_API_KEY`
repository secret. A missing secret or a failed call is a warning, never a failed job: the
pull request keeps its own text, and the release carries the raw commit list.

**`build-test.yml`**

- Trigger: `pull_request` targeting `dev` and `main`. No `push` trigger: `release.yml` runs
  the suite on every push. `paths-ignore`: `**/*.md`, `docs/**`, `LICENSE`.
- Permissions: `contents: read`.
- Concurrency group per ref, cancelling in-progress runs. The web workflows declare no
  concurrency and can race on tag derivation; this port fixes that.
- Steps: checkout, `actions/setup-dotnet@v4` with .NET 10, `dotnet restore`,
  `dotnet build --no-restore -c Release`, `dotnet test --no-build -c Release`. No trx logger
  and no result artifact: nothing read the trx, and a failed test's name is in the job log.

**`release.yml`**

- Trigger: `push` on `snd`, `dev` and `main`, same `paths-ignore`, plus `workflow_dispatch`
  for a release on demand (`gh workflow run release.yml --ref <branch>`; `GITHUB_REF_NAME` on
  dispatch is the chosen branch, so 17.4 derives the version unchanged).
- Permissions: `contents: write`, required to push a tag and create a release.
- Concurrency group per branch, not cancelling in progress, so two pushes cannot derive the
  same version.
- Steps, in order:
  1. `actions/checkout@v4` with `fetch-depth: 0`, which the tag-based derivation requires.
  2. `git fetch --tags --force`.
  3. `actions/setup-dotnet@v4` with 10.0.x.
  4. Derive the version per 17.4 by piping `git tag -l` into
     `tools/derive-version.sh "$GITHUB_REF_NAME"`, which writes the `version`, `channel` and
     `prerelease` step outputs.
  5. `dotnet test -c Release`. A failing suite never publishes; the job fails without
     proceeding to pack.
  6. `dotnet publish src/GalactiLog.App -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained
     -o publish/win-x64 -p:Version=<version> -p:SourceRevisionId=<commit sha>`. The output
     directory is pinned to the literal the pack step reads as `--packDir`.
  7. `dotnet tool update -g vpk --version 1.2.0`, pinned to the `Velopack` package version in
     `Directory.Packages.props`, then
     `vpk download github --repoUrl <this repo> --token ${{ github.token }} --channel <channel>`,
     with `--pre` when `prerelease` is true. This puts the channel's previous full package in
     the `Releases` directory, which is the condition under which the next step emits a delta
     package. The step runs with `continue-on-error: true`: a channel's first release has
     nothing to download, and the pack is then a full package only.
  8. Write release notes: `.github/scripts/release-notes.js` through `actions/github-script@v7`,
     writing `<runner temp>/release-notes.md`. The previous tag is the highest tag on the same
     channel (`alpha`, `rc` or stable) other than the version being built, falling back to the
     highest stable tag, then to the newest 50 commits when the repository carries no tag. The
     commit subjects and bodies in that range go to Gemini, which returns a one or two sentence
     summary and one plain-language line per commit, each ending in the commit hash. The file
     is the summary, a `## Changes since <previous tag>` list, and a compare link. When the
     secret is missing or the call fails, the list is the raw commit messages instead. The step
     sits after the tests and before the pack because the next step embeds the file.
  9. `vpk pack --packId GalactiLog --packVersion <version> --packDir publish/win-x64 --icon src/GalactiLog.App/Assets/GalactiLog.ico --mainExe GalactiLog.exe --channel <channel> --releaseNotes <runner temp>/release-notes.md`.
     The `--icon` file reaches Setup.exe, the Start menu and desktop shortcuts, and the
     Add or Remove Programs entry. GalactiLog.exe carries its own icon from the csproj's
     `ApplicationIcon`. `--releaseNotes` stores the file in the package and the channel
     manifest as `VelopackAsset.NotesMarkdown`, which is what the About tab (12.7) shows for
     an available update.
  10. `git tag <version>` and `git push origin <version>`, only after a successful pack, which
      is the ordering `build-deploy.yml` uses.
  11. `vpk upload github --repoUrl <this repo> --token ${{ github.token }} --publish --releaseName <version> --tag <version> --channel <channel>`,
      with `--pre` when `prerelease` is true.
  12. Generate release notes: `gh release edit <version> --notes-file <runner temp>/release-notes.md`,
      the same file step 9 embedded, so the GitHub release body and the About tab carry
      identical text. This edits the release step 11 created; it creates nothing.
  13. Prune old prereleases: keep the newest 2 on `snd` and the newest 2 on `dev`, deleting
      older ones with `gh release delete <tag> --yes --cleanup-tag`. Keep the newest 5 stable
      releases. These retention numbers are the web workflow's `KEEP=2` and `KEEP_STABLE=5`.

Step 11 is the only command that creates the GitHub release, and it is `vpk upload github`.
There is no `gh release create` anywhere in the workflow: both commands create the same tag
and release, and running both would fail on the second. `vpk` is the one that must run,
because it uploads the Velopack package assets and the `RELEASES` manifest the installed
application reads to find updates; a release created by `gh` would carry no update payload.

The release title is the tag name from `--releaseName`. The release body is the file step 8
wrote: user-facing prose with no version heading, no footer and no statement of how it was
written. GitHub's own generated notes are not used; the fallback when Gemini is unavailable
is the raw commit list the script assembled itself, so the body never depends on a second
API.

**`pr-description.yml`**

- Trigger: `pull_request` with types `opened`, `synchronize` and `reopened`, targeting `dev`
  and `main`. No path filter: a documentation-only pull request still gets a description.
- Permissions: `contents: read`, `pull-requests: write`.
- Concurrency group per pull request number, cancelling in-progress runs: only the newest
  push's description is worth writing.
- Steps: `actions/checkout@v4`, then one `actions/github-script@v7` step running
  `.github/scripts/pr-description.js`. The script lists the pull request's commits (subject
  and body, merges skipped) and changed files through the API, sends them with the shared
  writing rules to Gemini, and replaces the pull request title and body with the result: a
  title under 70 characters naming the single most important change, with no
  conventional-commit prefix, then a `### Summary` of one to three sentences and a flat
  `### Changes` list of at most eight bullets. The body carries no footer and no attribution.
  The current title goes into the prompt as a hint only.

**`branch-merge-policy.yml`**

- Trigger: `pull_request` targeting `main` and `dev`. No path filter.
- Permissions: `permissions: {}`, an explicit empty set.
- Runs on `ubuntu-latest`. No checkout, no actions.
- One shell step comparing `github.base_ref` and `github.head_ref`, passed through env
  variables (never interpolated into the script):

| Target | Allowed source | Otherwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | `dev` only | exit 1 |
| `dev` | `snd` only | exit 1 |

Enforcement is the failing status check. Blocking a merge requires marking the check
required in branch protection; the workflow cannot do that itself. The exact-string
comparison means `dev-hotfix` or `feature/dev` fails against `main`, which is intended.

## 18. Testing strategy

### 18.1 Coverage by project

**`GalactiLog.Core.Tests`**

| Area | What is asserted |
| --- | --- |
| FITS header parsing | Card types, `CONTINUE` concatenation, `HIERARCH` keywords including the malformed case, quoted strings with doubled quotes, `D`-exponent floats, blank-named cards excluded, repeated `COMMENT` and `HISTORY` collected into arrays, duplicate value keys last-wins, every rejection rule in 6.1.5 including the compressed-FITS skip. |
| FITS pixel reading | Each supported `BITPIX`, big-endian conversion, `BZERO`/`BSCALE` application including the unsigned-16 case, 2D and 3-plane shapes. |
| XISF | Signature and header length handling, attachment, inline, and embedded locations, each sample format, zlib and lz4 with and without byte shuffling, the unshuffle transform against a known vector, every rejection rule in 6.2.6. |
| Metadata extraction | The full field table in 7.1 including keyword priority; the HFR filename fallback including the fall-through on a zero header `HFR`; `camera_gain` null on a non-integer `GAIN`; the eccentricity and ellipticity conversion with its provenance; the plate scale formula and its null cases; `DATE-OBS` offsetless treated as UTC, with-offset converted to UTC, and unparseable yielding null (7.1.2). |
| CSV merge | A real CSV value overrides a header value; a blank CSV cell does not erase a header value; `HFR == 0` becomes null; `NaN` becomes null; the weather join by `ExposureStartUTC`; the eccentricity and guiding provenance stamps. |
| Session date | The solar-noon offset, the UTC-midnight fallback, the longitude resolution order in 8.3, the once-per-run warning. |
| Astro night | Astronomical dusk and dawn against the three hardcoded USNO rows below, 10 minute tolerance; monthly and weekly aggregation; the ISO week boundary; `mod360` and `mod24` correct for a negative `n` (a date before 2000). |
| Stretch | The MTF curve at known points; `stretchChannel` against captured reference outputs for a synthetic star field; the `mad == 0` flat-128 case; the `shadows >= 1` reset. |
| Debayer | Each of the four patterns against a hand-built 4x4 array; strip-wise debayering equals whole-frame debayering. |
| Resampling | Prefilter factor selection; output dimensions and preserved aspect ratio; a non-empty result; brightness monotonic after stretch (a frame whose highlights are lifted yields a brighter output). The lift is applied to the highlights rather than uniformly because the auto-STF solves for a midtone that maps the median onto 0.25, so a uniformly brightened frame returns at almost the same mean and the assertion would turn on the shape of the upper tail instead of on the stretch. No exactness assertion against any reference resampler: the resampler is Mitchell cubic, not Lanczos (11.2). |
| Name normalization | Whitespace collapse and casing, panel stripping, `NormalizeNgcName`, catalog priority ordering across all 25 patterns, alias curation keeps and drops, `BuildPrimaryName` for all four input combinations. |
| Scan filters | Every verdict in 10.2, glob against substring against regex semantics, folder rules matching ancestor segments, include narrowing per target type, nested include path deduplication, path confinement rejection. |
| Trigram | `similarity()` against captured PostgreSQL `pg_trgm` values for a fixed name set, hardcoded in the test. `word_similarity` is not implemented and not tested (9.7). |
| File safety | `FileSafetyTest` (2.1.3): a source scan over every non-test project asserting that no write-capable filesystem call occurs outside `src/GalactiLog.Core/Io/AppWriter.cs`; `FileSafetyTest.NoSkiaSharpPathBasedIoAnywhereInSrc`, asserting that SkiaSharp is never handed a path anywhere in `src/**` (2.1.2); and `NoSurveyImageFetchTest`, asserting over `src/**` and `tests/**` that no SkyView or DSS archive host appears and that the thumbnail pipeline under `GalactiLog.Core/Imaging` names no network type, so no survey image is fetched for a reference thumbnail (11.4, 19.2); the one survey host, hips2fits, is reached only by the client of section 11.3. Plus `AppWriter` unit tests: a path under app data is accepted, a path under the configured thumbnail cache is accepted, a path under a scan root is refused, a path outside all three is refused, a `..` traversal that escapes an allowed root is refused, and a scoped export writer refuses any path other than the one it was opened for and refuses everything after disposal. |

Astronomical twilight reference rows for the astro night test, taken from published USNO
tables. Hardcode these three in the test; they remove any need for an ephemeris library in
the test project. Tolerance is 10 minutes on each time.

| Site | Latitude | Longitude | Date | Astronomical dusk (UTC) | Astronomical dawn (UTC) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Greenwich, UK | +51.4778 | -0.0015 | 2025-03-20 | 20:00 | 04:09 |
| Flagstaff, US | +35.1983 | -111.6513 | 2025-06-21 | 04:34 (Jun 22) | 10:20 (Jun 22) |
| Sydney, AU | -33.8688 | +151.2093 | 2025-12-21 | 10:50 | 17:00 |

The test asserts that `sunAltitudeDegrees` crosses -18 degrees within tolerance of each
listed time, and separately that `darkHoursForNight` for each row equals the interval between
that row's dusk and dawn within 20 minutes because the function counts 10 minute samples, its result is quantized and can carry up to one sample of error at each end. A failure here is almost always a
degrees-versus-radians error in section 8.4.

The negative-`n` case (a date before 2000) exercises the pre-2000 path and asserts that the
altitude stays finite and in range. It does not catch a plain `%` in `mod360` or `mod24`: the
trigonometry is 360 degree periodic and `gmstHours * 15.0` turns a 24 hour wrap into exactly a
360 degree wrap, so a plain `%` leaves every `sunAltitudeDegrees` value unchanged. What catches a
plain `%` is the pair of assertions that `mod360` and `mod24` return a non-negative remainder for
a negative operand, stated as facts about those two functions rather than inferred from an
altitude.

**`GalactiLog.Data.Tests`**

| Area | What is asserted |
| --- | --- |
| Migrations | Apply cleanly on an empty file; produce the expected schema; are idempotent on re-run. |
| Pragmas | WAL, busy timeout, and foreign keys are actually set on a fresh connection. |
| Listing query | Every filter dimension; the group key including the empty-`OBJECT` collapse; the per-frame metric range semantics of 12.2.1, specifically that a group holding one in-range and one out-of-range frame is excluded and a group whose values are all null is included; sorting; paging; and that the aggregates describe the same set as the page. |
| Detail queries | Session grouping, per-filter medians, arcsecond conversion only for plate-scaled frames, the eccentricity modal-source exclusion and its count. |
| Stats query | Every field of the stats response against a seeded fixture with known totals. |
| Orphan pruning | Rows for missing files are deleted; rows under an unreachable root are not; the zero-discovery guard fires. |
| Merge | A merge writes a manifest, moves the frames, re-keys and appends notes correctly; unmerge restores the exact pre-merge state; a second unmerge is a no-op. |
| Catalog cache | Positive hit, negative hit, negative expiry, retry backoff not triggered on a 4xx, the SIMBAD dual-key write. |
| Settings store | Round trip of every settings section; alias cache invalidation on write. |

**`GalactiLog.App.Tests`**

Section 18.3.

### 18.2 Fixture policy

No user file is ever committed as a fixture. Every FITS and XISF fixture is generated at
test time by helpers in `GalactiLog.Core.Tests.Fixtures`:

- `FitsBuilder` writes a valid FITS file into a `MemoryStream` from a keyword list and a
  pixel array, handling card padding, the `END` card, block padding, endianness, and
  `BZERO`/`BSCALE`. It can also emit deliberately malformed files for the rejection tests.
- `XisfBuilder` writes a monolithic XISF from an XML fragment and a pixel array, with
  optional zlib or lz4 compression and optional byte shuffling.
- `CsvBuilder` writes `ImageMetaData.csv` and `WeatherData.csv` with configurable gaps,
  `NaN` cells, and zero HFR values.

Frames are small: 64 by 64 pixels for parsing tests, 256 by 256 for stretch and debayer
tests. The whole fixture corpus is a few hundred kilobytes generated on demand and nothing
is checked in.

Database fixtures are built by a seeder that inserts a deterministic library: 6 targets,
40 sessions, 900 frames, spanning two years, across two rigs and five filters, with known
totals so an aggregation assertion can name an exact number.

Network is never touched in tests. `SimbadClient` and `SesameClient` take an
`HttpMessageHandler`, and tests supply a stub returning captured response bodies stored as
plain text resources.

### 18.3 Headless UI test scope

Using `Avalonia.Headless.XUnit`. In scope:

- Every ViewModel: command enablement, property change propagation, filter state to query
  criteria mapping, sorting and paging state, autosave debounce behavior, progress event
  handling.
- View smoke tests: each screen's View constructs, binds to a populated ViewModel, and
  produces a non-zero layout without throwing. This catches the binding-path typos that
  compile fine and fail at runtime.
- Theme resolution: every resource key referenced by any View exists in the shipped theme
  dictionary. Implemented by scanning compiled XAML for `DynamicResource` and
  `StaticResource` keys and asserting each resolves.
- Keyboard shortcuts on the preview modal, asserted at the ViewModel level.

Out of scope: pixel comparison, real rendering output, drag interactions, and anything
requiring a display server.
